Executive Summary

This report provides a quantitative analysis to inform decisions about resource allocation in international agricultural research. It focuses on research aimed at raising agricultural productivity and examines how changes in productivity in different crops, regions, and farming systems are likely to affect economic growth, poverty reduction, human nutrition, and natural resource use at the global and regional levels. By quantifying the multidimensional impacts of productivity growth (for different commodities, regions, and farming systems), the report sheds light on how to move toward an efficient research portfolio that achieves high returns across multiple objectives. This has implications for USAID and other donor agencies regarding their R&D funding allocations to the CGIAR, Feed-the-Future Innovation Labs, and other mechanisms supporting international agricultural research.

Decision-making for research resource allocation occurs at multiple levels, or stages. At one level, donor organizations may need to allocate funding across multiple Centers or programs, or choose specific projects to fund. If general funding is provided to Centers or programs, then a second level of decision making is for Center or program leaders to select the projects to support with available program funds. At each stage, judgements are made about technical and institutional feasibility and the likelihood for success and widescale impact. The quantitative assessments in this report are designed to assist decision-makers with these judgements, especially on the potential of commodity research to achieve widescale impact across multiple objectives.

For a comprehensive approach to allocating resources for international agricultural research, we suggest a “staged” approach to decision-making. At the first stage, donor organizations could use relatively simple “parity rules” to allocate R&D resources among agricultural commodities at the global and/or regional levels. These parity rules can be adjusted to consider the multiple goals for R&D as well as give some considerations to the relative costs of developing and disseminating new technologies to smallholder farmers or other potential users. At a second stage, research program managers could lead more detailed exercises in ex ante benefit-cost analysis to guide project selection within commodity programs. At each stage, socioeconomic information (the parity rules and benefit-cost analysis) would bring demand-side considerations into research priority setting and technology design. The report gives illustrative examples of how this approach could be applied across CGIAR commodity research programs.

A major component of this report focuses on the first, higher-level program stage of research resource allocation. The primary audience for this analysis is the donor community: the governments, international organizations, and private foundations that fund international agricultural research. The suggested guide for research resource allocation at the program level is the “parity rule.” The parity rule posits that funding should be allocated across research programs in proportion to the benefits anticipated from the technologies developed by those programs. Of course, the goals for R&D are multidimensional – they include not only raising smallholder incomes, but also improving nutrition, reducing poverty, enhancing social inclusion, mitigating and adapting to climate change, and conserving natural resources. As a complement to the program focus, more detailed modeling helps address these multidimensional goals by employing more sophisticated socioeconomic and biophysical simulation models to derive estimates of how increases in agricultural productivity are likely to affect several of these dimensions. These simulations reveal potential tradeoffs among R&D objectives, depending on
the R&D emphasis given various commodities or commodity groups. For example, productivity

improvement in certain commodities may have large impacts on income growth but little impact on conserving agricultural land use or reducing GHG emissions. If a donor’s objective is primarily focused on climate change mitigation, it could give relatively more of its R&D funding to commodities that reduce net emissions. If a donor’s objective is primarily to raise incomes or reduce poverty, then it might give relatively more attention to commodities that have the greatest impact on that objective. The value of this quantitative analysis is that it can help to clarify these choices and trade-offs in R&D funding decisions.

The geographic focus for the international agricultural research considered in this report is a set of 103 low- and middle-income countries in Asia, Africa, and Latin America. Excluded are high-income countries in these continents and large or primarily temperate agricultural producers (namely, China, Brazil, and the Southern Cone countries of South America are excluded from the analysis). Results are presented for the whole set of 103 “target countries” as well as disaggregated among six regions (corresponding to the regional definitions used by the CGIAR in defining its programs).

One set of results uses a parity model to suggest an allocation of R&D funding across commodity programs. The parity model uses the current value of commodity production as a proxy for future benefits from research to improve productivity of that commodity. The commodity value is also weighted by national prevalence of poverty and child stunting to emphasize commodities of greater importance to these populations. The parity model is simple to implement but relies on strong assumptions to infer an optimal or efficient allocation of R&D resources.

A second set of results use an economic simulation model of the global agrifood economy. This model is considerably more complex but can make a more systematic assessment of how changes in agricultural productivity are likely to affect income, nutrition, and use of environmental resources. The economic simulation model looks forward to 2030, taking into account how changes in population, per capita income, and other factors are likely to affect the market demand for agricultural commodities. It also explicitly models how producer and consumer behavior might respond to changes in yields, prices, and market demand over the next decade. The economic simulation model provides a means to validate or refine the research allocations suggested by the simple parity model.

However, neither the simulation model nor the parity model takes into account the cost of R&D needed to achieve a given increase in yield or productivity. Instead, the report draws on evidence from past returns to R&D investments by CGIAR centers to offer some judgements about the likelihood of progress in the future. At the present time, explicit consideration of research costs, technology adoption pathways, and research benefits is probably best done to inform research project selection within commodity programs. The research managers, scientists, and socio-economists working within commodity programs are more likely to possess the specialized knowledge and information necessary to make informed judgements about technology needs and opportunities and the costs of technology development and dissemination in specific national and regional contexts. Eventually, systematic evidence from ex ante and ex post benefit-cost analysis of research projects could be built up to provide more sophisticated benefit-cost analysis for R&D funding allocation at the program level as well.

Table ES 1 provides a summary of key results of the multidimensional impacts of increasing agricultural productivity in the 103 target countries. The first column of figures shows the current value of production for six commodity groups and the aggregate value of these commodities by region. If the economic impacts of commodity research are strongly correlated with the current economic significance of the commodities, and if the R&D costs of raising productivity are roughly similar among commodities,

then the parity rule indicates an efficient R&D allocation rule that is likely to maximize economic returns across the commodity R&D portfolio. The poverty-weighted commodity values and value-shares (the 3rd an 4th column of figures in the table) give greater weight to commodities important to countries with a high prevalence of extreme poverty. The parity model applied to the poverty-weighted value, for example, gives greater importance to root and tuber crops, pulses and oilcrops at the expense of other commodity groups. This is because these crops are particularly important in Sub-Saharan African countries, where poverty rates are relatively high.

Table ES 1 also summarizes results from the simulation model. The table shows multiple dimensions of impact associated with a 25% increase in productivity. A 25% increase in the productivity in fruits & vegetables is projected to generate the highest income gains, followed by productivity gains in cereal grains. The productivity gain in fruits & vegetables is projected to only make small gains on the other dimensions of impact, however. Productivity improvement in cereal grains is projected to have much larger impacts on decreasing the population at risk of hunger and reducing agricultural use of land, water, and GHG emissions. For each of these impact dimensions, the “parity rule” applied to the simulation results indicates how R&D might be allocated across commodity programs to maximize the impact of the R&D portfolio on that objective. A decision-maker wishing to tackle several of these objectives at once would need to balance the portfolio allocation accordingly. Aggregating the impacts of a 25% commodity productivity improvement by region shows that the largest income gains and GHG emissions reductions would likely occur in South Asia.

Nutrient deficiency in human diets is recognized as a major cause of malnutrition with significant social and economic costs. Macro and micronutrient deficiencies have especially severe consequences for stunting growth in young children, which has both immediate and long-term consequences for human health and well-being. While Table ES 1 shows impacts of higher agricultural productivity on caloric adequacy, Table ES 2 extends this analysis to protein, iron and zinc. For zinc, the simulation model shows how productivity increases in the six commodity groups are likely to affect the population at risk of dietary inadequacy of this micronutrient. For protein, iron and other micronutrients, there is insufficient information to make this assessment. Instead, impacts are measured by changes in the “recommended nutrient intake (RNI) ratio.” An RNI of 1.00 means that the total nutrient availability in the diets of a population just equals the recommended nutrient intake for that population. To assure adequate nutrient availability for the entire population would require an RNI substantially greater than 1.00 to accommodate the unequal distribution of nutrients among individuals in the population. The simulation model indicates that raising cereal productivity would have by far the largest effect on improving RNI ratios for zinc, iron, and protein. This is due to the predominance of cereals in the diets of very poor and undernourished people, and thus the importance of grains as the primary source of these nutrients. Although overconsumption of carbohydrates and rising rates of obesity are growing problems in some countries, that issue might be better addressed by other public policies, food policy in particular, rather than by agricultural research policy. Agricultural research policy, on the other hand, can have major impacts on reducing undernutrition.

Whether a parity rule suggests an optimal or efficient allocation of R&D funding depends in part on whether the costs of technological development and dissemination are roughly similar across commodities. One indicator of future returns to research is evidence on returns from past investments in R&D. The report summarizes findings from recent reviews of ex post impact of CGIAR commodity research. R&D for most crops has earned moderate to high rates of return. Exceptions are banana/plantain and ruminant livestock, where there is only limited evidence of R&D impact so far (one

exception, however, is forage crop improvement, which has earned moderately high returns through its impacts on productivity in beef and dairy). With a few exceptions, research investments in crop improvement appear to offer significant potential to raise productivity.

Agricultural research programs may be structured not only along commodity lines but also around farming systems. Farming or food systems research is more integrative and aimed at adapting suites of technologies and practices to local needs. Table ES 3 illustrates how the parity model can be applied to guide R&D allocation among farming systems research programs. For 12 major farming systems in Sub- Saharan Africa, the table shows the total value and poverty-weighted value shares of farm production in that system, along with information on the total population, crop area, and number of ruminant livestock in each system. This information could be used to help select the priority farming systems for R&D investment and/or to guide the allocation of R&D resources among farming systems (for example, by using the poverty-weighted value share as a rule of thumb for its R&D budget share). Again, a second stage of priority setting employing benefit-cost analysis could be used to help select R&D projects within each farming systems research program.

Research programs organized around commodities or farming systems are multidisciplinary and develop a range of technologies. Crop and animal breeding improve yield potential as well as yield stability by incorporating tolerance or resistance to abiotic and biotic stresses. Innovations in agronomic and husbandry practices assure quality crop and animal nutrition and efficient and sustainable use of natural resources. Improved management and control of pests and diseases and better on-farm harvesting and storage practices help protect against yield losses. Quantitative analysis of potential research impacts can provide critical information for efficient project selection within research programs. And, when combined with estimates of the research project costs and time needed for successful technology development and diffusion, such analysis can be used to help select the projects offering highest expected returns across multiple objectives (like those illustrated in Table ES 1).

The report provides quantitative assessments of potential impacts of two classes of technologies – natural resource management (NRM) and integrated pest management (IPM) – that have relevance for international agricultural research. A key feature of these technologies is their focus on not only raising agricultural productivity but also enhancing environmental health and sustainability. Like new crop varieties or improved animal breeds, NRM and IPM need to be tailored to local conditions.

1. Executive Summary

Between 2022 and 2024, Accelerated Breeding introduced new methods for CGIAR-NARES breeding programs to achieve six end-of-initiative outcomes. The methods introduced by Accelerated Breeding were translated into a Results Framework aligned with its Theory of Change. The purpose of this document is to (i) capture 2022-2024 progress across CGIAR breeding teams using a set of indicators aligned with the Accelerated Breeding Results Framework, and (ii) translate insights from 21 crop-specific deep-dive sessions conducted in October and November 2024 into the 2024 indicator data and summarize associated insights and learnings. It complements other evidence of progress such as data sets in the Breeding Portal that are made openly accessible through the Global Market Intelligence Platform (GloMIP); peer-reviewed publications; insights from a NARES survey conducted among 94 National Agricultural Research and Extension Programs in Sub-Saharan Africa, and a large number of NARES program assessments. Overall, indicators are testimony to substantive methodological changes, learnings, and other outputs produced by the CGIAR breeding community between 2022 and 2024.
2. Introduction
Between 2022 and 2024, Accelerated Breeding introduced new methods for CGIAR-NARES breeding programs to achieve six end of initiative outcomes.
1. CGIAR-National Agricultural Research and Extensions Systems Breeding pipelines oriented towards specific market segments, enabling greater focus on farmers’ needs, drivers of adoption, and impact.
2. CGIAR breeding portfolio ensures gender inclusiveness and increases gender intentionality through the candidate varieties that are being developed.
3. Breeding pipelines use a revised organizational framework providing teams with operational clarity and effectiveness for pursuing breeding outputs.

4. Breeding networks implement stronger partnership models where National Agricultural Research and Extensions Systems (NARES) and Small and Medium-sized Enterprises (SMEs) have increased their contribution to the breeding process.
5. Breeding pipelines are supported by Trait Discovery and Deployment (TD&D) programs that deliver high-impact traits within elite parental lines.
6. Breeding pipelines have increased the rate of genetic gain, providing seed systems actors with farmer-preferred candidate varieties with step change in performance under farmers’ conditions.

The methods introduced by Accelerated Breeding were translated into a Results Framework aligned with its Theory of Change1 and organized into five work packages (ReFOCUS, ReORGANIZE, TRANSFORM, DISCOVER, and ACCELERATE) which included Center representatives from AfricaRice, CIAT, CIMMYT, CIP, ICARDA, IITA, and IRRI. ICRISAT joined in 2024.

3. Purpose of this document
This document summarizes the indicator information collected for the Accelerated Breeding Results Framework from 2022 to 2024.

Information was collected through annual surveys among breeders, and workplan reports. In 2023, the Breeding Portal was launched to document and track breeding program strategies and progress. Insights were summarized as “Innovation development” in the Program and Results Management System (PRMS) that drives the CGIAR Results Dashboard2.

In 2024, the annual survey was replaced with deep-dive sessions conducted with each CGIAR Breeding Program during October and November 2024. Compared to the leaner surveys, deep- dive sessions requested breeding programs to present evidence and discuss successes and bottlenecks in more detail. Work Package leads reviewed the presentations and evidence presented and categorized answers. They also drew on their wider knowledge of progress achieved, based on other interactions with these programs, such as through Work Package or individual meetings. The individual presentations are available from cgspace.org. (Table 1).

Therefore, and more specifically, the document (i) captures 2022-2024 progress across CGIAR breeding teams using a set of indicators aligned with the Accelerated Breeding Results Framework, and ( (ii) summarizes the final indicator data collected during the deep-dive sessions in 2024, and associated lessons learnt.

It complements other evidence of progress, such as: the more detailed data on Market Segments, Target Product Profiles, Breeding Pipeline and variety release data contained in the Breeding Portal and made openly accessible through the Global Market Intelligence Platform (GloMIP); peer-reviewed publications; and insights from a survey among 94 National Agricultural Research and Extension Programs in Sub-Saharan Africa (Das et al., 20253). Practices developed and used by CGIAR breeding are extended to and being adopted by NARES programs. Given the much larger diversity of NARES breeding programs, current states of NARES breeding programs have been assessed through 128 individual program assessments executed between 2019 and 2024. Details of those assessments are extensive and also not included in this summary.

Accelerated Breeding pursued a wide range of improvements. Center breeding teams needed to set priorities given time and resource limitations and could not make equal progress across all improvement ambitions. Also, access to Accelerated Breeding resources differed among crops, mostly given their variable importance in CGIAR target regions. Therefore, there is no intent to assess the performance of individual programs through this document.

Outcome

The introduction of business-oriented sheep fattening by The International Center for Agricultural Research (ICARDA) has revolutionized the economic landscape for youth and women in rural Ethiopia, leading to substantial job creation and income growth. ICARDA has organized 270,000 youth and women into groups and cooperatives, thereby facilitating the establishment of 49 sheep fattening groups and four legally registered cooperatives and integrating sustainable practices into local economies and supporting community development The sheep fattening activities in Ethiopia have been conducted as part of the Feed and Forage activities of the CGIAR Initiatives Sustainable Animal for Livelihoods, Nutrition, and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING) and Mixed Farming Systems.
Partners

Key partners include the Ministry of Agriculture, Ethiopian Agricultural Research Institute (EIAR), Regional Agricultural Research Centers (Amhara, Oromia, Central, Southern, and Southwestern), Debre Birhan University, Wachemo University, Jimma University, and media partners namely Fana FM and South Radio and Television Agency. This network of partners was bolstered by the involvement of non-governmental development organizations (NGO), namely, Ethiopian-based Charity and Development Association, and the UK-based Amanah Global Relief.
Why did we do this research?

Enhancing growth and reproductive performance in rams through research on improved feeds and forages to optimize sheep nutrition, promote accelerated growth rates, and improve overall flock health. By promoting locally available, affordable, and nutritionally rich forage options, the research reduced feed costs, benefiting resource- constrained farmers, particularly women and youth. Topics relating to collective action through groups and cooperatives, entrepreneurship and market-oriented approaches, financial literacy, gender and feed processing were integrated into the research because youth and women often face unique challenges, such as limited access to land, capital, skills and knowledge. The integration has helped to identify and mitigate these barriers, thereby enhancing sheep fattening as a sustainable pathway to economic stability and risk management through market- oriented approaches for farmers in rural Ethiopia.
Evidence
Job creation: The initiative created over 270,000 direct jobs, with 45% of the participants being women. This has significantly contributed to community resilience and economic empowerment.

Income growth: Beneficiaries reported an increase in annual income from ETB 16,000 (USD 570 to ETB 190,000 (USD 3653) by expanding their sheep fattening operations from four rams to 120 annually within a period of 3 years.

Participation and legal ventures: The program supported the formation and formal registration of four cooperatives and two enterprises ensuring that these ventures could access local support systems, engage in legal trade, and attract co-investment from the government and private sector.
Co-investment: Government co-investments included technical training, logistical support, direct funds and infrastructure development, helping to scale the initiative and enhance its sustainability.

“I have greatly benefited from participating in the sheep fattening program. Through the training, I learned how to scale my business from fattening less than 5 rams to fattening over one hundred rams within a period of 3 years. This knowledge has helped me track all my business transactions carefully and understand the importance of reinvesting profits instead of spending
the capital. With the current income from ram fattening, I can support my family financially and be a role model in my community.” Damitew Demise, Bonga, Ethiopia
Next steps

In the next phase, the program aims to technically support government initiatives, NGOs, and charity organizations to scale out and reach up to 500,000 youth and women, with an emphasis on achieving and maintaining over 50% female participation to ensure gender inclusivity. This expansion will include efforts to strengthen and scale up 100 new feed processing businesses that will support ready supply of balanced total mixed rations and foster partnerships with private sector actors to implement digital commercialization strategies, sustaining growth and market access. The initiative will also focus on building a more comprehensive framework to support economic resilience and long-term development, ensuring stable income and job creation for beneficiaries.

Overview

Under the CGIAR Initiatives, Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition, and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING) and Sustainable Intensification in Mixed Farming Systems (SI- MFS), a comprehensive training conducted on feed formulation and feed processing for sheep fattening in Ethiopia. The training targeted youth and women sheep fattening groups, aiming to enhance their knowledge and skills in optimizing feed management practices. ICARDA partnered with the National Agricultural Research Centers of Areka, Bonga, and Debre Berhan to deliver the training sessions. The objective of the trainings was to equip participants with the necessary expertise to formulate balanced sheep diets and efficiently process feed, thereby improving sheep productivity and promoting sustainable livestock feeding practices.

The trainings were conducted in Bonga, Doyogena, and Debre berhan between 15th March - 20 May 2023, engaging 175 participants. Training sessions were designed to be highly interactive, incorporating presentations, practical exercises, case studies, and group discussions to foster a collaborative learning environment.

Specific objectives of the training included equipping participants with the skills to formulate balanced sheep rations based on nutritional requirements, local feed resources, and cost- effectiveness. Participants were also trained in feed processing techniques, such as grinding, mixing, and pelleting, to ensure the production of high-quality feed with optimal nutrient distribution. The inclusion of women participants in each site highlighted the project's commitment to gender equality and women's empowerment in sheep fattening. Promotion of the use of locally available feed resources highlights commitment to sustainable practices.
Training Objectives
The objectives of the three-day training were as follows:
▪ To understand the nutritional requirements of sheep.
▪ To learn the principles and techniques of feed formulation for sheep.
▪ To gain knowledge of different feed ingredients and their appropriate use in sheep diets.
▪ To acquire skills in feed processing methods such as grinding and mixing for improved feed quality and digestibility.
▪ To explore cost-effective and sustainable feed-resourcing strategies.
Participants
The 175 training participants (105 male and 65 women) were from Bonga 75 youth (50 men, 25 women), Doyogena, 50 youths (30 men, 20 women) and Debre Berhan 50 youth (25 men,
25 women). The list of participants is attached as Annex II.
Course Structure
1. Introduction to sheep fattening
▪ Overview of sheep fattening industry in Ethiopia.
Importance of proper nutrition in sheep fattening.
▪ Factors influencing feed efficiency and profitability.
2. Nutritional requirements of sheep
▪ Essential nutrients for sheep and their functions.
▪ Understanding energy, protein, fiber, vitamins, and minerals requirements.
▪ Differentiating nutritional needs during different stages of sheep fattening.
3. Feed formulation
▪ Principles and techniques of feed formulation.
▪ Balancing rations for sheep using available feed ingredients.
▪ Evaluating feed quality and nutritional value.
4. Feed ingredients and their utilization:
▪ Common feed ingredients for sheep diets in Ethiopia.
▪ Nutritional composition and availability of locally sourced feed ingredients.
▪ Strategies for optimizing feed ingredient utilization and minimizing costs.
5. Feed processing techniques:
• Grinding and particle size reduction techniques for improved digestibility.
• Mixing and formulation of balanced sheep rations.
Introduction to pelleting and other feed processing methods.
6. Practical demonstrations and Hands-on exercises:
▪ Practical sessions on feed formulation software and tools.
▪ Hands-on experience in feed processing techniques.
▪ Group discussions and case studies to apply the acquired knowledge.

Group Assessment
The group assessment aimed to promote collaborative learning, problem-solving skills and critical thinking. Group assessment sessions are outlined below:
Feed formulation case study

Participants were divided into small groups and presented with a case study scenario involving a sheep farm in Ethiopia. Each group was tasked with formulating a balanced diet for a specific group of sheep based on their weight, age, and nutritional requirements. They

had to consider the availability of local feed ingredients, cost effectiveness and desired growth targets. The groups were required to work together, apply feed formulation principles, and use knowledge gained during the training to develop a comprehensive feeding plan. They were assessed based on the accuracy of their ration formulation, the appropriateness of ingredient selection, and the justification of their decisions.
Feed processing practical exercise

Another group assessment activity focused on feed processing techniques. Participants were divided into teams and provided with different feed ingredients commonly used in sheep diets. Each group was assigned the task of processing the ingredients into a pelleted feed using the available feed processing equipment. Teams had to demonstrate their understanding of grinding, mixing, and pelleting techniques to produce a high-quality feed with appropriate particle size and uniform nutrient distribution. The assessment criteria included the effectiveness of the feed processing methods employed, the quality of the final product, and the groups’ ability to troubleshoot and address any challenges encountered during the exercise.
Group presentation and discussion

To assess the participants' comprehension and communication skills, each group was assigned a specific topic related to feed formulation or feed processing for sheep fattening. The groups were given time to research and prepare a presentation on their topic, highlighting key concepts, best practices, and potential challenges. They then had to give their presentations to the entire training cohort, followed by a group discussion where participants could ask questions and engage in a constructive dialogue. The assessment criteria included the clarity and depth of the presentations, the ability to effectively communicate complex ideas, and the groups' active participation in the subsequent discussion. These group assessments provided participants with the opportunity to apply their knowledge, collaborate with their peers, and showcase their understanding of feed formulation and feed processing for sheep fattening in Ethiopia. The assessments not only evaluated their individual and group performance but also fostered a supportive learning.

4 Empowering youth and women through sheep fattening: A pathway to entrepreneurship, job 2 creation and economic growth in Ethiopia

In Ethiopia, sheep fattening is a transformative enterprise offering sustainable income, job creation and risk management for over 27,000 young people and women across the central, southern, southwestern, Amhara, Oromia and Addis Ababa areas. The market-oriented sheep fattening program offers a comprehensive suite of innovations aimed at increasing productivity and fostering business-oriented marketing opportunities. It is supported by a community of practice platform incorporating a livestock office, universities, the Ethiopian Institute of Agricultural Research, national research centres, media, microﬁnance institutions, cooperative offices, enterprise offices and the private sector.

The initiative has trained more than 5,000 youth and women who have fattened over 2 million sheep. It also provides essential initial investments that enable participants to start small-scale feed processing and marketing businesses, helping to alleviate feed shortages and reduce costs in local markets. By empowering youth and women, who often serve as primary caregivers for livestock, and by bridging market gaps, driving community-level economic growth, this project is creating a brighter future for Ethiopia's youth and women.

We will develop improved gender-sensitive business models for beef-cattle artificial insemination (AI) service providers in Vietnam, with a focus on economic performance and social responsibility. This will support the creation of business opportunities for rural men and women (offering the AI services), resulting in income generation and diversification. An increased number of AI service providers, offering quality service and semen from farmer-preferred breeds, is also likely to impact positively on adoption rates of AI. The use of improved beef-cattle genetics, combined with best- practice cattle management in relation to feeding and health-care, is expected to result in an increase in beef-cattle productivity and thus increased profitability of smallholder beef cattle enterprises.

Introduction

Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition and Gender (SAPLING) is one of the CGIAR Initiatives focusing on sustainable animal productivity. See here a description of the initiative. This initiative aims to contribute to transforming livestock sectors in target countries to make them more productive, resilient, equitable and sustainable. Contributing to SAPLING’s overall objective, the SAPLING Vietnam program (called Chan-Henh) aims to contribute to transforming pig and beef cattle value chains in the Northwest Highlands of Vietnam. Target sites are within the Mai Son District of Son La Province, specifically the communes of Chiềng Chung, Chiềng Lương, Mường Bon and Hát Lót.

Promotion of the adoption of pig and cattle artificial insemination (AI) is a key component of Chan-Henh. This is being achieved through working with both the AI service providers, strengthening both their technical capacity and business acumen as well as establishment of an AI service providers cooperative, and capacity building of the women and men smallholder farmers, through training on breeds, breeding and AI and exposure to AI. Introduction

Agriculture is central to the economy and livelihoods in Vietnam’s Son La Province, where the mountainous terrain and tropical climate support the cultivation of crops like maize, rice, tea, and various fruits, which are key for both local consumption and trade. Livestock, particularly beef cattle, is an essential component of the agricultural system, providing income through the sale of animals, manure for soil fertility, and draft power for farming. For smallholder farmers, beef cattle production plays a crucial role in their mixed farming systems, contributing significantly to household income and food security. However, farmers face several challenges that limit productivity and profitability. These include limited access to improved cattle genetics, which could enhance meat production, and the prevalence of cattle diseases, which affect herd health and growth. Additionally, the availability of high- quality feed is often constrained, especially during the dry season, impacting cattle growth. Profitability is further hindered by market fluctuations and a lack of organized value chains, which reduce the farmers' ability to secure stable and favorable prices for their cattle. Addressing these challenges through better breeding practices, disease control, improved feeds, and enhanced market access would greatly benefit the farmers and enhance the economic potential of beef cattle production in the region. This has been the aim of the CGIAR Initiative Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING) operating under the local project name of 'Chan- Henh' in Son La Province (Atieno et al. 2023).
Page 4 of 19

Under Chan-Henh a model was developed to promote use of artificial insemination (AI) in beef cattle. This model was developed in response to concerns from cattle farmers in Son La regarding the difficulty of finding quality breeding cattle and their high price (Le Thi Thanh and Marshall 2021a). AI has the advantage over natural mating of improving access to high quality genetics, reducing disease spread, and being cost-effective (in comparison to smallholders keeping their own bull). The adoption of beef cattle AI in Son La has traditionally been low (Hammond et al. 2010) due to both the lack of artificial insemination service providers, particularly in more remote locations, as well as lack of farmers awareness on the advantages of the technology (Le Thi Thanh and Marshall 2021a).

The model to promote the use of beef cattle AI presented here works with women and men AI service providers, women and men beef-cattle keepers, and partners including the Son La Department of Animal Health and Production, Mai Son Department of Agriculture and Rural Development, Mai Son Agricultural Service Center, and Chieng Chung, Chieng Luong, Muong Bon and Hat Lot Communal People Committees. It was tested in the Mai-Son District of Son La Province, where Chan-Henh operates. The model has been successful in both creating business opportunities in AI service provision as well as promoting AI adopting by smallholder cattle keepers, and is recommended for scaling to other locations within Son La Province and northwest Vietnam more broadly.
The Chan-Henh approach

The Chan-Henh project takes an integrated approach to improving beef cattle production and marketing, comprising: capacity building of farmers and service providers on innovations for improved beef cattle genetics, health-care and feeding; a farmers-groups approach for collective action, including on input acquisition and marketing; gender accommodative and transformative approaches to ensure innovation access and benefit is equitable; and a component to Improve nutrition of the producing households (Otieno et al. 2023). It also addresses pig production and marketing, including promotion of pig AI: the pig AI work will be reported separately.

Chan-Henh was Implemented between 2023 and 2024, within four target communes of the Mai Son District (Chiềng Chung , Chiềng Lương, Mường Bon and Hát Lót). It was funded through the One CGIAR Initiative Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING). Permission to undertake the project was granted by the People's Committee of Son La Province on March 25th 2023 according to Decision No. 963/UBND-NC.

The project was co-designed and co-implemented with partners and stakeholders. CGIAR partners included the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT (the Alliance) and the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) and local partners included the Son La Department of Agriculture and Rural Development (Son La DARD), the Son La Sub-Department of Animal Husbandry (Son La Sub-DAH), the National Institute of Animal Sciences of Vietnam (NIAS), the National Institute of Veterinary Research (NIVR), the Northern Mountainous Agriculture and Forestry Sciences Institute (NOMAFSI), the Vietnam National University of Agriculture (VNUA) and the National institute of Nutrition (NIN).

A key element of Chan-Henh was the use of farmer groups for improved access of the smallholder farmers to input and output markets, as well as being a forum for capacity development and co-create of solutions to issues pertaining to pig and cattle keeping. Given the inefficient function of the existing farmer groups engaged in cattle and pig production in Mai Son District (in terms of economic and financial sustainability, service offers, marketing connection and trading capacity (Cuong et al. 2023), Chan-Henh focused on developing and implementing strategic plans for upgrading the functioning and capacities of the existing farmer groups, and used that lesson to support the establishment and efficient operation of new farmer groups. Since 2023, SAPLING has been assisting eight farmer groups, comprising 120 members.

Activities with smallholder cattle keepers

Activities with smallholder women and men cattle keepers were aimed at increasing their capacity on, and improving their attitude towards, cattle AI. The activities comprised training on beef cattle breeds, breeding and AI, examining and treating reproductive diseases, as well as exposure to cattle AI through demonstration farms.
Training of cattle keepers on cattle breeds, breeding and AI

Training on cattle breeding, breeds and artificial insemination was achieved both through community workshop and trainings held within farmer groups. The training were a day in length and conducted by an expert team from NIAS (for the community workshops (Marshall and Le Thi Thanh 2023a) and by the Son La sub-DAH team for the farmer-group members (Son La Sub-department of Livestock Production, Animal Health and Fisheries 2024). All trainings were designed to be interactive, with group discussions and question and answer sessions. Topics included cattle breeds and their performance, the cattle reproductive cycle, how to select good breeding animals, cow heat detection, and artificial insemination, as well as taking care of pregnant and lactating cows. Materials supporting the training included posters (which remained in cultural centers (CGIAR Research Program on Livestock 2021), and training manuals which were given to each participant (Le et al. 2024 ), see Figures 2 and 3. Particular attention was paid to ensure that both women and men cattle keepers attended the training, though specifically inviting both women and men within households and ensuring that the training location was in a centralized and easy to access location. In addition to the women and men cattle keepers, local animal health care workers attended the training as well.
The respondents were very appreciative of the training, and noted that training of this nature had rarely (If ever) been offered before (Marshall and Le Thi Thanh 2023a).

Activities with artificial insemination service providers

Activities involving both women and men artificial inseminators and from Kinh, Thai and H'Mong ethnic groups aimed to equip them with high-quality skills in artificial insemination (AI) techniques, whilst ensuring AI service delivery was both professional and profitable. Activities comprised comprehensive training in the technical aspects of AI, alongside guidance on business operations. A cooperative was established to facilitate shared access to semen storage facilities, and partnerships were forged with semen suppliers to ensure a steady supply of quality genetics. Additionally, AI service providers were given booklets to track insemination procedures, monitor success rates, and assess the profitability of their services, enhancing both technical proficiency and business sustainability.
Training in the cattle AI technique, certification, and follow-on support

Training of women and men veterinary (animal health) workers and veterinarians on the technique of cattle artificial insemination was achieved through a 21 day training course (Marshall and Huyen 2023b). The course comprised both theoretical and practical sessions. Topics covered during the theoretical sessions included cattle reproduction, cattle breeding, semen including sexed semen, synchronization, heat detection, AI equipment and technique, pregnancy detection, embryo transfer, and reproductive diseases and their treatment. All theoretical sessions were interactive and all trainees were provided with a training manual (Le Thi Thanh and Marshall 2020a). The practical sessions comprised: examination and practice AI using cow uterus from different culled animals (heifers, cows etc.) provided by the slaughterhouse (Figure 5); practice AI on live cows destined for slaughter; on-farm examination of cows, synchronization and artificial insemination (Figure 6), as well as treatment of reproductive diseases. At the end of the course all trainees were examined for their skills on AI (practical) as well as theoretical understanding (oral examination). Those successfully completing the course were registered with the Animal Husbandry Research and Development Center for Mountainous Zone (ARDC - NIAS) and Issued with a certificate.

Following training, on-going support until project end was provided to the AI service providers through interactions, including field-visits, messages in Zalo group, phone-calls, and video calls, with the AI trainers. Business models studies were undertaken to consider different approaches to sustainable AI service delivery within Son La Province (Bravo et al. 2023a; Bravo et al. 2023b). A key recommendation from the study was a cattle AI service providers cooperative, which would serve multiple purposes including supporting operational capacity, reducing input and equipment costs, acting as a liaison between providers and various stakeholders (such as local authorities, NGOs, input suppliers, and farmers), disseminating technical knowledge related to cattle AI, Improved breeds, and animal husbandry practices. Based on this recommendation a beef-cattle AI service providers co-operative was established, which has played a core role in this model.

The AI co-operative established comprised four members, two men and two women, belonging to the Kinh, Thai and H'Mong ethnic groups. The co-operative leader is the communal veterinary of Hat Lot town, who was an established cattle AI service provider in Mai Son District. Two other members are
Page 10 of 19

communal veterinarians of Chieng Chung and Chieng Luong communes who wanted to become AI service providers for both cows and sows. The fourth member is a director of a beef cooperative and started to do cattle AI service in Muong Bon commune. The membership size of the co-operative was determined based on expected demand for cattle AI within the Chan-Henh project sites. As demand increases, or if the approach is scaled to neighboring sites, the number of members within the co- operative could increase

All co-operative members agreed to, and signed, a common operation regulation. The aim was to ensure that the co-operative supported all members, but with members accruing individual benefits. The regulations covered issues such as: assignment of operational sub-regions assigned to each member, to ensure manageable travel distances; charges for services for uniform pricing; the semen sources to be used; sharing of group costs, for example, shipping fees; recording practices; and other practices such as advise given to farmers on cattle reproduction and AI.

A large (35-litre) liquid nitrogen tank was provided to, and managed through, the co-operative lead. Specially the lead would be responsible for importing liquid nitrogen on a weekly basis and distributing to other co-operative members, as well as semen importation as required, with payment received to cover all costs.

Additionally each members was provided with a small (3 litre) liquid nitrogen tank (to be able to transport semen on the back on motorbikes), an insemination gun (CIDR Bovine applicator) and some consumables (insemination gel, gloves, 5ml cylinders, 18 gauge needles; and synchronization hormones – PGF2α (OvuprostTM), Ovurelin) to help them launch their AI provision businesses.

On semen, experts from NIAS connected the AI co-operative members with four input suppliers for cattle AI (semen and tools) including both state and private ones. The members considered the price, breeds of available semen, way of trading, and the convenience in receiving the inputs. Based on this an individual supplier was selected. Semen is purchased by the co=operative lead as needed, and stored under liquid nitrogen until required by a co-operative member for insemination.

The signing of the common operation regulations and distribution of equipment was undertaken during a workshop (Le Thi Thanh and Marshall 2024). At this time the AI co-operative members were also introduced to farmers, village heads, leaders of communes, and representatives from the District DARD, provincial DARD; and Agricultural Service Centre.

Communications within the co-operative is facilitated by a Zalo group comprising the AI members as well as NIAS experts on artificial insemination. Discussions have included the sharing of successful AI stories, AI and synchronization issues, diagnosis and treatment of reproductive issues (including by sharing videos and photos), jointly working together to perform AIs when many are being undertaken within a commune, amongst others.

Financial management of the co-operative has been as follows. For the first three months, the project supported the co-operative through the provision of liquid nitrogen, payment of half of the semen and semen transport fees (with the other half paid by the farmer group members receiving the AI), and coverage of re-insemination fees. After this time-period, the co-operative leader has been responsible for purchasing liquid nitrogen, when reimbursement from the co-operative members based on the volumes they use. Note the liquid nitrogen price to the members was set at cost-price, but compensating for liquid nitrogen loss from the main reservoir over time.

Recording tools

To further support the AI service providers, recording booklets were created to track both artificial inseminations and business profitability. These booklets, developed in both Vietnamese and English, are referred to as the AI Service Provider Recording Booklet on Service Provision (Marshall and Le Thi 2023 c,d) and the AI Service Provider Recording Booklet for Accounting (Marshall and Le Thi, 2023 e,f).

The AI Service Provision booklet enables providers to monitor all activities related to a specific cow and its insemination (Figure 7). It includes detailed records of the client, cow, and AI-related activities, along with dates for follow-up visits and outcomes of the inseminations. Each cow that undergoes insemination has a dedicated double-page spread, facilitating easy visualization of the activities conducted for that cow, such as synchronization, heat detection, insemination, and pregnancy detection. This recording booklet empowers AI service providers to track their clients effectively, plan follow-up visits with ease, and evaluate the outcomes of the artificial insemination process.

Strengthening linkages between the cattle keepers and the AI service providers

Connecting cattle keepers with AI service providers was a crucial aspect of promoting the adoption of cattle artificial insemination. This connection was fostered between farmer groups and AI service providers by having the providers in training sessions on AI (Son La sub-DAH, 2024). Additionally, these service providers took part in village meetings to discuss the benefits of utilizing AI in cattle farming, which helped promote their businesses and offered farmers with a reliable resource for livestock services (https://www.cgiar.org/news-events/news/promoting-the-adoption-of-saplings-innovations- through-village-sharing-events/). A Zalo group has been formed that consists of cattle keepers, AI service providers, AI experts, and researchers from NIAS. This group shares information related to cattle artificial insemination, including topics like cow births, calf care, management of pregnant and lactating cows, and post-calving treatment issues. The discussions are supplemented with pictures and short videos.

The AI service providers expressed that these linkages were essential for building relationships with potential clients, while farmers appreciated knowing their service provider and having direct contact with them.

About SAPLING

CGIAR’s Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition and Gender inclusion (SAPLING) is working in seven countries focusing on livestock value chains to package and scale out tried-and- tested, as well as new, innovations in livestock health, genetics, feed and market systems. SAPLING aims to demonstrate that improvements in livestock productivity can offer a triple win: generating improved livelihoods and nutritional outcomes; contributing to women’s empowerment; and, reducing impacts on climate and the environment. Its seven focus countries are Ethiopia, Kenya, Mali, Nepal, Tanzania, Uganda and Vietnam.

Background to training

Launched in Vietnam in 2022 until the end of 2024, the CGIAR Initiative on Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition, and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING) aims to enhance the livestock sector in Son La Province, situated in northwest Vietnam. The interventions were implemented through five work packages (WP), with WP1 concentrating on providing technical advancements in three key pillars of livestock productivity: genetics, feed and forages, and animal health.

Alongside offering technical assistance to farmers and enhancing the skills of veterinary personnel, the WP1 – Genetics component has established a cooperative of cattle artificial insemination (AI) service providers to improve the delivery of AI services in the region. The cooperative has four members, two men and two women, those belong to the Kinh, Thai and Mong ethnic groups. Each member was supported by the project with a small nitrogen tank, an inseminating gun, hormone and other equipment for heating synchronization and performing AI.

From May to October 2024, a business incubation training course was held for members of the AI service provider cooperative to improve their professionalism and increase profitability. This opportunity was also extended to four additional veterinarians who are interested in providing AI services and joining the cooperative. All eight participants had previously completed technical training courses organized by the National Institute of Animal Husbandry (NIAS) and received certificates, enabling them to professionally deliver AI services.
The training course focused on three areas:
Training on business plans
Training on marketing and sale skills

Location, modality

The initial two training sessions, which took place took place in-person at Bong Sen Hotel in Hat Lot town, focused on business plans and marketing and sales skills. In contrast, the monthly meetings and coaching sessions were held online.

Dates

A business plan training session took place over two days, 7–8 May 2024. Training on marketing and sales skills was held on 24 June 2024. Additionally, monthly meetings and individual coaching sessions occurred from May through to November.
Who conducted the training
The training was led by an independent consultant, Ms. Pham Thi Le, with support from members of SAPLING-WP4.
Objectives of the training
This training course aimed to enhance the professionalism and profitability of AI service providers. Specifically,

• The objectives of the training on business plans were i) to assess the current state of AI service provision of the AI service providers, ii) to strengthen the organizational structure and responsibilities of the cooperative, iii) to set revenue goals for both the cooperative and its individual members, iv) to create a comprehensive business plan for the cooperative, and v) to finalize the price list for the services offered.
• The objectives of the training on marketing and sales skills were to help each group member develop a marketing and sales strategy to achieve their individual and cooperative sales goals.

• The objectives of the monthly meetings and coaching were i) to review the progress and make necessary adjustments to the business plan, and ii) to help each group member create materials to promote their services in the community using platforms such as Zalo, Facebook, and local meetings.
Training agenda

Training on business plans involved participants first conducting a strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats (SWOT) analysis to assess their current AI service offerings. They then explored the potential for enhancing business efficiency through collaboration as a cooperative. Following this, they created operational guidelines for the AI service providers cooperative and established a system to track its performance. Additionally, they compiled a list of products and services available through the cooperative, along with their pricing, and set a revenue goal for the last six months of 2024. Finally, they discussed and formulated a monthly action plan.

Training on marketing and sales skills began with an introduction to the subject. Participants assessed the strengths and weaknesses of their current advertising and sales channels. This was followed by sessions on marketing and sales planning. Additionally, guidelines were provided for posting sales and completing orders on Facebook and Zalo.
See Annex 1 for the detailed training agendas.

Monthly meetings took place on the 25thof each month from May to November 2024, during which cooperative members shared updates on their businesses and discussed challenges they encountered. This information was used to make adjustments to the business plan of the whole cooperative. Individual coaching sessions were held monthly for each member according to their availability, aimed at reviewing their business plans and assisting them in creating promotional materials to market their services within the community through platforms like Zalo, Facebook, and local gatherings.
Training participants

The business incubation training course was conducted for eight AI service providers, including two women and six men. Four of these participants were already members of the AI service providers group formed by WP1-Genetics, while the other four were veterinarians looking to offer AI services and join the cooperative. All eight had previously attended technical training sessions organized by the Institute of Animal Husbandry (NIAS) and earned certificates, qualifying them to professionally provide AI services.
Results
1. Training on business plan
a. Evaluation of the current situation of AI service provision
Participants used the SWOT framework to analyze their current situation of AI service provision.
Strengths:

• All participants possess veterinary knowledge and they are employed by local communities, including communes, villages, and towns, where they carry out duties assigned by local authorities. Their responsibilities involve veterinary techniques and animal husbandry.

• All have attended training courses on AI for cattle and pigs from the Li-chăn and Chăn- hênh projects and were granted certificates, enabling them to professionally deliver AI services. Some of them have a certain number of customers with many successful inseminations for cattle, buffalo, and pigs.
• The AI service cooperative received strong support from the Chăn-hênh project in terms of technical skills and equipment (e.g., nitrogen tanks, semen, etc.).
Local authorities actively endorse the use of AI techniques to improve the quality of pig and cattle herds given AI’s outstanding benefits over traditional mating methods.
Weakness:

• The AI service providers cooperative is not operating systematically and effectively. Despite training by the Chăn-henh project, the group lacks ongoing connections and collaborative activities to maintain member engagement. Each member operates in different areas with significant geographic distances, making regular communication
challenging. The cooperative has not yet established operational guidelines, a business plan, or a service marketing strategy.

• Members of the cooperative work independently and provide services only when being contacted by customers without proactively marketing or seeking new clients, leading to low customer rates for the AI service.

• Skills of the cooperative members vary significantly. Some members have no confidence when handling challenging cases, therefore the cooperative leader takes on more work while some members lack work.

• Four participants (out of the AI service provider cooperative) completed training on AI for pigs and cattle but lack confidence in their skills due to limited practice opportunities, especially for cattle. Besides, there is low demand for AI services from farmers for both pigs and cattle, and the high-cost of equipment makes it challenging to have profit. Currently, they only offer pig AI by request and are not actively seeking customers.
Chăn-hênh opportunities:
• The rising demand for high-quality beef and pork presents an opportunity for AI to enhance livestock breeds, improving their productivity and quality.
• Consumers are increasingly concerned about the origin and quality of food. AI technology aids in tracing food origins and ensuring product quality, providing a competitive edge in the market.

• Mai Son District possesses favourable natural conditions for cattle and pig farming, yet local breeds with low yields remain the most common production challenges. The use of AI offers a chance to enhance breed quality, ultimately boosting their economic productivity and increasing income for farmers.

• Mai Son District has various organizations and projects aimed at promoting agricultural and livestock development. The AI service providers cooperative can partner with these entities to gain access to resources, expertise, and market opportunities.
Threats:

• Many farmers in rural areas have a limited understanding of animal husbandry and may not fully recognize the advantages of AI, leading to hesitance in embracing this technology. Additionally, their inadequate animal care practices contribute to low conception rates associated with AI.

• The cost of AI is still significant, which discourages customers from adopting it, particularly since they are accustomed to free traditional breeding methods. Moreover, farmers often seek out free AI services offered by government programs rather than choosing paid options.

• Numerous livestock-rearing households are situated in remote and isolated areas, which poses challenges for service providers to access them or results in unprofitability due to high fuel expenses for travel.

• AI services demand a high standard of quality, yet the revenue generated is minimal, often resulting in financial losses for providers. This is due to several factors: i) The likelihood of a cow becoming pregnant after a single AI is quite low, and even after three attempts, successful conception is not guaranteed. As a result, households are reluctant to pay if their animals do not conceive, making it less appealing for technicians to expand their services.

• Without financial assistance from the Chăn-hênh project, the service providers would not be able to purchase liquid nitrogen containers. Moreover, maintaining these containers is also challenging, as refilling a small one costs VND 80,000 and lasts only a week. With a small customer base, the expense of liquid nitrogen places a heavy financial burden on the cooperative.
b. Proposed solutions after SWOT analysis and discussions

The cooperative expanded to include 4 new members, bringing the total to 8 members, consisting of 6 men and 2 women. To better represent the variety of services it offers, the cooperative has been renamed Mai Son Veterinary Service Cooperative.
The members highlighted key factors essential for their service's success, including:
• enhancing the cooperative's internal capabilities.
leveraging opportunities from government programs and policies.
• partnering directly with private sector firms for services, breeds, and materials.
• obtaining backing from local authorities in conjunction with government programs.
The establishment of a cooperative focused on service provision, as suggested by the members, would tackle several key elements, including:
fostering mutual assistance among the members.
• maximizing each member's strengths.
formulating a collective business strategy.
• executing personalized business plans in designated local areas.

The cooperative decided to broaden its range of services and products to enhance profitability. This included offering disease treatment, veterinary medications and supplies, animal feed, breeding stock, probiotics, and molasses to farmers. This strategy would leverage the unique strengths of its members to collaboratively generate profits. For instance,
• Ms. Tho offers a significant supply of equipment, pig and cow semen, medicine, and reliable breeding sources for chickens, cows, and pigs. She is open to collaborating with
members, providing them access to these resources at discounted rates, which means they will not need to invest heavily to start their service.
• Mr. Day brings valuable technical knowledge and is willing to assist and mentor others when needed.

• When a member gets service orders that are distant from their home but close to other members, the cooperative has created a plan to link these members together and share the earnings from each order.
Improvement of the cooperative’s operation efficiency

The cooperative members reviewed and reached a consensus on the operating regulations and business plan for the cooperative to (i) enhance the provision of AI and veterinary services for livestock to meet the local needs, (ii) clarify responsibilities and promote teamwork among members, and (iii) ensure the cooperative's independent and effective functioning after the project's support concludes.

All members must adhere to the cooperative's operating regulations. The provisions of the regulations are reviewed and changed every six months according to actual requirements (see Appendix 1 for details). The regulations emphasize teamwork efforts, including:
• Building a spirit of cooperation, resolving conflicts together and making decisions together.
• Holding technical meetings and sales support plans on the 25th of every month.
• In addition to face-to-face interactions, online interactions take place via a general Zalo group account.
• Allocating geographical areas for providing direct services or cross-service referrals among members (Table 1).

Outcome

In Northwest Vietnam, the CGIAR Initiative on Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition, and Gender (SAPLING) is supporting a local initiative known as ""Chan-Henh."" This program aims to enhance smallholder production and marketing of beef cattle and pigs in the Mai Son District of Son La Province.

A primary objective of Chan-Henh is to improve the productivity of smallholder beef cattle and pig systems (Atieno et al., 2024). As part of this effort, the initiative promotes artificial insemination (AI) for pigs and beef cattle to provide farmers with better access to preferred genetics and enhance biosecurity. To this end, Chan-Henh supported AI service providers in technical training (Marshall and Huyen, 2023), developing business acumen (Le et al., 2024) and co-operative formation for collective action, including facilitating access to liquid nitrogen for semen storage. This was to ensure that professional AI services were available in the area, and that provision of AI services was profitable to the providers. Additionally, Chan-Henh trained women and men livestock keepers on breeds, breeding and artificial insemination, to help enhance demand (Marshall and Huyen, 2023c).

Here we report the number of households adopting either cattle or pig artificial insemination through the AI service provider co-operative members. In total 175 households adopted AI, 134 for cattle AI and 41 for pig AI. Using an average household size of 4.8 (Hammond et al., 2021) this corresponds to 840 people benefiting. The model for promotion of cattle and pig AI (which is being fully documented separately) will be promoted for scaling within other locations in northwest Vietnam.
Partners

The SAPLING initiative in Vietnam is supported by the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT and the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI). The National Institute of Animal Science, Vietnam, played a major role in supporting the beef cattle and pig AI work. The Sub-department of Livestock Production, Animal Health and Fisheries of Son La (Sub-DAH) also supported this work.
Why did we do this research?

Son La Province in northwest Vietnam is a region with a rich cultural diversity, where ethnic minorities make up about 83% of the population. Livestock, particularly beef cattle and pig farming, is essential to the local economy and culture, providing not only a source of nutrition but also a critical foundation for livelihoods. For many smallholder farmers, livestock represents both a financial asset and a means of economic resilience, while integrating livestock into crop farming systems enhances soil fertility through manure use, supporting sustainable agriculture.

Earlier studies in Son La identified low adoption of AI for cattle and pigs, including due to the lack of service providers, as a limitation to livestock production (https://cgspace.cgiar.org/handle/10568/107285). In response, Chan-Henh has been developing a model for promotion of AI, working with women and men AI service providers as well as smallholder cattle keepers. On the service provision side, veterinary workers have been trained in the technique of artificial insemination (Marshall and Huyen, 2023), undergone agri-business incubation to increase business acumen (Le et al., 2024) and formulated into a co-operative for collection action, including facilitation of access to liquid nitrogen. This was to ensure that professional AI services were available in the area, and that provision of AI services was profitable to the providers. Additionally, Chan-Henh trained women and men livestock keepers on breeds, breeding and artificial insemination, to help enhance demand (Marshall and Huyen, 2023c).
This approach aimed to ensure that professional AI services were accessible in the region and financially viable for
providers.

Next steps

Stakeholders in northwest Vietnam have expressed strong interest in scaling of the model to promote cattle and pig AI (which is being fully documented separately) to other locations within northwest Vietnam. The next steps will thus be to share the model with these stakeholders and provide support to them in adopting the model. Further efforts to promote the adoption of cattle and pig AI within the Chan-Henh sites will also continue.

Sustainable business models with a gender-sensitive approach   for cattle artiﬁcial insemination services in NWH Vietnam  Aura Bravo¹; Thinh Nguyen²; Phuong Nguyen²; Natalia Triana-Ángel¹; Thanh Huyen Le Thi³; Karen Marshall²; Stefan Burkart¹.  ¹International Center for Tropical Agriculture, Tropical Forages Program, Colombia; ² International Livestock Research Institute, Nairobi,   Kenya; ³ National Institute of Animal Science, Vietnam.  Contact: s.burkart@cgiar.org  CIAT / G Smith
Contact: s.burkart@cgiar.org
Introduction
Objective

The swift evolution of the Vietnamese cattle value chain can be attributed to a convergence of factors, e.g. public policies favoring a market-based economy, an expanding population, improved living standards, and geographical proximity to dynamic and ever-changing markets.
To assess the existing AI business model for cattle in NWH Vietnam and to provide actionable recommendations for enhancing the model, thereby addressing the issue of supply shortages.

The process of modernizing livestock production in Vietnam has exhibited distinct patterns based on the type of products (chickens, pigs, and cattle) and geographical regions (north, central, and south). As a result, beef production in NWH Vietnam is predominantly carried out by smallholders who have adopted technology to a limited extent.
Methodology
A qualitative and gender-sensitive methodology was employed to gather information, facilitating an examination of the prevailing AI service delivery model.

The central government and multilateral organizations have initiated mechanisms to advance beef production in Vietnam. These efforts are centered around enhancing the productivity of locals breeds through genetic improvement and the implementation of cattle artificial insemination (CAI), utilizing specialized crosses that possess significant adaptability to the conditions prevalent in the region.
Nine Key Informant Interviews were undertaken in Son La Province, involving AI cattle providers. The participants comprised seven men and two women, ensuring a gender-sensitive approach.

The conceptual framework is founded on the innovative business model design principles presented by Osterwalder and Pigneur (2010). Additionally, the triple-layered canvas business model introduced by Joyce et al. (2015) was employed, with specific emphasis placed on the social layer.

Nevertheless, enduring disparities in the adoption of CAI among cattle farmers persist due to constraints such as inadequate supply, restricted accessibility, and challenges related to the affordability of CAI services.
Results

• CAI business heavily relies on support from both government and development projects, offering training and certifying the technical skills, as well as providing essential inputs (Figure 1).
• Most participants within the service provision network, are men who engage in CAI service as a supplementary occupation.

• The existing provider network remains underdeveloped, with restricted geographical coverage. Mobility, as well as difficulties in reaching more remote and mountainous regions, constitute the primary obstacles.

• CAI service providers are required to possess a nitrogen flask for their operations. However, not all providers have the financial means to acquire one, nor procuring high-quality semen and liquid nitrogen.

• Several providers expressed concerns about the origin and quality of semen available in the market. They are typically obtained from Hanoi or Bac Ninh province, contributing to elevated transportation costs.

• Liquid nitrogen utilization falls short of its full capacity. To optimize its usage, a provider needs to offer services for 15-20 cows per month.

The prevailing value proposition of CAI service provision primarily revolves around the service itself, encompassing inputs and labor. Notably, success rates ranging between 60-80% are achieved for specific animal breeds. Moreover, the value proposition includes guidance on optimal breeds and crossbreeds to enhance local breeds, as well as veterinary consultations and services encompassing aspects like disease diagnosis and treatment, obstetric assessment, and nutritional guidance during pregnancy and post-delivery. The service package also features a guarantee that offers 2-3 additional attempts at a reduced price or even free of charge.
Conclusions
Enhancing the provision of CAI services requires the establishment of a local supply source for equipment, e.g. semen and liquid nitrogen.
Initiating a strategy involves a preliminary phase of bolstering the CAI service provision network in collaboration with farmer groups.
The social value acknowledged by suppliers is centered around several key aspects, including:
The expected influence on the social layer could manifest in terms of end users, social value and benefits, and the expansion of outreach.
• Enhancing the genetic traits and overall productivity of local breeds.
Comprehensive and advanced training to CAI technicians is necessary to enhance their proficiency and understanding of veterinary aspects, such as synchronization, obstetric examination, among others.
• Focusing on cattle with substantial economic value, characterized by larger body frames and higher carcass rates.
• Decreasing the time required for rearing.
• Lowering the vulnerability to diseases, encompassing both infections and the risks associated with inbreeding.
It is critical to train farmers regarding the advantages of CAI and equip them with the skills required for precise heat detection.

• The prevailing prejudgment in Ethiopia that indigenous goats do not adequately respond to improvements in level of care compared to crossbred goats is not true.
