KEY FINDINGS

This report covers the study area of the Sasakawa Africa Association Nigeria (SAA Nigeria) Use Case in the Northwest (Kano and Kaduna) and North Central (Nasarawa), based on interviews conducted in June and July 2023. The study sites are in Northwest (Kano and Kaduna) and North Central (Nasarawa).
Context

• Kano has the lowest number of literate people in the sample and highest number of people in the sample without formal schooling (for male and female study participants) among the three focus states. Almost all the heads of households in the Kano sample are Muslim; while 46 percent and 17 percent are Muslim in Kaduna and Nasarawa, respectively. In most of these communities, especially in Kano and Kaduna, women generally have mobility constraints from going to the farm or market or joining group meetings or community gatherings. Most people in the sample in Kano are in polygamous households, while mostly monogamous households comprise the samples in Kaduna and Nasarawa. Across all states, only a handful of single/widowed/separated heads were part of sample.

• Fewer households in the sample are likely poor in Nasarawa and more households in the sample are likely poor in Kano and Kaduna. There are more households who indicated they experience food insecurity in Kaduna and fewer households in Nasarawa, compared with Kano.

In terms of household structure, larger household sizes exist in Kano, while smaller household sizes and fewer younger children and youth in households in Nasarawa. Only 56 percent of households have youth members in Nasarawa compared to 85 percent and 94 percent in Kano and Kaduna, respectively. Land area cultivated is the smallest in Nasarawa, compared with Kaduna and Kano.

• Almost all households in the sample in Kaduna and Kano planted maize and rice; most sample households in Nasawara planted rice and maize, but more households planted cassava (44 percent of households in Nasawara compared to 5 percent in Kaduna and 22 percent in Kano).
Reach

• Women and youth participate to a significant extent in agricultural production, but men (especially older men) are more often considered as the main contributor to farm work and the main decision maker on the main plot.
• In 65 percent of households, female household members actively participate in farming (according to the household respondent).
In 70 percent of households, youth members actively participate in farming (according to the household respondent).

• However, men are considered the main decision maker on farm work on 92 percent of all plots, and non-youth members are considered the main decision maker on 93 percent of all plots (according to the household respondent).

• Based on separate responses of female and male respondents, more than 90 percent of women and youth contribute to agricultural activities for the Use Case focal crops (maize, rice, cassava), and the level of involvement of women and youth in farming is not significantly different with that of men or of their older counterparts. This is consistent across the three states.
¾ Reaching women and youth will necessitate making efforts beyond targeting the person who is considered the main decision maker in the household.

• There are large differences across states concerning women’s and youth’s participation in farming. Women participate in farming at a high level in Nasarawa, while youth participation in farming in Kaduna is highest. Women and youth participation in farming is lowest in Kano. There is also low youth participation in Nasarawa but this is because there are few youth members within the households in this sample (only 56 percent of households have youth members in Nasarawa compared to 85 percent and 94 percent in Kano and Kaduna).
• 79 percent of households in Kaduna and 92 percent of households in Nasarawa have female household members actively participating in farming, whereas in Kano, the rate is 25 percent.

• Youth household members in 82 percent of households in Kaduna actively participate in farming, whereas youth household members in 51 percent of the households in Kano and 53 percent of the households in Nasarawa actively participate in farming.

¾ Gender- and youth-specific activities may need to be considered within each state thereafter depending on the results. Qualitative inquiries could help to further understand why women are less active in farming in Kano and why youth are less active in Kano and Nasarawa.

• Literacy levels are quite high among female and male respondents.
• The majority of respondents (80 percent of women and 89 percent of men, and 94 percent of youth and 83 percent of non-youth) are reportedly literate.

• However, levels of formal schooling are lower than reported literacy rates, with a quarter of female respondents and 15 percent of male respondents not having received formal schooling, and 9 percent of youth and 21 percent of non- youth respondents not having attended formal schooling. Furthermore, a third of the sample completed only primary or elementary schooling.

¾ The level of complexities in advanced extension materials and ICT tools will have to match with the level of education of the target beneficiaries when designing an effective extension mechanism related to the Use Case technology.

• There is a paucity of professional extension services by government, non-government or private sector actors, especially for women. Both male and female respondents indicated they received low levels of government extension services, and this was even much lower among the youth. Social networks, radio and television programs are important for agricultural information sharing.
• Only 13 percent of male respondents and 9 percent of female respondents received government extension services.

• Private sector, particularly agrodealers, are a main source of agricultural advice for 22 percent of male respondents and 17 of female respondents, however, female youth reported the least access to these support services.

• Almost all female and male respondents indicated they received agricultural advice in the past, however, much of this advice was obtained from relatives or other farmers (for 53 percent of male respondent and 67 percent of female respondents), and much less of this agricultural advice is from government or private sector extension service providers.

• There are some differences across states regarding access to agricultural advice. In Nasarawa, the access to government extension is much better than in the other two states, with 32 percent of men and 29 percent of women reporting they accessed government extension services. TV programs are the most common main formal source of agricultural information, with 46 percent of men and 22 percent of women reporting that they access agricultural information from TV programs. In Kano, radio programs are the most common source of agricultural information, with 44 percent of women and 53 percent of men reporting that they access agricultural information from radio programs. In Kaduna, access to agricultural information is generally weakest; the main sources are radio programs, with 23 percent of men and 6 percent of women reporting it as their main source of agricultural advice. Twenty-two percent of men and 13 percent of women reported they accessed agricultural information via the private sector (agrodealers).

¾ Radio programs can be expanded and utilized more in Kaduna and Kano; while TV programs can be expanded and utilized more in Nasawara. In all states, agrodealers and traders play a role in agricultural information dissemination; training and access to improved seeds and knowledge among agrodealers and traders can be an important strategy. However, fewer women have access to such information using these sources, and therefore, ways to facilitate women’s access to these sources or alternative sources of information that attend to the needs/preferences of women must be explored and considered along with the social networks women often depend on for agricultural information.

• Digital technologies (including cell phones, smartphones, or other devices such as tablets or laptops) are not universally used and owned across farm households in the study area, and rarely serve to access agricultural advice.
• Access to agricultural advice through digital apps is currently very low (0 percent for both women and men), social media is only used by 1-2 percent of the sample.

• Women were less likely than men to report owning and using digital technologies, while youth and non-youth are equally likely to own and use digital technologies. Overall, 62 percent of female respondents versus 77 percent of male respondents reported owning a phone, though most of these are regular cell phones. Only 17 percent of female respondents and 27 percent of male respondents owned a smartphone. Youth are more likely to own and use smartphones whereas non-youth are more likely to own and use cell phones. However, in total, youth and non-youth are equally likely to own and use either a smartphone or a cell phone.

¾ Alternative approaches are needed to bring extension messages originating from digital tools to farmers, an issue pertaining to male and female farmers – though more critically so for the latter. Youth, a more tech-savvy generation, could be at the forefront of spearheading use of digital tools, though they would still need additional support.
• A third of the sample participate in groups or associations, but women are less likely to be part of a group than men, especially young women.

• Group membership is very low, especially in Kaduna and Kano. A gender gap in group membership exists in Kano, with only 13 percent of female respondents and 35 percent of male respondents being part of a group or association.

¾ Reaching women and youth through group-based extension services may require facilitating the creation of new groups for women and youth farmers or devising a more inclusionary strategy for them into existing groups. When working with group leaders, a purposive approach is needed to attenuate the lesser representation of women and youth. Alternative extension methods that do not require groups as such, could also be considered (e.g., male and female lead farmers).
Benefit
• We examined risk aversion, as an indication of willingness to innovation and try out new technologies, by women and men, and value of production per hectare by gendered household types.

• Most respondents are willing to accept some risks on their farming: 10 percent reported not willing to take risks; about a quarter would like to take risks; and the large majority is willing to accept some risks. Overall, more respondents in Kaduna are willing to take risks, and more respondents in Kano generally indicated that they do not like to take risks. Among the gender and age groups, male youth in Kano are most likely to be willing to take risks.

• Overall, households with women’s involvement in farming have higher value of production than those without. Moreover, households with youth involvement in farming also have higher value of production than those without, but the households with youth involvement only (no non-youth participating in farming) have lower value of production. This may be related to the household composition and availability of labor: households where women and youth are involved in farming may spend more family labor on their plots, thus resulting in a higher value of production.

• We also found regional differences. When looking at both mean and median, we only see a clear association between women’s involvement and value of production in Kaduna; and between youth’s involvement and value of production in Kano. Further in-depth analysis is needed to understand what drives these associations.

• Youth, given their willingness to take risks, may be a good target group for successful adoption of new agronomic technologies. When targeting non-youth, sufficient information may need to be provided more information on the extent to which the new tools could help mitigate risk and uncertainty in farm outcomes.
Empower
• We examined inputs to farming decisions, control over use of income, and access to and control over financial resources as key indicators of empowerment.

• Across all farming activities tracked, almost all male respondents reported contributing to most decisions, while only a third of female respondents reported contributing to most decisions and two-thirds contributed to some decisions. Most male respondents normally make the farming decisions on their own, while the majority of female respondents normally make the farming decisions jointly with the male decision-maker. About a quarter of women do not normally make decisions on any farming activity. Over half of women in Kano do not make decisions on farming activities, whereas only about 20 percent of women in Kaduna and around 10 percent of women in Nasarawa do not.

• Control over use of income is high among both women and men across all states, although gender gap still exists with fewer women having control over income from farming than men, especially in Kano.

• Access to and control over financial resources are generally low, especially in Kano and Nasarawa, where only around 43 percent and 36 percent of households are able to take a loan, compared with 75 percent in Kaduna. Gender gap exists in Kano, with only 27 percent of female respondents and 48 percent of male respondents achieving adequacy, i.e. their households have access to credit and the respondent has some input in financial decisions thereabout.

¾ Reaching women and youth may not suffice for them to also make active production decisions that will help them to ensure innovations benefit and ultimately empower them. Special attention to reducing gender-based, intra-household constraints and inequalities to decision-making in Kano will be needed. Finally, farmers struggle to access credit, thus requiring either agronomic recommendations that do not entail major investment or requiring facilitating credit access into the design of the envisioned intervention.
Transform
• Gender unequal attitudes persist in the study area: men are perceived as the main farmers and primary income earners and women as “helpers” on the farm and mainly responsible for domestic chores.

• Persistently strong attitudes supporting gender inequality in farming, livelihoods, and household chores exist. For example, eighteen percent of men and 15 percent of women disagreed to the statement “It is equally important to improve productivity on women’s plots as it is on men’s plots”. Fifteen percent of men and 10 percent of women disagreed to the statement “Husbands should help wives with household chores, like cooking and taking care of children” Overall, across a total of ten statements female respondents disagreed to 1.47 number of statements out of 10 supporting gender equality; while male respondents disagree to 1.91 number of statements supporting gender equality.

1. Introduction

This report serves as a youth and gender diagnostic assessment for the SAA Nigeria Use Case in the EiA Initiative. The SAA Nigeria Use Case combines three fertilizer recommendation tools (AKILIMO for cassava, Nutrient Expert (NE) for maize, and RiceAdvice for rice) in one digital interface that can be used on smartphones, tablets, laptops and desktops. Following the request of the “demand partner” SAA Nigeria, the decision support tools (DSTs) for fertilizer will be combined with advice on the planting or sowing windows. For cassava, this is already available as a module in AKILIMO, for maize and rice, this is under development. Modified versions of the RiceAdvice tool, RiceAdvice Lite (RAL) and AKILIMO, were tested in 2021 and 2022 (for AKILIMO, only the growing season 2021/2022). Following this technical validation, the Use Case demanded for an enhanced understanding of the context in which the tool will be used to ensure that it meets farmers’ requirements. In particular, the SAA Nigeria Use Case needed an improved understanding on how this tool will be useful for men and women farmers as well as for the younger and the older generations. The results presented in this study report will be instrumental in the scaling and dissemination phases of the Use Case.

We align our diagnostic assessment with the Reach-Benefit-Empower-Transform framework of Quisumbing, Meinzen-Dick and Malapit (2021) (Figure 1). This framework highlights the importance of not only reaching target beneficiaries, but also making sure that they benefit from any interventions, that the interventions further increase their empowerment, and lead to a transformation of any restrictive attitudes, norms, and power relations that create gender inequalities. Reaching women and youth with agronomic solutions and associated extension approaches requires including them in project activities (Quisumbing et al., 2023). Benefiting women and youth means the project should also improve their wellbeing, e.g., in terms of income, or mental of physical health (ibid.). However, beyond these steps, it is key to also strive to improve women’s and youth’s empowerment, i.e., ensuring they have the ability to make strategic life choices and act on them (Kabeer, 1999). Finally, sustained positive outcomes require that at community and societal levels, any harmful gender or youth norms, attitudes and behaviors are transformed towards more equality for all (ibid.).

2. Literature Review

A recent report published by the World Bank (2022) draws on the Nigeria General Household Survey (2018–2019) to highlight the gender gaps in labor force participation, document the drivers of the gender gaps in key sectors, highlight certain constraints including land and occupational segregation, and provide policy and programming recommendations to close the gender gaps. Similarly, Oseni et al. (2013), based on the earlier nationally representative General Household Survey Panel 2010-2011, provide insights in gender differences in the agricultural sector in Nigeria.

Oseni et al. (2013) show that women, like men, are heavily involved in agriculture in Nigeria, including producing staple crops and cash crops, and participating all along the agricultural value chain. At the national level, 55 percent of working-age women and 69 percent of men work in agriculture (World Bank 2022). Women in the North of Nigeria work far less, and 22 percentage points less than men in the North (46% compared to 68%, respectively). Such disparities between women and men do not exist in the South of Nigeria (ibid.).

However, women have smaller and less secure plots of land, less access to physical inputs such as fertilizer and herbicide, less use of labor, and less access to extension services. It is not surprising, then, that female farmers earn and produce much less than male farmers (Oseni et al. 2013; World Bank 2022). Female-managed plots, which average 0.3 hectares in size, are significantly smaller than male-managed plots, which measure 0.6 hectares on average (Oseni et al. 2013). Women are almost half as likely to cultivate cereals and greater than twice as likely to farm roots and tubers, vegetables, and melons (World Bank 2022).

Fewer women manage their own plots (World Bank 2022). The majority of female plot managers (63 percent) are widowed, separated, or divorced, while almost all male plot managers (94 percent) were married (World Bank 2022). Nationally, 67 percent of male managers report having the right to sell the plots under their control, as compared to only 31 percent of female managers (Oseni et al. 2013). While women can gain access to use and own land through marriage and inheritance, these options are quite complex and exclusionary given customary law and patrilineal inheritance systems (ibid). Women can purchase land, but intrahousehold dynamics and economic constraints create challenges for them to buy land (ibid).

Productivity (the value of output per hectare) on female-managed plots is 30 percent lower than that on male-managed plots at the national level, and 35 percent lower than that on male-managed plots in the North (compared to only 25 percent in the South) (World Bank 2022). Women’s lower productivity was explained by their limited use of inputs (e.g., fertilizer and herbicides), engagement in less valuable crop value chains, and use of less productive farm labor (ibid). Male plot managers are also more likely than female plot managers to use inputs, such as fertilizer (42 percent and 19 percent, respectively), herbicide (26 percent and 6 percent), and animal traction (28 percent and 3 percent) (Oseni et al. 2013).

Female farmers are also at a disadvantage in terms of access to agricultural labor: female farmers use fewer days of family labor, are less likely to hire outside labor, and, when they do, use fewer days of hired labor on their plots; while male farmers tend to hire outside male labor for assistance in their fields while also using more than three times the amount of male family labor than women (Oseni et al. 2013).

With regards to access to agricultural extension, only 3 percent of women plot managers in the North received extension services compared to 20 percent of men (World Bank 2022). This is important given that those plot managers who did participate in extension activities had 18% higher productivity. Women’s low participation in agricultural extension activities is due to: 1) current extension services may focus on crops mainly grown by men; 2) cultural norms may create barriers for men extension officers to interact with women farmers; or 3) outreach activities may target mostly male social networks (ibid).

Furthermore, Oseni et al. (2015) show that in the North, women produce 28% less than men after controlling for observed factors of production, while there are no significant gender differences in the South. In the decomposition results, the structural effect in the North is larger than the endowment at the mean. Although women in the North have access to less productive resources than men, the results indicate that even if given the same level of inputs, significant differences still emerge. However, for the South, the decomposition results show that the endowment effect is more important than the structural effect. Access to resources explains most of the gender gap in the South and if women are given the same level of inputs as men, the gap will be minimal. World Bank (2022) showed how gender norms contribute to gender inequalities in educational investments made in boys rather than in girls that assume men are breadwinners and women are supposed to stay at home and carryout domestic and caregiving duties. Differences in crop choice by women and men may be due to norms that designate cash crops as “male crops.” Gender norms can have an influence on how men extension officers interact with women farmers or other value chain actors. Norms may also prohibit women from registering their land in their names, and instead, registering in the name of male family members. Norms can impact women’s ownership of small versus larger livestock, which undercuts women’s economic potential. Norms around division of labor and value chain activities can shape women’s involvement in less remunerative value chains and activities. Norms may restrict women from using mechanized equipment that could reduce their labor and time burdens, and potentially increase productivity and profitability.

Similarly, Das et al. (2023) confirms strong gender norms around women’s participation in agricultural value chains in the north. Using data from 11,691 aspiring agribusiness entrepreneurs in Nigeria, they explore factors that drive sectoral choice, gender differences in the choice decision, and especially the role played by norms around gender roles. When given a choice of 11 agricultural value chains in a government program, they find the majority (54 percent) of the applicants chose to enter into the poultry value chain, and women were more likely to choose poultry than men. They find evidence of more restrictive gender norms in Northern Nigeria states, which lowers women’s likelihood of entering into agricultural value chains where the potential for profit may be higher. The gender bias in sectoral choice is also attributed to differences in work experience especially in agricultural activities and in the chosen value chain, as well as in land ownership. Women with more experience in male- dominated agricultural value chains exhibit lower self-efficacy, which could reflect the challenges they face when deviating from social norms to operate within nontraditional value chains.

These studies for the North and South suggest that policy should vary by region, and close attention to gender norms is needed, especially in the North. Moreover, several recommendations emerge to close the gender gap (World Bank 2022):

3. Data and Methodology
3.1. Data

The data from this survey was collected in June and July 2023 in three different States and nine Local Government Areas (LGAs): Kano (Bunkure, Kura, Tudun Wada), Kaduna (Ikara, Lere, Soba), and Nasarawa (Akwanga, Doma, Obi) (Figure 2A and Figure 2B). The LGAs were selected by i) environmental clustering, ensuring that the dominant environmental clusters that were considered relevant for the Use Case were present, ii) environmental conditions were suitable for at least 2 of the three focal crops (cassava, maize or rice), and iii) security considerations. In each LGA, 10 villages were randomly selected when at least two of the focal crops were assumed to be present as well as women involved in crop cultivation. During the training of enumerators, the lists of the 10 selected villages were confirmed and updated based on the enumerators’ knowledge of security and accessibility status of the villages (the rains had already started). In each village, a household list was composed via an interview with the village head and included information on cropping of the three focal crops and the involvement of female household members in crop production. From these lists, 24 households were randomly selected and divided into two lists of 12 households each. The second list served as back-up in case households of the first list were not available. Although the team initially intended to stratify households according to the involvement of women in crop production, this stratification was not put into practice given that in nearly all

Introduction

This meeting was convened with the primary objective of gathering essential feedback from secondary partners. These partners are poised to play a pivotal role in the utilization of the EiA (Excellent in Agronomy) solutions, leveraging their extensive network of farmers. The agenda encompassed in-depth discussions on EiA's cutting-edge agronomy tools, exploring feedback, and planning engagement.

The session commenced with a warm welcome from Alpha Kamara, the Station Head of IITA Kano. His address underscored the profound significance of collaborative efforts in addressing the pressing issue of food insecurity among Nigeria's farming communities. Christine Kreye, the Focal Lead for EiA in Nigeria, presented an overview of the EiA project, providing valuable insights into its broader scope beyond Nigeria's borders. To ensure a productive engagement, Thompson Ogunsanmi, the Scaling Specialist in EiA on the SAA use case, facilitated the interactions with the partners. He ensured their suggestions and inputs were captured and integrated into next steps

The partners represented a diverse array of organizations, each with a unique contribution to the shared objectives of the meeting. Among those present were KADA, OCP, GIZ, Smart Agribus, ANA, Kano ADP, INDORAMA, Notore, LIWEED, the Kano Innovation Platform, as well as dedicated teams from IITA/EiA and SAA. Partners’ expectations for the meeting were:
1. Gaining insights into the functionality of EiA tools.

AKILIMO/Fertilizer Recommendation and Scheduled Planting tools

Thompson presented an in-depth overview of the AKILIMO/Fertilizer Recommendation and Scheduled Planting tools for cassava. These tools, collectively known as AKILIMO, as part of the EiA initiative. 1. The Role of Behaviour Change in Achieving EiA Impact
Introduction

From seeds to solutions. The EiA Initiative is at the forefront of agronomy research, tackling today's global challenges. Understanding the factors that influence behaviours in agriculture allows EiA Use Cases to develop tailored interventions that address specific needs and preferences of
farmers and communities, ultimately accelerating the uptake of agronomy at scale.

Human behaviour is an important factor at the core of many of today’s most persistent challenges in agriculture such as low and variable yields, limited adaptation to climate change, low resource use efficiencies, and declining soil health. Addressing these challenges demands evidenced-based innovation and solutions that are designed having users and their r behaviours, their cultural context, and their needs and preferences in mind.

The EiA Initiative forms a part of CGIAR’s new research portfolio, delivering science and innovation to transform food, land, and water systems in a climate crisis. The initiative delivers targeted agronomic solutions to millions of smallholder farmers, prioritising women and youth, to enhance food and nutrition security, improve soil health, increase incomes and build climate resilience.

Achieving EiA’s goals often hinges on changes in farmer behaviour, such as adopting digital agro-advisory tools, actively engaging in field demonstrations, prioritising marginalised groups in farming, securing financial incentives and responsible risk mitigation, and peer-to-peer learning. Therefore, Behaviour change
(BeCha) strategies can enhance outcomes by removing barriers that prevent farmers from sustaining desired actions.

Though the systematic application of behaviour change strategies within EiA is still being explored, many use cases have started to address behavioural barriers. This report aims to review the current behaviour change processes in the use case and provide insights on the existing approaches and tools to guide behaviour change practice in the use case.
What is behaviour change?

It is good to first understand behaviour as the actions, habits or responses of an individual or group in a given context. Behaviour change is the evidence-based process of influencing farmers' and key agricultural stakeholders' behaviours that lead to the adoption (shift in behaviour) of new practices and technologies that lead to more sustainable desired outcomes. It is an evidence-based strategy that recognises that modifying people’s behaviour requires more than simply increasing their knowledge (UN Report 2021). It primarily involves identifying and understanding factors that hinder and facilitate the adoption of a desired behaviour. For example, the community adopts agroforestry techniques, which help to preserve forests and improve soil health. In general, behaviour is a state (i.e. what a farmer does), while behaviour change is a process (i.e. the act of altering that farmer's behaviour).

Behaviour change is often misconstrued as simply educating people about desirable actions (FAO, 2022). However, sustainably changing behaviour extends beyond mere knowledge transfer. Two key factors guide the design of behaviour change interventions, and a one-size-fits-all approach is not effective:

Bridging scientific evidence with tradition-driven solutions: To reach effective behaviour change interventions there is a need to combine scientific understanding with traditional knowledge. This approach prevents one-size-fits-all solutions and ensures that interventions align with people’s actions.

Tailored approach: Customising strategies and interventions to meet specific needs, circumstances, and preferences of individual farmers or communities. This approach ensures that the design of innovations or interventions considers behaviour change results and also recognises that a one-size-fits-all solution is unlikely to be effective in promoting sustainable agricultural practices.
Behavioural Change to Promote the Adoption of Agronomic Solutions
Behaviour Change Exploration

Behaviour change interventions in EiA Use Cases focus mainly on incentivising farmers to use agronomic advisory tools and adopt new agronomic practices, for example, site-specific fertilizer application, planting date decision support, new soil management practices or the use of climate information in agronomic planning, amongst others.
In behaviour change exploration, three key resources are identified as necessary for promoting behaviour change: time, competencies and ethical considerations.
Behaviour Change Resources

Time is a critical resource in agricultural behaviour change interventions, especially as EiA initiatives and projects are time-bound. The time required for an intervention varies depending on factors such as target behaviours, scale, approach, and resources available. Given agriculture's seasonal nature, timely implementation is crucial to avoid missed opportunities. Behaviour change itself takes time, requiring unlearning old habits and adopting new practices. As such, in urgent situations, focusing on high-priority behaviours and a simplified approach can accelerate the process.

The second resource is competencies. The competencies required for designing and implementing a behaviour change intervention depend largely on the chosen approach and the specific stage of the behaviour change process. In the context of agriculture, the specific skills required for designing and implementing a behaviour change intervention can vary widely. For example, in designing interventions – competencies in communication, persuasion, and understanding cultural nuances are essential for creating effective messages and materials. However, regardless of the approach (Adams, 2020), the following qualities are essential:
• Active listening
Curiosity and respect for local practices and people
Creativity and problem-solving
Facilitation and group participation skills
Technical knowledge in the intervention area (e.g., agriculture)

Ethical considerations are fundamental to effective behavior change interventions in agriculture. They build trust, ensuring participants feel respected and valued. Ethical practices promote transparency, informed consent, and fairness, fostering a sense of agency and ownership. By prioritizing ethical principles, interventions can be more effective, sustainable, and socially responsible. Ethical behavior also enhances the reputation of the organization or individual implementing the intervention, leading to increased credibility and influence. It's crucial to adhere to the ""do-no-harm"" principle, ensuring that programme goals are pursued without compromising ethical standards.
2. How Behaviour Change Occurs

While behaviour change function is still nascent in EiA, it is possible to synthesize and learn from a few notable progresses in how behaviour change occurs. To fully realise its potential, programs and initiatives can drive impactful change through innovative approach, historical and knowledge co-creation approach, empowerment or participatory approach, and structural and systemic approach (Ofosu-Ampong et al., 2024). For a detailed explanation of these approaches follow Framing behaviour change for sustainable agriculture: Themes, approaches, and future directions.
Innovative Approach

Innovation is a powerful catalyst for behaviour change. By introducing new varieties, digital technologies and new markets, we can reshape how farmers think, feel and act. Specifically, it focuses on how farmers respond to the allocation of these resources and programs, and how the farmers innovate in the absence of technologies. Innovative solutions from the use cases or programs can streamline processes for consistent innovative practices, making it easier for people to adopt desired behaviours.
For example, Akilimo provides site-specific recommendations that optimise productivity to existing problems, thereby motivating farmers to adopt new agricultural practices and behaviours.
Behavioural Change to Promote the Adoption of Agronomic Solutions
Historical and Knowledge Co-creation Approach

This approach represents a shift towards a more collaborative and inclusive perspective by considering historical and traditional agricultural knowledge and practices by farmers. It acknowledges the diversity of traditional knowledge systems influencing behaviour patterns and emphasizes the need for co-creation involving all stakeholders. It paves the way for community-enabled entry (trusted networks) and fosters deeper collaboration towards deciding and responding to the use case.

For example, research shows that fertilizer use follows customary practices among cassava farmers in Nigeria. This inertia can make farmers resistant to adopting new and more tailored approaches if the behaviour change approach neglects historical and traditional knowledge.
Empowerment or Participatory Approach

The participatory approach is the process where farmers or groups are allowed to actively participate in decision-making and the design and implementation of activities that affect their farming systems and lives. Most of the EiA Use Cases have consistently promoted this approach. Empowerment emerges as a critical factor within the agricultural system to foster a shift in the mindsets and actions of smallholder farmers.

For example, in Morocco, farmers were involved in co-designing the scaling strategy? of Conservation Agriculture (CA). By including farmers in the planning process, they gained a deeper understanding of the benefits, fostering a sense of ownership over the initiative.
Structural and Systemic Approach

This approach highlights how structures enable systems to function. The systemic approach places more emphasis on the ownership and control of resources, while the structural approach focuses on social relationships to unravel the social classes in the ownership and control of resources by individuals, groups or communities. The significant emphasis on this approach arises from its ability to determine whether or not a behaviour is necessary and justified within a use case.

For example, the Digital Green Use Case in Ethiopia details how the project's structure facilitates behaviour change (i.e. the adoption of new fertiliser practices) through its focus on the project background, trial design, implementation, data collection, and analysis of fertilizer treatment impacts on outcomes e.g. yields.
Guide to Designing Behaviour Change Strategies to Achieve the Impact Areas of EiA

From nudging for sustainability to shaping agricultural initiatives, a structural and systemic approach shapes the design of behaviour change interventions as informed by the theory of change (see e.g. digital green use case), based on the following stages:

Stage 1. Understand the behaviour in context: What is the problem to be addressed and what are important behavioural aspects to consider to solve the problem? What are the behaviour barriers and enablers of solving the problem through the proposed solution? Thus, there is a need to identify the target behaviours and understand their drivers.

Stage 2. Designing Effective Interventions: This involves deepening understanding of behaviours through community engagement and stakeholder consultation. Building on the insights towards identifying potential solutions, prioritise the intervention focus (i.e. barriers and enablers) and activities. Before full-scale implementation, the proposed strategy undergoes rigorous testing and refinement. Design thinking and human-centred design (HCD) can help to design effective interventions for behaviour change.

Use Case 1: Location, Context and Season-Specific Agroadvisory Decision Support Tool in
This use case promotes efficient fertiliser use and contributes to food security, improved nutrition and an increase in crop yields and
farmer incomes.
Context

In Ethiopia, the NextGen Decision Support Tool (DST) is developing a participatory intervention to motivate farmers to scale advisory services. By 2023, the pilot program, in collaboration with Digital Green, reached 50,000 farmers through digital and traditional channels, with over 16% adopting the recommendations, 20% of whom were women. Initially focused on wheat, the DST is now expanding to other crops, such as maize and tef.

To streamline various agro-advisory DSTs into a unified advisory system serving the nation, the experts conducted a ‘DST Harmonization’ exercise in 2024. Led by the Ethiopian Institute of Agricultural Research, this initiative involves a thorough field validation process of the advisories against blanket and local fertilizer recommendations across 2,500 farm sites for major crops in Ethiopia. Due to high approval rates, the DST is being implemented more broadly, aiming to reach over 87,000 farmers by 2024, highlighting significant changes in farmer participation and knowledge transfer. Farmers faced limitations in terms of access to information, technology, and financial resources, and may have been hesitant to adopt new practices that require significant changes to traditional methods. Introduction

The production of crops in many regions faces increasing difficulties due to declining soil fertility, erratic weather patterns, and limited availability of modern techniques (George, 2014; Ncube et al., 2009; St.Clair & Lynch, 2010). These issues are particularly pronounced in areas where smallholder farmers rely primarily on rainfed agriculture and have limited resources, rendering their livelihoods very sensitive to the effects of climate change and land degradation (Barbier & Hochard, 2018; Mendelsohn, 2008). Extensive research has been done on these areas with the aim to investigate ways through which productivity, resilience and sustainability may be enhanced.

Maize is an important crop in Ghana serving as a staple food for a significant number of households (Ragasa et al., 2014). The northern regions accounts for a considerable amount of Ghana's maize production, highlighting its importance not just as a food supply but also as a vital income generator (Ragasa et al., 2014; IFPRI & MoFA, 2020). The Upper West region situated within the Guinea Savannah zone, faces considerable challenges in crop production, primarily due to poor soil fertility, in-season drought, and sub-optimal agronomic practices (Adjei & Kyerematen, 2018; Atiah et al., 2022; Ragasa et al., 2014). Adopting technologies that can enhance production and address existing challenges will significantly benefit farmers.

The Excellence in Agronomy Initiative is committed to developing and delivering scalable agronomic solutions that align with the needs of its partners (EiA, n.d.). In collaboration with Degas, and regional and district MOFA, the Alliance Bioversity and CIAT aim to enhance the productivity and income of millions of smallholder farmers in Ghana. Recognizing the critical role of maize in the region and the significant challenges it faces, this initiative focuses on building the capacity and resilience of farmers, particularly in maize farming.

This demonstration project is designed to address the critical issues faced by farmers by integrating several agricultural technologies. The demonstrated technologies were designed based on the outcomes from trials conducted by Alliance Bioversity and CIAT in the 2023 year. The trials were conducted in sixteen sites in the Guinea Savannah zone, investigating suitable varieties, fertilizer recommendations and management practices such as ridging, and intercropping maize with cowpea. Identified technologies with high potential for resiliency included the selection of the Wang- Basig maize variety, a climate-smart hybrid variety. Wang-Basig is specifically selected for its drought tolerance and early maturity (MITA, n.d.). It therefore has the potential to buffer against the increasingly erratic rainfall patterns that have become common

Soil moisture conservation technologies – ridging and maize-cowpea intercrop, were included in the design, due to their potential to minimize yield loss, particularly in regions prone to drought (Bekele et al., 2021; Chemeda, 2022).

Ridging is crucial in increasing water infiltration and soil moisture conservation (Guzha, 2004). Ridging has been shown to improve the response of crops to both rainfall and fertilizer application (Jensen et al., 2003). In regions where farmers rely heavily on rainfall and often affected by midseason droughts, ridging stands out as a practical and effective method to enhance productivity. This technique can help mitigate the impact of droughts and optimize the benefits of applied fertilizers, leading to better crop yields.

Intercropping, which involves the cultivation of different crops together, provides a synergistic approach that optimizes resource use, enhances soil health, and boosts overall productivity (Lithourgidis et al., 2011). Moreover, cover-cropping with legumes, such as cowpea, has the potential to conserve soil moisture by reducing water evaporation beneath the canopy, further supporting crop resilience (Frye & Blevins, 1989; Liu et al., 2021). Intercropping cereals with legumes also contributes to food

security by diversifying production, reducing the risks associated with monocropping, and improving dietary nutrition through the output of two complementary products (Rehman et al., 2019; Rusinamhodzi et al., 2012). Additionally, legumes contribute to soil fertility by fixing atmospheric nitrogen, benefiting the companion cereal crops (Giller, 2001). This practice is particularly relevant for gender-responsive agricultural strategies, as legume cultivation is often dominated by women (Padmanabhan, 2007). As reported by Ndiritu et al., (2014), women are less likely to adopt agro-advisory content that directly contradicts established cultural norms.

From our last year work, we recognized that effectively addressing gender-specific challenges necessitates a targeted approach that includes crops of particular interest to women and other marginalized groups (Akpatsu et al., 2023). This demonstration builds on the previous year's recommendations to enhance interest and adoption of agricultural practices among both male and female farmers.

The intercropping of maize-cowpea was preferred because cowpea outperforms most legumes planted in the tropics, producing satisfactory yields with limited annual rainfall (Ayalew & Yoseph, 2022). Selecting cowpea variety with ground-covering characteristics will be crucial in conserving moisture. For this reason, the Padi tuya cowpea variety was selected. Padi tuya is moderately resistant to insects, diseases and striga and matures in 64-67 days. It is a white-seeded variety and is also well-suited for use as fodder due to high biomass production.

To complement these agronomic practices, the demonstration also introduces simple mechanization tools, such as push planters, fertilizer applicators and in-row weeders, which are designed to reduce the labour intensity of farming operations. In many regions, agricultural tasks like planting and fertilizer application are predominantly carried out by women, who often face significant physical burdens (Mensah & Fosu-Mensah, 2020). By incorporating these tools, the demonstration not only improves efficiency and productivity but also alleviates the workload on women, freeing up time for other important household responsibilities (IFAD, 2016).
The objectives of the on-farm demonstrations are to:
- Showcase the benefits of sustainable farming practices in enhancing farm resilience and support farmers in adopting these practices.
- Actively involve farmers and extension workers in the demonstration process, enabling them to learn and apply these techniques on their own farms.

Lessons

Farmers acknowledged the potential benefits of ridging but also expressed concerns about the practice, noting that it is labour-intensive. They showed interest in exploring alternative methods or finding ways to implement ridging through mechanization to reduce the physical burden.

The mechanization plot attracted the most interest among farmers. The farmers expressed willingness to adopt the use of push planters and fertilizer applicators. Farmers recognized the significant potential of these tools for saving time and labor. The mechanization tools are likely to have a more significant impact on women as planting and fertilizer application are traditionally considered women's work in many farming communities in the region. The time and labor savings provided by these tools are crucial, especially considering the additional household responsibilities that women typically manage.

Most farmers were eager to replicate the techniques they learned during the demonstration, with a strong preference for the mechanization plots. However, the research team needed to persuade some farmers to adopt the other two technologies as well. This eagerness to replicate the mechanization techniques demonstrates the farmers' willingness to incorporate mechanization equipment into their farming activities. Maize-cowpea intercrop also was well received by farmers, especially women farmers. Some women farmers were inclined to adopt intercropping, highlighting their strong interest in cultivating legumes.
Challenges

The timing of the demonstrations presented significant challenges in organizing farmers, primarily due to their eagerness to begin work on their fields immediately after the rainfall. Many farmers feared that any delay in planting could adversely affect their crop productivity, a concern that was further intensified by the late onset of rains this year. As a result, the urgency to capitalize on the available moisture made it difficult to gather farmers for the demonstrations at a time when they were focused on their own fieldwork.
Additionally, some farmers had already planted their fields by the time the

However, in a show of community cooperation, some farmers agreed to share portions of their land with fellow farmers who had no place to replicate, thereby enabling them to apply what they had learned during the demonstrations.

There was also a noticeable interest among some farmers in the mechanization tools showcased during the demonstrations. However, alongside this interest, farmers expressed concerns about the accessibility of these tools for use on their own farms. The challenge of acquiring or accessing mechanization equipment highlighted a gap between the interest in adopting these technologies and the practical ability to do so, pointing to a need for improved access to such tools to support broader adoption of mechanization in the region.
Next steps

- Conduct and organize the second round of fertilizer application and cowpea planting, providing training to farmers: The second fertilizer application will be done at week four or five after emergence, concurrently, cowpea planting will be carried out as part of the intercropping strategy. During these events, farmers will be invited and trained, the training will cover best practices for fertilizer application, including timing, dosage, and techniques that maximize nutrient use efficiency while minimizing environmental impact. Additionally, the training will emphasize the benefits of cowpea in improving soil fertility through nitrogen fixation and enhancing soil moisture conservation.

- Arrange field days at mid-season and during harvest to monitor progress and share insights: Field days will be strategically scheduled at critical growth stages—mid-season and harvest to allow farmers, extension agents, and other stakeholders to observe the progress of the demonstration plots. These events will serve as platforms for monitoring crop development, evaluating the effectiveness of the applied technologies, and identifying any challenges that may arise. During these field days, participants will have the opportunity to exchange insights, discuss observations, and learn from the successes and setbacks experienced during the growing season.
- Follow up with farmers to assess their progress with replication efforts and

These follow-ups will involve visiting the farmers' fields, observing the implementation of the practices, and providing additional guidance as needed. Feedback will be gathered in the process to improve support mechanisms and ensure that the practices are being effectively adopted and integrated into local farming systems.

- Explore ways to make mechanization tools accessible to farmers: Recognizing the challenges associated with acquiring and using mechanisation tools, efforts will be made to explore and implement strategies that can make these tools more accessible to farmers. Conclusion

The demonstration establishment at the two EiA communities was successfully conducted and provided the opportunity to showcase the potential of sustainable agricultural practices and mechanization tools. The good response from farmers, notably their willingness to replicate the learnt practices, indicates a high likelihood of widespread adoption. Moving forward, continued support, monitoring, and follow-up efforts will be critical to ensure that these practices take root and contribute to the region's agricultural sustainability and production.

Permanent link to cite or share this item https://hdl.handle.net/10568/159970 External link to download this item DOI Abstract/Description Accounting for 50-60% of the country's cereal production, maize is extensively cultivated across all six agroecological zones, standing second only to cocoa in economic importance. Despite its significance, maize production in the Guinea Savannah zone, which spans nearly half of Ghana's land area, faces numerous challenges. These include unpredictable weather patterns characterized by droughts and floods, soil degradation due to inadequate conservation practices, limited access to mechanization, and insufficient utilization of agroadvisories. Such factors collectively hinder efficient land preparation, planting, and harvesting, leading to increased labor costs, reduced productivity, and decreased resilience to climate change. In response to these challenges, AICCRA, as part of its drive to promote climate-smart agriculture (CSA) and one health, rolled out improved soil and production technologies. These activities were led by the Alliance Bioversty and CIAT in collaboration with the CSIR-Crops Research Institute and the Department of Agriculture of the Kumbungu District. The primary goal of this initiative was to enhance crop resilience and productivity through the evaluation and implementation of smart production and soil packages. These packages integrated three key components: agroadvisories, which provide farmers with timely and location-specific advice on weather, soil moisture, and pest/disease management; good agronomic practices; and essential crop production equipment, particularly simple mechanization tools. The initiative employed a standardized methodology to ensure consistency and reliability in data collection and analysis. Key activities included field demonstrations to showcase the integrated smart production and soil packages, comprehensive capacity-building programs for farmers and extension agents, and rigorous data collection to assess the effectiveness of the implemented packages. The use of agroadvisories was pivotal, as they offered farmers critical guidance on weather management, optimizing water use, and planning field-based activities, thereby reducing crop losses and enhancing yields. Additionally, agroadvisories facilitated proactive pest and disease management, minimizing crop damage and the reliance on chemical pesticides and fertilizers. Stakeholder engagement was a crucial aspect of this initiative. By organizing field days and other collaborative events, the project successfully involved government agencies, research institutions, NGOs, and the private sector. These engagements not only fostered collaboration and support for sustainable agricultural initiatives but also exposed a wider audience to the innovative technologies being implemented. The project also focused on promoting the widespread adoption and scaling of smart production practices across the agroecological zone, thereby enhancing agricultural productivity and sustainability. The capacity-building efforts provided comprehensive training and support to smallholder farmers and agricultural stakeholders on the use of agroadvisories, mechanization equipment, and sustainable agricultural practices. This holistic approach laid the groundwork for a comprehensive understanding of the potential benefits of smart production and soil packages in the Guinea Savannah zone. The findings from this research are expected to inform evidence-based decision-making and contribute to the development of sustainable agricultural practices in Ghana, ultimately supporting the livelihoods of smallholder farmers and boosting the national economy. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Accounting for 50-60% of the country's cereal production, maize is extensively cultivated across all six agroecological zones, standing second only to cocoa in economic importance. Despite its significance, maize production in the Guinea Savannah zone, which spans nearly half of Ghana's land area, faces numerous challenges. These include unpredictable weather patterns characterized by droughts and floods, soil degradation due to inadequate conservation practices, limited access to mechanization, and insufficient utilization of agroadvisories. Such factors collectively hinder efficient land preparation, planting, and harvesting, leading to increased labor costs, reduced productivity, and decreased resilience to climate change.

In response to these challenges, AICCRA, as part of its drive to promote climate-smart agriculture (CSA) and one health, rolled out improved soil and production technologies. These activities were led by the Alliance Bioversty and CIAT in collaboration with the CSIR-Crops Research Institute and the Department of Agriculture of the Kumbungu District. The primary goal of this initiative was to enhance crop resilience and productivity through the evaluation and implementation of smart production and soil packages. These packages integrated three key components: agroadvisories, which provide farmers with timely and location-specific advice on weather, soil moisture, and pest/disease management; good agronomic practices; and essential crop production equipment, particularly simple mechanization tools.

The initiative employed a standardized methodology to ensure consistency and reliability in data collection and analysis. Key activities included field demonstrations to showcase the integrated smart production and soil packages, comprehensive capacity-building programs for farmers and extension agents, and rigorous data collection to assess the effectiveness of the implemented packages. The use of agroadvisories was pivotal, as they offered farmers critical guidance on weather management, optimizing water use, and planning field-based activities, thereby reducing crop losses and enhancing yields. Additionally, agroadvisories facilitated proactive pest and disease management, minimizing crop damage and the reliance on chemical pesticides and fertilizers.

Stakeholder engagement was a crucial aspect of this initiative. By organizing field days and other collaborative events, the project successfully involved government agencies, research institutions, NGOs, and the private sector. These engagements not only fostered collaboration and support for sustainable agricultural initiatives but also exposed a wider audience to the innovative technologies being implemented. The project also focused on promoting the widespread adoption and scaling of smart production practices across the agroecological zone, thereby enhancing agricultural productivity and sustainability. The capacity- building efforts provided comprehensive training and support to smallholder farmers and agricultural stakeholders on the use of agroadvisories, mechanization equipment, and sustainable agricultural practices. This holistic approach laid the groundwork for a comprehensive understanding of the potential benefits of smart production and soil packages in the Guinea Savannah zone. The findings from this research are expected to inform evidence-based decision-making and contribute to the development of sustainable agricultural practices in Ghana, ultimately supporting the livelihoods of smallholder farmers and boosting the national economy.

1 INTRODUCTION
1.1 Background

Maize, cowpea, and groundnut are staple crops that play crucial roles in Ghana's food security and economy. Maize alone accounts for 55% of Ghana's cereal production, while cowpea and groundnut are key legumes grown widely across the country, especially in northern regions (MoFA, 2019). According to Ghana’s Ministry of Food and Agriculture, maize is grown on over 1.2 million hectares, cowpea on 180,000 hectares, and groundnut on 300,000 hectares, with the latter two serving as important sources of protein and soil fertility through nitrogen fixation (FAO, 2020). Maize serves as a primary cereal for human and animal consumption, while cowpea and groundnut are essential for dietary diversity, soil fertility, and economic resilience. These crops are particularly valuable for household food and nutrition security due to their high protein content and essential micronutrients, making them critical for addressing malnutrition in rural households (FAO, 2020).

Cowpea and groundnut are notably gender-responsive crops, often cultivated and managed by women in Ghana's smallholder farming communities. These crops provide women with income-generating opportunities and offer households access to affordable sources of protein. Studies show that when women have control over income from crops like cowpea and groundnut, household food security and nutrition outcomes improve significantly, as women tend to prioritize spending on food, education, and healthcare (Doss et al., 2018).

The reliance on rain-fed systems for these crops, however, exposes them to yield variability due to climate conditions. Cowpea and groundnut are particularly suited for Ghana's semi-arid regions, where they can withstand lower rainfall than maize. However, all three crops face challenges, including climate variability, limited access to improved seeds, and inconsistent fertilizer usage (Anim-Kwapong & Frimpong, 2016). Given their contributions to household income and food security, enhancing productivity in these crops is critical for achieving sustainable agricultural development in Ghana.

The Guinea Savannah Zone is prone to erratic weather patterns, including periods of drought and heavy rainfall. This variability affects maize, cowpea, and groundnut yields, leading to inconsistent production levels that undermine food security. While maize is sensitive to water availability, cowpea and groundnut are more drought-tolerant, making them essential crops for food security during dry periods (Gyasi et al., 2014). However, even these resilient crops face yield reductions under prolonged drought conditions.

Soil degradation is a pressing issue in the Guinea Savannah, stemming from unsustainable agricultural practices and inadequate soil conservation measures. Soil erosion, reduced fertility, and diminished water- holding capacity are common, leading to lower yields for maize, cowpea, and groundnut. Groundnut, in particular, requires well-drained, nutrient-rich soils, and degradation limits its growth and productivity. Promoting sustainable soil management practices can help address these issues and improve soil health over the long term (Braimoh & Vlek, 2006).

Limited access to mechanization is a major barrier to efficient farming in the Guinea Savannah. Without mechanized land preparation, planting, and harvesting tools, farmers face high labor demands and costs, particularly in cowpea and groundnut production, which involve labor-intensive harvesting. Mechanization can reduce drudgery, improve productivity, and make agriculture more attractive to younger generations, but affordability and accessibility of machinery remain challenges for smallholders (Diao et al., 2014). Mechanization can greatly benefit maize, cowpea, and groundnut production in the Guinea Savannah. In maize, mechanized planting and harvesting reduce labor costs and optimize planting density, leading to

For cowpea and groundnut, mechanized threshing and shelling reduce post-harvest losses and increase profitability by enabling farmers to process and store their produce effectively (Takeshima et al., 2013). In contexts where mechanization is accessible, research shows improved yields and reduced labor time for all three crops, with a notable impact on women, who typically perform labor-intensive tasks in groundnut and cowpea cultivation (Daum & Birner, 2020).

Agroadvisories and good agronomic practices play a crucial role in guiding farmers on planting times, pest control, soil nutrient and water management. It offers farmers timely, location-specific guidance on weather management, allowing them to plan planting and other field-based activities more effectively, thereby reducing crop losses and increasing yields. These advisories also provide critical weather information, especially available precipitation and soil moisture, enabling farmers to optimize water use and moisture- dependent activities such as land preparation, planting, and fertilizer application (Dheebakran et al., 2020). Furthermore, agroadvisories guide pest and disease management, enabling farmers to take proactive measures to prevent crop damage and reduce the use of chemical pesticides and fertilizers (Tambo et al., 2023). GAP in maize, cowpea, and groundnut production includes crop rotation, intercropping, conservation tillage, optimized fertilizer application, and pest management (Tittonell et al., 2012). Intercropping maize with cowpea, is a practice increasingly popular in the Guinea Savannah which maximizes land use efficiency and provides a diversified diet and income source. Its importance as a soil moisture management strategy is increasing in the face of climate variability where dry spells are becoming rampant.

To address these challenges and improve the resilience of crop production systems in the Guinea Savannah zone, it is crucial to evaluate and demonstrate the effectiveness of agroadvisories alongside smart production practices that incorporate simple mechanization equipment. Agroadvisories provide farmers with timely and location-specific advice on weather, soil moisture, and pest/disease management, helping them make informed decisions and enhance crop yields. The use of simple mechanization equipment reduces drudgery, improves the timeliness of farming operations, and enhances production practices.

This project activity, undertaken by the Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT (ABC) in partnership with the CSIR- Crops Research Institute (CSIR-CRI) and the Department of Agriculture of the Kumbungu District, aimed to promote smart production and soil packages in enhancing crop resilience and productivity within the Guinea Savannah zone of Ghana. The smart production and soil packages integrated three key components: agroadvisories, good agronomic practices, and essential crop production equipment as mechanization enablers. The activity's primary objectives were threefold. Firstly, it sought to assess the effectiveness of smart production and soil packages in improving crop yields and resilience. Secondly, the activity aimed to promote technology awareness and adoption through field demonstrations. Finally, the activity targeted the scaling up of successful interventions across the Guinea Savannah zone.

To achieve these objectives, the activity developed and employed a standard operating procedure for the field demonstrations, ensuring uniformity, accuracy, and dependability in data collection and analysis. This approach enabled the research team to gather reliable data and draw meaningful conclusions. The methodology involved several key activities, including conducting field demonstrations to display smart production and soil packages, providing comprehensive capacity building and training for farmers and extension agents, and performing detailed data collection and analysis to evaluate the effectiveness of these packages. This structured approach established a robust foundation for gaining an in-depth understanding of the potential advantages of smart production and soil packages in the Guinea Savannah zone.

Climate variability is a significant challenge in the Guinea Savannah zone. The project addresses this by promoting drought-tolerant crops like cowpea and groundnut, which improve resilience to climate stress. Integrating these crops into production systems alongside maize provides reliable food sources even in periods of low rainfall. Soil fertility enhancement through nitrogen fixation by cowpea and groundnut contributes to long-term soil productivity and reduces environmental degradation. Smart production

2. APPROACH

The implementation of the outlined activities employed a diverse approach for successful execution and impact, incorporating demonstrations, field days, and training programs, among other initiatives, to effectively showcase the benefits of improved crop production technologies.
2.1 Locations/Site

The beneficiary communities are Balinkpeng, Jakphi-Kukuo, Kunkulung, Gbanzogu, and Biegu in the Kumbungu District. These communities rely heavily on agriculture as the backbone of their economy, with a substantial portion of the population engaged in crop production, primarily focusing on yams, maize, and soybeans (Alhassan-Bawa, 2019). Research conducted during the project revealed that these crops were not only sold in local markets but also transported to other regions of the country (Alhassan-Bawa, 2019). In these communities, economically valuable trees, including shea trees, mangoes, and Dawadawa (Parkia biglobosa, also known as the African locust bean), provided additional economic opportunities (GSS, 2010). The project facilitated the processing and sale of shea butter and mangoes locally and nationally (Nguekeng et al., 2021; Kolavalli et al., 2020; Okorley et al., 2014). Residents of Balinkpeng, Jakphi-Kukuo, Kunkulung, Gbanzogu, and Biegu also engaged in inland fishing to supplement their income (Medium Term Development Plan, 2013). The project's findings confirmed that the fish caught were sold fresh in local markets or smoked and dried for preservation (FAO, 2016).

The district's strategic location near the regional capital, Tamale, made it an important hub for trade and commerce (MDTP, 2013). Trade and commerce thrived in the district, with numerous market centers and shops, including the Kumbungu Market, serving as a major trading hub for agricultural produce and other goods from Balinkpeng, Jakphi-Kukuo, Kunkulung, Gbanzogu, and Biegu (Kumbungu District Assembly, 2020). Small-scale industries, such as grain milling and blacksmithing, provided essential employment opportunities for residents of these communities and produced vital goods for the local population (Ministry of Finance, 2024). Livestock production was also crucial, with many farmers in Balinkpeng, Jakphi-Kukuo, Kunkulung, Gbanzogu, and Biegu keeping animals like goats, sheep, and cattle (GSS, 2010).
2.2 Community entry and sensitization

Engagement with local stakeholders was a cornerstone of the activity, focusing on building robust relationships with farmers, local leaders, and community groups. Through open dialogue and active listening, we gained a nuanced understanding of their distinct needs, concerns, and aspirations. This fostered trust, ownership, and inclusivity, laying the groundwork for a collaborative partnership. The collaborative approach ensured the activity's success and positive community impact. By working closely with farmers and local leaders, we gained valuable insights into their unique challenges. For instance, we discovered diverse crop and variety preferences, varied mechanization support needs, and distinct fertilizer recommendations. These insights enabled us to develop tailored solutions, enhancing agricultural productivity and resilience, and ultimately improving livelihoods. Initial engagement played a critical role in informing key decisions. We used the information gathered to select suitable sites for demonstrations and interventions, choose optimal crops and seeds for the local climate, deploy mechanization enablers efficiently, and provide targeted fertilizer recommendations for soil health. This thoughtful approach ensured that our interventions were responsive to the community's specific needs.

To establish a strong stakeholder engagement foundation, we identified key stakeholders and built robust relationships. We conducted community and district-level meetings to raise awareness about the activity's goals, strategies, and long-term benefits. These meetings facilitated open discussion, allowing stakeholders to

2.3 Development of Standard Operating Procedure

A comprehensive Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) was developed for demonstration establishment, ensuring consistency, quality, and scalability of the demonstrations. The SOP encompassed key elements described below.

• Experimental Design: The experimental design featured clear guidelines for setting up demonstrations, which included the establishment of treatment and control plots, replication, and randomization. Considerations were taken into account for climate, soil, and crop suitability to ensure the demonstrations were tailored to the local context. Additionally, farmer-managed plots were included in the design to facilitate participatory learning and engage farmers in the experimentation process.

• Data Collection: Data collection will be conducted using standardized protocols to gather information on climate-smart agricultural practices, such as conservation agriculture and agroforestry. These protocols will also cover agro-advisory services, including weather-based insurance and soil testing. Furthermore, data will be collected on farmer engagement and adoption rates to assess the effectiveness of the demonstrations. Accurate and reliable data collection methods will be employed, comprising surveys, interviews, and observations. Regular monitoring and evaluation of demonstration performance will also be carried out to track progress and identify areas for improvement.

2.4 On-farm Demonstrations
The establishment of demonstrations was a critical component of the program, designed to showcase the practical application and benefits of the improved crop production technologies.
2.4.1 Demonstration Design

The deployed technology bundle incorporated three improved crop varieties: Maize, Cowpea, and Groundnut. These varieties were produced using Good Agricultural Practices (GAPs) and guided by agroadvisories to ensure optimal growth conditions and productivity. The bundle aimed to enhance crop resilience and productivity by integrating advanced agricultural techniques and sustainable practices.
2.4.2 Technology Bundles
To showcase the effectiveness of these practices, six demonstration plots were established, each highlighting different aspects of smart production and soil management:

• Drought Tolerant Maize on Ridges (DTR): This plot demonstrated water conservation and soil erosion control techniques by planting drought-tolerant maize on ridges. The ridges helped to conserve moisture and prevent soil erosion, making it suitable for areas prone to drought.

• Drought Tolerant Sole Cropped Maize (DTL): This plot showcased the effectiveness of drought- tolerant maize varieties in sole cropping systems. The maize was planted on harrowed land, which improved soil aeration and water infiltration, leading to better crop performance under dry conditions.

• Drought Tolerant Maize Intercropped with Cowpea (DTC): This plot illustrated the benefits of intercropping drought-tolerant maize with cowpea. Intercropping improved soil fertility through nitrogen fixation by cowpea and enhanced pest management by providing a diverse cropping system, thereby reducing pest pressure on maize.

• Drought Tolerant Maize with SAM Enablers (DTS): This plot highlighted the efficiency of mechanized planting using simple agricultural mechanization (SAM) enablers. Drought-tolerant maize was planted using roller planters, which ensured uniform planting depth and spacing, leading to improved crop establishment and reduced labour requirements.

• Disease-Tolerant Groundnut (DTG): This plot demonstrated the effectiveness of selecting disease- resistant groundnut varieties to manage crop diseases. The disease-tolerant groundnut variety showed better resistance to common groundnut diseases, leading to healthier plants and higher yields.

• Farmer Practice for Maize (FPM): This plot served as a control to compare the effectiveness of the demonstrated practices. It followed traditional farming methods used by local farmers, allowing for a direct comparison between improved practices and conventional practices.
2.4.3 Plot Establishment
The demonstration trial was successfully conducted on a one-hectare plot, covering an area of 59 m by 42 m (2478 m²). Various treatments were laid out in designated plot sizes as follows:
• DTR, DTS, DTC, and FPM: Each treatment was allocated a 20 m by 20 m plot (400 m²).

Summary

Capacity development is a central element of the CGIAR that aims to strengthen the capacity of farmers and agricultural extension agents to implement good farming practices in Ghana, especially in the northern part. As part of the capacity development efforts, the EiA initiative, in consultation with CSIR – INSTI, has developed a practical training program based on the operationalisation of the Cropping Calendar digital agro-advisory tool to enhance the technical knowledge and skills of the extension agents and lead farmers. After developing and operationalising the features of the cropping calendar in 2024, this was the first time we had engaged with the extension agents in the Northern region – tamale, Savanna region – Damongo and Upper West region – Wa. Hence, this training phase is at the pilot stage to receive feedback to improve the digital tool.

This report provides a detailed description of the cropping calendar practical training implementation in terms of objectives, contents, processes, participants, feedback testing results, and recommendations for future steps.
