How do you manage wastewater and solid waste?

Hatcheries must ensure that any water discharged from the facility is devoid of pathogens. Implementing proper treatment and discharge practices will reduce the risk of disease within the ponds and their vicinity.

To treat wastewater, channel it from the ponds into a sedimentation pond. From there, treat the water using chlorination and dechlorination processes before discharging it. Do not discharge water close to the water supply intake point.

Waste products such as dead fish, wastewater and processing waste can transmit diseases in hatcheries. As such, proper disposal is necessary to reduce the risk. Bury or incinerate dead fish to prevent disease transmission, and dispose of solid waste according to local regulations and laws.

Introduction
Introduction to aquaculture

The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) defines aquaculture as farming aquatic organisms with some form of intervention by individuals or corporates who own the stock being cultivated in the rearing process to enhance production. Manipulating spawning, breeding and stocking density, providing aeration to supply dissolved oxygen (DO), feeding fish formulated feeds, and protecting them from predators are all forms of intervention in aquaculture. This definition implies that humans modify the life cycle of cultured animals, including Nile tilapia for aquaculture purposes as depicted in Figure 1.

For fish like Nile tilapia, farmers can manipulate their entire life cycle. In Africa, however, many farmers still collect broodstock from the wild. In commercial Nile tilapia culture, hormonal manipulation converts the sex of fish larvae into males, which are then nursed using high quality feeds to produce fish fry or juveniles for grow-out culture. To rear fish up to marketable size, farmers in Africa use two major types of grow-out systems: cage culture and pond culture. Some of them use healthy fish from their grow-out culture as broodstock.

Introduction to the curriculum

There are two types of aquaculture: noncommercial and commercial. Noncommercial aquaculture is mainly small-scale family-business ventures. They play an extremely important role in food security and the local aquaculture market chain. We developed this curriculum to help upgrade the aquaculture value chain, focusing mainly on commercial aquaculture. Since the main goal of commercial aquaculture is to maximize profits, this is one of the main performance indicators of its economic sustainability.

Fixed costs account for the bulk of operating costs of aquaculture operations. These include land, pond construction, cage frames, net bags, equipment, fish seed, fingerlings, feeds, feeding, oxygen supply, water pumping, water exchange and electricity. Provided that the farm is already in operation (meaning that costs are fixed), the main cost for practitioners is the operation itself. We developed this curriculum to help farmers improve the technical aspects of aquaculture, including a section that introduces the concepts of running an aquaculture business.

An aquaculture business should be economically viable or sustainable over time, which requires the business venture to be profitable and competitive to stay in the market. The latter requires improving the production process, as market demand changes over time. As such, producers should pay attention to changing consumer demand to keep them satisfied with the quality of their products, as well as the way their products are produced. To do this, producers must respect the legal, environmental and social sustainability of aquaculture while still earning profits.
Legal sustainability

As with any other industrial sector, the commercial aquaculture industry is governed by the laws and regulations of the particular country. Industrial stability is one of the main criteria that potential investors look for, and the laws and regulations are designed to make the sector stable. As such, legal and economic sustainability are linked, as investment is a necessary component to staying competitive in the market.
Social sustainability

Wherever their production facility is located, producers must make sure that aquaculture is acceptable to the local community. They must also ensure that their products are acceptable to the market, consumers and various interest groups that have a stake in the process, such as environmental groups monitoring the pollution effects. Moreover, production operations should benefit a broader proportion of society, including women, young people and the poor.
Environmental sustainability

Aquaculture should produce aquatic animals in responsible and ethical ways by reducing environmental pollution or eliminating it altogether. Producers should either reduce or mitigate all negative impacts of aquaculture to maintain the integrity of aquatic ecosystems where the production process is embedded. This will allow producers to continue production at the same site over time.

This course takes a holistic view toward designing and delivering a curriculum aimed at promoting a sustainable aquaculture production process that considers the total sustainability (economic, legal, social and environmental) of the business to ensure the future prosperity of the sector. The course also focuses on the need to inject new investments needed for upgrading current systems in order to improve both product quality and the production process.

One of the most important aspects of the aquaculture production planning process is to address the following questions on product and market characteristics, access to resources, and the operation model:
Products:
1. What species do you want to produce? (e.g. Nile tilapia)
2. How much do you want to produce? (e.g. target quantity in metric tons per crop)
3. Which quality do you want to focus on? (e.g. size, taste, food safety)

1.1.3. Narrative

Fish reproduction is an extremely complex process. Fish represent one of the most diverse groups of organisms among vertebrates in their patterns of reproduction. From an evolutionary point of view, fish are a versatile group with nearly every kind of adaptation for reproduction— structural, physiological, as well as behavioral. Most fish reproduce sexually and fertilize their eggs externally. However, some fish internally fertilize their eggs, such as live-bearing sharks, freshwater fish guppy, platy and molly. Most fish reproduce seasonally. The gonads in fish remain small during the nonreproductive season, and the gametes are generally produced only during the spawning season.

As a group, tilapia play a significant role in tropical aquaculture. In particular, Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus) holds great economic promise in providing food and nutritional security and creating rural employment. As tilapia farming expands worldwide, the demand for its seed for stocking in production ponds is also increasing, and the fish continues to be introduced into many regions outside its natural habitats. It is therefore important to understand the basic biology and ecology of tilapia, particularly in relation to its reproduction. This will help improve the efficiency of intensive seed production and minimize the impacts of tilapia farming on the environment.

Tilapia is a member of the family Cichlidae. Three genera are well known, namely Oreochromis, Tilapia and Sarotherodon. Tilapia are endemic to Africa, Jordan and Israel (more than 70 species), but only a few species are commercially important. Adult tilapia eat predominately vegetarian diets varying from macrophytes to phytoplankton, depending on the species. Many structural features are related to its feeding habits, such as a terminal mouth, slender notched teeth and long gill rakers, as well as long intestines that are seven to 14 times the standard length and suitable for processing a plant diet.

This session outlines the reproductive biology of fish in general and Nile tilapia in particular in relation to large-scale seed production of tilapia. We emphasize the practical aspects of seed production and include a short exercise at the end to apply the skills that students learn. At the end of this module is a list of references for further reading.
1.1.3.1. Reproductive cycle in fish

The reproductive cycle refers to the succession of processes in fish from immature germ cells to the production of mature gametes (eggs and sperm) that will finally unite and develop as the embryo. The process of formation, growth and differentiation of gametes is called gametogenesis. This leads to the formation of female oocytes (oogenesis) and male spermatozoon (spermatogenesis). The reproductive cycle in both males and females involves two major phases: the

growth phase, representing gonadal growth and development, and the maturation phase, leading to spermiation/ovulation and spawning. Spawning is the release of the mature gametes into the external environment. It is a highly synchronized event resulting in fertilization of the egg and embryo development. The successful progression of all these processes of the reproductive cycle resulting in production of good quality gametes is the basis for successful reproduction in fish. The physiological aspects of the reproductive cycle are discussed in session 1.2.
1.1.3.2. Size at first maturity of Nile tilapia

Species as well as strains of the same species can affect tilapia’s size and age at first maturity. Nile tilapia reaches sexual maturity at 20–30 cm or 150– 250 g in its natural environment. In aquaculture ponds or under stressed environmental conditions, however, Nile tilapia often reaches early maturity at 30–50 g.
1.1.3.3. Identifying male and female tilapia

Water temperature has a significant effect on sex differentiation, sex ratio and morphological development during early larval stages of tilapia. At increased temperatures, however, slow growth and body deformities can occur. Higher temperatures (34°C–36°C) significantly increase the proportion of males (69%–91%), but lower temperatures do not affect the sex ratio.

The best way to identify male and female fish is by the shape and size of the genital papilla, which is long and pointed in the case of males and blunt in the case of females. The female body has three openings on the outside: the anus, urethra and the opening of the oviduct in the form of a slit. Males are often larger than females of the same age and have two openings to the outside: the anus and the urinogenital aperture. These differences are easily distinguishable after the fish have grown to 10–20 cm or 100–150 g, and are more pronounced during the breeding season when males also develop a reddish color around the jaws. Plate 2 highlights the differences between a male and a female tilapia during the spawning season.
1.1.3.4. Mode of reproduction of tilapia

Tilapia are nest builders and substrate spawners. Tilapia spp. guard the developing eggs and fry in the nests, Oreochromis spp. females incubate their eggs and fry orally, and Sarotherodon spp. males and/or females incubate the eggs and fry orally. Nile tilapia is a maternal mouthbrooder that incubates its fertilized eggs in the oral cavity of the female fish, similar to other species such as Mozambique tilapia (O. mossambicus) and blue tilapia (O. aureus).

1.1.3.5. Fecundity and egg size in tilapia

Tilapia has low fecundity and relatively large eggs. Fecundity is the number of mature ova in the ovary, the number of ovulated eggs or the number of eggs deposited during spawning—all of which vary for fish of equal size. Nile tilapia can produce as few as 100 eggs to more than 3000 per spawn, ranging in size from less than 2 mm to larger than 7.9 mm. The volume of eggs ranges from 2.8 mm to 11.1 mm, each with a mean weight of up to 3.7 mg. Farmers can expect approximately 100–500 eggs from every spawning batch. For practical purposes, it is ideal to refer to the fecundity of tilapia as the “number of fry produced per year,” considering the environmental variables that affect egg and fry production.

Sunlight appears to have a significant role in the reproductive performance of tilapia. Optimal reproductive performance takes place in a normal daylength cycle, which is 12 hours of sunlight and 12 hours of darkness. Generally, high stocking densities slow the reproduction process in tilapia. Nile tilapia stocked in single compartments spawn more often than those stocked in groups. In tilapia seed production, there are mainly two types of systems for incubating eggs and rearing larvae. In the natural breeding system, producers can leave mouthbreeding females in the pond to incubate the eggs and release the free-swimming fry into the pond, where they can collect them for further rearing to fingerlings. Session 1.2: Reproductive physiology of Nile tilapia
1.2.1. Objective
Identify the complex interaction of environment (external) and hormonal (internal) factors that lead to successful reproduction and propagation of fish.
1.2.2. Learning outcome
By the end of this session, trainees will appreciate the role of the various factors that regulate the internal processes of reproduction in fish.
1.2.3. Narrative
The reproductive physiology of fish refers to

the overall progression of the physiological processes related to reproduction, from egg fertilization to embryo development, hatching, growth, puberty, male and female gonadal development, gametogenesis, sexual behavior, the timing of reproductive cycles, and endocrine and environmental control—all of which culminate in spawning. Internally, the endocrine (hormonal) system in fish associated with the brain-pituitary-gonadal axis is what regulates all these events associated with reproduction. These processes also interact with other important physiological functions in fish, such as growth, nutrition, osmoregulation and stress response. Many of these physiological attributes have contributed to the increasing popularity of tilapia in aquaculture, including tolerance to a wide range of environmental conditions, such as DO, salinity and high stocking densities. Environmental factors such as temperature, sunlight, seasonal rainfall, water quality and food availability are also known to significantly influence the physiological
processes connected with reproduction in fish.

Tilapia mature early and have relatively short reproductive cycles, and they are prolific breeders under culture conditions. There are two phases in fish reproduction: the growth phase (gametogenesis), and maturation phase (oocyte maturation in females and spermiation in males). Both are controlled by reproductive hormones from the brain, pituitary and gonad. Most fish can reach the growth phase in captivity (controlled conditions), but the maturation phase requires external hormone therapies. However, tilapia is an easy-to-breed fish that does not require any

inducement for maturation and spawning, as the reproductive processes are triggered naturally. This is one of the most significant advantages that has propelled Nile tilapia aquaculture, even in remote areas of their natural occurrence.
1.2.3.1. Environmental control of reproduction in fish

External environmental factors are what regulate reproduction in fish by triggering internal mechanisms into action. Fish live in a constantly changing environment that has a direct influence on the regulation of reproduction. The most important environmental factors that affect reproduction in fish include sunlight, water temperature, rainfall, stocking density, sex ratio, diet quality, presence of pheromones, substrates, water quality, diseases and parasites.
Sunlight appears to be one of the most important

external impulses that influences fish reproduction by its well-known effect on the brain-pituitary- gonad axis. Temperature has its own effect, but also in combination with sunlight. Suboptimal temperatures inhibit the development of gonads. Nile tilapia produces sperm above a temperature of 24°C but spermatogenesis is arrested at 20°C. Besides its direct effect on gonadal development, temperature affects reproduction through the metabolic rate influencing the endocrine process. Generally, high stocking densities slow the reproduction process in tilapia. Nile tilapia stocked in single compartments spawn more often than those stocked in groups. There is some indication that the pheromones from female tilapia attract males toward increased courtship behavior. Feeding Nile tilapia a diet containing optimal nutrients, including protein and lipids, significantly influences reproduction. For example, tilapia females fed diets with 20% and 35% protein had a higher output of eggs per spawn than those fed only 10%. Major water quality parameters also influence reproduction in Nile tilapia, including pH,
hardness, DO and salinity.
1.2.3.2. Endocrine control of reproduction

External factors controlling reproduction vary widely across fish species, but the internal mechanisms that regulate spawning are similar in most fish. The endocrine system is a collection of glands and organs that produce hormones and regulate the secretion of hormones that control various body processes, such as growth,

metabolism and reproduction. In fish, the endocrine system regulating reproduction acts through a cascade of hormones along the brain- pituitary-gonad (BPG) axis (the hypothalamic- hypophyseal-gonadal axis), also called the reproductive axis. The BPG axis sets the stage for the endocrine mechanism in fish to regulate the entire process of reproduction in conjunction with various environmental and social signals. The sensory signals from the environment and other factors are transmitted to the part of the brain called the hypothalamus. The gonadotropin- releasing hormone (GnRH) produced from the brain stimulates the secretion and supply of two pituitary gonadotropins (GTHs), namely follicle- stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing- hormone (LH) to control reproduction.

The pituitary gland, also known as hypophysis, is a small organ located on the floor of the brain in a cavity formed from the roof of the buccal cavity in fish. The anterior lobe (adenohypophysis), which regulates gonadal function in fish, and the posterior pituitary lobe (neurohypophysis), which serves as the major storage and transportation region, are the two major segments of the pituitary responsible for delivering hypothalamic hormones. The pituitary gonadotropins initiate the growth phase (FSH) and maturation (LH) of gametes.

Introduction
Introduction to aquaculture

The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) defines aquaculture as farming aquatic organisms with some form of intervention by individuals or corporates who own the stock being cultivated in the rearing process to enhance production. Manipulating spawning, breeding and stocking density, providing aeration to supply dissolved oxygen (DO), feeding fish formulated feeds, and protecting them from predators are all forms of intervention in aquaculture. This definition implies that humans modify the life cycle of cultured animals, including Nile tilapia for aquaculture purposes as depicted in Figure 1.

For fish like Nile tilapia, farmers can manipulate their entire life cycle. In Africa, however, many farmers still collect broodstock from the wild. In commercial Nile tilapia culture, hormonal manipulation converts the sex of fish larvae into males, which are then nursed using high quality feeds to produce fish fry or juveniles for grow-out culture. To rear fish up to marketable size, farmers in Africa use two major types of grow-out systems: cage culture and pond culture. Some of them use healthy fish from their grow-out culture as broodstock.

Introduction to the curriculum

There are two types of aquaculture: noncommercial and commercial. Noncommercial aquaculture is mainly small-scale family-business ventures. They play an extremely important role in food security and the local aquaculture market chain. We developed this curriculum to help upgrade the aquaculture value chain, focusing mainly on commercial aquaculture. Since the main goal of commercial aquaculture is to maximize profits, this is one of the main performance indicators of its economic sustainability.

Fixed costs account for the bulk of operating costs of aquaculture operations. These include land, pond construction, cage frames, net bags, equipment, fish seed, fingerlings, feeds, feeding, oxygen supply, water pumping, water exchange and electricity. Provided that the farm is already in operation (meaning that costs are fixed), the main cost for practitioners is the operation itself. We developed this curriculum to help farmers improve the technical aspects of aquaculture, including a section that introduces the concepts of running an aquaculture business.

An aquaculture business should be economically viable or sustainable over time, which requires the business venture to be profitable and competitive to stay in the market. The latter requires improving the production process, as market demand changes over time. As such, producers should pay attention to changing consumer demand to keep them satisfied with the quality of their products, as well as the way their products are produced. To do this, producers must respect the legal, environmental and social sustainability of aquaculture while still earning profits.
Legal sustainability

As with any other industrial sector, the commercial aquaculture industry is governed by the laws and regulations of the particular country. Industrial stability is one of the main criteria that potential investors look for, and the laws and regulations are designed to make the sector stable. As such, legal and economic sustainability are linked, as investment is a necessary component to staying competitive in the market.
Social sustainability

Wherever their production facility is located, producers must make sure that aquaculture is acceptable to the local community. They must also ensure that their products are acceptable to the market, consumers and various interest groups that have a stake in the process, such as environmental groups monitoring the pollution effects. Moreover, production operations should benefit a broader proportion of society, including women, young people and the poor.
Environmental sustainability

Aquaculture should produce aquatic animals in responsible and ethical ways by reducing environmental pollution or eliminating it altogether. Producers should either reduce or mitigate all negative impacts of aquaculture to maintain the integrity of aquatic ecosystems where the production process is embedded. This will allow producers to continue production at the same site over time.

This course takes a holistic view toward designing and delivering a curriculum aimed at promoting a sustainable aquaculture production process that considers the total sustainability (economic, legal, social and environmental) of the business to ensure the future prosperity of the sector. The course also focuses on the need to inject new investments needed for upgrading current systems in order to improve both product quality and the production process.

One of the most important aspects of the aquaculture production planning process is to address the following questions on product and market characteristics, access to resources, and the operation model:
Products:

2. How much do you want to produce? (e.g. target quantity in metric tons per crop)
3. Which quality do you want to focus on? (e.g. size, taste, food safety)

3. What are the by-products of the production process? (e.g. effluents, sludge)

1.1.3. Narrative

Fish reproduction is an extremely complex process. Fish represent one of the most diverse groups of organisms among vertebrates in their patterns of reproduction. From an evolutionary point of view, fish are a versatile group with nearly every kind of adaptation for reproduction— structural, physiological, as well as behavioral. Most fish reproduce sexually and fertilize their eggs externally. However, some fish internally fertilize their eggs, such as live-bearing sharks, freshwater fish guppy, platy and molly. Most fish reproduce seasonally. The gonads in fish remain small during the nonreproductive season, and the gametes are generally produced only during the spawning season.

As a group, tilapia play a significant role in tropical aquaculture. In particular, Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus) holds great economic promise in providing food and nutritional security and creating rural employment. As tilapia farming expands worldwide, the demand for its seed for stocking in production ponds is also increasing, and the fish continues to be introduced into many regions outside its natural habitats. It is therefore important to understand the basic biology and ecology of tilapia, particularly in relation to its reproduction. This will help improve the efficiency of intensive seed production and minimize the impacts of tilapia farming on the environment.

Tilapia is a member of the family Cichlidae. Three genera are well known, namely Oreochromis, Tilapia and Sarotherodon. Tilapia are endemic to Africa, Jordan and Israel (more than 70 species), but only a few species are commercially important. Adult tilapia eat predominately vegetarian diets varying from macrophytes to phytoplankton, depending on the species. Many structural features are related to its feeding habits, such as a terminal mouth, slender notched teeth and long gill rakers, as well as long intestines that are seven to 14 times the standard length and suitable for processing a plant diet.

This session outlines the reproductive biology of fish in general and Nile tilapia in particular in relation to large-scale seed production of tilapia. We emphasize the practical aspects of seed production and include a short exercise at the end to apply the skills that students learn. 1.1.3.1. Reproductive cycle in fish

The reproductive cycle refers to the succession of processes in fish from immature germ cells to the production of mature gametes (eggs and sperm) that will finally unite and develop as the embryo. The process of formation, growth and differentiation of gametes is called gametogenesis. This leads to the formation of female oocytes (oogenesis) and male spermatozoon (spermatogenesis). The reproductive cycle in both males and females involves two major phases: the

growth phase, representing gonadal growth and development, and the maturation phase, leading to spermiation/ovulation and spawning. Spawning is the release of the mature gametes into the external environment. It is a highly synchronized event resulting in fertilization of the egg and embryo development. The successful progression of all these processes of the reproductive cycle resulting in production of good quality gametes is the basis for successful reproduction in fish. The physiological aspects of the reproductive cycle are discussed in session 1.2.
1.1.3.2. Size at first maturity of Nile tilapia

Species as well as strains of the same species can affect tilapia’s size and age at first maturity. Nile tilapia reaches sexual maturity at 20–30 cm or 150– 250 g in its natural environment. In aquaculture ponds or under stressed environmental conditions, however, Nile tilapia often reaches early maturity at 30–50 g.
1.1.3.3. Identifying male and female tilapia

Water temperature has a significant effect on sex differentiation, sex ratio and morphological development during early larval stages of tilapia. At increased temperatures, however, slow growth and body deformities can occur. Higher temperatures (34°C–36°C) significantly increase the proportion of males (69%–91%), but lower temperatures do not affect the sex ratio.

Temperature and sunlight are the most important factors that influence spawning. Alone or in combination, these factors appear to trigger external impulses that influence fish. Optimal spawning temperatures for Nile tilapia range from 250C to 300C, but suboptimal temperatures inhibit the development of gonads. Besides its direct effect on gonadal development, temperature influences reproduction through the metabolic rate, which affects the endocrine process. In tropical regions, spawning can continue year-round, as ripe females school in midwater with non-territorial males and egg-brooding females. About four to seven batches of eggs are spawned in one mating.

1.1.3.5. Fecundity and egg size in tilapia

Tilapia has low fecundity and relatively large eggs. Fecundity is the number of mature ova in the ovary, the number of ovulated eggs or the number of eggs deposited during spawning—all of which vary for fish of equal size. Nile tilapia can produce as few as 100 eggs to more than 3000 per spawn, ranging in size from less than 2 mm to larger than 7.9 mm. The volume of eggs ranges from 2.8 mm to 11.1 mm, each with a mean weight of up to 3.7 mg. Farmers can expect approximately 100–500 eggs from every spawning batch. For practical purposes, it is ideal to refer to the fecundity of tilapia as the “number of fry produced per year,” considering the environmental variables that affect egg and fry production.

Sunlight appears to have a significant role in the reproductive performance of tilapia. Optimal reproductive performance takes place in a normal daylength cycle, which is 12 hours of sunlight and 12 hours of darkness. Generally, high stocking densities slow the reproduction process in tilapia. Nile tilapia stocked in single compartments spawn more often than those stocked in groups. Pheromones from females can attract males. Feeding and feed quality are

Fecundity increases during the initial period of maturity and growth, but decreases as the fish grow old. The optimal size of female breeders for tilapia seed production is 150–300 g, which produces about 200–500 fry per month. Smaller females produce many more eggs than larger fish with shorter spawning intervals of just over 100 days, while larger fish produce more eggs per clutch than smaller females. Larger eggs contain more yolk and result in larger, stronger and fast-growing fry.

1.1.3.6. Egg incubation and larval development

For tilapia, incubation time is inversely and linearly related to temperature. Time to hatching for Nile tilapia eggs varies from 2 to 3 days at 340C to 8 days at 170C, while the average duration of the incubation period and parental care is approximately 20 days. In tilapia seed production, there are mainly two types of systems for incubating eggs and rearing larvae. In the natural breeding system, producers can leave mouthbreeding females in the pond to incubate the eggs and release the free-swimming fry into the pond, where they can collect them for further rearing to fingerlings. In the artificial incubation and hatching system, producers collect the eggs and yolk sac fry from the mouth of incubating females and incubate the eggs separately in specialized hatchery systems. This system is best suited for large-scale production of good quality tilapia fry.

Water temperature has an important effect on various biological relationships. It affects sex differentiation, sex ratio and morphological development during early larval stages of tilapia, though at increased temperatures slow growth and body deformities are likely to occur. Temperature also affects the sex ratio in tilapia by increasing the proportion of males at higher incubation temperatures of 340C–360C.

Tilapia eggs pass through four stages before transforming into free-swimming fry (Plate 4). In Stage I, the eggs are light to dark yellow, in Stage II they are golden yellow and in Stage III they become golden brown with dots. Stage IV is the hatched yolk sac fry. The fry become free swimming when their yolk sac is absorbed.

Session 1.2: Reproductive physiology of Nile tilapia
1.2.1. Objective
Identify the complex interaction of environment (external) and hormonal (internal) factors that lead to successful reproduction and propagation of fish.
1.2.2. Learning outcome
By the end of this session, trainees will appreciate the role of the various factors that regulate the internal processes of reproduction in fish.
1.2.3. Narrative
The reproductive physiology of fish refers to

the overall progression of the physiological processes related to reproduction, from egg fertilization to embryo development, hatching, growth, puberty, male and female gonadal development, gametogenesis, sexual behavior, the timing of reproductive cycles, and endocrine and environmental control—all of which culminate in spawning. Internally, the endocrine (hormonal) system in fish associated with the brain-pituitary-gonadal axis is what regulates all these events associated with reproduction. These processes also interact with other important physiological functions in fish, such as growth, nutrition, osmoregulation and stress response. Many of these physiological attributes have contributed to the increasing popularity of tilapia in aquaculture, including tolerance to a wide range of environmental conditions, such as DO, salinity and high stocking densities. Environmental factors such as temperature, sunlight, seasonal rainfall, water quality and food availability are also known to significantly influence the physiological
processes connected with reproduction in fish.

Tilapia mature early and have relatively short reproductive cycles, and they are prolific breeders under culture conditions. There are two phases in fish reproduction: the growth phase (gametogenesis), and maturation phase (oocyte maturation in females and spermiation in males). Both are controlled by reproductive hormones from the brain, pituitary and gonad. Most fish can reach the growth phase in captivity (controlled conditions), but the maturation phase requires external hormone therapies. However, tilapia is an easy-to-breed fish that does not require any

inducement for maturation and spawning, as the reproductive processes are triggered naturally. This is one of the most significant advantages that has propelled Nile tilapia aquaculture, even in remote areas of their natural occurrence.
1.2.3.1. Environmental control of reproduction in fish

External environmental factors are what regulate reproduction in fish by triggering internal mechanisms into action. Fish live in a constantly changing environment that has a direct influence on the regulation of reproduction. The most important environmental factors that affect reproduction in fish include sunlight, water temperature, rainfall, stocking density, sex ratio, diet quality, presence of pheromones, substrates, water quality, diseases and parasites.
Sunlight appears to be one of the most important

external impulses that influences fish reproduction by its well-known effect on the brain-pituitary- gonad axis. Temperature has its own effect, but also in combination with sunlight. Suboptimal temperatures inhibit the development of gonads. Nile tilapia produces sperm above a temperature of 24°C but spermatogenesis is arrested at 20°C. Besides its direct effect on gonadal development, temperature affects reproduction through the metabolic rate influencing the endocrine process. Generally, high stocking densities slow the reproduction process in tilapia. Nile tilapia stocked in single compartments spawn more often than those stocked in groups. There is some indication that the pheromones from female tilapia attract males toward increased courtship behavior. Feeding Nile tilapia a diet containing optimal nutrients, including protein and lipids, significantly influences reproduction. For example, tilapia females fed diets with 20% and 35% protein had a higher output of eggs per spawn than those fed only 10%. Major water quality parameters also influence reproduction in Nile tilapia, including pH,
hardness, DO and salinity.
1.2.3.2. Endocrine control of reproduction

External factors controlling reproduction vary widely across fish species, but the internal mechanisms that regulate spawning are similar in most fish. The endocrine system is a collection of glands and organs that produce hormones and regulate the secretion of hormones that control various body processes, such as growth,

metabolism and reproduction. In fish, the endocrine system regulating reproduction acts through a cascade of hormones along the brain- pituitary-gonad (BPG) axis (the hypothalamic- hypophyseal-gonadal axis), also called the reproductive axis. The BPG axis sets the stage for the endocrine mechanism in fish to regulate the entire process of reproduction in conjunction with various environmental and social signals. The sensory signals from the environment and other factors are transmitted to the part of the brain called the hypothalamus. The gonadotropin- releasing hormone (GnRH) produced from the brain stimulates the secretion and supply of two pituitary gonadotropins (GTHs), namely follicle- stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing- hormone (LH) to control reproduction.

The pituitary gland, also known as hypophysis, is a small organ located on the floor of the brain in a cavity formed from the roof of the buccal cavity in fish. The anterior lobe (adenohypophysis), which regulates gonadal function in fish, and the posterior pituitary lobe (neurohypophysis), which serves as the major storage and transportation region, are the two major segments of the pituitary responsible for delivering hypothalamic hormones. The pituitary gonadotropins initiate the growth phase (FSH) and maturation (LH) of gametes.

Introduction

In April 2022, WorldFish transferred Genetically Improved Farmed Tilapia (GIFT) fry from its headquarters in Malaysia to Premium Aquaculture Limited (PAL) in Abeokuta, Nigeria. The transfer was part of an innovative initiative aimed at enhancing aquaculture sustainability and economic development in Nigeria. It was made possible through a collaboration with the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation and the West Africa Trade and Innovation Hub, which is funded by the United States Agency for International Development.

The vision of this strategic partnership is to establish a robust GIFT breeding population at PAL to disseminate fry and fingerlings for hatchery production and grow-out across Nigeria. PAL carefully cultivated and bred the GIFT fingerlings it received and expected to disseminate the F2 fingerling (second generation) to satellite hatcheries and smallholder grow out farmers in April 2024. Spearheaded by CGIAR’s Transforming AgriFood Systems in West and Central Africa project, this endeavor is poised to revolutionize aquaculture practices and seed supply within the country.

This comprehensive tilapia biosecurity manual is an integral component of this initiative. The manual provides crucial guidelines and protocols for ensuring the health and biosecurity of smallholder operations that farm tilapia. We hope it will prove instrumental in guiding fish farmers across Nigeria to protect their stocks from diseases. This, in turn, will enhance yields and ensure the long-term success of their aquaculture endeavors.

The aim of these collective pioneering efforts is to establish a resilient and biosecure environment for farming tilapia in Nigeria. In doing so, they will combine national goals of food security, economic prosperity and sustainable aquaculture practices.
What is biosecurity?
Biosecurity entails the following measures:
Establish and implement systematic procedures.
Prevent the introduction of infectious agents such as bacteria, parasites, fungi and viruses that can cause disease in an indoor or outdoor fish hatchery, nursery or grow-out.
Prevent the entry of infectious agents from external sources or within different sections of the same farm.
Why is biosecurity important?
It avoids harmful pathogens: Biosecurity is a standard prevention method that avoids contact between fish and infectious agents (pathogens).
It protects grow-out ponds: Biosecurity acts as a barrier to avert the onset of diseases.
It is a smart, inexpensive approach: Biosecurity is part of good aquaculture practices to use on any farm.
It saves time and money: Neglecting biosecurity measures can result in more time and financial resources spent on treating diseases when they occur.
• It is a good investment: Biosecurity includes simple, and sometimes, zero-cost measures that will keep pathogens away from fish and keep fish away from pathogens.
• It can be used anywhere: Biosecurity principles can be applied in large-scale and backyard or small- scale fish production units.
By doing smart things and being careful, we are helping our tilapia friends stay healthy and happy.

Why is biosecurity necessary?

Biosecurity is indispensable for fish production facilities. One of the main reasons is that it operates as a defense against introducing pathogens that can cause disease outbreaks. These pathogens can infiltrate the system through routine operational activities, potentially causing significant harm. They can be introduced from various sources, including new broodstock, new fry or fingerlings, contaminated equipment, birds and other animals, the water supply or visitors from other farms.

What is the role of biosecurity?
Disease prevention: Implementing robust biosecurity measures can prevent disease outbreaks, thus averting substantial financial losses and operational setbacks.
Effective pond design: A well-designed facility seamlessly integrates optimal biosecurity practices.
Investment protection: Biosecurity safeguards investments, ensuring consistent revenue generation.
Quality assurance: Ensuring the production of premium quality fish reinforces the trust of reliant farmers.

Implementing biosecurity measures effectively can uphold fish health and maintain grow-out profitability. Preventing the introduction of pathogens results in high quality fish production, reduced financial losses and sustained operations.
Prioritizing biosecurity measures will ensure the successful operation of a grow-out farm.
What are the advantages of biosecurity?
Biosecurity can help owners of grow-out farms minimize the following risks:
• disease outbreaks
• high rates of fish mortality
• high financial losses from fish loss
setbacks caused by production disruptions
• high operational clean-up costs after a disease outbreak
• project failure
loss of client trust in the quality of fry or fingerlings.

Even if a farm does a thorough clean-up following a disease outbreak, there is no guarantee that it will produce disease-free fish, as certain pathogens, like tilapia lake virus (TiLV), can persist within the fish. Implementing effective biosecurity measures, along with good management practices, is a more cost- effective approach than disease treatment.
Implementing biosecurity measures ensures a higher probability of overall success and contributes to long-term sustainability.

How are diseases introduced into grow-out ponds?

Diseases can infiltrate grow-out ponds through various pathways. When new fish are brought in from external sources, like other countries, different farms or the wild, they can carry harmful pathogens without showing signs of illness. A lack of robust biosecurity measures increases the chances of a pathogen getting into a hatchery.
Tilapia can harbor the following pathogens:
common protozoan parasites like Ichthyophthirius multifiliis, Trichodina sp., Eimeria spp., Myxosoma sp., Nosema sp., Henneguya sp. and Hexamita
• monogenean flukes
• helminths like Acanthostomum spp. and Acanthogyrus sp.
• bacteria such as Pseudomonas sp., Aeromonas sp., Flavobacterium columnare, Francisella sp. and Streptococcus spp.
• viruses like TiLV.

In addition to infecting fish, using a contaminated water supply that is not properly treated or contaminated equipment can introduce pathogens into grow-out ponds. To prevent this from happening, operators should take the following precautions:
• Minimize imports: Reduce the introduction of live fish from other countries or farms outside the facility.
• Seek expert guidance: Consult relevant authorities, like the Department of Fisheries, before importing fish. They can help identify reputable sources of fish that are free of harmful pathogens.

• Buy certified fish: Newly acquired fish should come with a health certificate that verifies they are free from harmful pathogens. Authoritative bodies should conduct essential tests on these fish to ensure they are healthy and free of pathogens.

• Quarantine new fish: Isolate new fish as a precautionary measure. The quarantine period helps hatcheries assess the fish for potential pathogens before mixing them with the existing pond population. Hasty mingling without proper assessment can lead to significant mortalities.
By adhering to these measures, growers can substantially reduce the risk of introducing diseases into their ponds and safeguard the health of their fish.
How can apparently healthy fish become sick?

It is puzzling how new fish that look perfectly healthy can become sick. Several factors can cause this, including transportation stress and disease. Transported fish may appear healthy, but symptoms can appear shortly after they are shipped. If fish undergo excessive stress during transportation, they will be at high risk of infection from pathogens, resulting in disease within just a few days. This usually happens with young or weak fish, resulting in high mortalities.
To prevent mortalities after transportation, operators should adhere to the following practices:
• Buy fish locally: Purchase fish from a nearby facility to avoid the stress of a long journey.

• Use a reliable source: Obtain fish from farms with no record of disease outbreaks. These farms are usually certified by the fisheries authorities and should provide a health certificate confirming the fish are free from harmful pathogens or diseases.
• Ensure optimal water conditions: Maintain favorable water quality in your ponds, including temperature, pH and oxygen levels, to keep fish healthy.
• Conduct routine checks: Regularly examine your fish for any signs of disease. Early identification, isolation and treatment of diseased fish will minimize losses and spread of the disease.
• Use timely treatment: If feasible, treat diseases effectively before introducing fish into a grow-out pond.
By implementing these steps, growers can substantially reduce the impact of transportation stress, fostering overall health and better survival rates of their fish.

How are diseases transmitted within a grow-out pond?

Diseases can swiftly propagate within a grow-out pond through various channels. One common avenue involves daily operational items becoming contaminated from multiple uses. These include buckets, nets, siphon hoses, footwear and other materials. Wild animals and visitors can bring in diseases as well.

Unintentional contact with diseased fish or pathogens can occur when contaminated items are used in routine operations, whether they are brought into a grow-out farm or contaminated during interactions with people or animals, like dogs, cats, squirrels and other stray creatures. This can, in turn, transmit pathogens to the fish.

To prevent diseases from spreading, it is important to implement strict biosecurity measures such as cleaning and disinfecting equipment regularly, making sure staff adhere to proper hygiene practices and maintaining vigorous pest control efforts.

Essential preventive measures are crucial steps in minimizing the spread of disease. Any items introduced into a fishpond, such as buckets or nets, must be disinfected to eliminate possible pathogens. During breaks between cycles, hatchery staff must disinfect all equipment used in a grow-out pond.
By vigilantly implementing these measures, grow-out farms can effectively prevent diseases from spreading, which will safeguard the health and vitality of their fish.
What are the key requirements for better biosecurity?
Before establishing a new hatchery, proper planning is crucial to meet the prerequisites for biosecurity. Consider the following aspects when selecting a site for a grow-out pond:

• Find a suitable location: Opt for elevated land to ensure proper drainage to prevent water logging. In addition, the site should be at a considerable distance from other ponds or farms to mitigate the risk of infection. Select a site with access to a reliable water source for filling and maintaining the pond.
• Avoid flood prone areas: Do not site a grow-out pond in flood prone areas. This will prevent damage to the facility from flooding and make it easier to implement biosecurity measures.
• Manage effluents: Treat effluent properly, and discharge it onsite.
• Ensure accessibility: Select a site with easy access to a road in order to transport fish and materials effectively.
• Use reliable utilities: Secure a reliable supply of electricity and clean water, both of which are essential for properly functioning ponds.
• Modify facilities: Make minor modifications to existing facilities to effectively implement better biosecurity measures.
What is the optimal design for a grow-out pond and best practices for biosecurity?

It is important to design an earthen grow-out pond for tilapia that has integrated biosecurity features. This is essential to prevent disease transmission and ensure the health and productivity of the fish farm. The following is an outline of an ideal design that focuses on biosecurity:

• Pond construction: Build the pond using high quality clay or loam soil that minimizes seepage and helps retain water. Include a properly compacted clay liner to prevent water infiltration and potential disease introduction.

• Water supply and exchange: Install water control structures, and implement an inlet and outlet system to control water exchange and flow and maintain water quality. Use a sedimentation basin to trap suspended solids before water enters the pond.

• Quarantine and isolation area: Designate a separate area within the farm for quarantine purposes. New fish should be quarantined for a specific period, and a health assessment should be done before introducing them into the main pond. If a vaccine is available, vaccinate fish in case of threat of disease.

• Single entry point: Establish a single entry point with proper footbaths and handwashing stations. Anyone entering the farm should go through disinfection procedures to prevent the introduction of pathogens.

• Fencing and predator control: Erect fences around the farm to prevent unauthorized personnel and potential predators from entering. Install bird netting or scare devices to deter birds, which can carry diseases.

• Water source treatment: Treat incoming water from external sources, such as rivers and canals, to eliminate potential pathogens. If necessary, implement sand filtration, UV treatment or chlorination to ensure water quality.

• Aeration and oxygenation: Incorporate aeration systems to maintain dissolved oxygen levels and minimize fish stress. Adequate oxygenation enhances fish health and reduces their susceptibility to diseases.
• Proper stocking: Avoid overcrowding the pond, which can lead to fish stress and disease outbreaks. Maintain optimal stocking densities to provide enough space for fish to move and grow.
• Feed management: Implement proper feeding practices to avoid overfeeding and water pollution. Use floating feeders or platforms to distribute feed evenly and reduce feed waste.
• Regular health checks: Designate a monitoring area for regular health checks and inspections. Address any signs of disease immediately with proper treatment.
• Proper waste management: Set up systems for effective waste management, including solid waste and uneaten feed. Prevent accumulation of waste, which can degrade water quality and promote disease.
• Emergency response plan: Develop a comprehensive disease outbreak emergency plan. Outline clear steps to take if a disease is suspected or confirmed, including isolation, treatment and reporting.
• Recordkeeping: Maintain thorough records of fish health, water quality, feed use and any administered treatments. Records help trace disease outbreaks and guide future management decisions.
• Education and training: Attend regular training programs to upgrade skills and knowledge on tilapia farming practices and biosecurity.

Remember that biosecurity is an ongoing process that requires vigilance, commitment and adaptation. Consulting with aquaculture experts and local authorities will help tailor your pond design to the specific needs of your region and fish farming operation.

Why is optimal water quality important?

For effective biosecurity practices, maintaining appropriate water quality is essential to prevent disease transmission and ensure the health and growth of the fish. Here are the recommended water quality requirements for a smallholder tilapia farm:
• Dissolved oxygen: Maintain dissolved oxygen levels above 5 mg/L. If required, adequate aeration or water movement can help maintain levels.
• pH: Keep the pH within the range of 6.5–8.5. Consistent levels prevent stress and support immune function.
• Ammonia and nitrite: Keep ammonia (NH3-N) below 0.5 mg/L and nitrite (NO2-N) below 0.1 mg/L. High levels are toxic to fish and weaken their immune system.
Nitrate: Maintain nitrate (NO3-N) below 50 mg/L. Elevated levels can lead to stress and affect growth.
• Turbidity: Maintain clear water with low turbidity. Clear water helps with detecting diseases and makes feeding more efficient.
• Water: Ensure that the water source is free from pathogens.
• Monitoring: Test water quality parameters regularly using appropriate testing kits. Monitor parameters such as pH, dissolved oxygen, ammonia and nitrite.
• Stocking density: Avoid overstocking, as it can lead to poor water quality and stress. Follow recommended stocking densities for tilapia.
• Feeding: Excess feed can lead to water quality issues.
• Preparation: Have a plan in place to address sudden changes in water quality. Be prepared to take corrective actions if parameters deviate from the desired range.
• Contamination: Control runoff and avoid chemical pollution to prevent pond water contamination. Limit access to the pond to reduce the risk of introducing pathogens.

By maintaining these water quality requirements, farms can create a healthier and more biosecure environment for their fish. Regular monitoring, prudent management practices and a commitment to biosecurity will lead to successful fish production.

What are optimal nutrition practices?

Nutrition is critical to run a successful fish farm, especially in a grow-out farm, as it directly influences growth, health and overall production. Providing balanced and appropriate nutrition ensures optimal growth rates, disease resistance and efficient feed conversion. Here are some nutritional aspects to consider for fish in a grow-out farm:

• Feed quality: Either use commercial pellet feeds specifically formulated to meet the nutritional needs of tilapia, or feed tilapia a diet with a balanced protein, carbohydrate, lipid, vitamin and mineral composition.
• Expiration date: Use feed before it expires to maintain its nutritional content and prevent contamination.
• Safe storage: Keep feed in a cool, dry place that animals cannot access to preserve its nutritional value.
• Fresh feed: Fresh feed, like trash fish or bivalves, can carry pathogens. Use fresh feed only if it can be treated to eliminate pathogens.
• Commercial pellet feeds: Commercial feeds generally carry a low risk of disease transmission.
• Feed management: Implement feeding practices that minimize waste and maximize consumption. Feed should be consumed within a short period to prevent degradation.
• Water quality: Maintain good water quality to support digestion and nutrient absorption. Poor quality water can hinder feeding and growth.
• Fish growth and health: Regularly monitor growth and overall health to ensure the fish respond positively to the feed.
• Feed transition: If changing feeds, gradually shift from one type to another to minimize stress and digestive disturbances.
• Recordkeeping: Keep records of feed consumption, growth rates and any observed health issues. Records help with adjusting feeding practices and identifying trends.
By following these nutritional principles, growers can enhance their potential for successful production while minimizing the risk of disease outbreaks.
By paying attention to these nutritional aspects and providing fish with a balanced and appropriate diet, you can optimize the growth, health and overall performance of your fish.
Plate 10. Keeping feed in a cool environment safeguards the integrity of its nutrient content.
How do you prepare your pond after harvest?

Cleaning up a grow-out pond after harvest is an essential step to maintain the health of the aquatic environment and prepare the pond for the next production cycle. Here are step-by-step instructions on how to clean up your pond after harvest:
• Drain the pond: After harvest, drain the water from the pond. This can be done using the existing drainage system or pumps. Allow the water to drain completely so that the pond is empty.
• Remove fish remains: Remove any remaining carcasses, uneaten feed and debris from the pond bottom. Use nets or other appropriate tools to collect and dispose of the remains.

• Clean infrastructure: If the pond is made of concrete structures or fiberglass tanks, scrub the walls and surfaces gently to remove any algae, biofilm and other residues. Use a hose to rinse the surfaces and remove any remaining debris.
• Inspect the liner or bottom: If the pond has a liner, inspect it for damage, and repair any tears or leaks. If the pond has a natural bottom, make sure it is level and free of any obstructions.

• Treat the pond for pathogens: If there have been disease outbreaks, disinfect the pond. Use appropriate chemicals or lime to eliminate pathogens. Be careful not to use too much, as that could harm the environment.
• Remove excess sediment: If too much sediment has built up, consider removing it to improve the pond’s water-holding capacity. Avoid disturbing the soil excessively to prevent erosion.
• Inspect and maintain infrastructure: Check equipment such as pumps, aerators and pipes, and clean and repair them as needed. Ensure that water inlets and outlets are functioning properly.
• Refill and recondition the pond: Begin refilling the pond with fresh water from a reliable source. If needed, add appropriate water conditioners to stabilize water quality.
• Plan for the next cycle: Evaluate the previous production cycle and identify areas for improvement. Plan stocking densities, feeding strategies and management practices for the next batch of fish.
• Implement biosecurity measures: Before introducing new fingerlings, put them through a quarantine period. Implement biosecurity measures to prevent diseases from getting into the facility.
• Keep records: Maintain records of the cleaning process, water quality measurements and any treatments applied. This information can be valuable for future reference and improvements.
• Give the pond a break: If possible, let the pond rest for a while to allow natural processes to restore the ecosystem.

Remember that the specific steps can vary based on your location and the type of pond. It is always a good practice to consult with local aquaculture experts to ensure you follow the best practices suitable for your situation.

What are optimal disinfection practices?

Disinfecting a pond after harvest may be necessary to control and prevent the spread of pathogens. However, it is important to exercise caution when using chemicals to avoid harming the aquatic ecosystem and environment. Here are some common chemicals used to disinfect a fishpond, along with their considerations:

• Calcium hypochlorite: This is a chlorine-based disinfectant commonly used to treat water. It can kill many pathogens, including bacteria, viruses and parasites. At high concentrations, however, it can be toxic to fish, so careful dosing and thorough rinsing are essential.
• Sodium hypochlorite: Household bleaches that contain sodium hypochlorite can be used as disinfectants. Use only as recommended, and rinse the pond thoroughly to remove residual chlorine.

• Copper sulfate: This is used to treat fungal and bacterial infections in ponds. It can be toxic to fish at higher concentrations and may harm aquatic plants and invertebrates. Use it with caution and according to the recommended dose.

• Potassium permanganate: This is effective against external parasites and bacteria. However, use it sparingly and with caution, as excessive use can harm fish and other aquatic life. It can also stain pond surfaces and water.

• Formalin: Formalin treats external parasites, fungi and some bacterial infections. It is toxic to fish and should be used carefully according to recommended doses. Proper aeration is crucial when using formalin.

• Hydrogen peroxide: Hydrogen peroxide can be used to treat fungal infections and improve water quality. It decomposes into water and oxygen, making it less harmful to the environment. Careful dosing is essential to prevent harming fish and other aquatic life.
Before using any chemical, consider the following precautions:
• Consult a local aquaculture expert or veterinarian to determine the appropriate chemical and dose for the specific situation.
Follow the manufacturer’s recommendations for application and dilution rates.
• Wear appropriate protective gear, including gloves and eye protection, when handling chemicals.
• Allow sufficient time for the chemical to react. Then thoroughly rinse the pond to remove any residual chemicals.
• Monitor water quality parameters such as pH and oxygen levels during and after treatment.
• Observe how the fish behave. Be prepared to take action if you see any negative effects.
• Apply suitable disinfectants at recommended concentrations and durations.
Remember, the goal is to effectively manage pathogens while minimizing harm to fish and the environment. Always prioritize the health of the aquatic ecosystem when using chemicals in a fishpond.

How do you manage vehicles entering the facility?

Stringent protocols for vehicles are important to minimize the risk of transmitting diseases within and beyond the hatchery. Unauthorized vehicles should be prohibited from entering the hatchery/farm premises. Install a disinfectant bath at the gate for vehicles to pass through to cleanse their wheels and undercarriage. Replace the disinfectant regularly according to the instructions on the label.

How do you manage people effectively?

It is important to minimize the risk of visitors transmitting diseases within and beyond the grow-out ponds. Neglecting protocols can inadvertently lead to fish infection, as individuals who have visited other sites may unknowingly carry pathogens that could contaminate the ponds. Likewise, frequent movement across different pond sections can also spread pathogens.
Growers should implement the following procedures to mitigate possible contamination from people:
• Control the movement of visitors: Regulate the movement of visitors to curb the spread of diseases.
• Implement hygiene measures at the entrance: Enforce the use of handwash and footbath facilities at the entrance to the pond facility.
• Prohibit unauthorized access: Prevent unauthorized individuals from entering the facility.
• Document visitors: Maintain a comprehensive visitors logbook to monitor their entry and exit.
• Escort entrants: Escort visitors into the facility.
• Maintain disinfectant: Replace the disinfectant regularly, as per the instructions on the label, to ensure its effectiveness.
By meticulously implementing these measures, grow-out ponds can strengthen their defenses against disease transmission through individuals.

How do you manage wastewater and solid waste?

Grow-out ponds must make sure that any water discharged from the facility is devoid of pathogens. Implementing proper treatment and discharge practices will reduce the risk of disease within the ponds and their vicinity.

To treat wastewater, channel it from the ponds into a sedimentation pond. From there, treat the water using chlorination and dechlorination processes before discharging it. Do not discharge water close to the water supply intake point.

Introduction to aquaculture

FAO defines aquaculture as farming aquatic organisms with some form of intervention by individuals or corporates who own the stock being cultivated in the rearing process to enhance production. Manipulations of spawning/ breeding and stocking density, provision of aeration to supply dissolved oxygen, feeding with formulated feeds, and protection from predators are the forms of intervention in aquaculture. This definition implies that humans modify the life cycle of cultured animals. The modification of the life cycle of Nile tilapia by humans for aquaculture purposes is depicted in Figure 1.

For fish like Nile tilapia, the whole life cycle can be manipulated. However, in Africa, broodstock is still collected from the wild by many farmers. In commercial Nile tilapia culture, the sex of fish larvae is converted to males by hormonal manipulation. Larvae are then nursed using high-quality feeds to produce fish fry or juveniles for grow-out culture. There are two major types of grow-out systems in Africa – cage culture and pond culture – to rear fish up to marketable size. Some of the healthy fishes from the grow- out culture can be used as broodstock.
Introduction to the curriculum

There are two types of aquaculture: (1) non-commercial aquaculture; and (2) commercial aquaculture. Non-commercial aquaculture is mainly a small-scale family-business venture. It plays an extremely important role in contributing to food security and contributes to local aquaculture market chain. This curriculum is developed to assist in upgrading the aquaculture value chain and focuses mainly on commercial aquaculture. The major goal of commercial aquaculture is to maximize profits. Profit is one of the main performance indicators of the economic sustainability of commercial aquaculture.
4 | P a g e

Fixed cost of aquaculture operations arising from land, pond construction, cage frame and net-bags, equipment, fish seed, fingerling, feeds and feeding, oxygen supply, water pumping/ exchange, electricity, etc., account for the operation cost. Provided that the farm is already in operation (i.e. fixed cost has been fixed), the major cost for a practitioner is the operation cost. This curriculum is mainly developed to help farmers to improve the technical aspects of aquaculture with a session (or several sessions) dedicated to introducing the concepts of aquaculture business.

The aquaculture business should be economically viable or sustainable over time, which requires the business venture to be profitable and competitive to stay in the market. The latter requires the improvement of the production process as the market demand changes over time. Hence, the producers also should pay attention to the changing consumer demand and keep consumers satisfied with the product’s quality as well as the way the product is produced. Therefore, producers must respect the legal, environmental and social sustainability of aquaculture while making profits.

Legal sustainability: As with any other industrial sector, commercial aquaculture industry is governed by the laws and regulations of the particular country. Industrial stability is one of the criteria potential investors look for, and the laws and regulations are designed to make the sector stable. Thus, legal and economic sustainability are linked as investment is a necessary component to stay competitive in the market.

Social sustainability: Aquaculture should be socially acceptable to the local community where the production facility is located, and the product should be acceptable to the market, consumers, and various interest groups in the society that have a stake in the process, e.g., environmental groups monitoring the pollution effects. Moreover, the production operations should benefit a broader proportion of society, including women, young people, and the poor.

Environmental sustainability: Aquaculture should produce aquatic animals in responsible and ethical ways by reducing/ eliminating environmental pollution. All negative impacts of aquaculture should be reduced/ mitigated to maintain the integrity of aquatic ecosystems that the production process is embedded, thereby enabling farmers to continue production at the same site over time.

This course takes a holistic view of designing and delivering a curriculum aimed at promoting a sustainable aquaculture production process considering the total sustainability (economic, legal, social and environmental sustainability) of the business to ensure the future prosperity of the sector. The course is also focusing on the need for injection of new investments to upgrade the current systems to improve both the product quality and the production process.

One of the most important aspects of aquaculture production planning process is to address the following questions on the product and market characteristics, access to resources and the operation model:
Product:
1. What species to produce? e.g., Nile tilapia (this curriculum focus on Nile tilapia)
2. How much (the producer wants) to produce? e.g., the target quantity per crop (tonnes/ crop)
3. What quality? e.g. size of fish, taste, food safety

4. For whom to produce: i.e., the target markets, e.g. local market, processors, export market
5. What quality is demanded by market? e.g., the quality expected by the market, such as non- contamination of antibiotic and chemical residuals
6. The nature of the product: e.g., live, frozen, processed, and the individual weight of fish at harvest
7. What is the capacity of market? e.g., what quantities the market can be absorbed without over supply (supply of fish more than the demand reduces farm-gate price)

Session objectives:

Session narrative:

Fish reproduction is an extremely complex process. Fish represent one of the most diverse groups of organisms among vertebrates in their patterns of reproduction. From an evolutionary point of view, fish are a versatile group with nearly every kind of adaptation for reproduction – structural, physiological, as well as behavioural. Most fish reproduce sexually, and fertilize their eggs externally. However, there are some fish with internal fertilization of eggs; for example, the live-bearing sharks, freshwater fish guppy, platy, molly, etc. that deliver the young ones. Most fish reproduce seasonally. The gonads in fish remain small during non-reproductive season, and in general, the gametes are produced only during spawning season.

Tilapia as a group plays a great role in tropical aquaculture with the Nile tilapia, Oreochromis niloticus, holds great economic promise in providing food and nutritional security and creating rural employment. As tilapia farming expands worldwide, the demand for its seed for stocking in production ponds also increases. Besides, the fish continues to be introduced in many regions outside its natural habitats. It is therefore important to understand the basic biology and ecology of tilapia, particularly in relation to its reproduction. This will help to improve the efficiency of intensive seed production and minimize the impacts of tilapia farming on the environment.

Tilapia is a member of the family Cichlidae. Three genera are well-known, namely Oreochromis, Tilapia and Sarotherodon. Tilapia are endemic to Africa, Jordan, and Israel (more than 70 species), while only a few species are commercially important. Adult tilapia eat predominately vegetarian diets varying from macrophytes to phytoplankton, depending on species. Many structural features are related to the feeding habit, such as a terminal mouth, slender, notched teeth, long gill rakers, and long intestines (7 – 14 times the standard length) suitable for processing a plant diet.

This session outlines the reproductive biology of fish in general, and Nile tilapia in particular in relation to large-scale seed production of tilapia. Emphasis is given to the practical aspects of seed production and a short exercise to apply the skills learned by students from this session is included. A list of references for further reading are compiled at the end of this Module.
Reproductive cycle in fish

The reproductive cycle refers to the succession of processes in fish from immature germ cells to the production of mature gametes (eggs and sperm) that will finally unite and develop as the embryo. The process of formation, growth, and differentiation of gametes is called gametogenesis. This leads to the formation of female oocytes (oogenesis) and male spermatozoon (spermatogenesis). The reproductive cycle in both male and female involves two major phases – the ‘growth phase’ representing the phase of gonadal growth and development, and the ‘maturation phase’ leading to spermiation/ovulation and spawning. Spawning is the release of the mature gametes to the external environment, which is a highly synchronized event resulting in fertilization of the egg and embryo development. The successful progression of all these processes of the reproductive cycle resulting in production of good quality gametes is the basis of a successful event of reproduction in fish. The physiological aspects of the reproductive cycle are discussed in session 1.2.
Size at first maturity of Nile tilapia

The size and age at first maturity of tilapia varies with species and strains within the same species. Under natural conditions, Nile tilapia reaches sexual maturity at a size of 20–30 cm (150–250 g). However, in aquaculture ponds or under stressed environmental conditions Nile tilapia often reaches early maturity (30 – 50 g).
Identification of male and female tilapia

Water temperature has a significant effect on sex differentiation, sex ratio, and morphological development during early larval stages of tilapia, although at increased temperatures slow growth and body deformities may occur. Increased temperatures (34 – 360C) significantly increase the proportion of males (69 – 91%), while lower temperatures do not affect sex ratio.

Male and female fish can be identified by the shape and size of the genital papilla that is long and pointed in the case of male, and blunt in the case of females. Female body has three openings to the outside – the anus, urethra, and the opening of the oviduct in the form of a slit. Male is often larger than a female of the same age and has two openings to the outside – the anus, and the urinogenital aperture. These differences are easily distinguishable after the fish has grown to the size of 10 – 20 cm or 100 – 150 g, and are more pronounced during the breeding season when the male also develops a reddish colour around the jaws. Mode of reproduction of tilapia

Tilapias are nest builders and substrate spawners. Tilapia spp. guard the developing eggs and fry in the nests; Oreochromis spp. females incubate eggs and fry orally; and Sarotherodon spp. males and/or females incubate eggs and fry orally. Nile tilapia is a maternal mouthbrooder in which the fertilized eggs are incubated in the oral cavity of the female fish, similar to other species such as O. mossambicus and O. aureus.

The mode of reproduction in Nile tilapia is quite unique. The males build a spawning nest (Figure 3) by defending a breeding territory where only the visiting females ready for courtship will be allowed. The courtship lasts for a few hours followed by spawning by female repeatedly releasing a string of about 20 – 50 eggs followed by the male fertilizing the eggs by gently passing right over the eggs and releasing milt. Then the overturning female immediately captures all the eggs into her mouth for oral incubation (Figure 3). Often fertilization of tilapia eggs takes place inside the female’s buccal cavity after the female sucks up the milt as well as the eggs into her mouth cavity for fertilization and incubation.

Temperature and photoperiod are the most important factors influencing spawning. The breeding behaviour of most species of tilapia begins when water temperature reaches 200C, and spawning starts at 220C. Optimum spawning temperature for Nile tilapia range from 25 to 300C. In tropical regions,

spawning may continue year-round. Ripe females school in midwater with non-territorial males and egg- brooding females. 4 to 7 batches of eggs are spawned in one mating.

Photoperiod appears to have a significant role in reproductive performance of tilapia with the optimum reproductive performance taking place in normal daylength (12 h light : 12 h dark cycles). Other environmental factors that influence tilapia reproductive performance indicators such as size at first maturity and broodstock productivity include feeding and feed quality. Provision of good quality feed results in bigger size at first maturity and spawning.
Fecundity and egg size in tilapia

A characteristic feature of tilapia is low fecundity and relatively large egg size. Fecundity can be expressed as the number of mature ova in the ovary, the number of ovulated eggs, or the number of eggs deposited during spawning, all of which may vary for fish of equal size. Nile tilapia is reported to produce between <100 to >3000 eggs per spawn with the egg sizes ranging from <2.0 to >7.9 mm. Volume of eggs range from 2.8 to 11.1 mm3, each weighing up to 3.7 mg mean weight. Approximately 100 – 500 eggs can be expected from every spawning batch. On a practical point of view, it is ideal to refer to the fecundity of tilapia as the ‘number of fries produced per year’ considering the environmental variables that can affect egg and fry production.

Larval development involves the functional development of the mouth, 4-5 days after hatching (DAH) along with the absorption of yolk and development of swim bladder that aids in buoyancy control. In the natural breeding system, the mouth-breeding females can be left to the pond to incubate the eggs and release the free-swimming fry to the pond from where they can be collected for further rearing to fingerlings. In the artificial incubation and hatching system, the eggs and yolk sac fry are collected from the mouth of incubating females and incubated separately in specialised hatchery systems. Reproductive physiology of fish refers to the overall progression of the physiological processes related to reproduction right from egg fertilization to embryo development, hatching, growth and puberty, male and female gonadal development and gametogenesis, sexual behaviour, timing of reproductive cycles, and endocrine and environmental control, all of which culminate in spawning. Internally, all these events associated with reproduction are regulated by the endocrine (hormonal) system in fish associated with the brain-pituitary-gonadal axis.
