5 THE CHALLENGES TO AND OPPORTUNITIES FOR CGIAR’S DIGITAL EXTENSION SERVICES

From research to rollout, challenges remain in getting the right information to the right people in the field. From validating site-specific data to adoption by farmers of digital technologies, to balancing site-specific recommendations with the need for information over large areas, these hurdles also present great opportunities.
Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics (ICRISAT)’s Plantix app works collaboratively with farmers to combat the diseases and pests that matter to them.
Trust: Navigating Digital Overload
Equity: Bridging the Digital Divide

• Leave no farmer behind. Farmers who do not have access to ICTs or regular contact with technicians are difficult to reach. These farmers (especially the women) are often uneducated, and have little access to the internet and mobile phone networks. Yet, reaching these farmers is essential to CGIAR’s mission. Bridging this digital divide means understanding how the poorest benefit from digital technologies, and how digitalization will directly and indirectly affect farmers who do not have digital access. For example, the International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center (CIMMYT)’s AgroTutor Mobile App provides specific information to 500,000 farmers in Mexico who have no extension agents. This allows for feedback, dialogue, and improved recommendations. In other contexts, SMS or IVR messages are more effective. Different solutions reach different farmers. Building national agricultural research systems’ digital capacity is an essential part of
the mission to leave no farmer behind.

• Make it simple and usable. It is essential to incorporate social and sustainable contexts into digital extension service projects in order to increase the number of farmers who engage with the project. It is one thing to download an app and another to correctly diagnose a problem on the farm and get proper help. Human-centric design places farmers at the center of the innovation and implementation process. For example, the International Crops

• Quality information. CGIAR is uniquely qualified to plan, build, and facilitate partnerships to democratize high-quality science, accurate data, and reliable tools. In partnership with local governments and national agricultural research systems, CGIAR ensures the distribution of quality, accurate, and relevant data.
• Trusted and tailored information.

Inaccurate advice and mixed information on issues of uncertainty or data privacy cause mistrust that is hard to repair. CGIAR has a distinct advantage because it can package science-backed knowledge through its partnerships with trusted start-ups, field entrepreneurs, donors, and governments. In short, CGIAR’s information comes from trusted sources. CGIAR’s information is also tailored: CGIAR integrates varied state-of-the- art data sources and modeling approaches. For example, ICRISAT’s Intelligent Agricultural Systems Advisory Tool leverages relationships between researchers, tech companies, and the government to deliver complex weather information. This information is then distilled into climate-informed advisories that are tailored to the needs of farmers.

• Big data. CGIAR has been collecting long- term data for many years in some regions. This work, combined with CGIAR’s advanced technologies and ICT skills, gives CGIAR scientists an advantage in tackling current and future problems in agriculture. For example, the 14-year-old Consortium for Improving

Agriculture-Based Livelihoods in Central Africa (CIALCA), which is led by the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA), Bioversity International, and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), is starting to yield data that can predict threats to food security across Africa. This information can be used to create early warning systems that prepare the population.

• Open data and data privacy. CGIAR provides data, knowledge, and tools for the public domain - through its Gardian platform, for example. CGIAR researchers are mindful of data privacy and the protection of farmers. Keeping up to date on privacy regulations, making data a public good, and encouraging partners to do the same are ongoing and important challenges for CGIAR. Such efforts are essential to safeguarding farmers from incorrect data privacy regulation in order to ensure that vulnerable communities are not exploited by digital technology and incorrect information.
Efficiency: The Power of Partnerships
Building long-lasting relationships. CGIAR

operates in more than 70 countries across institutions, sectors, and borders. Working with CGIAR creates powerful collaborative opportunities. For instance, digital services in Latin America connect a network of over 350 partners. These partners share the common goal of reducing climate change-related risk in agriculture. CGIAR has collaborative relationships that span more than 50 years. Because CGIAR can draw on a trusted network of partners, it can create successful digital extension solutions.
• Supporting the digital ecosystem. Digital tools are often developed by private-sector start-ups that have the know-how, time, and capital to invest in testing technology. However,

start-ups often need extra support to meet their developmental goals. Combining start- up innovation with CGIAR’s extensive scientific network delivers on both fronts. CGIAR can navigate relationships in different sectors to bring reliable information to farmers in a cohesive and organized manner. For example, the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI)’s Easy Harvest combines research and public and private-sector resources to offer farmers a fast and efficient method for booking combine harvesters during the busy harvest seasons in the Philippines.
Bringing a Message to Scale

• Triple bottom-line goals. CGIAR facilitates successful business models while improving livelihoods and helping the environment. CGIAR has triple bottom-line goals that ensure social, environmental, and financial progress. For example, the International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI) and Digital Green, a leader in developing technology, both use impact assessments to monitor their financial, social, and developmental goals. Tracking and monitoring goals and assessing impacts are an essential part of research.

• Digital infrastructure. Many countries lack sufficient policy, infrastructure, and institutional capacity for digital extension services and data sharing. CGIAR can create opportunities for these countries and build their strategies. Ultimately, CGIAR aims to unite its partners toward a common goal: tackling food insecurity and boosting food production across regions, countries, and sectors.

A PEST AND DISEASE EARLY WARNING AND ADVISORY SYSTEM
THE WHY, WHAT, AND HOW

Farmers in Isabela Province, Philippines, grow cassava for livestock feed and industrial use. Crop productivity in this region, as in most of Southeast Asia, is strongly limited by pests and diseases. In partnership with the Philippines Department of Agriculture, the International Center for Tropical Agriculture (CIAT) surveyed approximately 250 cassava farmers in Isabela Province in 2018. The survey documented pest, disease, and farm management data from 400 plots and 700 cropping events across two cropping seasons. CIAT scientists combined these data with climate and soil data that they gathered based on the GPS location of each plot. They used these combined data to build machine-learning models that focus on cassava
witches’ broom disease, the most prevalent disease in the region. These models employ recent weather data to predict the prevalence of the disease in a given plot.

The models’ predictions are 80% accurate. This degree of accuracy is very promising. CIAT aims to use these data to pilot an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered chatbot that monitors pests and diseases and administers early warning and advisory services. CIAT’s goal is for this service (i) to use model outputs to provide tactical advice, and (ii) to gather data for further model improvement. The service must also be accurate, efficient, and automated.

Lessons learned

The local weather and soil data are not very precise. Only one agrometeorological station is operating in Isabela Province, which means that the weather dataset is not specific enough. The contributing organizations used open data sources to obtain local weather data. Similarly, most farmers in Isabela Province have never had their soil tested. Consequently, the contributing organizations were unable to collect soil data via farm surveys. Instead, they used

the International Soil Reference and Information Centre (ISRIC) World Soil Information platform, which provides global data for soils of different depths and parameters. Accurately documenting survey data was challenging. To accomplish this, the contributing organizations developed a mobile app for rapid data collection and storage. The app was successful and the raw data were synced into an online database for storage and analysis.

Seed Information Exchange
THE WHY, WHAT, AND HOW

In Ethiopia, seed supply companies produce and distribute crop seed to farmers each season. Some areas experience seed shortages, while others have excess. This is due to a lack of communication and coordination. In order to address this challenge, Bioversity International and the Integrated Seed Sector Development (ISSD) program in Ethiopia have developed Seed Information Exchange. This online platform allows seed companies to make their stocks publicly visible. Any stakeholder that is looking for seed can use the platform to discover which companies have seed, where they are located, and how to access the supply. The platform aims to decrease misinformation and
increase transparency in the seed sector.

Seed Information Exchange has two components: an online web dashboard and an offline stock editor app that can be installed on any computer. Seed suppliers enter stock data using the stock editor. As soon as the device connects to the internet, the data go into the cloud and the online dashboard is updated. Seed buyers can use the web dashboard to learn about seed supply, availability, and location. Importantly, the Ministry of Agriculture of Ethiopia has approved this program and will be supporting it in the long term.

AGRIAPP: A MULTIFUNCTIONAL DIGITAL SERVICE FOR RICE FARMERS IN VIETNAM
THE WHY, WHAT, AND HOW

Agricultural extension agents and service providers do not have access to real-time, high-resolution data on how farmers manage their farms, for instance, about when they plant, what they plant, when they spray, and how these processes change between seasons. This dearth of information prevents the agents from helping farmers make decisions in a tailored, timely manner. Farmers are thus skeptical of these services and recommendations.

Digital innovations could help resolve these issues. High- resolution biophysical datasets are becoming increasingly accessible. AI can find patterns in huge, complex datasets. Mobile technology can collect farm data quickly and accurately. Used together, these technologies can analyze farm-level management information in the context of

huge datasets and rapidly deliver tailored, practical advice to farmers. This is exactly the idea behind AgriApp. AgriApp collects farm management data, accesses big datasets, and uses AI to rapidly generate and deliver customized recommendations directly to farmers.

AgriApp also offers income incentive to farmers. Data are collected from farmers in real time and then fed into the AgriApp system. This is packaged as traceable information that the farmer can use to earn additional income at the end of the season. In the short term, this traceability function will help AgriApp gather enough users to capture sufficient data. In the long term, farmers will experience real gains from the relevant, useful advice that the system generates.

DATA-DRIVEN AGRICULTURE
THE WHY, WHAT, AND HOW

In alliance with the National Cereals and Legumes Federation (FENALCE), CIAT has developed a system that enables farmers and local technicians in northern Colombia to compile their crop management information into a large dataset. These data are combined with multiple other data sources, including weather forecasts, to deliver crop management information in the form of a checklist- like report called FENALCHECK. The system was built from scratch, with a lack of reliable preexisting data. Within 2 years, its first recommendations proved to be successful in on-farm trials.1 The FENALCHECK report indicated which factors were associated with high yields and provided a checklist of recommended practices. These practices were sent to 575 farmers via IVR and SMS technology, so 90% of
these farmers had access to data-driven advice.

This system is driven by a multi-disciplinary, multi- institutional team that compiles and interprets data in the Sistema de Recolección de Información Agrícola (SIRIA) web platform and then translates it into practical, relevant recommendations. Diverse experts, including analysts, agronomists, researchers, knowledge managers, and communications personnel, help ensure that the recommendations are both accurate and accessible. The team explicitly abides by findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable (FAIR) data principles, and uses freely available data tools whenever possible.

Summary

Improving agricultural productivity in Ethiopia is crucial to alleviate poverty and meet growing food demand amid environmental stress and climate change. Agricultural innovation and access to digital agricultural solutions have the potential to boost productivity while reducing negative environmental footprints in agriculture and food system value chains. However, most smallholder farmers in Ethiopia have limited access to digital farming solutions. A disruptive approach is required to overcome crises in the sector and boost productivity to meet ecosystem needs and the related service demands of a growing population. Digital readiness is crucial to embrace and deploy existing technologies and transform agriculture.

With the world moving towards a digital economy over the past decade, Ethiopia has made significant progress in laying the groundwork for digital agriculture solutions. However, Ethiopia’s digital agriculture is still in its infancy, with very few digital service providers and a handful of government-led digital initiatives. An overview of Ethiopia’s digital agriculture ecosystem reveals that digital solutions are provided by a variety of public, private, international development and research institutions, and non-governmental organizations. Most of the digital solutions focus primarily on digital tools and advisory services for smallholder farmers. Less attention is paid to reliable digital data creation, big data storage and sharing, data analytics, and other critical digital content development components.

There are several challenges hampering the development of digital agriculture in Ethiopia. Access to advanced agricultural, knowledge, and information technologies is constrained due to weak digital infrastructure and facilities in the country. This includes limited data sharing policies and implementation guidelines to facilitate the collection and storage of, and access to, data to support digital solutions. The low digital literacy rate is another barrier to the expansion of ICT2 -based agricultural extension and consulting services. The majority of farmers have limited technical capacity to adopt digital services and products. Limited financing to support the launch and upscaling of digital products and services also limits the advancement of digital agriculture in Ethiopia.

Digital agriculture has the potential to support and incentivize agri-tech entrepreneurship to boost innovations and job creation in agriculture and related industries. However, opportunities for the private sector to fill technological gaps and provide efficient digital
2 Information and Communication Technology

solutions are not well utilized in Ethiopia. Public-private partnerships to catalyze agricultural digitalization remain nascent. Currently, few private sector initiatives and start- ups provide digital agriculture solutions. This is expected to change with recent government policy reform focusing on private sector-led growth, which opens the space for private sector innovation in diverse fields. The government’s ten-year development plan provides an opportunity to move towards digital agriculture. The plan aims to increase the share of private sector jobs in technology and digitalization from 50% to 80%, as well as to support and promote tech start-ups that have the greatest promise of large economic and social impacts.

Political and economic reforms ratified in recent years have significantly altered the digital infrastructure and connectivity landscape, paving the way for digital agriculture to thrive. The government’s recent telecom market liberalization, nationwide skill development, and enhancement of implementation capacity are important developments towards agricultural transformation, with an increased role of the private sector in offering digital solutions.

The potential for digital agriculture in Ethiopia is untapped. Reaping its benefits requires well-designed strategies and measures implemented at various levels. Fundamental measures that should be taken to accelerate digital agriculture in Ethiopia include: developing ICT3 infrastructure and big data analytics capacity; creating institutional mechanisms for high quality data management systems; supporting user- driven digital technology innovations; streamlining agricultural research, extension, and education systems to proactively accommodate digital products and services; and allowing the private sector to play an unrestricted role. The success of these measures relies on collaboration of state and non-state actors, including development partners, to harmonize efforts and create synergy among the digital agriculture interventions that are being developed.
Introduction

Ethiopia has a total land area of approximately 1.14 million km2.It is known as “the land of origins,” where many important archeological and paleontological milestones have been uncovered. It is Africa’s second most populous country, with an estimated 120 million people.4 In addition, the country has the largest and most diverse livestock population in Africa. Ethiopia has varied geography; its elevation ranges from 4,550

meters above sea level (Ras Dashen peaks) to 110 meters below sea level (Afar Depressions). The country is thus endowed with diverse agro-ecologies and biodiversity. Ethiopia is known as the Water Tower of East Africa due to its large, trans-boundary rivers.

Despite its potential, Ethiopia is still a developing country. Agriculture employs more than 75% of the population. Climate change, specifically variability in rainfall, has a significant impact on agriculture. Despite these challenges, the country has recently experienced healthy economic growth. In the 2019–2020 fiscal year, real GDP5 grew by 6.1% compared to 3.5% average growth predicted for sub-Saharan Africa as a whole.6 This rise in real GDP can be attributed to 9.6% growth in industry, 5.3% growth in services, and 4.3% growth in agriculture. The agricultural sector contributed 22.9% of GDP growth on average, with the crops sub-sector contributing 65%. The industrial sector contributed 42.6%, with the construction and manufacturing sub- sectors contributing 72.6% and 23.9%, respectively, to overall GDP growth in the industrial sector. The service sector has contributed to 34.5% of GDP growth.7 Despite recent rapid growth, nominal GDP per capita remains low at USD 1,0808 compared to USD 1,586 in sub-Saharan Africa and USD 11,312 globally.9

Although it is the engine of Ethiopia’s economic growth and provides a large portion of the country’s foreign exchange earnings, the agricultural system is characterized by low productivity, low input use, and limited capacity to respond to environmental shocks. As a result, the country faces a daunting challenge: produce more food for a rapidly growing population on low-fertility soils under uncertain climatic conditions and in a sector dominated by poor smallholder farmers who cannot afford adequate input use. To address this challenge, the sector must be transformed through effective use of technology throughout the entire value chain. Modernizing the system through digital transformation can boost productivity while also promoting resilience. Embracing the transformation of agriculture with digital solutions in big data analytics (e.g., programming, artificial intelligence, modelling), as well as digital communication of agricultural technologies, tools, and advisory services, is critical to attract youth to study and practice agriculture.

Digital transformation is the journey from an analogue society, where government, business, and social interactions take place in person, to a fully integrated inclusive digital economy where transactions become faster, cheaper, and more secure using technology, and where most interactions take place online.10 The term “digital economy” refers to economic activity that utilizes the enhanced interconnectivity of networks and the interoperability of digital platforms.11 It is born through the combination of two key network developments:12 (i) the internet, and (ii) IP13-enabled communications systems—such as mobile networks, electronic payment systems, and public service networks.

Digital technologies have been touted as potentially revolutionary solutions to improve the performance and sustainability of agricultural production systems through economic, social, and environmental dimensions. The agri-food sector can be made more efficient, inclusive, and environmentally sustainable through application of digital technologies, thereby increasing benefits to farmers, consumers, and society at large.14 Digital technologies can help to raise on-farm productivity, improve resource-use efficiency, and support climate resilience.15 Implementation of digital technologies can lead to notable improvements in primary production and supply chain and logistics performance, and reductions in food loss and waste.16

Digital agriculture (or “smart farming”) refers to the design, development, and use of digital technologies in agriculture and the wider agri-food sector.17 It encompasses a range of technologies that include sensors, robots, digital communication tools, blockchains, computational decision and analytical tools, and cloud-based technologies.18 In the context of the UN Sustainable Development Goals, digital agriculture has the potential to deliver economic benefits through increased agricultural productivity, cost efficiency, and market opportunities; social and cultural benefits

More specifically, it helps farmers to access technical information, obtain higher quality seeds, collect real-time data, improve the traceability of food, and enhance competitiveness.21 Therefore, it is an innovative solution to problems faced in the current global food system.

Evidence based on a meta-analysis of six studies shows that the transmission of agricultural information through mobile technologies has increased yields by 4% in sub- Saharan Africa and India and has enhanced the likelihood of adopting recommended agrochemical inputs by 22%.22 In Europe, an increase of 10% in digitization results in 1.4% growth in GDP per capita.23 Given its benefits as observed in many regions of the world, digital transformation of agriculture is essential for developing countries such as Ethiopia. Considering that agriculture is the basis of the global economy and people’s livelihoods, and has tended to be neglected in terms of the application of new technologies, agricultural improvement should be supported with the best available solutions (such as digital systems and technologies), targeting these to agriculturalists in developing countries, who are most in need.

Agricultural production systems

Ethiopia’s agricultural sector is dominated by small- scale farmers who practice rain-fed mixed farming with traditional technology and a low-input, low-output production system. Smallholder households account for more than 90% of total agricultural output.27 They generate income from agricultural production either in cash or through personal consumption. Despite efforts to commercialize and transform agriculture from subsistence to production of high-value crops, performance has been below expectations.28 The failure to achieve projected agricultural productivity levels is related to the coverage and quality of agricultural technology use, as well as the agricultural extension system in general, both of which could be addressed by promoting digital agriculture.
People, livelihoods, and agriculture

Ethiopia’s population was estimated at 120 million in 2021.29 Those under the age of 29 years account for 69% of the population (76 million people). The median age is 19.1 years. This brief summarizes WorldFish’s work on fish-based products in seven countries across three continents over the past 10 years. It is based on an e-learning event that brought country teams together to document approaches, lessons and research priorities. Fish- based products are a cornerstone of WorldFish’s work. Piloting and/or scaling products such as dried fish and fish powder have been a core component of its aquatic food system research for development and nutrition-sensitive programs, providing a link between production systems and consumer well-being.
Potential benefits of fish-based products:
L —
Nutrition & food security

Fish and fish-based products contain high levels of essential micronutrients, such as calcium, iron and zinc, as well as fatty acids, like omega-3, to support optimal human health. Their nutritional profile is particularly suited to meet the needs of women and children during the first 1000 days of life,1–3 as well as for growing brains in school-aged children. Often more affordable than other animal-source foods, fish and fish-based products are also rich in high-quality protein, contributing to healthy diets and food security for billions of resource-poor households.4–7 Fish-based products that use the whole fish during processing are more nutrient dense compared to the flesh only and can be prepared in powder form, making them suitable for infants, who have small stomachs.8

Many fish-based products are ready to eat or easy to prepare, and some can be kept without refrigeration. Such qualities are valuable for time-poor carers seeking to prepare nutritious meals at home or in public institutions, as well as in contexts that lack reliable cold chains and refrigeration, as is common in many low- and middle-income countries.
Convenience

Processing fish can add value, generating additional income for fishers and fish farmers, and/or providing income-generating opportunities for value chain actors, including women’s groups and young entrepreneurs.

Women’s empowerment

Fish-based products create opportunities for women’s participation in aquatic food systems and for their economic empowerment. In many countries, women lead fish post-harvesting operations and processing.9 Women’s employment in aquatic food systems can generate important income, which can facilitate greater household access to nutritious foods, increase women’s perceived social standing and lead to greater control over resources and to asset ownership. Increasing the visibility of women’s work and contributions to the fishery sector further supports shifts in detrimental social norms.

Inclusion

Fish-based products have potential to create more inclusive food systems. They can facilitate access to aquatic foods for marginalized populations that might not have refrigeration or live far from production systems. They can also be distributed in public food procurement initiatives, such as school meal programs (SMPs), enabling access for school-aged children.10 However, this potential depends on the affordability of such products for nutritionally vulnerable groups, as value addition is bound to increase costs. This highlights an area of tension between developing products for rural income opportunities and low-cost products for nutrition.

Sustainability

Aquatic foods can be produced with a lower environmental footprint compared to most terrestrial animal-source foods11–13 and can therefore be a key component of sustainable and resilient diets. Fish- based products can provide a useful pathway for dealing with seasonal abundance, thereby extending shelf life and availability, and reducing waste. Furthermore, making products from small indigenous fish species (SIS) uses an often-undervalued natural resource.1,14 Although SIS face several threats, exploring their polyculture with other aquatic animals can be a climate-resilient adaptation strategy.15

Partnerships

The development and scaling of fish-based products have potential to form a basis for strong multisectoral partnerships that further stimulate discussions on fish for improved nutrition and livelihoods, and sustainable fisheries management. These include public–private partnerships, engaging the non-for-profit sector, and creating new collaborations across fisheries and agriculture, health, education, social inclusion and equality, rural development, women and youths.

Across all seven countries covered in this brief (Figure 1), high malnutrition and low dietary quality are significant public health challenges. Stunting, a key indicator of the burden of malnutrition, ranges from 26.7 percent in Myanmar to 46.7 percent in Timor-Leste.16 Current annual per capita fish consumption differs widely, from 73 kg in Solomon Islands17—well above the world average of 20.5 kg9—down to 6.1 kg in Timor-Leste.18 Yet all seven countries report poor incorporation of aquatic foods in complementary foods for infants and young children, even though they have coastlines or inland waters that avail abundant aquatic foods. Reflecting on this opportunity, WorldFish activities on fish- based products have often targeted infants and children from conception until 2 years of age—also referred to as the first 1000 days of life—as well as pregnant and lactating women. Cambodia

Since 2012, WorldFish has led projects on fish-based products in Cambodia, where malnutrition costs up to USD 266 million annually. Use of SIS is considered one solution to address malnutrition in the country. These fish species, typically consumed whole, are rich sources of essential nutrients beneficial for infants and young children during the first 1000 days of life. The rice field fisheries system, or community fish refuge, which includes canals, refuge ponds, other associated waterways and flooded rice fields, is the source of open access fresh SIS for communities. Four SIS have been used to make products such as small fish powder, which has been promoted continuously by WorldFish for over 10 years and by Save the Children since 2016; another product is Num Trey, a supplementary snack promoted by UNICEF and Vissot, a Danish food company. The purpose of SIS product promotion has been to reduce the risk of micronutrient deficiencies in children, contribute to the targets of the National Strategy for Food Security and Nutrition, and use SIS during offseason periods. Fish powders made from SIS have been tested and found to be high in protein and essential micronutrients, such

as omega-3 fatty acids, zinc, vitamin B12 and calcium, and they have a long shelf life. WorldFish is scaling efforts with the aim to train producers to process small fish powder for sale, pilot commercial production and promote products through social media. Potential focal areas in the future include breeding and culturing small fish, as well as refining, diversifying and scaling out SIS products commercially.

Bangladesh

In 2012–2013, WorldFish initiated a project in Bangladesh to improve the nutritional status of children under 2 years old and pregnant or lactating mothers. This innovation project aimed to increase protein and micronutrient intake and dietary diversity through fish consumption in the first 1000 days of life. Activities included coordinating production systems, distribution and promotion, and using locally sourced small fish dried in a community-run facility. Nutrition field facilitators conducted nutrition education alongside social marketing activities at the community level. The project developed dried fish powder as a complementary food for infants and fish chutney/pickle for mothers, both containing additional ingredients like onion, garlic, spices and oil. Nutrient content analysis showed a rich nutritional profile. Although only representing a small number of participants, the endline survey found significant improvements in anemia status and food consumption scores among the target groups.19 Two additional projects focused on interventions for value addition where a private sector partner, Bengal Fish, processed fish for urban communities. Another initiative with ethnic hilltribe communities used a similar approach, with an additional focus on gender equity, though it faced challenges because of COVID-19 restrictions. The projects also faced affordability and accessibility issues from the high cost and scarcity of small fish. Efforts were made to develop quality standards for fish-based products, which the government adopted, and also to scale up the project’s impact through links with entrepreneurs and ongoing market- oriented initiatives. Further research is needed to assess the long-term impact of fish-based products on nutritional status and improved livelihoods, and to provide comprehensive solutions that also address declining coastal fisheries resources.

Timor-Leste

From 2017 to 2020, WorldFish Timor-Leste worked with a rural coastal women’s group to improve livelihoods through the sale of fish-based products, mainly fish powder. The group received training in microenterprise establishment and marketing to sell fish powder to urban consumers; however, members faced challenges when it came to sustaining activities after project completion. Nevertheless, there remains substantial opportunity for scaling fish powder and similar fish-based products that are safe, culturally acceptable, convenient to prepare and do not require refrigeration. In particular, WorldFish has investigated the potential for supplying fish and fish powder in the national SMP. Nutrient content analyses of three fish powders by WorldFish partner CSIRO—two made by the women’s group using marine and farmed fish, and one sold commercially—found that all had outstanding macro and micronutrient profiles that could contribute significantly to the recommended nutrient intake for school-aged children. In 2023, WorldFish also successfully piloted supplying fresh tilapia to 1000 students from nearby fish farms, using iceboxes on motorbikes to overcome the lack of cold

chain facilities. However, research also indicates that supplying fish to all SMP students would require a substantial proportion of national fisheries production.20 This supply challenge, as well as affordability and food safety issues, were discussed at a WorldFish-organized workshop by government and development partners, including one that had included a locally made fish powder in the SMP in four municipalities. Further research is planned on fish powder scalability trade-offs and the mosaic of approaches required to supply fish to all SMP students.

India

Recognizing the potential of aquatic foods, WorldFish India implements innovative strategies to enhance dietary diversity and micronutrient intake, especially among women, children and other vulnerable populations. WorldFish started piloting projects with school feeding initiatives in Odisha in 2019 and Assam in 2022, using marine and freshwater small fish to produce dried fish products, with the aim to improve nutrition and health outcomes. In Odisha, the project promoted carp–mola polyculture and the provision of fresh fish, which was difficult to sustain because of cold chain and supply limitations. The approach changed to include easy-to-use fish powder and paste for children in preschool and school meal programs, and dried fish for adolescent girls and pregnant and lactating women. Acceptability tests among participating tribal communities were successful. This influenced the Government of Odisha to promote hygienic certified dried fish production by engaging Women Self-Help Groups through a 5-year livelihood project with WorldFish. In Assam, awareness programs promoted the consumption of fish powder among 10,300 children in preschools and primary schools in 2022 and 2023, with plans for further expansion. Product testing and certifications addressed the government’s concerns on food safety. In a third state, Bihar, the focus is on empowering caretakers to prepare fish powder at home using locally available small fish and through effective social and behavioral change communication strategies. WorldFish plans to scale up these efforts in collaboration with local communities and governments by developing value-added fish products and assessing their impact on nutritional status.

Zambia

Since 2017, WorldFish Zambia has promoted the consumption of fish-based products to encourage adequate dietary intake for pregnant and lactating women, infants and young children. WorldFish trialed two partnership approaches for scaling the production of nutritious fish-based products: (1) at a commercial scale with the private sector and (2) at the household level through women farmers. Working with companies such as Sylva Food Solutions and EUNIMOS, WorldFish produced instant porridges using locally available ingredients fortified with fish powder from kapenta (Limnothrissa miodon and Stolothrissa tanganicae), a pelagic small fish rich in iron, iodine, vitamin A and zinc. Laboratory analyses showed good nutrient levels for both porridges, ranging from 10.8 to 15.5 g of protein and from 1.7 to 6.1 g of fat per 100 g of dry weight. Qualitative taste testing indicated that children generally liked the smell, appearance, texture and flavor. The porridges’ short preparation time was valued among women to help engage fathers in child feeding. Moreover, WorldFish worked with small and medium enterprises to produce quality products, including smoked fish, fish sausages and fish pies. To scale these products at the household level, women received training to make fish powder with SIS from ponds and lakes. A recipe book demonstrated how to integrate fish powder into popular dishes, and was promoted at festivals and through digital media. Collaborating with Mississippi State University, the Department of Fisheries and the Ministry of Health, WorldFish trained caregivers, businesspeople and community health

workers on the importance of consuming fish and preparing recipes using fish powder—important since many of the fish caught are sold and exported. Future work could target urban and peri-urban areas and investigate safe fish powder storage. Additionally, advocacy for the integration of fish powder into homegrown SMPs, reaching more than 2.3 million pupils in Zambia, could boost more nutritious meals.

Myanmar

From 2021 to 2023, WorldFish Myanmar worked with two local business—FedWell Foods and MMKM Food Company—to develop nutritious fish-based products using small pelagic fish for children and pregnant and lactating women. The partner company was identified through local business networks and a competitive bidding process. Four products were developed—porridge, cookies, chickpea balls and noodles— each containing small fish powder, chickpea powder, moringa and orange sweet potato as the main ingredients. Spices were added to improve consumer acceptability after sensory testing. Nutrient content analyses showed the products are high in protein, calcium, iron and zinc. Designs for packaging were developed by a branding agency, resulting in the Happy Fish brand. Marketing occurred through social media, cooking events with celebrities, and stalls at fairs and nutrition events. Other information materials, including a cookbook, were also produced. Youths and women were engaged as sales agents and provided with nutrition and financial literacy

training, and they received sales commissions. The company is currently producing 200–300 packages per month. Challenges included disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic and the country’s political crisis, as well as daily power outages affecting production and the rising costs of ingredients. The products are more nutrient-dense but more expensive than similar products. There is good potential for fish-based products to support nutrition among target populations, such as by developing products tailored for the prevention and treatment of malnourishment, thereby reducing reliance on imported products; however, addressing affordability and improving nutrition awareness are critical.

Solomon Islands

WorldFish Solomon Islands has focused efforts on improving fish handling and aquatic food safety, rather than specific fish- based product development. From 2016 to 2020, WorldFish worked with the West ‘Are’Are Rokotanikeni Association to trial solar-powered freezers managed by rural women saving’s groups. Current work focuses on developing a fish handling training package in partnership with Solomon Islands National University and national and provincial government fisheries staff and also on piloting a youth-led processed fish business. Fish consumption is high at the national level; however, nutritionally vulnerable groups such as women, young children, and people living further inland consume lower amounts. Fish-based products are important in Solomon Islands cuisine—in particular, canned tuna is commercially produced in the country, widely consumed and part of the national identity. Developing other fish-based products has potential to increase consumption for specific groups while supporting rural livelihoods and covering seasonal shortfalls in catches. For instance, opportunities exist to improve infant and young children feeding practices and the diets of pregnant and lactating women through fresh fish. Other ongoing work includes developing nutrition-sensitive fisheries guidelines and establishing a national program with government and other partners to improve fish handling. Future work could explore the cultural acceptability of fish-based products, such as fish powder, as a complementary food, as well as consider their feasibility as avenues for income generation.

Key lessons and research priorities

For over 10 years, WorldFish has been leading innovative and nutrition-sensitive projects on fish-based products. Several key lessons emerged from the shared work on developing fish- based products, which we have synthesized next. To continue our scientific work and scaling for impact, strategic research priorities are also highlighted.
1. Work to develop fish-based products can aim for
impact in nutrition, livelihoods and women’s economic participation. However, ensuring product affordability while also providing decent income for small-scale producers remains an area of tension.

The objectives of WorldFish projects on fish-based products have spanned multiple impact areas, including nutrition, livelihoods and women’s economic participation. Improving nutritional intake among vulnerable groups has been the main theme of most projects. In particular, activities have aimed to diversify diets, promote micronutrient intake and contribute to addressing issues such as stunting and underweight among children by leveraging fish consumption. Many of the same projects have also promoted local production and sale of fish-based products to enhance rural livelihoods and the economic participation of women, while a couple have focused predominantly on value adding for rural income generation without a specific nutrition component. This highlights the potential multifaceted benefits to be obtained through the development of fish-based products. However, questions remain on the affordability of such products, particularly on how to ensure a fair price for producers as well as access for those who need them most.

Future research could usefully consider affordability, profitability and accessibility trade-offs, as well as consumer product uptake and behavior change to understand enablers and barriers to access. Product development work could also consider options to use different parts of the same fish for different value-added and nutrition-supplement products.

2. Marine, freshwater and farmed fish are an important source of nutritious, tasty and culturally acceptable products, from powders to pickles to porridges. Other aquatic foods such as seaweed may also offer potential resources for future product development.

Across the seven countries, there are examples of fish-based products made from freshwater, marine and farmed finfish, reflecting the aquatic resources available in each context. For instance, freshwater SIS have been central to the past 10 years of work on fish-based product development in Cambodia and Bangladesh. This typically undervalued natural resource is caught in open access fishing grounds and provides a free or low-cost input that keeps the resultant fish powder product affordable and accessible to many. However, like products reliant on natural marine resources, maintaining a reliable and sufficient supply of fish is an ongoing challenge, compounded by habitat degradation and climate change.

Similarly, a variety of products have been developed to suit the tastes and preferences of the different contexts, including fish powders, dried fish, fermented pastes, chutneys and porridges. Fish powder has been the main product developed and scaled across six countries, largely because of its high

nutrient density, shelf-stable properties and suitability for feeding infants and children. In particular, it addresses common fears of children choking on fish bones. Some fish powders are made by pounding or grinding dried whole fish, while others include spices and/or other nutrient-rich ingredients, such as prawns and moringa leaves. The versatility of fish powder is further highlighted through the various ways its consumption is promoted. In some countries, it is used alone as a seasoning to add to local foods, while elsewhere it has been incorporated into an array of products, including noodles, cookies, chickpea balls and instant porridge. Product refinement to improve consumer acceptability in terms of taste, smell and ease of use was highlighted as an important step for successful uptake of recipes. Furthermore, consideration of how new or enhanced foods integrate into local cooking styles and meals, as well as gender considerations, was also an important criterion for success. These considerations underscore the importance of designing products and projects that leverage traditional practices and knowledge, while promoting culturally relevant interventions in improving dietary diversity and nutrition.

Future research could also explore the potential of aquatic foods other than finfish to create or complement nutritious and sustainable fish-based products, such as seaweeds, bivalves or other aquatic plants, which in certain contexts could have the added advantage of supporting women-led fisheries.

3. Fish powders and similar context-specific products have good potential for improving undernutrition in vulnerable population groups, particularly infants during the first 1000 days of life, pregnant and lactating women, and school-aged children.

Improving nutrition and health outcomes of nutritionally vulnerable groups has been the core aim of most fish-based products developed through WorldFish. In all seven countries, diversifying diets and improving the nutritional intake of children in the first 1000 days of life is an important priority. Multiple products have been designed as complementary foods, such as fish powders and porridges, targeting infants and young children ranging from 6 months to 2 years of age. Engagement of mothers and pregnant or lactating women is critical for reaching this age group. Importantly, most fish-based products developed have been analyzed for their nutrient composition.

School-aged children are another key target population for fish-based products, and possibilities to include fish in SMPs have been considered to varying degrees across most of the seven countries. For example, WorldFish teams in both India and Timor-Leste recently piloted supplying fish and fish-based products to preschools or schools as part of SMPs. Supplying fresh fish met similar challenges in both contexts, particularly associated with the lack of cold chain infrastructure and time required for meal preparation. The project in India has since transitioned to developing fish-based products, which are easier to administer, targeting children and their mothers. Countries in Africa also mentioned challenges associated with incorporating fish powder into SMPs because of cost and supply issues, while in some Southeast Asian nations, like Cambodia, fresh fish is included in the government's SMP as an affordable animal- source food, and in Myanmar some organizations are testing fish powder as part of supplementary programs.

Future research could design impact evaluation studies using rigorous methods to assess the efficacy, effectiveness, cost-efficiency, safety and equity considerations of fish- based products at improving public health outcomes, such as dietary quality, nutritional status and early childhood development indicators. Moreover, formative research studies to explore cultural belief systems and acceptability of feeding fish-based products to infants, young children, and pregnant and lactating mothers would help inform context- specific products and programs. These could be paired with studies on willingness to pay and sensory acceptability. There may also be opportunities to promote fish-based products in biofortification efforts and as a locally produced ingredient in ready-to-use supplementary foods and ready- to-use therapeutic foods aimed at the prevention and treatment of moderate acute malnutrition (MAM) and severe acute malnutrition (SAM), respectively.
4. Ensuring the safety and quality of fish-based products from both formal and informal food production channels is critical for consumers and producers alike.

Across WorldFish projects, fish-based product development has been promoted through a range of production channels to suit different objectives and contexts—from supporting rural microenterprises, to engaging networks of women-led producer groups, to contracting commercial manufacturers. Ensuring fish-based products are good quality and safe to eat is critical for consumer health and confidence as well as producer reputation and business viability, regardless of how or where or by whom the fish product is produced. Food safety is a particular concern in relation to public food provision such as SMPs, although it is arguably just as important when fish-based products are made for sale in rural village markets. Countries vary in terms of their regulatory environments and requirements for certifications or licenses to sell locally made products. In contexts where informal food systems are central to people’s access to food, development of food safety standards should aim to be inclusive of different types of production systems and not exclude small-scale or home-based producers. Good fish handling practices also need to be embedded throughout the whole fish supply chain and involve all fishery actors, starting from fishers. Delivery of widespread fish handling training as part of low- cost government services has potential to reduce food safety risks in aquatic food systems—an approach being tested as
part of ongoing research in Solomon Islands.

Further research is also required into packaging options, shelf life and storage requirements of certain fish-based products to build consumer confidence, particularly in public food procurement contexts. Investing in research and projects that support hygienic fish handling practices in formal and informal food systems is needed to ensure that safe and nutritious products are accessible to nutritionally vulnerable groups.

5. The production and sale of fish-based products can support the economic empowerment of women and provide a platform for sharing nutrition information. Women’s involvement in fish value-adding through processing and in the sale of products generates important

income that directly supports their economic participation and empowerment. In rural areas, where women often face even higher barriers to engage in income-generating activities, decentralized production models provide good opportunities for their involvement. BACKGROUND

Multiple micronutrient powders—globally standardized prepackaged vitamin/ mineral sachets distributed by donors such as the United Nations International Children's Emergency Fund (UNICEF)— have helped reduce global rates of stunting and anemia among vulnerable infants and young children (IYC), yet have had less impact on protein malnutrition. In contrast, dried fish powder (DFP) made from pelagic small fish such as Kapenta (Limnothrissa miodon and Stolothrissa tanganicae) provide important macro- and micronutrients even when consumed in small quantities that accommodate IYC’s tiny tummies.

DFP provides high-quality animal- sourced protein, lipids (e.g., essential fats and fat-soluble vitamins such as vitamins A, D, E, and K), and other nutrients such as zinc and vitamin B12. Our goal is to incorporate a small amount of locally sourced DFP into a complementary instant porridge that is 1) both tasty/acceptable to vulnerable IYC (and other household members) and 2) will fill protein and micronutrient gaps among such IYC.
SCALING FISH POWDER IN ZAMBIA ACTIVITY

To help us reach this goal, our Scaling Fish Powder for Adoption in Rural Zambia activity builds directly upon results from FishFirst! Zambia: Research for Development and Scaling Staple-Fish Products for Enhanced Nutrition in the First 1,000 Days of Life (2020-2023). These results included a nutrient analysis of locally sourced Kapenta DFP, two sensory panels of dishes fortified with a DFP-based protein/micronutrient blend we call Complementary Food for Africa+Dried Fish Powder (ComFA+Fish), collaboration with our private sector partner in Zambia, Sylva Food Solutions, to produce ComFA+Fish Plain and Vanilla Instant Porridges, and a third sensory panel to test the acceptability of the porridges among adults prior to testing their acceptability among IYC in 2024. For Sensory Panel I, caregivers (N=42) evaluated seven attributes—aroma, appearance, texture, taste, sweetness, convenience, and overall acceptability—of four ComFA+Fish dishes. For Sensory Panel II, 42 caregivers evaluated IYC’s “global liking” of ComFA+Fish Complementary Maize Porridge. For both panels, the dishes were highly acceptable to a majority of participants. COMFA+FISH INSTANT PORRIDGE MACRONUTRIENTS: INFANTS AT 6–8 MONTHS

At this age, infants should continue to be breastfed, and breast milk should provide approximately 400 calories (kcal) per day, which equals approximately 65% of estimated kcal needs. For the average healthy breastfed 6-8- month-old, complementary food should be provided two to three times per day. For 6–8- month-olds, the reference weight for the calculations below is 7.9–8.9kg (male infants).
▪ Kcal: One ComFA+Fish Instant Porridge sachet two times per day provides 377 kcal, which equals approximately 50% of the estimated kcal needs for 6–8-month-olds.1,2
▪ Protein: One ComFA+Fish Instant Porridge sachet two times per day provides 10.8g of protein, which equals approximately 100% of the estimated protein needs for 6–8-month-olds.3-5
▪ Lipids: One ComFA+Fish Instant Porridge sachet two times per day provides 1.66g total fat, which equals approximately 5% of the estimated fat needs for 6–8-month-olds.1,3,5
COMFA+FISH INSTANT PORRIDGE MACRONUTRIENTS: INFANTS AT 9–11 MONTHS

At this age, infants should continue to be breastfed. For the average healthy breastfed 9–11-month-old, complementary food should be provided three to four times per day. For 9–11-month-olds, the reference weight used for the calculations below is 9.3–10kg.
▪ Kcal: One ComFA+Fish Instant Porridge sachet three times per day provides 565 kcal, which equals approximately 60% of the estimated kcal needs for 9–11-month-olds.1,2

Multiple micronutrient powders—globally standardized prepackaged vitamin/ mineral sachets distributed by donors such as the United Nations International Children's Emergency Fund (UNICEF)— have helped reduce global rates of stunting and anemia among vulnerable infants and young children (IYC), yet have had less impact on protein malnutrition. In contrast, dried fish powder (DFP) made from pelagic small fish such as Kapenta (Limnothrissa miodon and Stolothrissa tanganicae) provide important macro- and micronutrients even when consumed in small quantities that accommodate IYC’s tiny tummies.

Foreword

The consumption of pelagic whole small fish during the first 1,000 days of life—which is the period of time from conception until a child reaches two years of age—is associated with opti- mized health, nutrition, and cognitive development among infants and young children as well as with reduced stunting and anemia. Pelagic whole small fish are a protein-rich and nutrient -rich animal source food that is popular in Zambia and across sub-Saharan Africa. Because they are consumed whole, pelagic small fish are rich in more than 15 micronutrients such as calcium, vitamin A, iron and zinc, all of which play important roles in infants’ and young children’s cognitive and physical development.

The Government of Zambia is promot- ing the consumption of nutrient-dense foods— including dried fish powder combined with other locally sourced, seasonally available, nutrient-dense powders made from, for example, orange-fleshed sweet potato, dark green leafy vegetables (e.g., dried pumpkin leaves), groundnut, soybean, and cassava. In addition to being used to fortify complementary foods for vulnerable young children, dried fish powder can enhance the nutrition and flavor of traditional dishes for vulnera- ble older children, adolescents, and adults. This is in-line with ongoing
initiatives by the Government of Zambia to promote dietary diversity to enhance household’s nutrition security.
In addition to complementary feeding practices for infants and young children, we support and encourage:
1. Breastfeeding within the first hour of life;
2. Breastfeeding exclusively for the first six months of life;
3. Introduction of nutritious semi-solid and solid foods at six months of age;
4. Continued breastfeeding up to two years of age and beyond.

The Government of Zambia commits to work with its stakeholders—including the donor community, the private sector, research organizations, academia, not-for-profit organizations, and local communities—to ensure a sustainable and resilient value chain for pelagic whole small fish. A resilient value chain that works for all income brackets will ensure that all households

Complementary Maize Porridge

ComFA+Fish Complementary Maize Porridge is a complementary food for infants and young children that is made from small pelagic fish that have been dried, roasted and ground into a fine powder and cooked with ground white maize meal, groundnut powder, and orange-fleshed sweet potato (OFSP) powder (or other sweet potato powder if OFSP powder is unavailable locally) into a nutrient-dense porridge. The fish powder can be made from a variety of pelagic small fish species such as Kapenta (Limnothrissa miodon and Stolothrissa tanganicae), Chisense (Potamothrissa acutirostris and Poecilothrissa moeruensis), Dagaa (Rastrineobola argentea), etc. Roasting the dried fish over low heat prior to grinding is recommended to lengthen the powder’s shelf life and enhance the dish’s flavor.

Savory Cassava Bites

ComFA+Fish Savory Cassava Bites are an easy side dish or snack made from dried small fish powder, cassava flour, orange-fleshed sweet potato (OFSP) powder, and spices such ginger powder and dried curry leaves. The fish powder can be made from a variety of pelagic small fish species such as Kapenta (Limnothrissa miodon and Stolothrissa tanganicae), Chisense (Potamothrissa acutirostris and Poecilothrissa moeruensis), Dagaa (Rastrineobola argentea), etc. Roasting the dried fish over low heat prior to grinding is recommended to lengthen the powder’s shelf life and enhance the dish’s flavor.
Ingredients
½ cup roasted dried small fish powder
2 ¼ cups cassava flour
2 teaspoons Irish potato powder
2 teaspoons ginger powder
12 pieces dried curry leaves, crushed into fine pieces
¼ cup onion powder
3 teaspoons sugar
2 teaspoons garlic powder
2 teaspoons salt (optional)
2 cups water (or more as needed)
2 teaspoons orange-fleshed sweet potato powder
Preparation
Mix all the dry ingredients in a bowl.
Add the water and gently mix just until the water and dry ingredients are barely combined: overmixing causes the dough to have a tough texture.
Gently shape the dough into 50 round bites, each approximately 2 inches in diameter.
Pre-heat the vegetable oil in a deep pot until it reaches 191degrees Celsius.

Deep fry a few bites at a time until golden brown and crispy on the outside, turning frequently with a slotted utensil to ensure even browning. The oil needs to maintain 191 degrees Celsius. If the oil’s temperature is too low, the cassava bites will absorb too much oil. If the oil’s temperature is too high, the outside of the cassava bites will burn before their centers are fully cooked.
Check one cassava bite in the batch to ensure that it’s center is fully cooked.
Savory Cassava Bites can be eaten warm or at ambient temperature.

Foreword

The consumption of pelagic whole small fish during the first 1,000 days of life—which is the period of time from conception until a child reaches two years of age—is associated with opti- mized health, nutrition, and cognitive development among infants and young children as well as with reduced stunting and anemia. Pelagic whole small fish are a protein-rich and nutrient -rich animal source food that is popular in Zambia and across sub-Saharan Africa. Because they are consumed whole, pelagic small fish are rich in more than 15 micronutrients such as calcium, vitamin A, iron and zinc, all of which play important roles in infants’ and young children’s cognitive and physical development.

The Government of Zambia is promot- ing the consumption of nutrient-dense foods— including dried fish powder combined with other locally sourced, seasonally available, nutrient-dense powders made from, for example, orange-fleshed sweet potato, dark green leafy vegetables (e.g., dried pumpkin leaves), groundnut, soybean, and cassava. In addition to being used to fortify complementary foods for vulnerable young children, dried fish powder can enhance the nutrition and flavor of traditional dishes for vulnera- ble older children, adolescents, and adults. This is in-line with ongoing
initiatives by the Government of Zambia to promote dietary diversity to enhance household’s nutrition security.
In addition to complementary feeding practices for infants and young children, we support and encourage:
1. Breastfeeding within the first hour of life;
2. Breastfeeding exclusively for the first six months of life;
3. Introduction of nutritious semi-solid and solid foods at six months of age;
4. Continued breastfeeding up to two years of age and beyond.

The Government of Zambia commits to work with its stakeholders—including the donor community, the private sector, research organizations, academia, not-for-profit organizations, and local communities—to ensure a sustainable and resilient value chain for pelagic whole small fish. A resilient value chain that works for all income brackets will ensure that all households

Bean-Vegetable Soup

ComFA+Fish Bean-Vegetable Soup is a savory dish made from whole pelagic small fish that have been dried, roasted and ground into a fine powder and cooked with dried bean powder and pumpkin leaf powder or another dark green leaf vegetable (DGLV) powder of choice (such as powdered sweet potato leaves, powdered spinach leaves, etc.). The dish also includes dried mushroom powder (any mushroom variety of choice), as well as onion powder, cassava flour, soybean flour, garlic powder, and vegetable oil. The fish powder can be made from a variety of pelagic small fish species such as Kapenta (Limnothrissa miodon and Stolothrissa tanganicae), Chisense (Potamothrissa acutirostris and Poecilothrissa moeruensis), Dagaa (Rastrineobola argentea), etc. Roasting the dried fish over low heat prior to grinding is recommended to lengthen the powder’s shelf life and enhance the dish’s flavor.

Savory Cassava Bites

ComFA+Fish Savory Cassava Bites are an easy side dish or snack made from dried small fish powder, cassava flour, orange-fleshed sweet potato (OFSP) powder, and spices such ginger powder and dried curry leaves. The fish powder can be made from a variety of pelagic small fish species such as Kapenta (Limnothrissa miodon and Stolothrissa tanganicae), Chisense (Potamothrissa acutirostris and Poecilothrissa moeruensis), Dagaa (Rastrineobola argentea), etc. Roasting the dried fish over low heat prior to grinding is recommended to lengthen the powder’s shelf life and enhance the dish’s flavor.
Ingredients
½ cup roasted dried small fish powder
2 ¼ cups cassava flour
2 teaspoons Irish potato powder
2 teaspoons ginger powder
12 pieces dried curry leaves, crushed into fine pieces
¼ cup onion powder
3 teaspoons sugar
2 teaspoons garlic powder
2 teaspoons salt (optional)
2 cups water (or more as needed)
2 teaspoons orange-fleshed sweet potato powder
Preparation
Mix all the dry ingredients in a bowl.
Add the water and gently mix just until the water and dry ingredients are barely combined: overmixing causes the dough to have a tough texture.
Gently shape the dough into 50 round bites, each approximately 2 inches in diameter.
Pre-heat the vegetable oil in a deep pot until it reaches 191degrees Celsius.

Deep fry a few bites at a time until golden brown and crispy on the outside, turning frequently with a slotted utensil to ensure even browning. The oil needs to maintain 191 degrees Celsius. If the oil’s temperature is too low, the cassava bites will absorb too much oil. If the oil’s temperature is too high, the outside of the cassava bites will burn before their centers are fully cooked.
Check one cassava bite in the batch to ensure that it’s center is fully cooked.
Savory Cassava Bites can be eaten warm or at ambient temperature.
