4) Data collection and timeline

The evaluation included three major survey rounds: a baseline survey conducted between January and April 2018; a midline survey conducted following one year of program implementation between July and October 2019; and an endline survey following three years of program implementation conducted between February and March 2021. The primary intervention activities, including the formation of VESAs, commenced immediately in the study subdistricts following the baseline, and implementation continued through summer 2021. The one-time transfers of poultry and cash were delivered in April 2019, approximately four months prior to the one-year follow-up survey. Figure 2 summarizes the overall timeline.

The sampling frame was constituted by PSNP households reporting a child aged 0 to 36 months at baseline, and a simple random sample of households meeting these eligibility criteria was selected.13 The target sample included 3,494 households, and the realized sample was 3,314 households or roughly 17 households per subdistrict.14 In the one-year follow-up, 3,220 of the realized sample households were surveyed for an attrition rate of 3%, and in the three-year follow-up, 3,098 of the sample households

In each survey round, surveys were conducted with the primary female (defined as the primary caretaker, usually the mother, of the index child aged 0—3 at baseline) and the primary male, if present (defined as her husband or partner). Key outcomes of interest included demographic characteristics, participation in the PSNP and SPIR interventions, savings and assets, agriculture, livestock production, consumption and food security, infant and young child feeding practices, maternal nutrition, and depression and well-being. Each survey respondent provided informed oral consent; ethical review and approval of the trial was provided by the Institutional Review Boards at IFPRI and at Hawassa University.
5) Outcome variables

The analysis in this paper focuses on five pre-specified families of outcomes: assets, financial inclusion, income from agriculture and livestock, non-agricultural income, and consumption and food security. We will report the average standard treatment effects for these five outcome families as well as the treatment effects for each specific variable. While the majority of outcomes of interest are measured only at the three-year follow-up, a subset of outcomes were also measured in the one-year follow-up survey. For the five average standard treatment effect coefficients, we also report q-values robust to the analysis of multiple hypothesis estimated across the set of ASTEs (Simes 1986).16

For assets, we analyze total asset value and the value of productive assets, consumer durables, and livestock assets as measured at the three-year follow-up; at the one-year follow-up, only livestock assets are reported.17 For financial inclusion, we analyze any access to credit, access to formal credit, and total credit accessed over the past year, as well as a binary variable for any savings and the current savings balance. World Development 173(January 2024): 106414. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.worlddev.2023.106414 Permanent link to cite or share this item https://hdl.handle.net/10568/132862 External link to download this item DOI https://doi.org/10.1016/j.worlddev.2023.106414 Abstract/Description Many cash transfer programs include complementary nutrition training, with the aim of encouraging households to use transfer resources toward improving child nutrition. Evidence indicates that these bundled programs, if intensive and well-implemented, can be effective in improving child nutritional status. However, little is known about how adding nutrition training to transfer programs affects their economic impacts. In particular, few studies have assessed whether nutrition programming may induce reallocation of transfer resources from physical capital to human capital. Scarce evidence also exists as to whether these tradeoffs depend on the transfer modality. We study a pilot program called the Transfer Modality Research Initiative in Bangladesh (TMRI), designed as a randomized controlled trial. TMRI provided cash or food transfers, with or without intensive group-based nutrition behavior change communication (BCC), to mothers of young children in poor rural households. We find that adding nutrition BCC to cash or food transfers leads to larger impacts on both consumption and assets potentially surprising, given that the transfer value is unchanged. Analysis of mechanisms suggests that these effects occur through the BCC inducing increases in income generation, through investments in livelihoods. Suggestive evidence indicates that the effects of TMRI s BCC are plausibly due to the intensive group-based format, which increased social capital for participant women and their household members, as well as improved participant women s agency and self-confidence, knowledge, and input into household decisions. Results indicate that adding nutrition BCC to cash or food transfer programs do not necessarily induce a tradeoff between investing in human capital versus physical capital, but can rather strengthen impacts on both if appropriately designed. Abstract: We study the impact of one-season transfers framed for agricultural investment combined with agricultural support services on decision making among smallholder households in Senegal and Malawi using data from randomized control trials. In Senegal, we find evidence that the program increased the decision power of male household heads at the expense of other males in the household after two years. We cannot disentangle the impacts of the farm planning program and the lump sum transfer that comprised that program. In Malawi, we observe that over two years male program recipients exhibit increased decision- making power, while male non-recipients see reductions in decision-making power. These results are broadly due to both the transfers and the intensive agricultural support services. Changes in decision power seem to flow not just from control of income, but also from shifting household norms linked to program participation. Only in Malawi do we note some suggestive evidence that decision making power increases among female program recipients.

1. Introduction
As transfer programs have gained popularity in the developing world as a

tool for improving the livelihoods of poor households, interest has grown in studying the consequences of these programs for the dynamics of decision making within families. This question is important from a number of perspectives. Cash transfers can directly affect bargaining power, which in turn affects how household resources, including transfers, are used.1 While bargaining is not directly observable, decision making has been shown to be a good proxy in a number of settings (Lundberg and Pollack 1996; Duflo 2012; Browning, Chiappori, and Weiss 2014). Additionally, women’s participation in decision making is seen as an important component of increasing women’s empowerment more generally, which is often a primary or secondary goal of many transfer programs. At the same time, many transfer programs are accompanied by other types of support services, and less is known about how such services may interact with transfers or operate independently to further affect household decision making. In this paper, we study the impact of one-season, lump sum transfers combined with agricultural support programming on a range of household decision-making outcomes in the context of programs for smallholder farmers in Senegal and Malawi.

A growing literature examines the link between cash transfers and household decision-making processes, and specifically how the receipt of cash transfers affects the identity of these decision makers. Such papers generally use decision making as a proxy for bargaining power, studying how increasing the unearned income controlled by a household member through a transfer affects their bargaining power. In a general collective model of the household (Chiappori 1988; 1992), bargaining power is represented by the weight on each household member’s utility function, and can be conceptualized as the influence of the household member’s preferences on final household decisions. Bargaining power is composed of many

factors including individual unearned income, leading to the link with the transfer literature.2 Other components of bargaining power include characteristics such as education, age, individually held assets, and cultural norms. It should also be noted that bargaining power is a relative concept, and increased bargaining power for one household member should functionally mean decreased bargaining power for some other household member.
To date, most transfer programs that have been studied focus on transfers

that occur at regular intervals, in many cases without specific end dates. Theoretically, as transfers lead to a permanent increase in unearned income for the recipient, the motivation for a link to bargaining power for such transfers is that they result in a permanent stream of income controlled by them and accessible in most cases outside of any cooperative solution to household bargaining. The study of one-time transfers presents an interesting question; without the promise of long- term stream of income, such one-time transfers should not affect bargaining power in the same way. However, such transfers have the potential to impact decision making in two ways. First, norms regarding control of the transfer income may lead the recipient to make decisions regarding that income, which in the short run could be observed in answers to survey questions regarding who makes decisions. Second, if the transfers are effectively invested, sustained increases in income controlled by the transfer recipient can result. If so, we should observe a longer term increase in the recipient’s bargaining power (as proxied by their decision- making power).

Support services, including different types of training programs, are often offered in conjunction with transfer programs and while their link to household decision making is less direct than transfers, there are also channels through which these effects many occur. Programs which directly address gender relations and other household decision-making dynamics can shift behavior by changing household norms. At the same time, trainings that increase an individual’s skills or more directly involve them in economic activity can increase their bargaining power

The programs studied here combine transfers with support services and have

the primary goal of improving farmer livelihoods by increasing agricultural production. Both are evaluated through the use of randomized control trials. The Senegal project included a comparison group that received monthly advisory visits conducted by an animateur (a farmer from the area trained to implement the program), a group that received those visits and a farm management plan (FMP) intended to help the farmers effectively allocate their resources over the year, and a group that received the visits, the FMP, and a one-time cash transfer worth approximately USD200. An interesting component of the Senegal program was that one of its explicit goals was to increase family participation in decision making, particularly regarding agricultural activities. We collect data over two years; support services were administered in both years, but the transfers were only given once, at the beginning of year 1. Results from the Senegal study on other household outcomes show that the transfers resulted in one-year improvements in crop production, and increased holdings of livestock and agricultural equipment that were sustained over two years. No robust impacts of the management plan alone are identified (Ambler, de Brauw, Godlonton 2020).

The Malawi project cross-randomized transfers and support services. The transfer treatment included a control group, a group that received a series of three cash transfers over one season, and a group that received a series of three transfers in a combination of inputs and cash over the same season. The cash transfers were given at planting ($36), mid-season ($22), and harvest ($26). The input transfers were given on the same schedule, were of equivalent value, and approximately 50 percent of the value was given in kind in the form of seed, hoes, inoculant, and storage sacks, while the remaining half was given in cash. The support services were administered in a cross-randomized treatment that included a control group receiving only standard services offered by our partner, and a treatment group that received intensive technical advice and an FMP from a trained extension worker. In Ambler, de Brauw, and Godlonton (2023) we show that in Malawi the program led to large increases in crop production and household consumption over two years, driven by increased expenditures on inputs, only when farmers received both a transfer (of either type) and intensive extension in the first year. In this paper, we find some suggestive evidence after two years that the

program solidified the decision-making power of male household heads, and reduced the decision-making power of male non-recipients in the household. In Malawi, there is some evidence that the program increased the decision-making power of female recipients after two years. The main findings from Malawi are that in both years, male recipients see their decision-power grow with program receipt (both transfers only and transfers and support services), while male non-recipients see their decision-power decline. The results are not linked only to treatments that are also associated with increased household production and consumption, and are not connected only to transfer receipt. Decision making is also impacted by receiving agricultural support services without transfers, suggesting programming can impact decision making through multiple channels. that

2. Experimental Design

To study how one time transfers may lead to changes in household decision making, we consider the impacts of two related, but distinct, transfer and agricultural support services projects on measures of household decision making. In this section we describe the relevant elements of the design of each project. Further details can be found in Ambler, de Brauw, and Godlonton (2020 and 2023).

A. Senegal

The Senegal project was conducted in partnership with the Fédération des Organisations Non-Gouvernementales du Sénégal (FONGS), an umbrella group of autonomous farmers associations with near national coverage. We work with eight associations located in central and western Senegal during the 2014/2015 and 2015/2016 agricultural seasons. The total sample is 600 households, comprising 15 villages in each association and 5 households in each village.

Project implementation largely occurred through an animateur, a farmer from the local area (but not the same village), who was trained to provide the support services the project offered. Animateurs worked in one or two villages, so randomization occurred at the animateur level to ensure that no animateurs would have to administer more than one treatment. Animateurs were mostly male and fewer than half had a high school education. Randomization was stratified by association and number of villages per animateur, in 11 distinct stratification cells.7 A timeline of project activities can be found in Appendix Figure A1. Animateurs and their associated households were allocated into one of three groups:
Comparison group: Advisory visits only

The comparison group for our analysis received the light-touch treatment of monthly advisory visits from their animateur. These advisory visits were intended to assist farmers with issues related to their farms, principally regarding management issues. Animateurs were not trained to provide technical advice. Households in the comparison group also participated in the FONGS Basic Agricultural Assessment (BAA), which is a survey-like instrument administered three times during the project. The BAA served to measure progress, and also as a tool for households to learn about their financial situation.
FMP group: Advisory visits and farm management plan

This group received the same services as those in the comparison group, and also completed an FMP with their animateur in both years prior to the beginning of the agricultural season. The goal of the FMP was to improve production-related

Guided by the animateur, farmers created a schedule of activities, thought through likely challenges, and preemptively devised solutions. FMP + Cash group: Advisory visits, farm management plan, and cash transfer

Farmers in this group received all the same services as those farmers in the FMP group, and received a one-time cash transfer of approximately USD200 timed near planting of the first year of implementation to help them carry out the FMP designed in the first year. The size of the transfer was equal to approximately 15 percent of the baseline value of crop production. The transfer was only given once, at the beginning of year one, while the support services (including the FMP) continued for two years. The transfer was unconditional, but heavily framed for agricultural investment and implementation of the FMP.8 The transfers were distributed to household heads.
We expect that the infusion of resources in the FMP + Cash treatment could

have a direct effect on household decision making. However, in this context, because the transfers were given directly to the household head (almost always male), we do not necessarily expect that the program would increase the decision- making power of women or other males in the household. However, if the transfers increase the decision-making power of the household head, we may observe reduced participation in decision making for other household members. Changes in decision making after one year only may indicate only control over the transfer itself, while changes lasting into the second year may indicate that the transfers led to lasting changes in decision making linked to the increased livestock holdings observed in Ambler, de Brauw, and Godlonton (2020). When considering the potential of the FMP alone to impact decision making we focus on the way in which it was conceptualized as a tool for promoting joint planning and decision-making among adults in the entire household. As such, the FMP alone has the potential to

B. Malawi

The project in Malawi was conducted in partnership with the National Smallholder Farmers Association of Malawi (NASFAM), a nationwide organization that provides farmers with both social and commercial services. NASFAM operates through self-organized farmer clubs. In this study we worked with 120 farmer clubs in the Dowa and Ntchisi districts of central Malawi. The clubs averaged ten members each, leaving us with a target sample size of approximately 1,200 smallholder farmers. Project implementation was conducted during the 2014/2015 and 2015/2016 agricultural seasons. Appendix Figure A2 details the project timeline and experimental design.

Because a large component of the project (to be detailed below) was conducted by extension agents, clubs were first assigned to extension agents. Treatment randomization was then done at the club level, and stratified by extension officer, an indicator for above the median share of females in the club, and an indicator for above the modal club size. The project involved two cross- cutting interventions: a transfer treatment and an intensive extension treatment. Transfer treatment: Control
Transfer treatment: Control

Farmers in the control group of the transfer treatment received only standard NASFAM services, and no additional resources. If the farmer was newly registered, they received a seed loan equal to about two-thirds of the value of the seed disbursement given in the other groups, but which was repayable with interest to NASFAM. Other farmers received no capital support.
Transfer treatment: Cash

Cash transfers were distributed during the agricultural season of the first year of implementation, in three tranches, equal to about $84 in value. As in Senegal, the total value of the transfer was equal to about 15 percent of the baseline value of crop production. Farmers were given disbursements of $36 (November 2014), $22 (February 2015), and $26 (April 2015). As in Senegal, the transfers were unconditional, but heavily framed for investment in specific agricultural inputs appropriate at the time of each transfer. Transfers in Malawi were allocated to the NASFAM club member, not the household head, who could be either male or female. 64 percent of club members in our sample are female.

Transfer treatment: Inputs

The third group of farmers received a combination of cash and inputs, timed at the same time as the cash transfers. The first disbursement was comprised of seed, inoculant (a nitrogen fixer), and hoes. The second was given in cash to pay for ganyu (day-labor, which was the relevant input for these farmers mid-season), and the third included improved storage sacks, strings, and cash for harvest-related activities.9 Again, transfers are distributed to the NASFAM member.
Extension treatment: Standard services

The control treatment for the extension intervention received only standard NASFAM extension services. This is primarily a lead farmer approach, where a NASFAM member is selected by other farmers to be a lead farmer. The lead farmer then receives trainings from NASFAM extension agents and is encouraged to share that knowledge with other farmers in their area, primarily through group-based activities.
Extension treatment: Intensive extension

Farmers in this group receive the standard NASFAM services, and additionally receive individual extension support from trained, professional extension agents. As in Senegal, the support included farm management planning, but in Malawi it also included individualized technical support. Farmers received at least three one-on-one visits from extension agents over the season. A detailed FMP was completed during the first visit, and subsequent visits focused on support to complete the FMP and to help with any technical issues farmers were experiencing. These services were directly targeted to the club member, not the entire household. To support the project, NASFAM hired 15 additional extension agents. The transfer treatment was conducted only in the first year of implementation, but the extension treatment was implemented in both the first and second years.10

The analysis for the Malawi data collapses the two transfer treatments. Therefore, we study the impacts of the transfers and intensive extension alone and in combination, following Ambler, de Brauw, and Godlonton (2023) who found that sustained increases in production and consumption were attributable only to the combined package, allowing us to study whether those increases are linked to changes in household decision making. A finding that the decision-making power of the recipient increased over two years for those receiving both interventions would suggest that transfer recipients were able maintain a level of control over that new income, resulting in increased bargaining power. Conversely, a finding that any kind of transfers leads to only short-term changes in decision-making power would indicate recipients controlled the transfer itself, but that those transfer did not fundamentally alter relative household bargaining power.

Though the agricultural support services offered by this program did not directly aim to increase the roles of various household members in decision making as in Senegal, this training program does have the theoretical capacity to effect this change. Club members, men and women, who receive training from extension agents may have more agency and knowledge with regards to production. They may also learn skills, both technical and management related, that result in changes in the way household decision-making is organized.

The midline and endline data are complete household surveys supervised by the research team. These instruments collected a large amount of data on agricultural outcomes and other household welfare measures. They contain a section on decision-making asking for the identity of the household decision makers in a variety of household activity categories, and additionally contain questions about decision-making over crop production on a crop-by-crop basis, and livestock decision making by animal. Innovation Next Innovation ACTIVE: 2012 to present Cash transfer programs are an increasingly popular form of social protection, aimed at reducing poverty and food insecurity among vulnerable populations. There are at least a billion beneficiaries of such programs in low- and middle-income countries, with numbers increasing in response to the COVID-19 pandemic. CGIAR researchers at the International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI) have shown the effectiveness of these programs in reducing poverty and examined their impacts in other areas, such as improving education and child nutrition, and sustainably reducing intimate partner violence. IFPRI s experimental evaluation of the conditional cash transfer program PROGRESA in Mexico was one of the first rigorous economic impact evaluations of a national anti-poverty program and the world s first randomized impact evaluation of a large-scale conditional cash transfer program. When the Mexican government launched PROGRESA in 1997, the program was viewed as revolutionary, not only for its integration of health, nutrition, and education interventions into social protection programming, but for its intent to be rigorously evaluated to improve implementation and demonstrate program effectiveness. IFPRI research has illustrated the potential for cash transfer programs to support other areas of well being, including household labor supply, child labor, food security, asset holdings, maternal and child nutrition, and women s empowerment IFPRI collaborated with the Government of Mexico and academic partners on the first evaluation of the PROGRESA program, showing that the program reduced poverty and improved health and education. This research was used to justify the program s national expansion, which reached one in five Mexican households as the PROSPERA program in 2015. IFPRI s evaluation of PROGRESA helped to usher in a global evaluation culture regarding social-protection programs. Moreover, the findings led PROGRESA to serve as a model for social-protection policy and programming in other countries, both inside Latin America and more broadly. Following PROGRESA, IFPRI played a major role in informing national social protection policies, evaluating national cash transfer programs in Brazil, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, and later in Turkey, Ethiopia, Mali, and Egypt. IFPRI research has also illustrated the potential for cash transfer programs to support other areas of well being, including household labor supply, child labor, food security, asset holdings, maternal and child nutrition, and women s empowerment. One recent study provided the first insight into how combining cash transfers with nutrition behavior change communication (BCC) can positively impact child nutrition and sustainably reduce intimate partner violence. The research was based on the Transfer Modality Research Initiative (TMRI) in Bangladesh, a two-year randomized controlled trial in collaboration with the World Food Programme that was the first to distinguish between the impacts of cash alone, and cash plus nutrition BCC. The BCC provided nutrition messages through group-based trainings, home visits, and community meetings. IFPRI s evaluation found that cash transfers alone did not improve child nutrition, but cash plus BCC decreased stunting by 7.3 percentage points, almost three times the national average decline over the same period. Furthermore, research found that intimate partner violence against women was significantly lower in households receiving cash plus BCC, and these reductions persisted four years after the trial ended. While prior work showed that cash transfer programs can reduce intimate partner violence, the Bangladesh trial was the first to show that complementary programming can sustain drops in violence over the longer term. The findings have demonstrated the profound impacts of adding BCC to transfer programs and have influenced program design in Bangladesh and beyond. Also, agricultural production is often characterized by a gender inequitable balance, which means that men are frequently the decision-makers, controlling the production of main agricultural commodities. Key to this practice is the efficiency principle, by increasing resource-use efficiencies of major inputs. Increase adoption rates of new technologies by using video-mediated extension services. A randomized controlled trial will be implemented in Bihar, India. Provision of climate advisory services includes four steps: 1) Generation of climate and crop information; 2) Translation of the information into actionable advisories; 3) Transferring the advisories through various dissemination channels; and 4) Uptake of the advisory by end users.

In the DeRISK SE Asia Report “Advancing climate resilience in agriculture via climate information services in Myanmar”, it was suggested to integrate the use of climate information services and climate-smart agriculture as part of the Good Agricultural Practices (GAP) for key commodities, and to support delivery mechanisms for climate information services, including mobile-based technologies [4]. However, the current climate information that is available does not meet the needs of fish farmers, especially in terms of downscaled information, reliability, and accuracy [5]. Information available on Radio and TV is most commonly used, but it only provides weather information for a few days and lacks the advisory component.
Due to the current political situation in Myanmar and for

security reasons, the provision of digital climate advisory services is considered an opportunity for promoting existing digital services. Fish farmers have experienced many challenges such as insufficient fish seed supply, limited access to finance, and a lack of rice-fish farming technology. Improved access to formal credit for fish farmers will enable them to reduce their reliance on informal sources of credit with high interest rates [5]. To fill this gap, the Alliance established a partnership with Village Link Company Ltd in Myanmar within the context of the project DeRISK SE Asia and the CGIAR research initiative Asian Mega- Deltas. The innovation developed under this partnership provides monthly and weekly climate advisory to 5,000 fish farmers in Irrawaddy Delta, associated with the provision of loans to selected farmers through microfinance institutions (MFIs). Village Link developed decision trees for different fish growth development stages under different climate scenarios for the different townships.

The Alliance provided Village Link with additional training on the use of Decision Trees and made AccuWeather data easier accessible via a temporary web page. Based on the weather forecasts and decision trees, Village Link translated the forecast information into actionable, tailored, context-specific advisories targeted to the townships, which were disseminated through its digital platform — web page, Htwet Toe mobile phone App, and Htwet Toe Facebook page.
Fish farmers can access the information through their mobile phones and provide feedback via the Htwet Toe app call center.

Fish farmers were also provided with digital literacy training to improve their access to and use of the advisories, and potential access to MFIs based on Village Link pre-credit scoring for further assessment [3].

The provision of monthly and monthly climate advisories to fish farmers was part of a collaboration between the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT (the Alliance) and the Village Link Company Ltd (Village Link). As part of the scope of this work, Village Link provided monthly and weekly climate advisories to 5,000 fish farmers from 20 townships in four regions, including Irrawaddy Delta. The advisories were based on Decision Trees for fish farming adjusted according to the weather forecasts for each township. The monthly and weekly climate advisories were disseminated through Village Link’s digital platform — web page, Htwet Toe mobile application, and official Htwet Toe Facebook page.

WorldFish provided technical support in the Decision Tree development. Village Link selected the townships and the Alliance provided easier access to AccuWeather weather forecasts, reorganizing the data through a temporary web page for easier use. The information provided via the Village Link platform includes monthly and weekly weather forecasts and related advisories. The advisories are prepared according to the location, time, and risks, based on the forecasts, growth stage, and relevant farming activities such as pond renovation, water management, fish stocking, feeding, disease control, etc. For example, in Irrawaddy, October is the end of the monsoon season when the weather is normally rainy. With it come risks of damage to the pond embankments, loss of fish due to flooding, change in water temperature and pH, reducing dissolved oxygen on cloudy days. In this case, the advisories may include the preparation of embankments to prevent fish loss due to flooding, preparation for moving fish to a temporary location, feeding methods during rainy and cloudy days, recommendations to increase dissolved oxygen in the pond, fishery
etc.
The monthly and weekly advisories are uploaded to and disseminated through Village Link’s Htwet Toe mobile phone application [1], Htwet Toe web page [2] and Htwet Toe official Facebook page [3].

By the end of September 2023, Village Link provided 1 monthly and 10 weekly advisories to farmers and each of these reached an average of 98.808 users and had 806 engagements on social media (liked, shared and follow up questions).

In addition, eight series of digital literacy trainings were provided to 221 farmers (67 women) so that farmers can access the monthly and weekly advisories via mobile phone. App features also allow users to share the content to other social media such as Facebook, Messenger, Twitter, Telegram, and WhatsApp, among others.

According to pre-credit scoring, Village Link referred the fish farmers to MFIs that include LOLC Myanmar Microfinance, Maha Microfinance, and Vision Fund. So far, 264 fish farmers in Twantay and Maubin have been referred to MFIs to obtain a loan to support management and improvement of their fish farms.

Key Messages
Dairy norms and practices are gendered and require transformational approaches to increase women’s benefits from farmer-led scaling approaches.
“Champions for Transformation” adapts GROOTS Kenya’s champion model to support women in dairy communities in Kenya to strengthen women’s leadership and peer learning in collectives.

The challenge

Climate change is severely affecting livestock production systems in East Africa. Efforts to enhance resilience, or the capacity to anticipate, cope with and recover from climate impacts are essential to sustain livestock-dependent communities.

Scaling climate-smart livestock practices through locally-led institutions may increase adaptation capacities. Dairy innovations that improve efficiencies in milk production have the potential to mitigate livestock emissions, a key priority in the national agenda.
Intra-household gender relations both shape and are

shaped by the uptake of new farm innovations. Gender- blind approaches can reinforce existing inequitable power relations in dairy households. Gender norms and practices often influence women’s and men’s dairy activities. In married households in Western Kenya, men typically own dairy cows and women provide substantial labour in everyday activities, such as milking, feeding and cleaning sheds in semi-intensive and intensive production systems. Despite women’s significant labour contributions, their potential to earn or decide how to use income from milk sales is often limited (Bullock et al. 2023, Tavenner and Crane 2018).

Opportunities to learn about climate-smart practices are similarly gendered.

Dairy norms and practices are gendered and thus require transforming gender relations to increase women’s abilities to benefit from farmer-led scaling approaches, specifically their access to information, technologies that reduce labour and income management. The innovation is comprised of sequential steps, mapping the champions, organizing them into groups, then strengthening women’s leadership in collectives through training on group dynamics and financial literacy followed by male engagement that addresses inequitable intra-household relations. Finally, over time and through women’s engagement in the champion model process, the next generation of women champions will advocate for grassroots women as county and subcounty level coordinators and

Extension services often target men because men own cows and often have more time than women to socialize (Figure 1). Women are often busy with household tasks and have limited time to attend training events. Unequal access to information further limits women’s participation in deciding whether to try out an innovation. Labour-intensive innovations may also unintentionally increase women’s labour burdens in dairy production.
Integrating socially inclusive approaches is essential to ensure that farmer-led scaling is both inclusive and supports social equity in dairy households.

Partnership to support socially inclusive scaling

ILRI sustainable livestock systems gender team partnered with GROOTS Kenya to co-create a socially inclusive scaling approach in Bomet County, Kenya. GROOTS Kenya is a national movement of over 5,000 women- and girl-led self-help groups and community-based organizations. The organization was founded in 1995 because of the low visibility of grassroots women in development processes and decision-making forums.

GROOTS Kenya scales and sustains a grassroots movement for women and girls, promotes women and girls’ leadership, economic empowerment of women and girls and resilience building to impacts of climate change and eliminates injustices against women and girls.

They use a champion model, which is a community-led approach to development wherein grassroots champions identify, conceptualize and solve problems. Champions are women or men who are agents of change or individuals who understand their community needs and actively and intentionally try to change their situation, in part by promoting women’s agency in their communities.

Community-based organizations and self-help groups play a central role in network building, supporting peer-to-peer mentoring, learning, and locally-led development. Engaging with stakeholders, namely public and private sector actors, ensures the sustainability of the model in communities.
Our innovation

The “champions for transformation” innovation adapts GROOTS Kenya’s champion model to dairy communities to increase women’s potential to benefit from access to information about climate-smart practices and manage dairy income.
Setting the foundation (2023)
Conduct a context analysis to select sites

GROOTS reviewed secondary data and interviewed stakeholders such as government officials in the livestock sector to learn more about dairy opportunities. Three wards in two subcounties were selected based on the need for dairy capacity building amidst higher levels of poverty relative to other sites where ILRI is working. Working in underreached and marginalized wards also provides greater opportunities to strengthen institutional presence and capacity.
Create women-led savings groups

Six seasoned champions from other locations, one of whom was a man, travelled to the three wards (Kipreres in Bomet east subcountry and Sigor and Kongasis in Chepalungu subcounty). They met with community members and grassroots women and men engaged in dairy production. They conducted six gender- disaggregated group discussions to gather information about climate change, dairy and gendered opportunities and challenges. Ten groups were created and will be registered
in Bomet County.
Implementing responsive and transformative approaches (2024)
Mentor and strengthen group capacities

A training programme will be developed and tailored on a group-by-group basis to build the capacities of group members. Seasoned champions, some of whom are Kalenjin in dairy households, will mentor women in the newly formed groups for three to four weeks to create a strong and sustainable collective.

Gender transformation takes time and men’s engagement should be continued and strengthened. Men and women will engage in gender dialogues to collectively discuss and reflect.

The Challenge

Climate change adaptation processes can be uneven and may reinforce inequitable power relations and outcomes (see Eriksen et al. 2021). Less powerful actors are often excluded from important decision-making during the design and development of adaptation interventions (Coger et al. 2022). This can perpetuate the design of programs that, unintentionally or not, exclude groups based on differential resource base and capacities in communities. “One-size-fits-all” approaches will not garner inclusive adaptation at scale. Furthermore, within households, unequal relations and dynamics often limit women’s agency and subsequently, capacities to learn, lead, and scale adaptation.
1. Local actors exercise limited agency in leading climate adaptation solutions

While top-down interventions are common, there is growing recognition of the need to innovate ‘with’ rather than innovate ‘for’ local actors such as dairy farmers in Kenya (Ndege, Marshall, and Byrne 2024). Dairy farming households are at the forefront of climate change adaptation and have been innovating and learning new ways to cope with climate uncertainties including drought and rainfall variability (Habermann et al. 2022).
2. Gender norms and practices generate inequitable distributions of burdens and benefits in households

Women and men’s differential access to, and ownership of resources, and agency in decision- making over important assets, including livestock is often shaped by gender norms and practices (Baltenweck et al. 2024). These inequities underpin and create socially differentiated adaptation processes and abilities in Kenya (Marty et al. 2023).

In dairy households of Nandi and Bomet counties in Kenya, despite women’s significant labor contributions, gender norms constrain women’s access to resources and limit their control over key decisions (Tavenner and Crane 2018). Women often carry out practices such as feeding, milking, and carrying fodder, yet have limited control over decisions around income from milk sales or uptake of innovations. Men, considered heads of households, gain access to extension services more than women, and may autonomously make decisions on uptake of dairy technologies (Bullock, DuttaGupta and Miriti n.d.).
3. “One-size-fits-all” solutions fail to support diverse households’ adaptation capacities

Rather than relying on top-down, one-size-fits-all solutions, adaptation must prioritize flexible, locally led approaches tailored to capacities of diverse households and groups with differential access to resources and opportunities.
Approaches that fail to accommodate differential perspectives and capacities may unintentionally exclude and deepen vulnerabilities to climate

change (Eriksen et al. 2021). Dairy households in Kenya are diverse and have different resources and adaptation capacities (Vernooij et al. 2024a). Households with more capital and assets, with dairying as a major source of income, may adopt climate technologies at higher rates compared to resource poorer households where dairy production is less commercialized (Vernooij et al. 2024a).

In Nandi and Bomet counties, intensive and semi-intensive practices are common methods of dairy production, but may vary depending upon availability of labor, capital, and land and asset ownership. Given the diverse practices and socioeconomic characteristics of dairy households in this region, adaptation capacities differ and necessitates a shift from adoption of predefined solutions to flexible approaches tailored to diverse needs and adaptive capacities in dairy households (Vernooij et al. 2024b). Livestock-oriented interventions that intentionally consider gender can support advances towards more equity (Baltenweck et al. 2024). In addition, differences in infrastructure and livestock service provision imply that extension agents’ capacities to reach remote communities vary across dairy producing regions in Kenya (Kiptot and
Franzel 2015, Odhiambo et al. 2019).

To address these challenges, adaptation in dairy requires diverse approaches to ensure households with different resources and capacities can access information about farmer-led innovations. For adaptation to be socially inclusive, flexible approaches are needed, tailored to capacities of diverse households and groups with differential access to resources and opportunities.
Box 1: Key definitions
Adaptation: Process of adjusting to actual or expected climate change and its effects, the process of moderating or avoiding harm, and ability to benefit (adapted from IPCC 2014).

Adaptation pioneer households: Positive deviant households who are better at adapting to climate change than others in the same circumstances (Habermann et al. 2024). They outperform other farming households facing the same climate challenges and are willing to share knowledge in networks and learning spaces like farmer-to-farmer field days.

Co-design: A participatory process of equal collaboration, decision-making and repeated consultations with partners, including local communities, recognized as experts and not beneficiaries in the locally led adaptation process.

Equity: Principle of fairness in burden sharing and serves as a basis for understanding how the impacts and responses to climate change (including costs, benefits, and opportunities) are distributed. Gender equity recognizes the diversity of different groups of women and men (see Tye et al. 2023).
Grassroots women: Women who have historically been excluded from decision-making spaces and perceived as passive beneficiaries of development projects instead of agents of change (GROOTS Kenya

Locally led adaptation (LLA): Adaptation that involves a “shift in power to local stakeholders” (Rahman et al. 2023). Local actors have individual and collective agency over adaptation priorities and how adaptation takes place (Tye et al. 2023).

Positive deviance: An approach that works with “outliers who succeed against all odds” and can offer “potential solutions for complex social problems” (Herington and van de Fliert 2018). Practical applications of positive deviance in development contexts initiated in domains like child nutrition and health and expanded to include gender and agriculture (Sternin and Choo 2000; Steinke et al. 2019; GIZ 2023).

Pioneer positive deviance approach (P-PD): An approach developed by a team at ILRI to address issues of adaptation to climate change. It focuses on identifying and learning from individuals within a community who find unique, successful solutions to common challenges despite having no additional resources or advantages. By studying these “positive deviants”, communities can discover locally effective practices that can be adopted and scaled, making solutions more sustainable and tailored to specific needs (Habermann et al. 2024).
Our Innovation

Our innovation combines two socially inclusive approaches, piloted in and tailored to dairy producing households and community in western Kenya. Together these approaches address each of the above-mentioned challenges that undermine socially inclusive adaptation.

We draw upon core principles of locally led adaptation (LLA) and co-designed approaches with diverse actors from dairy households and communities. LLA emphasizes the value of local knowledge and shifts control over adaptation priorities and decisions to local actors (Coger et al. 2022; Rahman et al. 2023). Key principles of LLA include 1) Devolving decision-making from external

to local actors; and 2) Recognizing the value of local actors’ knowledge and agency in developing their own solutions (Coger et al. 2022). LLA principles recognize inequitable norms and relations as barriers to women’s equal participation in decision- making and support their equitable access to services and resources, and greater exercise of agency and leadership (Tye et al. 2023).

Our innovation works with multiple approaches focusing on actors with differential capacities to learn and lead adaptation in dairy. It seeks to: 1) Address inequitable norms and practices through deliberate efforts to plan and scale adaptation with women and men in dairy households and groups; and 2) Tailor locally led solutions to the unique needs and capacities of women and men in diverse households.
Synergies in action: Scaling with households and champions in groups

Household approach: The first approach works with households as part of the Pioneer Positive Deviance (P-PD) approach to scale farmer-led adaptation solutions developed by “adaptation pioneer households” (APHs). APHs are positive deviant dairy farming households implementing innovative feed and fodder practices in Nandi and Bomet counties of Kenya. These APHs outperform other farming households facing the same climate challenges and are willing to share knowledge in networks

and learning spaces like farmer-to-farmer field days (Habermann et al. 2022). This approach deliberately incorporates practical strategies to increase women’s learning opportunities and capacities to lead adaptation practices during field days, strengthen their partnerships with extension and farmer networks, and by doing so, support inclusive scaling of locally led adaptation (DuttaGupta and Bullock 2023).
• Extension officers engaged men and women in APHs to plan field days to identify gender specific priorities and encouraged them both to invite participants from their networks.

• During these planning meetings, extension officers found that members of the same household often had different interests and needs (Omayio et al. 2024). For instance, though dairy was the primary focus, women expressed interest in other livelihood activities such as poultry and kitchen gardening.

• Field day audiences were sex-disaggregated to create an environment where women felt comfortable speaking openly (Omayio et al. 2024). Inviting other women from their groups and networks and leading demonstrations enabled women in APHs to have greater visibility, decision-making agency, and confidence in their ability to learn and lead.
• Additionally, demand-driven training sessions promoted shared learning within households, covering topics like dairy nutrition, fodder agronomy, animal health, adaptive breeding and record keeping.
Box 2: An extension officer’s experience of planning field days with adaptation pioneer households

Esther Omaiyo, a sub-county livestock extension officer in Nandi County has been working with adaptation pioneer households (APHs) as part of the Pioneer Positive Deviance (P-PD) approach to support farmer-led adaptation and scaling.

“It is very different from what we normally do as extension,” Esther explains. She elaborates how they planned with APH members to understand gender-specific priorities and practices they wanted to learn and lead during field days “… we ask each household member what do you want to be trained on, what are the needs, what are your interests… whom do you want to train? And it was very interesting because you will find that the household is one but inside there are so many people who have different interests.”

Champions for transformation approach: The second approach works with local champions and grassroots women-led groups in Bomet, Kenya. Adapted with GROOTS Kenya, this approach is based on their community-led champion model, where grassroots women leaders, referred to as champions, take the lead in driving change and implementing interventions in their communities. Building on the premise that those who are most affected by social

issues are best placed to identify solutions, organize resources, and inspire collective action, this approach supports women-led peer learning in collectives and strengthens their leadership capacities (Bullock and DuttaGupta 2023). Local champions engaged in discussions with community members to then form and mentor women-led dairy groups in Kipreres ward of Bomet East and Sigor and Kong’asis wards in Chepalungu sub counties of Bomet, Kenya.

• These groups — led by grassroots women — are spaces of mutual support and knowledge exchange. As part of these groups, women can increase their collective agency and potentially benefit from access to resources and learning opportunities, often in ways they cannot as individual women within households. Grassroots women have historically been excluded from decision-making spaces and often perceived as passive beneficiaries of development projects instead of agents of change (GROOTS Kenya 2024). Men are included in the groups as engaging them to support women's leadership positions in groups can help inform pathways for more equitable decision-making in households.

• After the groups were formed, a stakeholder workshop involving county officials, civil society, and GROOTS Kenya champions was conducted followed by a champion-led needs assessment. Findings from the needs assessment revealed training demands in areas like livestock feeding and nutrition, disease prevention, and manure management, with participants favoring hands- on learning through exchange visits to farms and on-site trainings with demonstration.

These socially inclusive approaches were piloted, and synergies identified to advance equitable adaptation to better reach and address diverse needs of heterogenous dairy households. We recognize that any single approach will likely exclude, while synergies between multiple approaches can bolster adaptation capacities and provide opportunities for APHs and grassroots group members to lead and learn from and with each other. Insights and learnings informed efforts to bridge the household and the champions approach through knowledge exchange and on-site learning of farmer-led innovations that work, and multistakeholder interactions and platforms that include women and men from diverse households.
Principles in action for equitable locally led adaptation
Our innovation is rooted in four core principles, each operationalized through practical actions and collaborations. These principles focus on

engaging different actors in adaptation and scaling, promoting learning and leadership of women and men from diverse dairy households, fostering equal collaboration, reflecting and co-learning with partners, and addressing inequitable gender norms in the community (Figure 1).
1. Deliberately engage diverse actors to learn and lead adaptation and scaling
Practical actions to operationalize this principle included the following:

• Women and men in APHs led adaptation practices through peer-to-peer knowledge exchange with women-led groups during a field day. Over 100 participants from the women-led groups attended the field day. Topics covered during the field day included those identified through needs assessment in the groups, including feed and fodder practices, kitchen gardening, poultry management, and animal health.

• The field day provided a platform for showcasing adaptive solutions using easily accessible and affordable resources. Farmer-led dairy solutions were showcased using locally available materials for livestock feed, and through practices such as storing silage in small batches in bags. These practices addressed resource limitations and were appropriate for households with limited access to and ownership of resources like land to
produce fodder.

In-situ training sessions were hosted at farms in three sub-locations across Bomet County to sustain learning and networks formed during the field day. These trainings, co-designed with GROOTS champions, APH members, and extension officers, addressed specific needs of the women-led groups. Topics included livestock nutrition, kitchen gardening, water management,
and value addition.

• Grassroots women gained hands-on learning during the field day and in-situ training sessions at farms showcasing farmer-led innovations. They became part of adaptation pioneer networks with extension and other farmers.
• These efforts help bring to the forefront those who may not typically hold leadership positions, such as women in APHs and grassroots women, to learn, lead, and scale adaptation practices.
Box 3: Women in adaptation pioneer households learn, lead, and scale adaptation

A feedback session with APHs revealed gender-specific priorities and opportunities to support women’s capacities to learn, lead, and scale adaptation. Women showed interest in actively participating in planning processes and scaling of adaptation practices. Suggestions include: “…involve young families, both husband and wife so that they can do all the activities together such as gardening from the beginning of the project and for the husbands to respect the wife’s gardening. They shouldn’t plant fodder in the kitchen garden.”

Emily Yebei is an adaptation pioneer and local pastor in her community. Together with her husband Tomas Yebei, their sons, and members of two other APHs, she hosted the field day with more than 100 participants from the women-led groups. Emily explains how this field day was different from the previous ones. “I have hosted the previous field days; this one is very different. I have seen women from humble backgrounds and if you can encourage these women… they will be somewhere, and I think the poverty levels will also go down because you went to the grassroots.” Emily emphasized the importance of these learning exchanges happening on farms, and not as seminars in hotels. “When they come to our home, they remember what they learned. They’ll say, ‘This sukuma wiki, I brought it from Mrs. Yebei’s farm,’ and they’ll remember how to plant it.”

Women in other APHs who co-hosted the field day agreed with Emily, stating that improving women’s learning capacities is beneficial for all because women are implementers: “… when you teach a woman, they will go with that thing she has learned and go implement.”

They further highlighted that these opportunities not only support women’s learning but also capacities to lead and scale adaptation practices through groups. When groups learn together, “ten will go and teach twenty” so networks can grow faster.

2. Collaborate and connect partners with equal say in decision making
Practical actions to operationalize this principle included the following:

• Equal collaboration between partners including APHs, dairy households, members of women- led groups, non-governmental organizations, and sub-county livestock extension officers from Bomet and Nandi counties to assess gender- specific priorities and demand driven learning needs.

• Planning meetings were held prior to the field day with all partners to share the learning needs of the groups with the APH members. Key practices were selected based on the needs of grassroots women-led groups.
• Demonstrations during field days were conducted collaboratively by men and women in APHs, extension officers, and other partners, fostering shared leadership roles.

• Networks between grassroots women, women and men in APHs, and extension officers were strengthened during the field day and in-situ training sessions. Partners exchanged knowledge with women and men group members during in-situ trainings, ensuring diverse households gained practical skills.
GROOTS Kenya champions and APHs worked together to mentor participants from the grassroots women-led groups, supporting equitable learning opportunities.
3. Pilot, reflect, co-learn, and adjust complementary socially inclusive approaches
Practical actions to operationalize this principle included the following:

In-situ training sessions at farms in Bomet County provided opportunities for co-learning among diverse stakeholders. GROOTS Kenya champions and APH members collaboratively conducted these training sessions and provided tailored practical guidance to women and men from diverse dairying households.

• Approaches were customized to match the differential needs and capacities. Practices like fodder planting, poultry management, and kitchen gardening were adjusted to align with resources accessible to the participants.

• Iterative feedback from stakeholders was integrated, adjusting strategies to reflect local insights and challenges. This flexibility enhanced the effectiveness of scaling efforts by incorporating lessons learned at key junctures in the process.
Box 4: Women-led group members learn from the APHs during the field day

A woman from one of the grassroots women-led groups balances multiple roles as a farmer and community pastor. On her farm, she grows beans, maize, indigenous vegetables, and fodder crops like Napier grass and sweet potatoes for her dairy cows. While her husband oversees dairy activities with a hired worker, she manages tasks like planting and weeding vegetables.

During the field day, she learned about dairy feeding practices and poultry management, and found connecting with an extension officer particularly helpful. “I have also learnt how to prepare chicken feeds; I had always wished to learn about that, but I am glad I learnt about that today, I even took the number so that I can ask more questions about the same later from the officer.”

Another participant and member of a women-led group, who balances various roles to provide for his family, including that of a farmer, a catechist, and a bodaboda rider, found learning about silage making to be valuable. “Silage preparation is something I had never learnt before, and now I know how important it is to plan and store feed for the cows, especially during droughts."" This was echoed by a woman member from another group who shared about learning how to use silage bags. ""We used a random black polythene bag, but now I have learned that air is not supposed to get inside, and we should use
proper silage bags.”
Women-led group members learn how to use silage bags. Photo credit: Photo ILRI/Tanaya DuttaGupta

Learning how to use locally available materials and adjust practices based on access to resources like land were reported by participants to be especially useful. A farmer and group member who manages poultry and a single dairy cow with his wife, plans to adjust practices learned during the field day based on the land they own. “I can see that people are very serious especially the women they are going to implement. And then another thing is that the things we have seen here are the things that we have that we can use to improve our lives,” he highlighted.

A single mother from another group, who has a kitchen garden, and two dairy cows, plans to implement the learning and share with others. “I will practice myself and teach my neighbors too so that they can learn too how to grow crops, how to feed the dairy cows so that we can earn a living, and people won't look down upon us anymore. After gaining knowledge now we have power,” she explained.
4. Address inequitable norms and work on changing behavior
Practical actions to operationalize this principle included the following:
• Deliberate efforts to address wider community norms can help dismantle barriers to women’s equal participation in learning, decision-making, and leadership roles.

Led by “men for women” champions from dairy communities, the forum discussed norms and practices in households, women’s decision- making agency, sharing of dairy benefits and labor responsibilities, along with gender-based violence and unpaid care work among other key topics.

• Field day and in-situ trainings at farms created spaces for women to lead activities and share knowledge. These spaces amplified women’s voice and confidence and supported their agency in scaling adaptation practices.

Box 5: Men’s engagement forum addresses inequitable gender norms

Men from APHs participated in a community forum dialogue around gender norms and practices in dairy households. Acknowledging it is rare for them to share how decisions are made within their households, the adaptation pioneers described how they work together with women in APHs to share responsibilities and benefits.

“Men should discuss farm income with their wives… I advise men to not take away most of the dairy income and leave the family with very little. This is not good,” advised Tomas Yebei, an adaptation pioneer.

At the moment, men have been elevated up there and our women are down there to an extent they are too dependent on us even on buying basics… When a woman is empowered, the society is empowered… There should be communication between the

Way forward
Assess impact: Understand effects of the piloted approaches with households and groups, along with their synergies, on gender relations and practices within diverse dairy households in the community.

Identify transferable lessons: Learn from existing equitable practices, and strategies that work well and have transformative potential. Then identify key transferable lessons to pilot the approaches with other communities.
Sustain outcomes: Continue collaborations with partners to sustain outcomes and ensure uptake of approaches by key actors, such as agricultural and livestock extension.

Scale to other geographies and systems: Based on the transferable lessons learned, implement the approaches in other geographies and systems, for instance, with farming households and groups in agropastoral and pastoral communities of Kenya and beyond.

Key Messages
Scaling locally-led adaptation can unintentionally deepen the inequitable division of burdens and benefits if the process does not address the gendered impacts of new practices.
“Scaling with households” integrates gender-responsive planning with household members to increase women’s capacities for learning and leading socially inclusive locally-led adaptation.
Strengthening women’s partnerships with extension staff and farmer networks increases their agency in shaping adaptation scaling.
The challenge

Climate change is severely affecting livestock production systems in East Africa. Efforts to enhance resilience, or the capacity to anticipate, cope with, and recover from climate impacts are essential to sustain livestock-dependent communities.

Scaling climate-smart livestock practices, such as innovations in feeds with and through locally-led institutions may increase adaptation capacities. Dairy innovations that improve efficiencies in milk production have the potential to mitigate emissions from the livestock sector, which is a development goal in the national agenda.

Intra-household gender relations both shape and are shaped by the uptake of new farm innovations. Gender-blind approaches can reinforce existing inequitable power relations in dairy households. Gender norms and practices often influence women’s and men’s activities in dairy. In married households in Western Kenya, men typically own dairy cows and women provide substantial labour in everyday activities, such as milking, feeding cows and cleaning sheds in semi- intensive and intensive production systems.
Despite women’s significant labour contributions, their potential to earn or decide how to use income from milk sales is often limited (Bullock et al. 2023, Tavenner and Crane 2018).
Opportunities to learn about climate-smart practices are gendered.

Extension services typically target men, who often have more free time than women who are busy with household tasks and do not have time to attend training events. Unequal access to information further limits women’s participation in deciding whether to try an innovation. Labour-intensive innovations may unintentionally increase women’s labour burdens in dairy production.
Integrating socially inclusive approaches is essential to ensure that farmer-led scaling is inclusive and supports social equity in dairy households.

In this brief, we describe an innovation that supports locally-led adaptation that is “controlled by local people, grounded in local realities, ensures equity and inclusivity, and is facilitated by local networks and institutions” (Westoby et al. 2021, Rahman et al. 2023).

Our innovation integrates gender into an existing project that uses ‘positive deviance’ to identify and work with successful ‘pioneer’ farmers in a community to scale existing climate-smart practices through knowledge networks and farmer field day events (Habermann et al. 2022). Pioneer farmers implement climate-smart feeding practices and share their knowledge with others in the community, primarily through farmer field days. They are also typically men. However, dairy is a household enterprise and multiple family members, wives in particular, provide substantial labour and time in dairy activities.

The household approach was piloted with adaptation pioneers and, in this case their wives, to ensure that gender-specific concerns and priorities inform and impact scaling activities. This is primarily through co-creation processes in which adaptation pioneers and household members meet with local extension agents and partners to plan farmer field days together. Women in these planning activities actively participate in shaping the agenda and, in so doing, have created a demand-driven gender- responsive locally-led adaptation approach. Women and men lead and learn together, and reflection dialogues are incorporated to collectively assess the process and make changes as needed. These activities are not linear but iterative and often complement and inform one another to improve socially inclusive scaling and
equitable benefit distribution in households.
Our innovation
Incorporate gender-specific priorities in planning field days

Household members and extension staff met in the early stages of planning field days. Typically, extension staff, whether women or men, speak to men in married households. The ILRI gender team developed guidelines to integrate social inclusion principles when engaging with household members. Specifically, extension staff were encouraged to engage women to learn about gender-specific priorities and needs. Women’s perspectives and recommendations led to changes in the organization and content of field day activities.
Women found training events on climate-smart fodder and feed practices to be interesting, however, they generally exercise limited agency in decision-making about the uptake of such innovations.

During co-creation processes, women expressed interest in leading and learning about alternative activities that they manage or control, such as kitchen gardens and poultry production. In many households, diverse practices are common and support synergies with dairy production (e.g., manure and compost application in kitchen gardens to improve productivity). Certain fodder species, for example, specific sweet potato varieties, also function as both food and fodder and may be planted in kitchen gardens near the home.

Because of local gender norms and relations, women are reluctant to speak up in the presence of men in public spaces. In mixed group audiences on farmer field days, men who were attending were more likely to interact with the facilitator of the training event. Recommendations to increase women’s participation were to organize field days into gender-disaggregated audiences to encourage women to speak up and interact more with training session facilitators.
Include and enhance women’s knowledge networks.

Engaging in planning discussions also led to changes in network sharing. Previously, the project worked with only the pioneer farmer networks. In the household approach, both the pioneer and his spouse’s networks were included. Women’s and men’s knowledge networks were contacted and invited to attend farmer field days. Women thus expanded their knowledge networks with other women and community members, thereby expanding overall networks that scale climate-smart dairy practices.
Reflect, review, and refine the approach.

Multiple opportunities for reflection were incorporated into the approach, such as feedback workshops with adaptation pioneers and their spouses to review experiences from women’s and men’s perspectives. Feedback sessions were also conducted with stakeholders and participants to discuss what went well and what should be improved at the conclusion of each field day.
Women recognize their important roles and their contributions to the success of dairy activities and recommend that women learn and lead alongside men in households and communities.
