Introduction Bread is a global staple food that plays a vital role in food security [1]. Over the past decades, the change in food habits has tremendously increased the demand for wheat-based foods, such as bread, in developing countries [2]. Wheat flour is the main raw material for the processing of bread. It has proteins with superior baking properties [3]. Regardless of the unique qualities of wheat flour proteins for bread-making, wheat flour is low in health-promoting bioactive compounds, such as beta-carotene [4]. Wheat flour contains high amounts of digestible starch [5] with a high glycemic index, making wheat bread unsuitable for consumption by patients suffering from diabetes, hypertension, and other cardiovascular diseases [6]. Furthermore, the soaring prices of wheat on the global market and concerns over the increase in importation in sub-Saharan Africa warrant the interest to partially substitute it in bakery applications. This would reduce dependency on wheat imports and lower the cost of production for bakeries and consequently generate more profits. Vitamin A is an essential micronutrient for human health. It is primarily involved in vision, reproduction, growth, and cellular communication [7,8]. Vitamin A deficiency (VAD) is a prevalent health problem in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) and South Asia. It results from consumption of diets low in bioavailable vitamin A [9,10]. Limited access to diets rich in vitamin A has been a major factor contributing to the high prevalence of VAD among populations in SSA [11,12]. VAD is one of the leading causes of childhood blindness, morbidity, and mortality from infections in children and pregnant women in low and middle-income countries [12]. According to the World Health Organization Database, approximately 190 million preschool children and pregnant women suffer from VAD worldwide [12]. A previous study by [9] has further reported 40% of children below five years are deficient in vitamin A. Strategies, such as dietary diversification, vitamin A supplementation, and food fortification, are being explored to address vitamin A deficiency. These approaches are however not feasible and sustainable [12]. Further, animal food sources rich in vitamin A, such as dairy products, fish, and meat, are not consumed regularly by the majority of poor households in developing countries [10,11]. Alternatively, these households obtain about 82% of their total dietary vitamin A from plant-based foods [12]. For these reasons, plant-based foods and biofortified crops, such as sweet potatoes, offer cheap and sustainable alternatives for alleviating VAD [10,13]. Among the carotenoids, -carotene is the most important provitamin A carotenoid. It is found in fruits, leafy green vegetables, orange, and yellow vegetables [8,10]. Biofortified orange-fleshed sweet potato (OFSP) is being grown and promoted as a food-based strategy to address the problem of VAD in SSA [11,14]. OFSP is rich in beta-carotene, a precursor for Vitamin A. An ex-ante assessment by [13] demonstrated that OFSP could largely contribute to fighting VAD in SSA. A different study by [10] recommends OFSP as a long-term strategy in combating VAD in children in SSA. About 100 125 g of boiled or steamed OFSP adequately provides the recommended dietary intake (RDA) of retinol equivalent per day in children below five years [10,13,15,16]. Unlike many vegetables, OFSP is also a good source of energy, antioxidants, vitamins C, E, K, B vitamins, and minerals such as phosphorus, potassium, and dietary fiber [17]. OFSP is bulky, highly perishable, and mainly consumed as boiled or steamed in SSA. However, the majority of the urban population has a low preference towards boiled sweet potato [18]. Efforts to expand the processing and utilization of OFSP in SSA are still in progress. It is currently processed into a pur e for partial wheat flour substitution in the production of bread by bakeries in SSA [19,20]. The pur e is prepared by washing, peeling, steaming, and mashing sweet potatoes which retain more than 90% of beta-carotene. Conventionally, the production of flour by drying has been a practical approach for enhancing the shelf-life of sweet potatoes. Although this saves on problems related to perishability, storage and transportation, significant loss in carotenoids occurs [21,22]. Regardless, several studies have reported the use of OFSP flour as an ingredient in baked goods [3,21,23,24,25,26]. Therefore, the incorporation of OFSP pur e in foods is a more ideal approach for potentially improving vitamin A dietary intake [27] in Kenya and SSA in general. A study by [28] revealed a high preference and willingness to pay for OFSP bread among consumers in urban areas. Thus, OFSP bread can help in fighting VAD in children, pregnant women, and lactating mothers in urban areas [29]. Bakeries in SSA are currently substituting wheat flour with up to 30% of OFSP pur e in the production of sweet potato bread [19]. However, the potential to increase the current substitution level to produce a more nutritious composite bread exists. A few studies have reported sweet potato pur e as an ingredient in baked goods in regard to their sensory attributes, physical properties, consumer preference, and contribution to vitamin A [27,28,29,30,31]. A recent study by [5] found that increasing the proportion of OFSP pur e concentration (10 to 50%) in bread improves the bioacccessibility of -carotene and alters the digestion of starch, beneficial for human health. However, there is limited information on the effect of substituting wheat flour with different proportions of OFSP pur e on nutritional and some physicochemical properties of sweet potato bread. The shelf-life of bread is relatively short. It is limited mainly by staling and spoilage by microorganisms, such as Bacillus subtilis, yeast, and molds. There has also been an attempt to assess the shelf-life of bread substituted with 30% OFSP pur e [31] but more information on different levels of substitution is required. OFSP flour has recently been shown to decrease staling in wheat OFSP composite bread [3]. On the contrary, OFSP pur e can support microbial growth and act as a source of contamination in bread if good hygiene practices are not observed [32], hence the need for microbial quality assessment. To date, there is no information on the influence of OFSP pur e proportion on microbial quality and shelf-life of bread. The objectives of this study, therefore, were: (1) to develop sweet potato composite bread from different proportions of wheat flour and OFSP pur e, and (2) to investigate the effects of wheat flour substitution with 20 50% of OFSP pur e on proximate composition, -carotene, color, water activity and microbial shelf-life of the composite bread. 2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Materials Sweet potato pur e was prepared from fresh OFSP roots of the VITA variety at the pur e processing company in Homa Bay County, Kenya. It was prepared following methods described by [33,34]. The sweet potato roots were washed, hand-peeled, trimmed, and cut into 0.5 cm-thick slices using a mechanical slicer. Then, the slices were steamed for half an hour at 100 C. The cooked sweet potato was cooled for 1 h on trays and comminuted into a pur e using a pur eing machine (OMAS Food Machinery, AEE1T0, Euro ingredients limited, Oggiona con Santo Stefano, Italy). The pur e was vacuum packed in 5 kg plastic bags and immediately stored in the freezer ( 20 C). The frozen pur e was delivered to International Potato Centre (CIP-Nairobi) in ice-cold boxes and stored at 20 C before analysis. All the ingredients: commercial baker s flour (United Millers Limited, Kisumu, Kenya, protein content 10% on dry matter basis); bread improver (VITABAKE D 300, Pack Ingredients, Nairobi, Kenya), formulated with corn starch, ascorbic acid, calcium carbonate, and baking enzymes ( -amylase and hemicellulase); salt (Kensalt Ltd., Mombasa, Kenya), sugar (West Sugar Co. Limited, Kakamega, Kenya), baker s yeast (Dalet Foods, Nairobi, Kenya), and cooking fat (Bidco, Africa Ltd., Thika, Kenya) were purchased from a retail outlet in Nairobi. All the ingredients were purchased from a retail chain store in Nairobi and formulated as shown in Table 1. Wheat flour was mixed with OFSP pur e in the ratios of 100:0, 80:20, 70:30, 60:40, and 50:50. These were used to prepare 20, 30, 40, and 50% sweet potato pur e bread. White bread was prepared with 100% wheat flour as a control for the study. Table 1. Ingredient formulation for wheat flour OFSP pur e composite bread (g/kg). Bread Making The bread was produced by straight dough according to [31,35] with modifications. The dough for each treatment was prepared in three replicates while maintaining the processing conditions for both sweet potato bread and wheat flour bread (control). Yeast was dissolved in warm water at 30 C, followed by mixing of the dry ingredients (Table 1). Melted fat, sweet potato pur e, and other ingredients were then mixed (Tombak bakery and confectionary F2 mixer). The ingredients were mixed for 3 min at low speed, followed by 5 min mixing at high speed. After complete mixing, the dough was weighed, cut into 450 g portions, and molded into rolls. The molded doughs were placed in baking tins smeared with a layer of oil and proofed at 30 C for 45 min at 85% relative humidity. The proofed dough was baked in a preheated oven (F MAK Rotary Oven, Turkey) at 230 C for 30 min [24]. The loaves of bread were depanned and cooled on clean and sanitized shelves at (23 1 C) for 2 h [36]. The bread samples were vacuum-packed and aseptically transferred to the laboratory for analysis. 2.3. Sample Preparation The bread was sliced manually using sterilized kitchen knives. Nine slices were selected from each bread for analysis. They were equally selected from the center, and both ends of each bread. The crust was manually cut and separated from the crumb and grinded separately for beta-carotene analysis. The crust (20 mm 20 mm ~4 mm) and the crumb (20 mm 20 mm 20 mm) were also prepared manually for color measurement. Samples for proximate composition and water activity analyses were milled without the separation of the crumb and the crust. Bread samples for the analysis of water activity and microbial profile were analyzed immediately while the rest of the samples were kept in a clean and sanitized oven space at 25 C to mimic the normal shelf storage conditions for bread. Sample preparation, extraction, and analysis were performed under golden-yellow lights to prevent the degradation of beta-carotene. All the samples were analyzed for moisture content, protein, fat, fiber, ash, -carotene, color, water activity, total viable counts, and fungal counts. All the analyses were performed in triplicate. 2.4. Determination of Proximate Composition in Bread Moisture content, crude fat, crude protein, crude fiber, and total ash were determined according to the Official Methods of Analysis of AOAC International [37]. 2.4.1. Determination of Moisture Content The moisture content was determined by the method of AOAC 934.01 [37]. Two grams (2 g) of well-homogenized bread samples were transferred to the dried weighed dishes. The samples on the dishes were dried in the oven for 2 h at 105 C until achieving a constant weight. The dried samples were removed from the oven, cooled in a desiccator at room temperature, and reweighed: M o i s t u r e ( % ) = ( W 1 W 2 ) 100 S w (1) where W1 is the weight of the dish and fresh sample, W2 is the weight of the dish and dried sample, and Sw is the sample weight. 2.4.2. Determination of Total Ash Content The ash content was determined according to the methods of AOAC 942.05 [37]. Two grams (2 g) of the sample were weighed and placed into a dry crucible of predetermined weight. The sample-containing crucibles were charred on a hot plate and placed in a muffle furnace at 550 C. The samples were ignited for 6 h. The samples were removed from the furnace, cooled in a desiccator at room temperature, and weighed: T o t a l A s h ( % ) = ( W 1 W 2 ) 100 S w , (2) where W1 is the weight of the ash and crucible after incineration, W2 is the weight of the empty crucible, and Sw is the initial weight of the sample. 2.4.3. Determination of Crude Fat The fat content was performed by acid hydrolysis and Solvent extraction method as described by AOAC 920.39 [37]. Five grams (5 g) of the sample were weighed in a 300 mL hydrolysis tube and hydrolyzed with 100 mL of 4 N HCl at 170 C for 1 h. The samples were filtered, dried in an oven (at 70 C) for 8 h. The dried samples were transferred into extraction thimbles and extracted for fat using SER 148 Solvent Extractor (VELP Scientific, Italy) with petroleum ether as the extraction solvent. The receiver flask was then dried in the oven at 100 C for 30 min to evaporate traces of the solvent. The flask was cooled in the desiccator to room temperature and reweighed: C r u d e F a t ( % ) = ( W f W ) 100 S w , (3) where Wf is the weight of the receiver flask and extracted fat, W is the weight of the empty receiver flask, and Sw is the weight of the sample used. 2.4.4. Determination of Crude Fiber The crude fiber content in bread was established according to the AOAC 978.10 methods [37]. Two grams of defatted sample were transferred into a 1 L beaker and digested on a hot plate with 25 mL of 2.5 M H2SO4 for 30 min. The volume was maintained at 200 mL with hot distilled water while stirring the sample during the digestion process. It was then filtered through the glass wool on a Buchner funnel. The second digestion step was conducted using 2.5 M NaOH. The sample was filtered again through the same glass wool. The residue on the glass wool was rinsed with 3 mL of ethanol. The glass wool together with the residue were dried in an oven at 105 C for 30 min until a constant weight (W1) was achieved. The oven-dried samples were then incinerated in a muffle furnace at 600 C for 3 h. The incinerated sample was cooled in a desiccator at room temperature and reweighed: C r u d e F i b e r ( % ) = ( W 1 W 2 ) 100 S w , (4) where W1 is the weight of the crucible and sample before incineration, W2 is the weight of the crucible containing ash, and Sw is the weight of the sample. 2.4.5. Determination of Crude Protein Protein content was performed by the Kjeldahl method as described by AOAC [37]. Exactly 0.5 g of the bread sample was weighed into 100 mL digestion tubes, and 10 mL of concentrated H2SO4 was added with 2 g of Kjeldahl tablet (catalyst). Samples were digested until a pure colorless solution was obtained. Kjeldahl distiller was used for distillation with 35% NaOH (w/w) to release ammonia from the sample. The distilled ammonia was collected in a flask with 50 mL of 4% boric acid mixed with bromocresol green and methyl red indicators. The distilled sample was titrated against 0.1 HCl. The protein content was calculated by multiplying the value of nitrogen by a factor of 5.7 [38]: C r u d e p r o t e i n ( % ) = ( a b 14 5.7 ) 100 W (5) where a is the normality of the acid, b is the volume of the standard acid used (mL), W is the weight of the sample (g), and 5.7 is the conversion factor for protein from % nitrogen. 2.4.6. Available Carbohydrates The percentage of available carbohydrates was calculated by subtracting the total contents of moisture, total ash, crude protein, crude fat, and crude fiber content from 100%: Available carbohydrate = 100 ( M o i s t u r e ( % ) + P r o t e i n ( % ) + F a t ( % ) + A s h ( % ) + F i b e r ( % ) ) (6) 2.4.7. Gross Food Energy The gross energy content of bread was estimated by Atwater s conversion equation [39]: F o o d e n e r g y ( k c a l g ) = ( % A C 4 ) + ( % T F 9 ) + ( % C P 4 ) (7) where AC is the available carbohydrate, TF is total fat, and CP is the crude protein. 2.4.8. Quality Control All the proximate composition analyses were performed in triplicate. Cereal-based food (FC 290, PT-FC-770) from LGC Standards Proficiency Testing UK, previously used for proficiency testing in the lab, and an in-house quality control food material (wheat bran), were used as reference materials for quality control. 2.5. Extraction and Quantification of Beta-Carotene 2.5.1. Extraction of -Carotene in OFSP Pur e Composite Bread -carotene extraction in bread was conducted by saponification and extraction with hexane as described by [40] with modifications. Approximately 2 g of each sample (crust and crumb) was weighed separately in 25 mL screw-capped glass tubes. Then, 6 mL of ethanol (with 0.1% butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT)) and 250 L of echinenone (internal standard) were added. The samples were further homogenized, vortexed for 1 min, and incubated in a water bath (SW23GB, JULABO) at 85 C for 10 min. This was followed by the addition of 120 L of 80% KOH (w/v) to each tube, mixing, and further incubation at 85 C for 5 min. The tubes with the samples were removed from the water bath and immediately cooled in a bucket full of ice. Distilled water (5 mL) was added to each tube while still immersed in ice and vortexed for 1 min. This was followed by the addition of 3 mL hexane ( 99.8% HPLC grade, Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA,) and mixing on the vortex mixer for 1 min. The tubes were then centrifuged (Eppendorf, Centrifuge 5810) at 3000 rpm for 10 min. The upper phase of hexane was extracted using a Pasteur pipette into separate clean 25 mL Pyrex glass test tubes. The extraction and separation processes were repeated thrice by adding 3 mL hexane to each sample pellet in the tubes. -carotene extraction was confirmed to be complete after obtaining a white residue and a clear upper liquid phase. The extract was washed by addition of 5 mL of distilled water, vortexing, and centrifugation at 3000 rpm for 5 min. The upper hexane phase was separated into 15 mL clean test tubes and evaporated under a stream of nitrogen using a nitrogen evaporating machine (N-Evap machine, Organomation, Model OA-8125, River Rd, Berlin, MA, USA) with a water bath at 40 C. Dried tubes with carotenoids were then reconstituted with 5 mL of methanol and tetrahydrofuran (HPLC grade) (85:15 v/v) and filtered through a 0.2 m PFTE syringe filter into amber vials for HPLC analysis. 2.5.2. Extraction of Beta-Carotene in Orange-Fleshed Sweet Potato Pur e -carotene extraction in OFSP pur e was performed according to [41] with some modifications. Approximately 1 g of the sample was weighed (in triplicate) in a 25 mL test tube, followed by the addition of 5 mL methanol and 250 L of the internal standard. The sample was vortexed for 1 min and incubated at 70 C for 10 min. The sample was vortexed, centrifuged for 10 min (at 3000 rpm), and the upper phase was transferred into 25 mL volumetric flask. Tetrahydrofuran (THF) (5 mL) was added to the sample in the tube, mixed on the vortex for one minute, centrifuged, and separated. The extraction was repeated three times. The flask was filled to the mark with THF and mixed on the vortex for 1 min. Two milliliters (2 mL) of the extract were transferred to a separate tube and washed by adding 3 mL of distilled water, 4 mL of hexane, and 0.5 mL of methanol. The samples were centrifuged for 3 min at 3000 rpm. The upper phase (hexane) was separated and dried in a stream of nitrogen using the N-Evap machine. The dried tubes were reconstituted with 2 mL of methanol and THF (HPLC grade) (85:15 v/v) and filtered through a 0.2 m PFTE syringe filter into 2 mL-amber vials for HPLC analysis. 2.5.3. HPLC Conditions Ten microliters (10 L) of each sample were injected into the HPLC (Waters Alliance, 2695 Separations Module, Milford, MA, USA) with an auto-sampler and a UV-Vis photodiode array detector (PDA-2996). Empower software controlled the entire system and data acquisition. The extracts were resolved on a 150 mm 4.6 mm, YMC C30, 3 m particle size HPLC column (Wilmington, NC, USA) utilizing a reverse-phase gradient HPLC method. The mobile phases were methanol/tert-butyl methyl ether/water (85:12:3, v/v/v, with 1.5% ammonium acetate in the water-mobile phase A) and methanol/tert-butyl methyl ether/water (8:90:2, v/v/v, with 1% ammonium acetate in the water-mobile phase B). A linear gradient elution was employed and set as follows: 0 1 min, 100% A; 1 10 min, 90% A; 10 22 min, 45% A; 22 33 min, 5% A; 33 37 min, 5% A; 37 39 min, 100% A; 39 40 min, 100% A. The flow rate was maintained at 0.4 mL per minute and a run time of 40 min [40]. 2.5.4. Quantification of -Carotene in Pur e and Bread All-trans, 13-cis, and 9-cis -carotene in the samples were identified based on their absorption spectra and retention time of their respective pure standards. Quantification was performed using the calibration curves of pure -carotene standards after correcting for extraction efficiency based on recovery levels of echinenone [40]. 2.5.5. Contribution of OFSP Pur e Wheat Composite Bread to Vitamin A Requirement Retinol activity equivalents (RAE) were calculated according to the conversion factor of 12 g of -carotene to 1 g of retinol [42]. Vitamin A activity of the cis-isomers of -carotene was estimated to be half of the trans- -carotene [21,43]. The contribution towards the recommended daily vitamin A body requirement to different groups: children (4 8 years), adolescents (10 18 years), adult males and females (19 65 years), and pregnant and lactating mothers was based on a portion of 100 g for each bread sample. 2.6. Determination of Color in Bread Color measurement was based on Hunter L* (a measure of lightness), a* (a measure of greenness to redness), and b* (a measure of blueness to yellowness) values. The color of bread was determined using a Hunter color meter (Lovibond LC100, Parkland Dr, Sarasota, FL, USA) with standard illuminant D65, observation angle of 10 , and an aperture of 30 mm [21,36,44]. The Hunter color values for the crust (20 mm 20 mm ~4 mm) and the crumb (20 mm 20 mm 20 mm) of bread were determined separately by pressing the chroma meter against the transparent glass petri dish (60 15 mm) filled with approximately 100 g of the sample. The instrument was calibrated using a standard white reference tile with values L* = 98.63, a* = 0, and b* = 0. Three readings were recorded from different positions of the petri dish with the sample. All the samples were analyzed in three replicates. The psychometric color terms chroma, hue angle, and delta E were calculated according to the methods of [45,46], as follows: C h r o m a = a 2 + b 2 (8) H u e a n g l e ( h ) = t a n 1 ( b a ) , (9) E = ( L 1 L 0 ) 2 + ( a 1 a 0 ) 2 + ( b 1 b 0 ) 2 , (10) where L0, a0, and b0 are Hunter color values of white bread and L1, a1, and b1, are experimental color values of different sweet potato composite breads. 2.7. Determination of Water Activity in Bread Water activity (aw) was determined by a water activity meter (Aqua Lab Series 4TE, Decagon Devices, Inc., NE Hopkins Ct., Pullman, WA, USA) [31]. The instrument was calibrated with 0.5 mol/kg, aw = 0.984 potassium chloride standard solution at 25 C. Water activity was determined after 0, 3, and 6 days of storage. The analysis was performed in triplicate. 2.8. Microbial Analysis of Bread Total mesophilic (total viable bacterial counts) and fungi were carried out to determine the microbial load of the bread samples by pour plate method according to [47,48] with modifications. Briefly, twenty-five grams (25 g) of each bread sample was mixed with 225 mL of sterile buffered peptone water, agitated vigorously, and allowed to settle. A ten-fold subsequent serial dilution series was performed with 0.85% saline water (NaCl) to obtain a colony count of 1 10 3/mL. Precisely 0.1 mL of each serial dilution was spread evenly and separately on Petri dishes with solidified plate count agar (PCA) for total counts and potato dextrose agar (PDA) for enumeration of yeasts and molds. All the analyses were performed in triplicate. Cultured PCA plates were incubated at 30 C for 48 h, while PDA plates were incubated at 25 C for five days. The colonies were enumerated and recorded after incubation. Microbial quality evaluation was conducted on day 0, day 3, and day 6 of storage. The analyses were performed in triplicate. 2.9. Statistical Analysis The experimental data were subjected to statistical evaluation using analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey s test to determine the significant differences between bread quality characteristics of the various formulations. Pearson correlation was also performed to establish the relationship between the variables. The analyses were conducted using the statistical software for social sciences (SPSS 26.0, SPSS, Inc., Chicago, IL, USA). The statistical significance was defined as (p < 0.05). Executive Summary

Malawi faces significant challenges in nutrition, economic development, and climate resilience. The Orange- Fleshed Sweet Potato (OFSP) puree offers a scalable solution that addresses these interconnected issues. Developed by the International Potato Center (CIP), OFSP puree is a nutrient-dense product with the potential to reduce Vitamin A deficiency, enhance food security, and drive economic growth through value addition and market expansion. By integrating OFSP puree into the food system, Malawi can advance its health and economic goals while supporting the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 2 (Zero Hunger) and SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-being).

OFSP puree’s adaptability to local conditions and its versatility in institutional and household settings position it as a transformative innovation for Malawi’s food systems. However, realizing its full potential requires addressing critical challenges such as limited processing capacity, restricted vine availability, financial constraints for farmers and processors, and low consumer awareness. These barriers must be tackled through strategic interventions that build infrastructure, expand demand, and foster public-private partnerships.

Scaling OFSP production and puree utilization in Malawi faces several interlinked challenges. Access to quality planting materials restricts the supply chain, while smallholder farmers need more financial and technical support to scale production. Processing capacity needs to be developed, with only three processors currently operational, far short of the 12 required to meet projected demand. Additionally, consumer awareness and acceptance still need to be higher, particularly in rural areas where the benefits of OFSP puree are not widely known. Support policies further complicate scaling efforts, with limited incentives for processors and distributors to invest in infrastructure and product development.
Three overarching objectives, drawn from a stakeholder’s consultation, guide this scaling strategy:
1. Improve nutrition and food security by integrating OFSP puree into school feeding programs, reaching 4.4 million children by 2030 and reducing Vitamin A deficiency.
2. Strengthen economic empowerment by increasing smallholder farmer incomes by 20%, creating 10,000 jobs across the value chain.
3. Promoting climate-smart farming practices and adopting drought-tolerant OFSP varieties will enhance environmental resilience and reduce food shortages during dry seasons.

The scaling strategy emphasizes targeted interventions to address key bottlenecks in production, demand, finance, and policy to achieve its ambitious objectives. Central to this approach is enhancing the supply chain by establishing ten vine multiplication centers, increasing vine availability by 200% by 2030. Complementing this, 5,000 farmers will receive training in sustainable farming practices to boost yields and resilience against climate challenges.

On the demand side, the strategy aims to integrate OFSP puree into national school feeding programs, creating a dependable market while addressing child nutrition. Community-based cooking demonstrations and engagement initiatives will further drive household adoption, ensuring that OFSP puree becomes a staple across diverse dietary contexts.

Financial barriers are tackled through partnerships with microfinance institutions, unlocking $2 million in credit for farmers and processors. This is coupled with financial literacy training to empower stakeholders to make informed investments and sustainably scale their operations.

The strategy advocates for robust policy and regulatory support to ensure the long-term success and credibility of OFSP puree. Collaborating with the Malawi Bureau of Standards, it will establish and enforce quality assurance protocols to build consumer trust. Additionally, efforts to incorporate OFSP puree into national food security policies will cement its role as a strategic crop, fostering institutional backing and sustainability.
The scaling strategy unfolds in three phases to ensure structured growth:
1. Foundation Phase (2023-2025): Focus on building infrastructure, piloting OFSP puree in school feeding programs, and initiating farmer training and microfinance support.
2. Scaling Phase (2026-2030): Expand production and processing capacity, integrate OFSP puree into broader food systems, and intensify community engagement to drive demand.

Integration Phase (2031-2040): Transition to a market-led model with minimal public support, ensuring long-term sustainability through private sector investment and strengthened distribution networks.
Projected Impact

By 2030, the scaling of OFSP puree is expected to achieve the following transformative results. Nutritionally, it will reduce child malnutrition by 10% and increase Vitamin A intake by 30%. Economically, it will create 10,000 jobs, and boost smallholder incomes by 20%. Environmentally, it will promote sustainable farming practices, reduce food shortages during droughts, and lower agricultural emissions.

The successful scaling of OFSP puree in Malawi hinges on collaborative action. Stakeholders, including government agencies, private sector partners, and NGOs, must work together to address bottlenecks, invest in infrastructure, and advocate for policy alignment. Through these collective efforts, OFSP puree can become a cornerstone of Malawi’s food systems, driving sustainable development and improving the lives of millions.]

1. Introduction

The Orange-Fleshed Sweet Potato (OFSP) is a biofortified sweetpotato cultivar characterized by its distinct orange hue, a result of selective breeding to increase beta-carotene content levels—a precursor to Vitamin A. OFSP’s high beta-carotene content supports efforts to address Vitamin A deficiency, a key public health issue affecting vision, immune function, and overall health. Regular consumption of OFSP and other beta-carotene- rich foods can help meet the body’s Vitamin A requirements. In its puree form, OFSP serves as a versatile, nutrient-dense base for a range of food products, including baby foods, soups, stews, and sauces. By enhancing the nutritional content of these foods, OFSP puree provides the health benefits associated with high beta- carotene intake and broadens the appeal of OFSP across various consumer groups.

OFSP presents significant opportunities to address Malawi’s food security and economic resilience challenges. As a nutrient-rich crop adapted to local conditions, OFSP can improve household nutrition, enhance smallholder farmer income, and bolster resilience to climate and economic shocks. Value addition through the production of OFSP puree further enhances market potential by extending the product's shelf life and facilitating distribution and sales through formal markets and institutional channels. By integrating OFSP puree into local food systems, the crop is elevated from a traditional food product to a high-value ingredient used in diverse baked goods and snacks, supporting a resilient supply chain and reducing reliance on imported ingredients such as wheat flour. Strategic scaling of OFSP puree production offers pathways for sustainable development, economic empowerment, and strengthening food security in Malawi.
Unlocking the Potential of OFSP Puree for Sustainable Development in Malawi

Processing OFSP into puree enhances its utility. It transforms it into a shelf-stable, adaptable product for diverse applications in institutional settings, including hospitals and school feeding programs. Amidst rising wheat costs—up by 20% globally over the past two years (World Bank, 2023)—and increasing climate challenges, OFSP puree offers Malawi a climate-resilient alternative that reduces dependence on imports in wheat. Malawi’s agricultural sector faces significant pressures, with droughts impacting approximately 30% of arable land and contributing to a 25% decline in maize yields in recent years (Malawi Ministry of Agriculture, 2022). Given its low input requirements and drought tolerance, OFSP is well-suited to Malawi’s conditions, aligning with the Malawi National Agriculture Policy goal of increasing domestic food production by 25% by 2025 (Malawi Ministry of Agriculture, 2016). Scaling OFSP puree processing presents an opportunity to strengthen Malawi’s food security and resilience.

The expanding demand for nutritious, affordable food products in Malawi’s processed foods market—growing at an estimated 5% annually— presents a significant market opportunity (USAID, 2020). OFSP puree is well-suited for various baked goods and snacks, enabling small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) to lower production costs and offer healthier options (Muzhingi, 2020). OFSP puree serves as a cost-effective and nutritious ingredient for the baking industry, capable of replacing up to 60% of wheat flour in various baked and fried goods. Additionally, the puree can reduce the sugar content in doughs by as much as 70% and the amount of oil by 30%, thereby lowering the overall production costs of wheat and wheat-based products by 12-20% (CIP, 2020; MITC, 2022).OFSP puree is a healthy alternative that reduces reliance on wheat flour and enhances the nutritional profile of baked and fried products, enabling them to reach both formal and informal markets. Crucially, this strategy aims to improve the incomes of smallholder farmers by creating a reliable market for OFSP roots. This scaling initiative is expected to generate new jobs across the production, processing, retail, distribution, and retail sectors. Women,
who comprise around 60% of Malawi’s informal workforce, stand to gain significantly from employment opportunities arising from OFSP puree innovation (World Economic Forum, 2021).

Scaling OFSP puree production (Fig 1) also has the potential for substantial social impact. Integrating OFSP puree into school feeding programs could reach an estimated 500,000 children, thereby enhancing their nutritional intake and reducing child malnutrition rates (World Food Programme, 2023). Access to essential vitamins and minerals would support healthier growth and development among Malawi’s population, including children, women and youth.

The scaling strategy for OFSP puree aligns closely with Malawi’s national health, agriculture, and nutrition policies, emphasizing biofortification, food security, and the reduction of micronutrient deficiencies. As a government-endorsed biofortified crop, OFSP supports Malawi’s commitment to improving health and nutrition outcomes. This strategy also contributes to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 2 (Zero Hunger) and SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-being), by promoting food security and reducing malnutrition.

2. Current Landscape of OFSP Puree in Malawi

The Orange-Fleshed Sweet Potato (OFSP) puree market in Malawi is emerging but has yet to reach optimal scale. Approximately ten bakeries and food vendors in urban centers, including Blantyre and Lilongwe, integrate OFSP puree as a healthier ingredient in bread and snacks (USAID, 2020). Current OFSP puree production is estimated at 5,000 metric tons annually, significantly below the 15,000 metric tons required to satisfy rising demand across consumer markets and institutional programs (International Potato Center [CIP], 2023).
Potential for Institutional Feeding Programs

Institutional feeding programs, notably those in schools and community centers, present a considerable opportunity to increase OFSP puree utilization. These programs could consume up to 6,000 metric tons of OFSP puree annually, potentially benefiting approximately 825,000 children by providing nutritious meals that support health and improve educational outcomes in 778 primary schools and 140 pre-primary schools (World Food Programme, 2023). Bridging the current production gap to meet this demand is critical to fully integrate OFSP puree into Malawi’s food systems.
Stakeholder Insights and Challenges in Scaling OFSP Puree in Malawi

The scaling of OFSP puree requires coordinated efforts across a diverse network of stakeholders, as identified during the stakeholder scaling workshop. Table 1 summarizes the roles, challenges, and needs of key stakeholders in scaling OFSP puree in Malawi. Approximately 15 SMEs and local processors require significant investment to expand their currently limited processing capacity. Around 10,000 smallholder farmers face challenges in accessing quality vines and establishing reliable market linkages, which impacts the consistency of root supply essential for puree production. Non-governmental organizations (NGOs), research organizations (such as CIP), and government agencies (e.g., United Purpose) play a critical role in supporting farmers through training for both farmers and extension workers. However, these organizations require additional resources to scale their efforts effectively.

Background: The Need for Multistakeholder Agriculture Knowledge Hub

Within the CGIAR’s Mixed Farming System Initiative (MFS)1, the International Water Management Institute Nepal has piloted a Multi-Stakeholder Agriculture Knowledge Hub (MSAKH) as one of the socio-technical interventions under the initiative in the mid-hills of Nepal. The initiative has been conducting action research since 2022 in Halesi Tuwachung Municipality and Gurbhakot Municipality located in Surkhet and Khotang districts respectively to find possible solutions to improve the livelihood of farmers and foster gender transformative changes.

Within this context, MSAKH aims to bring all the local and municipal stakeholders at each site together to discuss their existing problems in agriculture, learn from each other’s experiences, find common solutions to problems, and promote sustainable mixed farming practices. The hub also holds the potential to be a strong entity to advocate for public and private sector policy changes and empower farmers to negotiate better subsidies, inputs, and prices for their products. Currently, various organizations working in agriculture within these areas are functioning in silos (Bastakoti et al., 2024). As a result, the interventions they implement, and their knowledge and learning are limited to the targeted area and population. MSAKH seeks to break down these silos promoting collaborations and creating momentum for transformative change. Furthermore, the hub can serve as a strong social network for women, Dalits, and other marginalized farmers, helping them strengthen their social connections and role in agriculture-related matters within their households, communities, and wards.

This guideline outlines the methodological steps taken to form MSAKH in MFS sites. It lays out the guiding principles, the formation process, and the activities conducted under MSAKH. It also highlights the preliminary observation, opportunities, and challenges for the long-term sustainability of MSAKH. The insights gained from the process of forming the MSAKH in the mid-hills of Nepal can be adapted and applied to the establishment of other types of local multi-stakeholder platforms.
What is MSAKH?

The concept of a Multi-Stakeholder Agriculture Knowledge Hub is derived from the multi-stakeholder platforms commonly found in Nepal’s forestry and nutrition sectors (Rana et al., 2009; Gaihre et al., 2019). The MSAKH, like a multi-stakeholder platform, is an inclusive and participatory hub designed to bring together relevant stakeholders from various levels. Its long-term goal is to establish an institution that benefits smallholder farmers through knowledge sharing, capacity building, and advocacy programs aimed at changing policies and practices to better support smallholder farmers (K.C et al., 2023). The MSAKHs in MFS sites are currently formed

at the local scale targeting localized and specific issues and solutions. However, the actors connected to the platform can be from regional, national, and international levels. In the future, similar MSAKHs can be established at different levels and can be linked with each other.
The current objectives of MSAKH at the research sites are as follows:

• Establish a participatory platform to engage a wide range of local stakeholders, including women, Dalit, and other disadvantaged groups, in dialogue, decision-making, and collaborative implementation of activities related to Mixed Farming Systems (MFS).
• Serve as an information hub for diverse aspects of mixed farming systems, such as cultivation techniques, post-harvest processes, and market-related information.

• Create a forum to share indigenous and scientific knowledge, experiences, and successful best practices from other regions. This will ensure a coordinated approach to adopting and scaling socio-technical innovations that meet farmers' needs—while also considering the preferences of female farmers—and are suitable for the local context.
• Conduct advocacy campaigns to update agricultural provisions in line with the needs of stakeholders, including diverse farmer groups, agro- entrepreneurs, and the private sector.
• Provide capacity-building training and conduct awareness campaigns for stakeholders on relevant topics tailored to their roles and needs.
• Monitor and document agriculture-related activities—such as trainings, input distributions, and other initiatives—carried out by municipalities, INGOs, NGOs, and academic institutions in the area.
• Facilitate the upscaling of MFS through policy advocacy and resource mobilization.
Who is currently involved in MSAKH?

As the name suggests, MSAKH comprises multiple stakeholders, including farmers, agro-entrepreneurs, ward/municipality representatives and officials, agro-vets, financial institutions, community-based organizations (CBOs), and private entities such as cold storage operators, collectors, processors, and retailers. Among these, some stakeholders—such as farmers, ward representatives, cooperatives, and agro- vets—have become regular members. However, others have yet to formalize their participation. Non-members have expressed positive attitudes toward MSAKH and occasionally attend meetings.

IWMI and CIMMYT have appointed social mobilizers to support the research team in piloting MSAKH. These social mobilizers are locals with experience in agriculture, serving as Junior Technical Assistants. They are familiar with the local context and are in regular contact with the farmers and other relevant stakeholders in the area. Their role involves facilitating the formation of MSAKH in the sites within both municipalities.

The research team comprises biophysical scientists, agriculturists, and social scientists with expertise in feminist approaches. They have been responsible for conceptually designing MSAKH, supporting social mobilizers in its formation, and providing technical input. Additionally, as part of the action research, the team has been observing and documenting MSAKH's progress and the challenges it encounters. The primary objective of their research is to evaluate the conditions under which such platforms become beneficial for all stakeholders and sustainable over time.
This document presents the initial reflections as part of the broader research.
Principles followed for establishing MSAKH in MFS sites:

The principle used to establish the MSAKH is based on the CGIAR guidelines developed and adopted for the creation and management of multi-stakeholder platforms to coordinate integrated water resources management in the Central Rift Valley Lakes Basin of Ethiopia (Kassa et al., 2024). These principles were also adopted to form MSAKH in Nepal, considering the country's socio-cultural, institutional, and agricultural settings.

i) Inclusivity: Inclusion was prioritized in the formation of MSKH. For this, the research team including social mobilizers reached out to relevant stakeholders representing diverse backgrounds to share the importance and benefits of the platform. To ensure equal access to opportunities under MFS initiatives, the research team developed inclusion criteria for selecting stakeholders to participate in piloting MFS innovations and capacity-building training.

ii) Equity and Equality: MSAKH promotes the meaningful participation of women, Dalits, indigenous groups, poor farmers, and other disadvantaged actors working in various sectors within MFS. For example, meetings are typically scheduled at times and locations convenient for these groups. Additionally, two MSAKH platforms were established in each municipality to ensure that female participation is not limited by distance or time constraints.

iii) Clear Communication: Clear communication and equal access to information is one of the principles that MSAKH adheres to. The objectives of MSAKH and its significance were communicated to relevant stakeholders, including Municipality and Ward representatives, as well as to local farmers and other community members. Additionally, stakeholders are encouraged to share information about the platform. However, many residents still need to be informed about the innovation.

iii) Collaboration: The MSAKH encourages its members to network and collaborate with stakeholders outside the platform. The research team also supports MSAKH members in connecting with local, provincial, and federal actors by inviting them to various events organized under the MFS initiative. Additionally, IWMI and CIMMYT are planning exposure visits for MSAKH members to agriculture training/research centers, with the aim to expand their networks and foster collaboration.

iv) Transparency and accountability: MSAKH follows a participatory approach and maintains open and transparent processes. Decisions are made collectively, and members are encouraged to share new information about agricultural opportunities or challenges on the platform. Currently, IWMI researchers closely monitor the platform, but in the long term, the Municipality is expected to take over this responsibility.
v) Flexibility: MSAKH is designed to adapt to changing needs, priorities, and circumstances. This also means that the membership of the hub can be expanded, and leadership can be adjusted as needed.

vi) Sustainability: Currently, MSAKH operates as a loose network and has not been formally registered under the Municipality. However, MSAKH has been established with the long-term goal of remaining functional, if stakeholders find it necessary for knowledge sharing and problem-solving. So far, current members are eager to expand MSAKH and want the Ward and Municipality to take ownership of its sustainability. They have communicated their concern to the Ward and Municipal representatives. It is expected that they will take ownership.

vi) Knowledge/skill sharing: MSAKH promotes the culture of participatory knowledge/skill sharing. It encourages stakeholders to support the enhancement of each other’s capacity so that everyone benefits together.
The Case Study: The MSAKH in MFS sites

Brouwer et al. (2019) proposed four stages for designing an MSP: initiation, adaptive planning, collaborative action, and reflective monitoring. We are following a similar approach to design MSAKH. Although MSAKH is currently in the formation and adaptive planning stage, few activities under collaborative actions and reflecting monitoring is also undertaken. This section outlines the steps we have taken to form and develop MSAKHs.
Formation of MSAKH: The initiation stage

i) Identifying the organizational gap: In both municipalities, the research team conducted a scoping study to assess the existing opportunities, challenges, priorities, and needs of diverse groups of farmers and relevant stakeholders. A capacity assessment of MFS stakeholders was also carried out at the local, provincial, and federal levels. The findings revealed that, at the local level, farmers rely on each other for various farming activities. Informal networks, such as forest user groups, savings and credit groups, mothers' groups, women’s groups, and water groups, exist in the

study areas. However, these platforms do not function as spaces for sharing problems or exchanging agricultural knowledge, nor do they provide a means for farmers to unite and negotiate with stakeholders, such as Ward /Municipality

representatives and market intermediaries (Bastakoti et al., 2024). As a result, their ability to advocate for themselves has been weakened. Some farmers recognized this issue and sought support from the research team to establish such a network (Figure 1).

ii) Need assessment: After the scoping study and capacity assessment, representatives from the Municipality, farmers, and other stakeholders were consulted regarding the institutional gap within the Municipality that prevents farmers and relevant stakeholders from coming together on a single platform. The concept of such a platform was also presented, drawing on suggestions from some farmers. Later, during the innovation selection process for piloting MFS socio- technical innovations, farmers from both municipalities were surveyed about their interest in joining the platform. The response was overwhelmingly positive, prompting the MFS research team to select MSAKH as one of the socio-technical innovations to pilot at the MFS sites (Figure 3) . iii) Briefing about the MSAKH: Social mobilizers were deployed in both municipalities to facilitate the formation of MSAKH. During this process, the social mobilizers reached out to diverse groups of farmers and stakeholders who were not consulted before and briefed about the MSAKH. They were also asked about their interest in joining the platform. This way women, Dalits, the elderly and other marginalized groups were not left out and their interests were assessed.

v) Formation of the MSAKH: In March and April 2024, MSAKH was formed in both municipalities with the support of the farmers, MFS research team, social mobilizers, and municipality staff. The hubs were formed in Gurbhakot, in the presence of the ward chairpersons (Figure 4). The stakeholders selected the hubs’ chairpersons in a participatory way. In all the hubs, male members took the leadership positions while females took the vice chairperson or treasurer positions. During the formation meeting, the objectives of the hub were clarified. The members also introduced themselves and exchanged their contact information. Likewise, trust-building exercises were also conducted during the formation meeting to strengthen the bonding of the stakeholders. A session on MSAKH was also conducted during
Innovation Packaging and Scaling Readiness workshops in Surkhet and Khotang, where the workshop participants identified enablers of MSAKH and challenges related to it (Figure 5).

vi) Linking MSAKH with the MFS interventions: MFS interventions have been linked with MSAKH. Most of the members in the MSAKH are from the piloting areas of MFS interventions on Micro irrigations, and fruits and fodders cultivation. As such the farmers of the areas have received either micro-irrigation tools, fodder, fruit samplings, or all of these interventions. This linkage has brought positive results as the members have found more reasons to interact with each other and are also sharing the experience of using the tools to grow fruits and fodder. This has also helped in cultivating the habit of sharing experience, problems and future plans with each other. Likewise, during the process they have also been sharing their experiences with Ward/Municipality representatives.
Multi-Stakeholder Agriculture Knowledge Hub: The Adaptive Planning Phase

This stage includes deepening the understanding and trust among stakeholders, identifying issues and opportunities, generating visions for the future, and examining them, agreeing on the strategies, identifying actions and responsibilities of the different stakeholders, and communicating outcomes (Brouwer et al. 2019). The following activities were conducted:

Regular meetings and discussions: Currently, monthly meetings are held under MSAKH, with the participation of farmers, municipality staff, ward representatives, social mobilizers, and cooperative staff. Social mobilizers, along with the Chairperson, facilitate these meetings. During these sessions, farmers share their experiences of growing seasonal crops and discuss the seasonal agricultural calendar. The meetings also include discussions on the selection of participants for training. Additionally, stakeholders who have attended capacity-building training organized by various organizations share what they have learned with other members.

Furthermore, the stakeholders discuss MSAKH's plans, and the steps required to ensure its sustainability. So far, the concrete action plans for MSAKH have not been developed, however, it is expected to be developed in the year 2025.

Capacity Building Programs: A half-day sensitization workshop on Gender roles and responsibilities was conducted in all the MSAKHs. Likewise, considering the needs and demands of the stakeholders, IWMI organized training on Start and Improve Your Business (SIYB) in both municipalities. The training focused on the basics of account-keeping and entrepreneurship development. Selecting interested women farmers for such capacity-building training is mandatory.

Strengthening networks of MSAKH: The social mobilizer in Khotang created a Messenger group to establish a virtual platform where stakeholders can share information and experiences. Through this platform, farmers are directly connected with municipality/ward representatives, staff, and the Agriculture Knowledge Center. So far, participants have been using this platform to exchange information. Additionally, the research team has been inviting CGIAR scientists, NARC scientists, provincial and national staff working under the Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock, agro-vets, and others to participate in various workshops organized under the MFS initiative. This has helped expand the networks of MSAKH and increase its visibility.
Future Plans: Collaborative Actions and Reflective Monitoring

Collaborative action: The hub is expected to be registered under the Ward or Municipality. The formalizing process will occur gradually after evaluating the short- term impact of the hub. Meanwhile, the members will also revise the goals, objectives, rules, and regulations of the MSAKHs. Likewise, as mentioned above, they will also develop an action plan for the activities to be undertaken and will also allocate responsibilities among stakeholders for its functioning.

Reflective monitoring: The participatory reflective monitoring process is yet to be set. In November 2024, IWMI and CYMMIT scientists assessed the challenges and opportunities of scaling MSAKH in both municipalities. The participants of the workshop included farmers, Ward/Municipality representatives/staff, experts from the province and federal government offices, JTA, Agro-vets, suppliers, social mobilizers, and the IWMI and CIMMYT scientists. This workshop was useful for monitoring and reflecting on the progress of MSAKH. In addition, the activities for the year 2025 were also laid out. The stakeholders proposed various activities, including: i) Registration of MSAKH under Municipality/ Wards ii) Regular meetings & information/knowledge sharing iii) Leadership capacity strengthening of members to lead the network iv) Financial support & resource mobilization v) Advocacy of favorable policies vi) Exposure visits & networking opportunities.
Preliminary reflections
These reflections are based on the research team's interactions, both in groups and individually, with stakeholders from both municipalities.

• Participants have recognized the knowledge hub as a valuable platform for sharing knowledge and information related to agricultural production and marketing. It is also useful for negotiating fair market prices for farm produce and inputs and accessing services such as subsidies provided by local governments.

• Linking MFS (Micro-Finance Services) interventions on micro-irrigation, fruit, and fodder production with the MSKH (Multi-Stakeholder Knowledge Hub) has been effective. The positive outcomes of micro-irrigation practices have helped build trust between farmers and the research team, including social mobilizers. This trust has also extended to municipality representatives, farmers, and vendors, enhancing their confidence in MFS activities.

• Both mayors and respective ward chairs have expressed positive feedback regarding the hub. They believe it has the potential to inspire youth and other farmers to continue farming practices. They also see the hub as a platform that brings together multiple actors to better understand and collaboratively address shared challenges. Additionally, municipality representatives and ward chairpersons from other wards have shown interest in replicating the hub model in their own areas.

• The distance of the meeting venue is a barrier to participation for private- sector actors. Cooperatives, agro-vets, entrepreneurs, and extension workers are typically based in market areas, which are far from the villages where farmers reside. As a result, some of these actors are reluctant to attend monthly meetings due to the time and cost of travel.

• A clear governance structure for the MSAKH needs to be developed and formally endorsed by its members. This should include a detailed action plan, division of responsibilities, and a framework for implementation to ensure consistent progress and momentum.

• The role of social mobilizers has been crucial in establishing and maintaining the MSAKH. While their involvement is intended to be temporary, with the expectation that hub members will assume full responsibility in the future, stakeholders are currently highly dependent on them. The process of transferring responsibilities must therefore be carefully planned and discussed with stakeholder members to ensure a smooth transition.
Challenges
The research team has reflected on these challenges based on their interaction with the stakeholders and their personal reflections on being involved in the MSAKH piloting process.
• Male Dominance in Leadership Roles:

In all the knowledge hubs, male members have taken up the leadership positions. Female members, in many areas, have been hesitant to hold executive roles. Reasons they have mentioned include fear of additional work burden, lack of confidence, and challenges in traveling to attend training in other areas. This highlights the need for targeted capacity-building programs, such as self-esteem-building workshops, mentoring opportunities, and technical skills training to empower women and other disadvantaged groups to assume leadership positions.
• Meeting Members’ Expectations:

The sustainability of the platform depends significantly on its ability to fulfill stakeholders' immediate expectations. If the hub fails to deliver tangible outcomes within 1–2 years of its formation, there is a risk of it becoming dysfunctional.
• Securing Adequate Financial Resources:

The MSAKH requires financial resources for its operation. While current expenses are modest and covered by the MFS initiative, this support will not continue indefinitely. To ensure long-term sustainability, the hub must develop strategies to secure independent funding sources.
• Building Technical Skills:

Hub members need a range of skills, including networking, coordination, fundraising, data and information management, monitoring and evaluation, and leadership. However, members currently lack these skills. Training programs should be implemented to address these gaps and enhance the hub's functionality.
• Ensuring Inclusion:

Inclusion is a key objective of the MSAKH but ensuring equitable representation and meaningful participation of marginalized groups, including women, Dalits, and other disadvantaged communities, remains a challenge. Formal and informal barriers often hinder their involvement. The MSAKH must create a safe, supportive environment that encourages the participation and representation of these groups.
• Fostering Cooperation Among Multiple Actors:

During the IPSR workshop, stakeholders identified trust issues as a significant challenge to the sustainability of the MSKH. Past instances of dysfunction in saving groups, cooperative groups, mother groups, and farmer groups at MFS sites have often been attributed to trust breakdowns. To address this, the
MSAKH must implement effective mechanisms for communication, conflict resolution, transparency, and accountability.
Conclusion and the way forward

The establishment of Multi-Stakeholder Agriculture Knowledge Hubs (MSAKH) in Khotang and Surkhet marks a promising step toward enhancing mixed farming systems (MFS) in Nepal's mid-hills. The progress made in forming these knowledge hubs reflect the stakeholders' interest and recognition of the benefits MSAKH offers. These hubs have the potential to foster sustainable livelihood practices in the mid- hills by connecting various actors to improve productivity, strengthen market linkages, and influence local policies.

As this approach is still in its early stages, ongoing support is crucial to developing effective collaborative action plans. Strengthening stakeholders' capacities will be vital for managing MSAKHs, fostering a learning-oriented culture, building capabilities for action, securing resources and funding, and conducting reflective monitoring and adaptation (Brouwer et al., 2019).

Looking ahead, the lessons learned from these pilot sites will provide valuable insights to decide whether to establish similar multi-stakeholder platforms elsewhere. However, before scaling up this model, additional time is required to support further development and ensure the maturity of these pilot initiatives.

The Mixed Farming Systems Initiative aims to provide equitable, transformative pathways for improved livelihoods of actors in mixed farming systems through sustainable intensification within target agroecologies and socio-economic settings.

Through action research and development partnerships, the Initiative will improve smallholder farmers' resilience to weather-induced shocks, provide a more stable income and significant benefits in welfare, and enhance social justice and inclusion for 13 million people by 2030.

Activities will be implemented in six focus countries globally representing diverse mixed farming systems as follows: Ghana (cereal–root crop mixed), Ethiopia (highland mixed), Malawi: (maize mixed), Bangladesh (rice mixed), Nepal (highland mixed), and Lao People's Democratic Republic (upland intensive mixed/ highland extensive mixed).

1 Background
1.1 Overview of Mixed Farming Systems

Mixed farming system (MFS) is predominant in the global south. Mixed crop- livestock systems are estimated to cover about 2.5 billion ha of land globally and, in the developing world, they supply around 75% of milk, 60% of meat, and 41–86% of cereals consumed (Herrero et al., 2010). In MFS, farmers integrate crops, trees, and livestock systems to diversify risk from single-crop production, use labor efficiently, access cash, and add value to products. MFS has the potential to maintain ecosystem function and health, and to help prevent agricultural systems from becoming fragile (Holling, 1995). However, key drivers of change- population pressure, urbanization, migration, climate change, water scarcity, changing eating habits, and unstable food prices are deepening inequalities in resource access. All these drivers are obstructing progress towards achieving sustainable development goals (Herrero et al., 2010).

To improve the overall performance and sustainability of MFS, their sustainable intensification requires integrated systems research to identify context-specific pathways toward efficient, resilient, and scalable MFS that preserve natural capital and offer equitable benefits for all (Hoeschle-Zeledon et al., 2021). The Sustainable Intensification (i.e., production of more food on the same piece of land while reducing the negative environmental impacts) of Mixed Farming Systems can deliver critical outcomes that result in multiple impacts at scale, minimize sectoral trade-offs and leverage/maximize synergies in MFS (Hoeschle-Zeledon et al., 2021). The CGIAR’s Initiative on Mixed Farming System (SI-MFS) aims to address these challenges through sustainable intensification of mixed crop-tree-livestock systems to deliver more productive and equitable livelihoods, along with reduced environmental footprint. SI-MFS intends to provide gender-transformative pathways to achieve this goal by deploying locally viable socio-technical innovations that will maximize synergies and minimize trade-offs between the systems’ biophysical and
social components (Hoeschle-Zeledon et al., 2021).
1.2 Nepal’s context

In Nepal, small and medium holder farmers practicing a mixed farming system (MFS) dominates the agriculture practices. Farmers follow multiple cropping practices integrating crops with vegetables, fruits and raising livestock. This system typically involves strong integration where livestock provides manure for crop production and crop residues provide feed for livestock. MFS is primarily practiced in rain-fed environments on fragmented land in the mid-hills and the mountains (Neupane and Koirala, 2023).

In the Nepalese context, the needs of farmers practicing MFS are overlooked prioritizing commercial farming by providing subsidies to promote mono-cropping, the use of herbicides, and improved crop varieties. Policies, institutions, and technologies are also designed for adult male farmers giving less attention to the needs, challenges, and priorities of women and elderly farmers. Further, inadequate investment, infrastructure, agro-advisory tools, underdeveloped markets, labor shortage, climate-induced risks, and weak agriculture governance foster challenges to MFS. As a result, farmers’ interest in agriculture is decreasing whilst attracting them to non-agriculture sectors (Koirala and Neupane, 2023).

This indicates a pressing need to rethink the existing agriculture system. In the context of growing labor migration, feminization of agriculture and increased fallow land, mixed farming systems (MFS) can be a vital strategy. MFS has the potential to enhance the current mixed farming system by utilizing the same quantity of natural resources and employing effective crop management and animal husbandry techniques. With policy, program, and technological interventions, MFS may provide an important opportunity to upscale agroecological innovations and improve the livelihoods of resource-poor farmers (Neupane and Koirala, 2023). Within this context, In Nepal, the International Water Management Institute (IWMI) and the International Maize and Wheat Improvement Centre (CIMMYT) are conducting action research on SI-MFS in Gurbhakot Municipality, Surkhet district and Halesi Tuwachung Municipality, Khotang district. These mid-hill regions of Nepal were selected as they are prone to drought. The research began in 2022 and is intended to be completed by 2025.
1.3 Stakeholder demand and participation

In December 2022, group discussions and in-depth interviews were held with farmers, and relevant stakeholders in both areas with the objective of understanding the farming system, farmer’s needs, opportunities, and challenges of agricultural practices in the area. Based on these discussions, the team made a list of eight potential technical innovation bundles. These innovation bundles are listed in the table below.

3 Challenges and Opportunities for scaling Multistakeholder Agriculture Knowledge Hub
3.1 Background

During consultations with farmers and municipality/ward representatives, it is observed that there is a gap in both formal and informal institutions that unite and serve as a common platform for local stakeholders to discuss problems, challenges, and opportunities, and share knowledge related to the agricultural sector. To address this gap, Multistakeholder Agriculture Knowledge Hubs (MSAKHs) were established in Halesi Tuwachung Municipality, Khotang, and Gurbhakot Municipality, Surkhet, with the objective to:

• Establish a participatory platform to engage a wide range of local stakeholders, including women, Dalit, and other disadvantaged groups, in dialogue, decision-making, and collaborative implementation of activities related to Mixed Farming Systems (MFS).
• Serve as an information hub for diverse aspects of mixed farming systems, such as cultivation techniques, post-harvest processes, and market-related information.

• Create a forum to share indigenous and scientific knowledge, experiences, and successful best practices from other regions. This will ensure a coordinated approach to adopting and scaling socio-technical innovations that meet farmers' needs—while also considering the preferences of female farmers—and are suitable for the local context.
• Conduct advocacy campaigns to update agricultural provisions in line with the needs of stakeholders, including diverse farmer groups, agro- entrepreneurs, and the private sector.
• Provide capacity-building training and conduct awareness campaigns for stakeholders on relevant topics tailored to their roles and needs.
• Monitor and document agriculture-related activities—such as trainings, input distributions, and other initiatives—carried out by municipalities, INGOs, NGOs, and academic institutions in the area.
• Facilitate the upscaling of MFS through policy advocacy and resource mobilization.

In March 2024, the MSAKHs were established in Ward 6 and 7 of Halesi Tuwachung Municipality, and Ward 12 and 14 of Gurbhakot Municipality, in the presence of the research team, social mobilizers, municipality staff, and ward chairpersons. The stakeholders selected the chairpersons of the hubs through a participatory process. The stakeholders involved in the hubs include subsistence farmers, small-scale agriculture and livestock entrepreneurs, financial cooperative staff, members of community forest user groups, local-level agrotechnicians, agro-vet owners, cold storage owners, and others.
3.2 Stakeholder Discussion Summary

The group identified inadequate time to participate in the hub's activities and a lack of financial resources to operate the MSAKH as major challenges for scaling the initiative. Another concern raised by the participants was the difficulty in reaching common solutions to problems. They noted that varying needs, interests, and political ideologies among stakeholders could make it challenging to reach a consensus. Additionally, they mentioned challenges in engaging technical experts, who may not be available to attend every meeting. To address these issues, they suggested holding in-person meetings every 2-3 months, with information and knowledge being shared throughout the year.

The participants strongly urged the municipality/ward to take a leading role in facilitating the MSAKH and support its formalization under the Ward/Municipality. They also recommended using municipal resources, such as halls, telephones, and human resources, to reduce the long-term costs of operating the MSAKH. Furthermore, they suggested that many local farmers and stakeholders are unaware of the platform, so promoting the MSAKH to local communities, as well as to stakeholders at the ward, municipality, provincial, and federal levels, would help attract diverse actors and facilitate scaling.

The participants emphasized the importance of encouraging participation from women and marginalized groups, creating an inclusive environment where they can meaningfully engage and represent the group. They also suggested that the Ward/Municipality develop a supportive environment for the MSAKH by implementing policies, such as providing incentives to MSAKH members, to help it thrive.

1 Summary

Mekong Delta region has the largest sweetpotato production in Vietnam. In general, sweetpotato is moderately tolerant to salinity and heat and considered as a climate resilient crop. All parts of sweetpotato from vines to roots can be used for multiple purposes such as animal feeding, human consumption, biofuel, and various forms of processing. The global market for sweetpotato is growing, and there is a great potential for the Mekong region to increase sweetpotato production by incorporating it in the rice cropping system as well as utilizing the coastal sandy-soil zone.

However, there are some challenges to promote sweetpotato for smallholder farmers in the Mekong Delta region. It takes 4-5 months to harvest sweetpotato, which is too long to incorporate into the rice cropping system. Currently, the rice-sweetpotato rotation is only implemented in some areas in Vinh Long province. Furthermore, there are specific trait preferences for Southeast Asia, such as purple flesh and yellow flesh with high dry matter content, which limit variety options for growers, resulting in the dependency on single sweetpotato variety and its informal seed systems. Third, there is an emerging disease in the region in which major varieties in the Mekong region appear to be susceptible.

To address those challenges, International Potato Center (CIP) has initiated a breeding experiment under the CIP sweetpotato Asia short duration breeding pipeline (BP00052). The first batch of true seeds are orange flesh with high dry matter (above 29%). This short-duration genotypes have a great potential to be adopted in the rice cropping system as they can be harvested in 3 months instead of 5 months. It can be for exporting to China or domestic market if the traits meet local demand.

True seeds with elite crosses (humid tropics) were sent from San Ramon, Peru to Vietnam in September 2023 and germinated at Potato, Vegetable, Flower Research Institute (PVFC) in Da Lat, Lam Dong Province, Central Highlands of Vietnam where the temperature is stable year around.

The observation yield trial (OT) was conducted with 1324 genotypes from 9 families in the campus of the Cuu Long Rice Research Institute from late January to late April (90 days). The cuttings were sent from PVFC. Two checks were selected from locally available varieties for a comparison purpose: one is Khoai Lang Mat from Central Highlands which is Vietnam’s only commercial orange flesh variety. Another one is Khoai Sua, a white flesh local variety grown in the Mekong Delta region of Vietnam.

The selection of genotypes for the next advanced trial was made based on the following steps: step 1: the number of marketable roots equal to or above 1.7; step 2: Vine vigor - score 2 or 3; step 3: Remarks about diseases (discarding all with the comment on diseases); step 4: the number of damaged roots by weevils, nematodes and/or pathogens; step 5: the number of marketable roots above 2.0 or above; step 6: high dry matter content (above 28%); step 7: disease damage 1 or above; and step 8: the number of marketable roots equal to or above 2.3. Step 9: the number of vines in their mother plants in Dalat equal or larger than five.

Overall, 167 genotypes (10.7% of the total genotypes) were selected in consultation with partners and the next experiment will be planned starting in July to August when new planting materials and experiment fields are ready.
This report outline the process and result of the observation trial, as well as other relevant activities such as stakeholder consultation and a household survey.

A stakeholder meeting was organized in Vinh Long Province to understand local needs, concerns and interest among farmers, researchers and the government, especially Vinh Long crop production department and MARD Mekong office. “Training of Trainers Guide to Improving Child Health and Nutrition through Diets, Feeding and Hygiene Practices” has been prepared under various projects implemented by International Potato Center (CIP), Bangladesh. In the future, we want to use Community Nutrition Scholars (CNS) to train mothers using this training guide. The aim of this training is to cultivate potatoes without traditional farming, to enhance agricultural development by cultivating orange-fleshed sweetpotato and vegetables in home gardens, easy access to vegetables and variety of nutrients in vegetables increases tendency to eat promoting healthy eating habits and helps to learn techniques of cooking process while maintaining quality of nutrients. Through this guide awareness on nutritional value of potatoes, orange-fleshed sweetpotatoes and sweetpotato vines will be increased, as well as awareness on the role of vegetables in cash crops and healthy development will be improved.

By utilizing spaces around our residence, we can grow vitamin A rich sweetpotatoes, potatoes, green vegetables and fruits. This will allow our families to consume fresh produce as needed, thereby reducing the need to purchase vegetables from the market, which will help save costs. As a result, the nutritional needs of the family can be met and by selling vegetables income may be generated which then can be used to purchase other essential nutritious foods.

In addition to essential nutrients information on healthy sanitation, safe drinking water, and water related information through the implementation of agricultural practices have been included.
