SESSION 1: POTATO PRODUCTION THROUGH ZERO-TILLAGE WITH STARW MULCH FOR HOUSEHOLD CONSUMPTION AND INCOME

Topic Potato Production Through Zero-Tillage with Straw Mulch for Household Consumption and Income • To bringing coastal fallow land under crop cultivation. • To know the technique of zero-tillage potato production. Objectives • To encourage family members especially women and children to engage in zero-tillage potato cultivation. • To meet the vegetable requirements of the family and generate income by selling the surplus. • To improve soil fertility by use of mulch (mulch by rice straw or rice stubble left after harvesting) Method Discussion and practice Duration One hour Materials Module and flipchart

The potato is one of the most important food crops in the world, serving as a staple food in about 40 countries. In Bangladesh, it is a significant part of the diet. Coastal areas in Bangladesh comprise about 30 percent of the total land area, yet potato cultivation is uncommon there. The primary challenges for potato farming in these regions include poor soil tilth, high salinity levels (ranging from 2-25 dS/m), and scarce ir- rigation water. Consequently, a large portion of land remains fallow during the Rabi season after harvesting the Aman rice. To address these issues, the Bangladesh Agricultural Research Institute (BARI) has developed a zero-tillage potato cultivation technique that utilizes rice straw mulch. This innovative method can sig- nificantly benefit farmers in coastal areas.
Advantages of zero-tillage potato production:
Fallow land can be converted to productive farmland.
Due to tillage, potato can be planted 15-20 days
earlier.
• Reduced production costs due to the elimination of tillage, less labor and irrigation requirement.
Lower labor and irrigation requirements.
• Increased soil fertility through the use of rice straw mulch.
Most importantly, increases yields.

ZERO-TILLAGE POTATO CULTIVATION TECHNIQUES:

Time of Planting: If you plant potatoes after harvesting Aman rice, ideally between the first and third weeks of December, you can expect optimal yields. You need to plant potatoes in such conditions, if you walk barefoot in the mud, your feet get stuck, but your feet don’t get muddy.
Varieties: Salt-tolerant varieties like BARI Alu-72 and BARI Alu-78, as well as heat-tolerant varieties like BARI Alu-73 and BARI Alu-79, are suitable for zero-tillage cultivation.
Seed Size: It is best to plant whole seed potatoes weighing 40-50 grams. If the seed potatoes are large, they can be cut into pieces, each with at least two eyes.

Seed Treatment: If the seed potatoes were not treated before storage, soak them in a 3% solution of boric acid, Provax-200 WP, Amister Top, Bavistin-50 WP, or Vitavax-200 (mix 3 grams of powder in 1 liter of water) for 10-15 minutes before sprouting. After soaking, dry the seed potatoes in the shade. If the potatoes are cut, dry the cut pieces in the shade for 3-4 hours before planting and coat, them with ash.

Planting Method: Generally, seed potatoes are planted in rows, maintaining a row-to-row distance of 16 inches (40 cm) and a seed-to-seed distance of 8 inches (20 cm). When planting, press the seed potato into the soil to a depth of one-third of its diameter. Cover each seed potato with compost or organic manure at a rate of 40 kg per decimal. Then, cover the planted seed potatoes with a 6-8 inch (15-20 cm) layer of straw, applying fertilizer on both sides of the row.

Fertilizer Dosage and Method of Application: Usually, apply 1.2 kg of urea, 800 grams of TSP (Triple Super Phosphate), 1 kg of MoP (Muriate of Potash), 400 grams of gypsum, 40 grams of zinc sulfate, and 30 grams of boron per decimal of land. However, the dosages of fertilizers and manures may vary based on the fertility of the soil. At planting, apply half of the urea and MoP, along with other fertilizers. Apply the remaining half of urea and MoP at 30-35 days after planting, followed by light irrigation after top-dressing.

Diseases and Control Measures: Major potato diseases include late blight, bacterial wilt, potato scab, stem rot, and viral diseases, with late blight being particularly dangerous. Outbreaks can occur during foggy weather or prolonged cloudy skies with drizzle. During such conditions, spray Dithane M 45, Acrobat MZ, or Secure at a rate of 2 grams per liter over the entire potato plants.
Harvesting and Yield: Harvest zero-tillage potatoes 75-85 days after planting. The average yield of potato grown in this technique is 60-80 kg per decimal of land.

Zero tillage potato cultivation is a profitable technique. It is possible to earn average Taka 40,000 to 45,000 per bigha of land by cultivating potato in this technique. Adopting zero-tillage potato cultivation can in- crease cropping intensity and productivity in coastal saline areas.

CULTIVATION TECHNIQUE OF ORANGE-FLESHED SWEETPOTATO:
A) Sweetpotato Vine Production Techniques:

Sweetpotatoes are typically propagated using vines. Vines are grown in seedbeds and transplanted to the main field in the subsequent season. To produce 220 vines, plant 20–25 cuttings in an area of 40–50 square feet. To cultivate sweetpotato in one decimal of the homestead area 220 vines is required. In this case the following steps are to be followed:
Step 1 - Site Selection and Land Preparation:
Choose a raised area within or near the homestead that gets enough sunlight and has well-draining loamy soil. Prepare the sweetpotato seedbed by thorough plowing or digging with a spade.
Step 2 - Fertilizer Application:
Mix 4-5 kg of cow dung, 20-25 g of urea, 18-20 g of TSP (Triple Super Phosphate), and 18-20 g of MOP (Mu- riate of Potash) thoroughly into the soil of the seedbed 2-3 days before planting the vines.
Step 3 - Preparation of Cuttings:

Harvest sweetpotatoes planted the previous year when they mature around (mid Chaitra) early April month, which is ideal for making vine cuttings. Collect cuttings from disease-free, healthy, vigorous, and mature vines. Each vine cutting should be 20-25 cm long and have 4-5 nodes per segment.
Step 4 - Planting:

Plant the cuttings in prepared soil immediately after harvesting potatoes in the month of Chaitra (April/ May). Maintain a row-to-row distance of 1.5-2 feet and a cutting-to-cutting distance of 1 foot. Ensure that 2-3 nodes are buried in the soil. Light irrigation should follow immediately after planting the cuttings.
Step 5 - Collection of Vines:
To propagate sweetpotatoes, gather healthy, fresh, vigorous, and pest-free vines during October - November (Kartik-Agrahayan).

B) Sweetpotato production through modern technique:
Soil and Climate:

Orange-fleshed sweetpotatoes grown in sunny, raised and well-drained land. Sandy loam soils are optimal, but with proper management, they can be cultivated in various soil types. The plant performs best at temperatures ranging from 22 to 25°C, which promotes highest carbohydrate accumulation. Soil temperatures below 10°C hinder plant growth.
Land Preparation:
Prepare the land thoroughly with 5-6 plowings, cross plowings, and harrowing.
Planting Time:
The ideal time for planting orange-fleshed sweetpotato vines or cuttings is from mid-October to November (Kartika to Mid Agrahayan).
Vine Planting Method and Number of Vines:

Plant the first and second sections from the top of the sweetpotato vine, with preference for the first sec- tion as it yields higher. Each vine should be 10 to 12 inches long and have two to three nodes buried below ground when planted in rows. Maintain a spacing of 30 cm between plants and 60 cm between rows. Pest Control Management:
In our country, sweetpotato diseases are rare in the field. However, the following insects occasionally attack sweetpotatoes:
Sweetpotato Weevil: This pest affects both field and stored tubers, rendering sweetpotatoes unsuitable for consumption.

Control Measures for Sweetpotato Weevil: Before planting, soak the vines in a pesticide solution made by mixing one milliliter of Benicron or Dimicron with one liter of water for twenty minutes to prevent sweetpotato weevil infestation. This treatment effectively eliminates adult insects, larvae, and eggs. If infestation occurs after planting, apply 8 grams of Diazine-14G or Carbofuran-5G along the rows and lightly irrigate. Additionally, pheromone traps can be used to capture male weevils effectively.

Harvesting and Yield: Orange-fleshed sweetpotatoes are ready for harvesting approximately 120–135 days after transplanting, typically in March or April. Topic Importance of Balanced Diet and Nutrition • To be aware about nutrition and diet. Objectives • Benefit of balanced diet and good nutrition. Method Discussion Duration One hour Materials Module and flipchart

The primary goal of a diet is to maintain a strong, healthy, and functional body. While any food can satisfy hunger, it does not necessarily support health or meet the body’s nutritional needs. Malnutrition can affect both the undernourished and the affluent. Therefore, understanding proper nutrition and diet is essential for everyone.

Few people suffer from malnutrition solely due to insufficient food intake. Instead, most people become malnourished by consuming food without considering its nutritional content. Often, malnutrition goes unnoticed because its effects can be subtle and not immediately obvious. Long-term deficiencies in vitamins and minerals can suppress hunger signals, making it difficult for individuals to recognize their nutritional needs. Malnutrition not only affects productivity but also leads to health problems, which in turn impacts overall economic well-being.

Eating only three meals a day is not enough to maintain a strong, active, and healthy body. It’s essential to be mindful of both the nutritional content and quality of your food. Ensuring that your diet includes nutrient- rich foods is crucial for sustaining overall health and functionality.

Malnutrition persists in our nation largely due to insufficient knowledge about nutrition. To combat this issue, it is essential to increase nutritional awareness, ensure balanced food consumption, employ appropriate cooking techniques, and manage family meal distribution effectively. By carefully selecting nutrient-rich foods and preparing them properly, we can break the cycle of malnutrition and improve overall health.

Vegetables supply essential vitamin A and mineral salts, which are crucial for meeting the body's nutri- tional needs and maintaining overall health. The model for climate-informed agricultural advisories being tested in Cambodia is based on the ""Local Technical Agroclimatic Committee"" (LTAC) approach [4], originally developed by the International Center for Tropical Agriculture (CIAT) in Latin America [1,5]. LTAC is a dialogue process that seeks to understand local climate behavior and generate local-specific recommendations to reduce risks. It includes scientists, technicians, representatives from the public and private sectors, and farmers. This process produces a tailored agroclimatic bulletin, which contains the seasonal climate forecast for the region, the potential impacts on crops for specific conditions in time and space, as well as recommendations for agricultural production planning and decision- making, and is distributed to farmers.
COUNTRY: Cambodia
Comments: Starting with 22 communes in 6 districts of Kampong Speu and Battambang provinces, it has been expanded to 12 communes in 4 districts of Prey Veng and Takeo provinces in the LMB.

The LTAC approach was initially implemented in Cambodia by the DeRISK SE Asia project benefitting about 11,000 rice and cassava farmers in Kampong Speu and Battambang provinces between 2021 -2023 [1,5,7]. It has now been expanded to the Lower Mekong by the CGIAR Asian Mega-Deltas initiative.

Gender relevance: 1 - Significant. The project has a target to disseminate agro-climatic bulletins to both men and women through cooperatives and local authorities (69% of farmers received advisories are women). Multiple dissemination channels were used to reach different user groups, including both non- digital (posters, meetings) and digital (Telegram) [3].

Cap Dev relevance: 2 - Principal. Provincial and district level training on agroclimatic bulletin content and how to share information with farmers is a key activity. The trainings organized by the project were attended by PDAFF and District Office of Agriculture extension officers, leaders of agricultural cooperatives (ACs), local authorities, and representatives of existing projects/programs [1,5].

Climate Change relevance: 2 - Principal. Climate change is a priority in this activity capturing the significance of the use of climate information for short- and long-term farm planning and decision- making [3].
ELABORATION OF OUTCOME/IMPACT STATEMENT

For the development and dissemination of agroclimatic advisory, LTACs are established at provincial level. The committees include relevant partners and stakeholders, such as the Provincial Department of Agriculture, Forestry, and Fisheries (PDAFF), the Provincial Department of Water Resources and Meteorology (PDoWRAM), technical experts from District Office of Agriculture (DOA), leaders of agricultural cooperatives (ACs), and commune authorities [1,5].
These  committees  develop  tailored  advisories  based  on  rice  Crop

These committees develop tailored advisories based on rice Crop Decision Trees (CDTs), with specific response strategies for each crop stage under different climate scenarios (normal, wetter, drier) [2,6]. To date, the CDTs have been developed for all 24 provinces in Cambodia, providing a national database for agroclimatic advisory for farmers at the provincial level [2].

In 2023, LTACs were established in Prey Veng and Takeo provinces in the Lower Mekong. Using the provincial CDTs, the advisories were tailored to match the specific farming conditions at the district level. In each province, two seasonal bulletins were developed during the wet season. AC leaders disseminated the agroclimatic advisories to farmers via multiple channels: posters in public areas, Telegram (a messaging App), and face-to-face communication. AC leaders also distribute printed bulletins to individual AC members and other farmers in their communities.

The project team with PDAFF and DOA, trained 76 AC leaders and local authorities to share agroclimatic information with farmers, Telegram groups were set-up (one in each of the 4 districts, with a total of 116 members, including 24 women), AC leaders, local authorities, and DOA extension officers for sharing up-to-date weather forecasts to farmers. The forecast was provided by the Department of Meteorology (DOM). More than 6,000 farmers (69% female) from 26 ACs (12 communes across four districts) of Prey Veng and Takeo provinces were provided with agroclimatic bulletins. These contained information on variety selection, land preparation, planting methods, soil fertility and water management, pest control, and harvesting dates [3]. This has helped them to better manage climate-related risks such as excessive rainfall, flooding, drought, and pest outbreaks. Farmers using the advisories reported a reduction in rice seed rates/volumes, irrigation expenses, and a decrease in the of planting materials, pesticides, and fertilizers [3].

Preface

Cambodia is one of the most vulnerable countries to the impact of climate change. While climate risks play an important role in agriculture, smallholder farmers' lack of adaptive capacity makes it more difficult for them to cope with changing weather patterns and extreme climatic events. Therefore, agricultural advisory based on climate and weather forecasts can help farmers to reduce climate risks by adapting farming practices and hence maintain their yield and income.

DeRISK SE Asia promotes the application of seasonal climate forecasting and innovative insurance solutions to climate risk management in the agriculture sector in SE Asia. The project is led by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) and implemented by the University of Southern Queensland (USA) and the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT.

In Cambodia, the project began in 2019 by mapping the demand for climate services at the livelihoods level through a series of climate risk workshops across all agroecological zones, followed by the characterization of the existing network of actors supporting climate services (CS). Based on these data, the project partners decided to pilot Local Technical Agroclimatic Committees (LTACs) in Battambang and Kampong Speu Provinces. The LTAC approach was originally developed in Colombia by the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT to co-develop agroclimatic advisory with local partners.

The pilot in Cambodia was led by the International Institute of Rural Reconstruction (IIRR) with technical support from the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT, working closely with the GDA's Department of Agricultural Land Resource Management (DALRM), the Regional Integrated Multi-Hazard Early Warning System (RIMES) and with PDAFF in both provinces. The LTACs were implemented for two years, during the rainy season of 2021 (June – November) and the rainy season of 2022 (June – November). The approach was centered around the co-development of agroclimatic advisory by the members of the LTAC committee for rice and cassava farmers in Battambang and Kampong Speu based on the seasonal climate forecast.

This manual is based on the lessons learned from piloting LTACs in the two provinces and is intended for the relevant departments and ministries, such as PDAFF, NGOs, private sector, management committees of agricultural cooperatives, and other stakeholders, as a practical guide in coordinating and implementing LTACs in the country.

Background

DeRISK SE Asia aims to develop climate risk management strategies, decision support tools, and innovative insurance solutions that will safeguard smallholder farmers and business sectors from physical and financial disasters associated with climate change. As part of the project, a pilot was conducted in Kampong Speu and Battambang provinces for the co-development and dissemination of agro-advisories based on the seasonal forecast.

The Local Technical Advisory Committee (LTAC) approach was introduced at the provincial level. The LTAC brings together different types of technical stakeholders considered critical in the generation of climate information, the translation of climate information into agro-advisories, and the dissemination and use of these. Members included representatives from PDAFF, the Provincial Department of Water Resources and Meteorology (PDoWRAM), Agricultural Cooperative (AC) leaders, private sector partners, and representatives from other projects or programs active in the province. The process was facilitated by IIRR and RIMES with technical support from the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT.

The LTAC was implemented during the rainy season, from May to November 2021 and 2022. A series of LTAC meetings were facilitated before and during the cropping season to co-produce and disseminate agroclimatic bulletins based on seasonal forecasts. Bulletins were provided to farmers with follow-up meetings, training with AC leaders and local authorities, and support of a digital application called Specialized Expert System for Agro-Meteorological Early Warning for Climate Resilient Agriculture (SESAME), developed by RIMES for mobile phones.
Project partners have developed this manual based on the lessons learned with the LTAC approach over a 2-year period and with support and input from the LTAC members.
Objectives
To provide guidance on the implementation of the LTAC approach in the context of Cambodia through specific steps and tools.

This manual is the guide for implementing the LTAC, in which extension workers and relevant development practitioners can produce locally specific agroclimatic bulletins with seasonal climate information and agro-advisories to mitigate climatic risks.
How to use the manual

This manual is intended for LTAC members and those who provide related climate services to farmers in local communities, such as PDAFF Extension staff, PDOWRAM staff, district agricultural officers, NGOs, development projects/programs, and the private sector.

This manual provides background on the LTAC approach, including key components of the LTAC and LTAC member composition, and introduces key sequential steps in implementing the approach. Each step will be presented with clear objectives, processes, and materials for implementation.
The procedure in this manual can be broken down into five steps, as shown below and illustrated in Figure 1.0, Page 11.
Step 1: Establishment of the LTAC
Step 2: Development of the agroclimatic bulletin
Step 3: Dissemination of agroclimatic bulletins
Step 4: Promoting the application of agroclimatic advisories
Step 5: Field visits and review meetings for improvement of results and process

Each step includes a set of activities that the facilitator of the LTAC approach carries out with the LTAC members over several meetings. The worksheets throughout this manual explain the activities of each step in more detail. When developing the program, it is critical to examine when each phase is carried out during the year to ensure that local agroclimatic bulletins are timely developed and disseminated to farmers for making decisions on the planning and management of crops.

This manual is not meant as a blueprint. Activities can be adjusted based on the context and specific circumstances of the LTAC, but key components with underlying principles of the LTAC approach should be acknowledged.
Key components of the LTAC
The graphic below shows the three key components of the LTAC:
(1) Carry out a process of implementation and sustainability of the LTAC by local stakeholders with capacity-building.
(2) Generate, in a participatory way, adaptation measures for each region and crop, based on local agroclimatic prediction.
(3) Disseminate the agroclimatic bulletin focused on the needs of famers, to facilitate decision making for their planning and farming activities.
The LTAC is implemented by local stakeholders, with required capacity building, which ensures ownership by the local stakeholders and leads to sustainability of the LTAC.

From climate information, the LTAC generates adaptation measures against predicted climate risks. A participatory approach does this to make sure the local context is considered when developing the adaptation measures.
The adaptation measures generated at the LTAC are disseminated to farmers to support their informed decision-making for the planning and farming activities.
The LTAC approach promotes key principles such as a participatory approach, combining scientific expert and local knowledge, demand driven, local ownership, and an iterative learning process.
Composition of the LTAC Members

The member composition of the LTAC is critical. First, the lead facilitator must be familiar with and have relevant technical skills in agriculture and meteorology. However, he does not to be an expert on either of these, as both areas need to be represented by experts and officers from relevant government agencies. In addition, farmers from the target communities should be represented to ensure that the agro- advisory information is appropriate and practical to their local conditions. Representatives from existing development projects or programs and the private sector can further help spread the agroclimatic bulletins to a larger number of beneficiaries.

Before the first LTAC meeting, members need to be identified through consultation with project partners, PDAFF, and PDOWRAM in target provinces or with other climate service providers. Relevant stakeholders, including PDAFF, PDOWRAM, other government institutes, development projects/programs in the province, and the private sector, should be invited to join the LTAC. Furthermore, agricultural extension networks, farmer networks, and digital applications that allow for information sharing (e.g., Facebook Messenger, Telegram groups, SESAME App, Tonlesap App, and so on) should be identified from the start, as understanding the primary communication channels in the target areas assists in the proper dissemination of agroclimatic bulletins. For instance, in Cambodia, Facebook messenger is widely utilized by farmers in communities, including agricultural cooperative (AC) leaders. Similarly, Telegram is mostly utilized by government officials and agricultural extension officers.

The number of LTAC members can range from 10 to 15, making accommodating each LTAC meeting easy. However, as mentioned above, LTAC members should represent different types of technical expertise, with key members from both agriculture and meteorology backgrounds and farmer representatives from communities, as well as relevant stakeholders that can facilitate wider dissemination of the information, such as the private sector and relevant projects/programs. To enhance gender equity, women should be encouraged to participate in the LTAC.
Steps for the LTAC implementation

Prior to LTAC implementation Crop Decision Trees (CDT) were prepared with technical assistance from the Cambodia Agricultural Research and Development Institute (CARDI). CDTs include agro-advisories for relevant crops under different seasonal climate scenarios, based on crop calendars, farming practices, climate risks and response strategies. A national validation workshop and subsequent provincial validation workshops are required to make them suitable for each target province.

The CDTs were also incorporated into the SESAME app, so that extension officers and/or farmers can also access agro-advisories via smartphone. Every time the LTAC meets, the climate smart farming recommendations from the CDT can be extracted based on the latest seasonal climate forecasts and used to generate draft agroclimatic bulletins. See Annex 1 for the format of the CDT.

ESTABLISHMENT OF THE LTAC  The  LTAC  members  need  to  have  a  common  issue  of  interest  that  brings  them

The LTAC members need to have a common issue of interest that brings them together and for which they are willing to contribute their expertise, mobilize their networks, and invest their time. During the first step of the LTAC implementation, potential members must be well informed and agree on the purpose, planning of activities, and their role.
Objective of this step
The overall objective is to establish the LTAC with members who agree on the purpose, planning, and roles for the co-development and dissemination of agroclimatic bulletins for farmers.
Specifically

1. Participants understand the scope and background of LTAC implementation and identify which tasks each institution performs, their target crops and places they work in, and their interest in participating in the LTAC.
2. Build coherence among members in terms of the mission, goals, and activities for the establishment of the LTAC, and create a work plan for LTAC’s operation.
3. Inform them on climate forecasts, the tools and products they can use to access this information, and relevance for agricultural decisions
4. Provide seasonal climate forecasts for the next three months and the potential benefits and limitations of using the forecast for decision-making on planning and crop management.
Materials

You will need flipcharts, marker pens, masking tape, a brief document on the background and lessons learned in the LTAC implementation from previous pilots and this LTAC manual, an announcement about seasonal climate forecasts from DOM/MoWRAM, and a list of attendance.
Issues to consider

It is essential to include a meteorologist from PDoWRAM from the start of the LTAC process so that he or she fully understands the objectives and LTAC approach and procedures. At the same time, PDoWRAM staff can provide further information on important climate variables and climatological characteristics, as well as essential information such as major climate risks in the target province.

Forecast variables available, such as rainfall and temperature

6. Worksheet 1a: Background information on the LTAC

The LTAC is a dialogue process among a diversity of local actors including scientists, technicians, representatives from the public and private sectors, and farmers, which seeks to understand the climate’s possible behavior in a locality, and to generate agro-advisories to reduce risks associated with expected climate variability. This dialogue is then used to create an agroclimatic bulletin that contains the region’s climate prediction, its possible impact on crops or livestock for specific conditions in time and space, as well as climate smart recommendations around decision-making for each productive sector. In general, climate predictions produced by each country’s meteorological service are provided in the LTAC meeting, and the LTAC members, from various institutions, identify climate-smart agro-advisories to the climate predictions, and then the climate predictions and the agro-advisories are shared with local extension officers and farmers in the form of agroclimatic bulletins.

It is also important to foster procedures that increase the institutional capacity of agroclimatic bulletin development, particularly for local actors.

The successful implementation of the LTAC requires a joint vision and commitment from participating institutions. For this reason, it is recommended that all involved institutions meet to discuss and agree on its objectives, expected outputs and outcomes, organizational structure, and roles and responsibilities.

a. What should be the role and contribution of my institution within the LTAC? b. Which institutions should be invited to participate in the LTAC?

The development of   crop decision trees for   climate risk management  Kwang-Hyung Kim, Angelica Barlis, Leo Kris Palao,   Bandit Mienmany, Pablo Imbach, Cornelis Swaans  December 2022
KEY MESSAGES
• Crop Decision Trees (CDTs) are an important systematic tool for the development of climate risk responses based on sub-seasonal and seasonal forecasts.
• CDTs are unique in that they combine the need for a harmonized standardized model at the national level with the ability to tailor responses to the local level.
• CDTs generate tailored agricultural advisories to farmers to cope with climate risks occurring at sub-seasonal and seasonal time scales, taking location and crop growth stages into account.
• CDTs can be easily integrated in digital tools and platforms for scaling and automating agro- climatic advisory.
Introduction

Sub-seasonal and seasonal forecasts (SSFs) with sufficient lead time (from 1 month to 6 months) can help farmers to make informed decisions regarding their agricultural activities. The biggest challenge with this is translating SSF information into agriculturally-relevant information that can trigger timely action alerts for farmers and other agricultural stakeholders.

One way to make SSFs useful to the agriculture sector is developing the CDTs based on SSF information for selected crops. CDT will provide recommendations for climate-smart farming practices based on the upcoming 1–6-month SSFs, utilizing mainly rainfall information but also including temperature information in a case-by- case manner. Through sequential scaling down approaches from national to province, district, and commune, location-specific traditional knowledge and valuable experiences on best practices and experiences from local experts and champion farmers can be collected and shared with fellow farmers using the CDT.

In order to use the climate-smart farming in CDTs, additional key recommendations information should be collected, in order to develop a Climate Crop Calendar (CCC) for each crop. A crop calendar is the arrangement of crops according to the chronological order of the crop life cycle and the corresponding crop management practices. The crop calendar can also illustrate some seasonal conditions (start - end time of a crop) and climate variables (monthly rainfall, monthly temperature). A more systematic approach connecting the crop calendar with the seasonal climate conditions and climate-related events during the growth stages of a crop is CCC.

CDT provides proper and farming timely recommendations for a specific crop growth stage (or a specific month) based on SSFs using the information in CCC, where each crop growth stage is linked with farming activities, major climate risks, and major pests and diseases occurring at individual stages. CDTs have been implemented in multiple countries, such as Tonga, Vanuatu, Samoa, Lao PDR, Cambodia, Myanmar, and the Philippines as of October, 2022, through various

• The development of CDTs involves collecting and systemizing local-specific crop information, CCC, and seasonal climate scenario-based BFPs and effective coping practices to major climate risks, with future consideration of the integration of CDTs in digital tools and platforms for scaling and automating agro-climatic advisory.

BACKGROUND INFORMATION

The Asian Mega-Deltas for Climate and Livelihood Resilience (AMD) is a CGIAR initiative, which aims to create resilient, inclusive and productive deltas, which maintain socio-ecological integrity, adapt to climatic and other stressors, and support human prosperity and wellbeing, by removing systemic barriers to the scaling of transformative technologies and practices at community, national and regional levels. The AMD Initiative also addresses challenges to nutrition security, financial investment, gender equity and social inclusion, and to the natural resources on which the resilience of the entire system depends by building strong policy-science partnerships working with diverse actors and aligning them towards common goals.

One of the activities under AMD Initiative is to develop climate-risk maps and adaptation plans for the targets regions of Asian Mega-Deltas following participatory mapping approach (CS-MAP). In CS-MAP, local knowledge is very important in identifying affected areas, the level of climate risks and adaptation measures taking into account local contexts (natural resources, infrastructure and production activities). Starting from mid-2022, CS-MAP has been carrying out at 13 provinces of Vietnam, 4 provinces of Cambodia in the Mekong River Delta, and 10 districts belonging to 3 divisions of Bangladesh. As the outputs of CS-MAP, climate- risks and associated adaptation plans have been identified for every agriculture land area by local stakeholders from different administrative levels.

From farmers’ perspective, impacts of climate risk and feasibility of adaptation measures can be seen through a very site-specific angle that influenced by farm/household capacity (land quality, labor, capital, education, etc.), gender equity and other social norms. Therefore, besides the macro and meso planning, resilient and sustainable agriculture development should also be considered at the micro or grassroots level. Farmer-level verification of proposed climate-adaptation measures will provide important guidance for AMD to create its significant impacts at deltas level.
Within the framework of AMD, farmer-level verification of CS-MAP aims at:
▪ Understanding farmer/community perspective on climate risks and workable options to cope with their risk-prone conditions
Identifying the grassroots constraints and willingness of male and female farmers in adoption of adaptation measures;
▪ Empowering farmer/community by involving both male and female farmers in climate-planning and decision making processes;
▪ Informing planning and strategy development of local and central government.
OBJECTIVES OF THIS GUIDELINES

This document is developed for facilitators and researchers/advisors who support the participatory evaluation of CS-MAP results at community level. It provides a basic framework to conduct a Focus Group Discussion (FGD) with participation of farmers, extension workers and village leaders. The Guidelines only describe the 3- step process and simple tools that are commonly applied in the Participatory Rural Appraisal (PRA) and Rural Rapid Appraisal (RRA). The process can be adjusted depending on local bio-physical and social conditions.

It is assumed that climate-risk maps and proposed adaptation plans have been developed at higher administrative level and are available for community-level evaluation. Participatory mapping is outside the scope of these Guidelines.
STEPS OF THE COMMUNITY-LEVEL EVALUATION
The focus of community-level evaluation is to capture farmers’ feedback of CS-MAP outputs, including perception of risk level and feasibility of proposed adaptation measures.
STEP 1: PREPARATION
1.1. Facilitators

For each validation meeting, at least 1 or 2 facilitators are required. Facilitators are members of the CS-MAP team, who did facilitation in CS-MAP consultation workshop at higher level (i.e. district level). For each step in the evaluation process, the facilitators are responsible to guide discussion, encourage all the participants to contribute inputs, record and summary outputs. Facilitators should prepare themselves the checklist of the items needed for the evaluation meeting.
1.2. Revision of climate-risk and adaptation measures for the targeted community

The target community can be delineated by the administrative boundary (e.g. commune/union or village) or natural boundaries based on topography (landscape as valley, hill, and mountain) or hydrological conditions (watershed, irrigation system…).
1.3. Pre-prepared information and data

STEP 2: PARTICIPATORY EVALUATION OF CS-MAP AT COMMUNITY
The evaluation process mainly follows participatory approach and consists of 3 sessions.
Session 1. Overview of the CS-MAP outputs (30 minutes)
Facilitators provide all participants a brief of following topics:
- CS-MAP objectives, implementation and findings that are relevant to the target community
- Available/practicable adaptation options from similar environments
- The purpose and expected results of the validation meeting

Depending on readiness of infrastructure (i.e. electricity and meeting venue) and facilities (i.e. projector and screen), facilitators can use either the pre-prepared slides (see 1.5) or hard copies of maps and pictures to communicate to participants.
Session 2. Individual evaluation (45 minutes)

The purpose of this session is to capture individual perception of climate risk and their evaluation of proposed adaptation measures, which are introduced in Session 1. Output of this session will be the qualitative input for next discussion session, and the quantitative data for further analysis.
- First, facilitators provide each participant a hard copy of the questionnaire (Annex 2) and guide them fill out the form individually (30 minutes).
- Facilitators then collect all filled forms and do quick statistic and develop a list of most common issues (15 minutes).
Session 3. Group evaluation (90 minutes)

- Necessary investments (e.g. irrigation, crop variety, fertilizers…) and technical supports (30 minutes)

The agricultural sector in most developing countries remains less productive and inefficient due to multiple constraints, including limited extension and advisory services.

Extension and advisory services have multiple contributions: help to transfer new knowledge and information, promote new technologies, facilitate farmers’ access to inputs and outputs markets, and provide real-time support on emerging issues.

In most developing countries, extension and advisory services are delivered through traditional approaches, which have various limitations, including limited coverage, high cost of operation, and inadequate real-time and tailored support to farmers. .

The limited access to extension and advisory services can be associated with inadequate policy and strategy, poor rural and agricultural infrastructures, poor service delivery models, and other socio-economic and environmental factors.

1. Introduction

Smallholder poultry production is integral to rural and agricultural households’ livelihood in developing countries, including Africa and Asia. Various studies show that smallholder poultry production significantly contributes to household income, food and nutritional security ( Wong et al. 2017; Birhanu et al. 2023b). It also has a sizable contribution to women’s empowerment and job creation. However, despite various research and development efforts in the previous decades, the production and productivity of the sector have remained quite low due to multiple production, marketing, policy and institutional constraints (Birhanu et al. 2021; Birhanu et al., 2023a; Anyona et al. 2023). Most farmers keep small flock sizes, mainly using low-input, low-output production practices for subsistence and income generation. Producers have limited access to better inputs and output markets, with weak horizontal and vertical coordination and linkages. Moreover, poultry product demand is highly seasonal, and there is significant price fluctuation associated with socioeconomic and cultural factors (Birhanu et al. 2022). Higher transaction costs, limited access to roads and other infrastructure, limited bargaining power and limited access to information restrict household access to better markets. Transforming the sector from subsistence-based to market-oriented commercial production requires integrated interventions, including improved genetics, health, feed, management practices, access to extension and advisory services, access to finance, capacity building, market linkages, collective actions and coordination ( Birhanu et al. 2021; Birhanu et al. 2022; Yakubu et al. 2023).

An increasing trend in poultry product consumption—associated with increasing population, urbanization, increasing income of the middle-class population, and preference for white meat over red meat—has created opportunities and challenges for smallholder producers. The opportunities could be associated with a broader market for eggs and meat. At the same time, the challenges would be strong competition with the emerging commercial sector in peri-urban and urban areas. An increasing demand in urban areas requires standardized products and better production and management practices from smallholders. However, given their large number and dispersed in remote locations, where there are significant infrastructural, institutional, technical, and policy-related challenges, individually, smallholder farmers cannot cope with existing and emerging challenges and exploit opportunities. Organizing farmers enhances collective actions, peer-to-peer learning, and access to inputs and output markets such as improved breeds, feeds, health services, finance, training, and advisory services (Fischer and Qaim 2014; Mutonyi 2019; Missiame et al. 2023). Moreover, sustained access to better inputs and value-added output markets requires strategies to link producers to different market opportunities.

Based on the above backgrounds, as part of the CGIAR initiative on Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition, and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING), the Tropical Poultry Genetics Solution (TPGS) is implementing different interventions that enhance the production and productivity of the sector including developing a business model for scaling improved tropically adapted breeds. The scaling business model involves organizing farmers in groups and linking them with inputs, suppliers, and marketing actors for sustained adoption and use of farmer-preferred and locally adapted breeds. Considering the vital role of organizing farmers in groups and creating market linkage, this document is developed as a reference material when establishing farmer groups/organizations and linking them with various input suppliers, service providers, and marketing actors. The document is generic and can be applied to smallholder-based agricultural production and marketing activities. However, the proposed approaches can be amended and adjusted based on the country’s local contexts, policies, and strategies.
2. The role of group formation in smallholder agricultural production

Most smallholder farmers live in rural areas in highly dispersed locations and far from input and output markets. These areas have poor rural infrastructure, weak institutions, limited access to markets and services, limited information and low access to innovative technologies. They experience multiple production, marketing and consumption challenges that individual actions cannot easily address but require collective actions (Abdul-Rahaman and Abdulai 2020; Ruzzante et al. 2021). Empirical evidence suggests that organizing farmers in groups is a good strategy for addressing most of the production and marketing challenges (Birhanu et al. 2017; Abdul-Rahaman and Abdulai 2018; Bachke 2019; Abdul- Rahaman and Abdulai 2020; Bizikova et al. 2020; Bairagi and Mottaleb 2021; Ma et al. 2023; Tran et al. 2023).

Farmer organizations can be defined as groups formed to address the different interests of farmers. These organizations can be formal or informal and have different forms, including cooperatives, associations, self-help groups and commodity-based producer organizations (CRS and MEAS 2015; Bizikova et al. 2020; Fernando et al. 2021). Farmer organizations can also be classified into three board categories: general interest groups, cooperatives and commodity-based organizations. Interest groups represent farmers’ interests in policy and program development, mobilize resources and information for farmers, organize capacity building and address other issues that attract farmers’ interest. Cooperatives are business organizations owned and managed by farmers and other actors in the value chain to fulfill members’ needs for agricultural inputs and services and create demand for their produce. Usually, cooperatives facilitate the distribution of agricultural inputs, collect, store and add value to products, deliver large quantities to markets, and provide other services such as credit, savings and insurance. Commodity-based organizations are specialized groups of farmers organized based on a specific crop or livestock commodity that comprises various actors in the value chain, including producers, marketing actors, and input and service providers. Farmers’ organizations can function at different levels, such as village, kebele, district or region. Usually, the groups are independent, non-governmental and voluntary.

The essential role of organizing farmers in groups is documented in various empirical studies (Markelova and Mwangi 2010; Shiferaw et al. 2011; CRS and MEAS 2015; Agarwal, 2018; Gugerty et al. 2019; Bizikova et al. 2020; Kassie et al. 2020; Ma et al. 2023). Farmer groups enhance collective actions that reduce transaction costs and help to obtain better market prices (Abdul-Rahaman and Abdulai 2020). Organized farmers can take advantage of economies of scale, express their needs, have better lobbying ability, and be in a good position for buying inputs and bulking and selling outputs. When farmers are organized, their voices can be easily heard, and their contribution to the research and development agenda can be significant. On the other hand, isolated and individual actions of farmers restrict them from fulfilling their production and marketing objectives due to limited access to input and output markets, inadequate capital, technical and social capacity, and other institutional and organizational factors. Organized farmers can easily access technology through linkages with service and input providers, including the research and extension system. Research and development institutes are also more likely to work with a group of farmers than individual farmers. Farmers who participated in farm organizations or groups have been found to have better economic and social gains compared with others (Shiferaw et al. 2011; Abebaw and Haile 2013; Abate et al. 2014; Verhofstadt and Maertens 2014; Abdul-Rahaman and Abdulai 2020).

As indicated above, a sustained transformation of traditional smallholder-based poultry production requires organizing farmers in groups for collective actions and establishing effective linkages along the value chain. Organizing farmers helps to promote farmer adoption of improved production and marketing practices; enhance service delivery; reduce transaction costs; improve farmers’ bargaining power; encourage farm work; empower rural women; improve members’ economic, social and innovative performances; and improve

value additions. When smallholder poultry farmers are organized, they can easily access improved technologies such as poultry breeds, feeds, vaccines, treatment drugs, and other assets such as feeders and drinkers. Moreover, farmers organized in groups can be suitable partners for research and development activities.

Although there is no single best approach to organize framers in groups, based on various empirical evidence suggested by researchers and development experts working in the area (CRS and MEAS 2015; Kassie et al. 2020), the following approaches can be adopted for smallholder poultry producers in developing countries. The approaches can be broadly classified into three stages and nine steps (Figure 1). The institutions that facilitate1 the group formation or organizing of farmers should have a good understanding of the sector and part Startup of the value chain actors.

2.1 Stage I: Startups
2.1.1 Step 1: Define the goal and scope of the proposed group formation

The formation of farmers’ groups should be based on clear and achievable objectives with predefined scopes, without unrealistic assumptions. Objectives of group formation may include enhancing access to technologies and better management practices, improving technical efficiency, access to better markets and credit; empowering women through different strategies; enhancing members’ economic, social and innovative performances; and increasing participation in the value chain through value addition (Francesconi and Wouterse 2015; Di Marcantonio et al. 2022). The groups should be manageable and organized by homogeneous people with similar interests and economic conditions.

2.1.2 Step 2: Understand the characteristics of target farmers

Smallholder farmers in developing countries are very heterogeneous. However, farmers in different geographies have specific characteristics and interests in production and marketing activities that differentiate them from others. Hence, understanding the target farmers’ characteristics is critical to establishing a successful farmer organization. This could be done through formal and informal approaches, including quick assessments regarding their interest in group work and vision for improved technologies-based production and marketing activities. Farmer characteristics may include age and gender composition, social and cultural settings that affect group formation, practices in farm and non-farm activities, average income, assets holding, land sizes, distance to main roads, and other socioeconomic activities associated with poultry production practices. At this stage, it is also important to know if the target farmers are part of existing farmers’ groups, have experience participating in similar groups and are interested in joining the proposed poultry-based groups.
2.1.3 Step 3: Identify potential leaders

The success and failure of farmers’ organizations depend partly on leadership style and management skills. Partners who facilitate the formation of the proposed farmer groups must ensure the presence of potential leaders among the target groups. Potential leaders can be identified using predefined criteria, including experience in group/community leadership, interest in leading the group, communication skills, education, technical skills and interest in poultry-based business. The potential leaders should include a mix of people from different age and gender groups.
2.1.4 Step 4: Talk to the local community leaders/administrators

Engaging local administrators and partners on the ground is vital to the sustainability of the proposed group formation. From the inception stage, local administrators should be involved through formal and informal meetings and discussion forums. The facilitating team can arrange a brief meeting and discuss the need to organize farmers, their alignment with the country’s policy, and their contribution to the development of the poultry sector. Facilitators should clarify the goal and scope of the proposed group formation, create awareness, and receive the necessary feedback and support from the community leaders and other stakeholders on the ground. Community leaders and farmer-organizing units should be part of the implementing partners.
2.1.5 Step 5: Establish the group

Once the goal and scope of the proposed group are defined, farmers are characterized, potential leaders are identified, and community leaders and partners are engaged, a community awareness meeting can be held to promote the idea and encourage targeted farmers to join the group. At this stage, interested farmers can be registered using appropriate formats. This meeting can clarify the needs and goals of group formation, nominate the identified leaders, obtain approvals and formally establish the groups. In this meeting, the need to develop a farmers’ group should be explained to participants, and farmers could ask questions to get clarification on important issues and share their expectations of participating in the group. The members can also elect potential member farmers who can work in different roles for the next few years.
2.1.6 Step 6: Develop the organizational structure

Facilitators and elected leaders can develop the organizational structure of the group. However, facilitators and group leaders may not start from scratch and can tailor and adopt similar organizational structures used in different farmer groups in their local or other areas. The organizational structure in the proposed farmer groups should reflect various relationships between the members of the groups, and facilitators and group leaders can choose from various options that maximize individual contributions while minimizing challenges (Bolman and Deal 2017). The organizational structure should show the types of committee members, the roles and responsibilities of different committee members, directions of information flow, and decision-making processes. As a starting point, the structure should be simple and easily amendable at any time and able to be developed with technical help from other local partners. However, according to Bolman and Deal (2017), the following questions can be considered while organizing the group’s structure (Box 1).

2.2.1 Step 7: Build the capacity of the group

Building the capacity of group leaders and other members is important for establishing successful groups (Ashby et al. 2009). As indicated above, leadership plays a critical role in the success and sustainability of group formation. Among other things, facilitating teams and partners on the ground should focus on raising good leaders through capacity building. The capacity-building efforts should focus on multiple dimensions of group formation, such as productive, organizational, entrepreneurial and sociopolitical dimensions (Valleur 2017). This can be achieved through formal and informal training, experience sharing, coaching and advisory services, and financial and material support. Various trainings can be provided on identified issues that help fulfill the groups’ missions and goals. Nevertheless, capacity- building efforts should be planned and properly implemented with partners and stakeholders. For instance, capacity building in time management, such as long meetings, record keeping, leadership style, fairness and communication, will significantly contribute to the success of group formation (CRS and MEAS 2015). The role of capacity building at the initial stage of group formation is documented in some empirical studies (Ahado et al. 2021).
2.2.2 Step 8: Plan and implement activities

After establishing the farmers’ group and capacity building, based on the goals of the group formation, potential interventions that improve the production and marketing activities of the group members should be identified, planned and implemented. This may involve identifying and analyzing problems, identifying possible solutions, prioritizing issues and

solutions, checking the feasibility of solutions, and developing detailed action plans (CRS and MEAS 2015). Activities should be prioritized and ranked based on importance and available resources, considering the farmers’ existing situation and local conditions. For smallholder poultry producers, this may include linking the groups with input suppliers, service providers and marketing actors; identifying and promoting additional value chain activities such as establishing product aggregation and marketing centres; adding more people to the group; expanding production and marketing activities; and building the technical skills of farmers. The group leaders should adopt dynamic approaches in implementing the proposed activities.
2.3 Stage III: Regular activities
2.3.1 Step 9: Monitoring and evaluation

Monitoring and evaluation should be integral to the group formation process and the entire management system. The monitoring component refers to keeping regular records of group activities, verifying that planned actions are taken according to the plan and adjusting ongoing activities to align with the group’s goals. On the other hand, evaluation may refer to looking back to confirm whether the proposed objectives have been met and identifying strategies to improve future activities to meet the group’s mission (CRS and MEAS 2015). Monitoring and evaluation activities can follow a participatory approach and are conducted jointly by group leaders, facilitators, local partners and other stakeholders. This would be led by the facilitating institution supported by other stockholders supporting this activity. One of the main responsibilities of facilitators would be establishing the monitoring evaluation system as part of supporting the proposed group and documenting lessons learned for scaling in different areas.
3. Linking organized groups with inputs and output markets
3.1. Market linkages and smallholder farmers

In most developing countries, the smallholder poultry value chain is characterized by low production and productivity with limited competitive advantage with emerging commercial sectors in urban and peri-urban areas. Access to inputs and output markets is the main constraint identified by almost all empirical studies on technology adoption and productivity (Adesina et al. 2014). Findings from such studies suggest linking smallholder farmers with input suppliers and central markets as essential interventions to enhance production and productivity and transform the sector from subsistence-based production to commercial production (Ebata and Hernandez 2017; Birhanu et al. 2022). Farmers’ participation in market-oriented production enhances household income, nutrition, job opportunities and other livelihood activities. Therefore, linking farmers with value chain actors using various strategies is one of the best approaches to enhance smallholders’ access to input and output markets. Linking farmers with inputs and output markets is not establishing an ad-hoc sale but developing long-term and formal business relationships among various value chain actors (Shepherd 2007). However, as indicated above, farmers must first be organized to establish effective linkages, as organized groups can be easily linked with various value chain actors.

Farmers’ linkage arrangements may consist of service provision (such as the delivery of improved breeds, vaccines, drugs, feeds, other assets such as feeders and drinkers, and providing training and advisory services); investing in value chain activities; formal and

informal contractual agreements; purchasing arrangements for outputs; full vertical cooperation with other value chain actors; asset sharing; contract farming; and other informal linkages and ad hoc arrangements (Dannson et al. 2004; Ferris et al. 2014b). For sustained adoption of technologies and improved livelihood outcomes, farmers can be primarily linked with input suppliers, such as improved breeds, feed and vaccine and treatment drug suppliers, and output markets with traders and institutional buyers, such as school feeding programs, universities and hospitals. To begin with, facilitators may focus on linking organized farmer groups with local input suppliers using various approaches. This process should involve local partners and stakeholders in government offices and non- government organizations working on input and output market linkages.

Strategies for creating market linkages can be broadly categorized into input and output market linkages (Figure 2). Although both adopt similar approaches, examining them separately helps to understand some of the specific issues among input and output marketing actors. Inputs market linkages involve exploring farmers’ needs and requirements; identifying potential inputs and service suppliers and initiating linkages; enhancing farmers’ awareness and understanding; organizing a joint discussion forum and determining the linkage type; developing an action plan; and facilitating implementation and evaluation. Linking with output markets involves establishing product collection/aggregation centers; identifying potential buyers/markets; organizing a discussion forum between producers and buyers; specifying contracts and developing risk management strategies; developing an action plan; and facilitating implementation and evaluation.

3.2 Strategies for creating linkages with input suppliers

Establishing successful and long-term inputs market linkage requires well-thought-out and carefully planned activities based on the context of each location. The linkage created should be based on win-win principles, where smallholder producers, input and service providers, and marketing actors benefit mutually. Establishing sustained inputs market linkages involves the following activities.
3.2.1 Explore farmers’ needs and requirements

Working with individual farmers involves higher transaction costs for companies or firms, and organizing them in groups should be an important step, as indicated above. To establish successful linkage, it is important to understand farmers’ production objectives, gender and age compositions, production and marketing practices, available resources for scaling existing production activity, production environment, and their current and potential capacity for market-originated production.

The smallholder farmers’ demand for inputs and the service requirement usually depend on their production objectives, the adopted technologies, the technical and financial capacity, and other socioeconomic factors. The production practice they adopt (intensive vs extensive production) also determines their input type. Moreover, farmers in each area may not always need all the recommended commercial inputs, as they can also use locally available sources or a mix of locally available and commercial inputs.

Despite the dynamic nature, it is essential to understand the type, quality and volume of inputs and services required by farmers in each period. Although this needs continuous assessment, it can generally be achieved using a mix of approaches, including formal assessments such as checklists of inputs and services required by farmers and their willingness and ability to pay for the inputs.
3.2.2 Identify potential inputs and service providers and initiate linkages

Due to asymmetric information and inadequate capacity and skills, smallholder farmers have limited ability to identify appropriate input suppliers and service providers. Since most of them live in rural areas with minimal access to roads, information and other infrastructures, they have limited capacity to access most value chain actors. Therefore, facilitators must first identify potential input suppliers (i.e., individuals, companies, etc.) relevant to smallholder farmers and begin a discussion with them to initiate the linkages. This may primarily involve identifying the inputs farmers require for production and marketing activities and the capacity and willingness of suppliers to work with smallholder farmers in each target location. This could be done through a rapid assessment, including reviewing the company’s expertise and activities, collecting customer information, key informant interviews, and reviewing documents. Working with existing commercial companies would be the best strategy for the poultry sector. Facilitators can approach commercial poultry companies or agents that can supply key inputs such as improved breeds in the area and major feed, vaccine and drug suppliers.
3.2.3 Enhance farmers’ awareness and understanding

Using the information generated from Steps 1 and 2, facilitators can quickly match farmers’ demand for products and services and the capacity and readiness of companies/individuals to supply the smallholder farmers. This may help to confirm whether the identified potential actors are appropriate for creating successful linkages. About SAPLING

CGIAR’s Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING) is working in seven countries focusing on livestock value chains to package and scale out tried-and-tested, as well as new, innovations in livestock health, genetics, feed, and market systems. SAPLING aims to demonstrate that improvements in livestock productivity can offer a triple win: generating improved livelihoods and nutritional outcomes, contributing to women’s empowerment, and reducing impacts on climate and the environment. Its seven focus countries are Ethiopia, Kenya, Mali, Nepal, Tanzania, Uganda and Vietnam.
Acknowledgements

This work was conducted as part of the CGIAR Initiative on Sustainable Animal Productivity. CGIAR research is supported by contributions to the CGIAR Trust Fund. CGIAR is a global research partnership for a food-secure future dedicated to transforming food, land, and water systems in a climate crisis.
Background to training

The Tropical Poultry Genetics Solutions (TPGS) program, led by the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI), aims to enhance the consumption of chicken products through its nutrition-sensitive interventions in various countries, including Ethiopia and Kenya. The intervention focuses on promoting the consumption of chicken meat and eggs, primarily leveraging participating households in on-farm chicken testing as a foundational entry point. This intervention specifically targets children under five years of age, pregnant women, breastfeeding mothers, and women of reproductive age. Women are disproportionately affected by nutritional deficiencies due to factors such as reproductive biology, low social status, poverty, and lack of education. Undernutrition diminishes women’s resilience and makes them more vulnerable during childbirth, increasing their susceptibility to infections and reducing their reserves for recovery from illnesses. Over the past 10 months, integrated nutrition education has been delivered to these target groups through digital and paper-based tools, featuring monthly interactive sessions, including demonstrations and cooking activities. Nutrition education has been provided to both TPGS on-farm chicken performance testing participant households and other non-participant farmers within the project villages in the two countries. This activity is linked to the CGIAR Sustainable Animal Productivity for Livelihoods, Nutrition and Gender Inclusion (SAPLING) Work Package 2— Innovations and practices for safe livestock-derived foods consumption as part of diverse diets.
Location and modality
The training was provided face-to-face and held in Kenya and Ethiopia.
Dates
This training was held from March–October 2024.
Who conducted the training?

The National Agricultural Research System of Ethiopia and Kenya, most notably the Central Ethiopia Agricultural Research Institute (CEARI) and the Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO) provided this training.
Objectives of the training
The main objectives of the training were:
Addressing Malnutrition
• To identify and address major malnutrition challenges faced by target communities, particularly among vulnerable groups such as pregnant women and children under two years.
Promote Animal Source Foods Consumption

• To promote the importance of consuming animal-source foods, especially chicken products (meat and eggs), rich in essential nutrients vital for growth, development, and overall health. This may include encouraging families to incorporate chicken and eggs into their daily diets to enhance dietary diversity and nutritional intake.
Enhancing Nutritional Awareness

• To assess and enhance current knowledge regarding the benefits of animal-source foods among community members. Identify knowledge gaps and inform the development of effective educational programs aimed at changing dietary behaviours. The initiative also seeks to foster
healthier eating habits by emphasizing the value of including chicken and eggs in meals, encouraging families to make informed dietary choices.
Community Engagement

• To encourage both participant and non-participant households to improve chicken production and consumption practices, ensuring that the intervention scaled out a diverse segment of the community. This objective includes evaluating the effectiveness of community engagement strategies to promote inclusivity. Furthermore, the initiative aims to establish a feedback mechanism to gather insights from participants about their dietary practices and attitudes toward animal-source foods, allowing for continuous improvement of educational programs.
Promote the utilization of technology

To leverage digital tools, such as a nutrition literacy application, to enhance learning about the benefits of animal-source foods and assess their uptake among farmers. This objective includes evaluating the effectiveness of technology in promoting better nutrition and reaching a wider audience to facilitate ongoing education regarding the importance of chicken products.
Training agenda

The training agenda includes a comprehensive overview of essential nutritional topics, focusing on five key sessions: “Why Nutrition Matters,” “Family Nutrition,” “Maternal Nutrition,” “Child Nutrition,” and “Hygiene and Sanitation.” Each session included thematic areas that emphasized the importance of nutrition at various life stages. Participants explored the significance of food groups, dietary diversification, and the crucial roles of chicken, eggs, and meat in promoting health and growth. Emphasis was placed on maternal nutritional needs during pregnancy and lactation, as well as optimal feeding practices for children from birth to 24 months. Additionally, the agenda highlighted safe food handling practices and the importance of hygiene in ensuring proper nutrition, ultimately aiming to enhance overall health and well-being within families.
Training participants

A total of 301 households participated in the nutrition education, with 230 from TPGS on-farm chicken performance testing participant households and 70 from non-participant households. In Ethiopia, 44 participants—36 from on-farm chicken performance testing participants and 8 from non-participant households—indicated interest from non-participant households. Comments or next steps

Following the completion of these training sessions, participants are expected to experience a positive behavioral change in their dietary consumption, leading to improved nutritional status. To support the ongoing impact of the training, we will graduate a select group of farmers as champions who will serve

as leaders in their communities, promoting sustainable practices and encouraging others to adopt healthier nutritional habits. These champions will play a vital role in ensuring the sustainability of project activities fostering a culture of improved nutrition within their households and among fellow farmers. Additionally, end-line data will be collected to assess the impact on nutritional status and consumption patterns, providing valuable insights into the effectiveness of the training and guiding future initiatives. This comprehensive approach aims to enhance individual health outcomes and build a resilient community committed to ongoing nutritional education and support.

Introduction

Agricultural research in Ethiopia began in the early 1960s. The earliest agricultural research center was the Debre Zeit Experiment Station, a constituent station of Alemaya College of Agriculture, Emperor Haile Selasie University. Almost at the same time, the national research system, IAR was established in 1966, by proclamation No 42/58 (1958 E.C.). The Swedish-Ethiopian regional agricultural development branch- the Arsi Rural Development Unit (ARDU) was founded in 1966 (SIDA, 1966), and became operational in 1972 (CADU, 1972). The CGIAR research institute, ILCA, was established in 1982 to promote livestock development in Africa. All these institutions did their part to improve livestock productivity through improving animal feed inter alia.

The scope of this review is limited to the topic of forage research in Ethiopia, with a focus on native Forage species. Therefore, the foregoing discussions do not go beyond simple presentation of stories of forage research processes, achievements, and gaps in the research, collected from published and unpublished literature found at various national and international research institutions.

From the research achievements of the pioneering institute CADU-ARDU, it is evident that wholistic, system-based research and development approaches were more fruitful than isolated single item-based approaches. Although sustenance could not be maintained for various reasons, there is evidence that improved forage crops developed by CADU have made their way to the farm gates of smallholder farmers in Arsi (ARDU, 1983). Additionally, CADU researchers have laid the groundwork for the fruitful approach of screening and developing varieties from indigenous material (Carlson, J., 1972; Thulin, M., 1972). Now, after half a century of research (with “staggering” achievements), benefits of focusing research efforts on native forages are vivid. Box 1.1 is a case in point.

A review of published and unpublished literature revealed that a total of 59 indigenous forage species (31 legumes and 28 grasses) have undergone evaluation for their forage value. Of these, 6 legume varieties and 9 grass varieties have been registered/released (NVRC, 2018). This number does not correspond to the exotic species that have been introduced and evaluated in the country since forage research began. Apart from a few species: Oats (Avena spp), Rhodes (Chloris gauana), Guinea grass (Panicum maximum), vetches (Vetch spp) Lucerne (Medicago sativa) desmodiums (Desmodium intortum and D. uncinatum) which remain valuable forage crops in districts of Ethiopia, other large numbers of introductions failed important selection criteria (adaptation, yield and quality). Some temperate grass species such as rye grass (Lolium spp) are destroyed by rust. Most of the previously selected and recommended oats varieties (Lulseged G. Hiwot, 1981), suffer from crown rust, although resistant varieties have been developed. Oats

remain the only successful annual forage grass species. The exotic clovers (Trifolium repens, T. pretense and others) cannot compete with the native clover species in terms of adaptability and herbage yield.
Box 1.1: Desho, the mysterious indigenous forage grass

Desho grass (Pennisetum glaucifolium) is an indigenous perennial grass forage variety developed from native ecotypes germplasm collected jointly by the Debre Zeit Agric Research Center (DZARC) and Areca Agricultural Research Center (AARC) of the Southern Nations Nationalities and Peoples Region (SNNPR) around Wolayta Zone. The grass is tussoky, rhizomatous, erect, up to 2 meters tall. The dense stem and foliage is glossy, so named glousifolius. Forage yield varies widely with soil fertility and moisture. Mean dry forage yield per harvest ranged 5.6 – 8.8 t/ha DM. While yearly (3 cuts) yield (under irrigation), ranged between 21.0 t/ha (Areka-DZF-590) to 24.59 t/ha (Kindukosha-DZF-591). At its best location (Wondo Genet) with fertile soil and abundant soil moisture, the mean DM yield ranged 25 – 39 t/ha (Solomon Mengistu et al, 2017; Tekalign Yirgu et al, 2017). Among the “pro-poor” forage technologies, three varieties of desho officially released by DZARC have provided hope to the smallholder farmer (Fig. 1). MoARD and NGOs have desiminated planting material almost throughout the highlands of Ethiopia. Farmers plant desho in their backyard on small plots and use the green fodder to feed lactating cows and young stock. Desho ha gained nationwide popularity. Some farmers have taken up multiplying propagation material as a business and make money by selling bunches of vegetative (stem cuttings and rhizome splits) to neigbouring farmers and even to distant areas, hundreds of kms away. The business has spread dramatically.
