3.7 Plantain fruit pulp dry matter yield determination

To determine the edible dry matter produced by plantain, the dry mass of the edible pulp needs to be determined. A precondition for this procedure is that the plantain fresh fruit hand or finger yield (3.5) and the plantain fresh fruit pulp yield (3.6) have been determined.

Step 1: Cut the peeled fruit fingers (pulp) collected in 3.6 into thin slices, mix the slices and take a sub-sample of 250–400 grams, record the fresh mass of the fruit pulp sub-sample and place it in a paper bag or other container suited for drying in a forced-draft oven.
Step 2: Dry the sub-sample to constant mass and weigh again, record the dry mass of the fruit pulp sub-sample.
3.7.1 Calculations
First, calculate the proportion of dry matter in the fruit pulp sub-sample.
Proportion of dry matter in fresh fruit pulp = Fruit pulp dry sub-sample (g)
Fruit pulp fresh sub-sample (g)
The edible fruit dry matter yield is:
Edible fruit dry matter yield (kg/m2 year–1) = Fresh fruit pulp yield (kg/m2 year–1) × Proportion of dry matter in fresh fruit pulp

Note: Because the totals are constituted from a number of bunches that may have been harvested at different dates and over a long period, all masses of all variables need to be summed for each plot over the entire trial lifespan and then be used for the calculations of the different yields.
4. Biomass determination of the vegetative biomass after bunch harvest

Plantain loses a large portion of the biomass between flowering and bunch maturity. Depending on the variety all leaves may be dead and only some dead mass may remain. Figure 3 shows a schematic approach for how to dissect the plantain plant after bunch harvest.
Figure 3. Cutting the plantain plant after bunch harvest to obtain the plant parts to determine vegetative biomass

Cut along the red lines to remove the leaves, including the dead leaves (which may be the majority in varieties susceptible to black sigatoka leaf disease). Cut the corm from the base of the pseudostem. The yellow lines indicate where to take the minimum number of pseudostem slices to determine the pseudostem biomass. It is advised that five samples be taken, i.e. the three indicated here plus one additional to each side of the center.

Step 1: The leaf biomass is relatively easy to determine by cutting off all leaves at the emergence point from the pseudostem (although the leaves are forming the pseudostem [Fig. 4] it is feasible to cut at any convenient point on the leaf petiole close to where the petiole bends off the pseudostem).

Step 2: Weigh the fresh mass of all leaves and take a sub-sample by cutting two to four entire leaves into small pieces and weighing the fresh sub-sample. Dry to constant mass and weigh the dry sub-sample.
Step 3: Harvesting the pseudostem is more challenging as it has a very high water content, and the water will run out from the cut surface immediately (Fig. 4).
Figure 4. A slice through a plantain pseudostem

The pseudostem consists of the petioles of the leaves forming several layers until the flower stalk emerges from the corm and grows through the center of the pseudostem (red dotted circle). The leaf petioles (roughly traced in black for one leaf) consist largely of large caverns that are usually filled with water. In this image the outer dead petioles have been removed.

It is recommended that the pseudostem be cut right above the soil surface and placed with the cut surface over a bowl to capture the water. If available, the entire pseudostem should be weighed fresh and then be dissected into slices of about 20 cm length serving as sub-samples to determine the dry matter content. When slicing the pseudostem, it is as important to capture the water that runs from the slices. Weigh three to five of the slices fresh (more if the pseudostem is longer) and record the fresh mass. The slices will then be cut into smaller pieces. At this stage the draining water does not need to be captured as it would be driven from the material in the oven. However, the entire amount of slice material needs to be cut up and dried to constant mass.

Step 4: Harvesting the corm involves the separation of the corm of the harvested plant from the corms of eventual suckers. This is best done with a straight cutlass or a spade by pushing it vertically down between the harvested plant’s corm and those of the suckers. The corm is then lifted from the soil and the roots are cut off at the corm’s surface. Clean the corm from attached soil. Corms are usually semi-spheres but can be almost spherical. Place the corm cut surface down and cut the corm into quarters by cutting across the middle in two directions. If the pieces are small, you can choose one piece and cut it into smaller pieces, weigh the sub-sample fresh, and dry to constant mass.
If the corm is large and the mass of one quarter too large to dry, then one piece needs to be cut in half again (forming 1/8 of the corm) and that piece is cut into small pieces to be dried.

The leaf biomass dry matter is calculated by multiplying the proportion of dry matter in the sub-sample [equation (11a/11b)] with the fresh mass of the leaves [equation (12a/12b)].
Proportion dry matter in the leaf sub-sample = Leaf sub-sample dry mass
Leaf sub-sample fresh mass
If the percentage dry matter is preferred use:
Percentage dry matter in the leaf sub-sample = Leaf sub-sample dry mass Leaf sub-sample fresh mass × 100
Leaf dry matter (kg/ha) = Proportion dry matter in leaf sub-sample × Fresh mass (kg) of leaves
Or, if using dry matter percentage is preferred:
Leaf dry matter
(kg/ha)
(kg/ha)
Percentage dry matter in leaf sub-sample × Fresh mass (kg) of leaves
The biomass of the pseudostem and the corm are calculated in the same manner using the fresh mass and the proportion or percentage dry matter of the respective plant parts.
To obtain the plant vegetative biomass dry matter, the leaf, pseudostem and corm biomass dry matter values are added together.

Note: This procedure produces the vegetative biomass dry matter data of a single plant and should not be used to extrapolate to the vegetative biomass dry matter of the entire farm or a hectare. To obtain reliable biomass dry matter data, it is necessary to harvest several plants or the entire plot of plantain to sum their biomass data and divide by the occupied area and the time from planting to end of harvesting.

1.2 Procedure for the taking sample from the field
Step 1: Identify the right harvest time

Chickpeas are typically ready for harvest when the pods start to dry up and become yellow or brown in color and feel dry and crisp to the touch. This usually occurs around 90–110 days after planting, but timing can vary depending on the variety and growing conditions. Monitor the crop regularly as it nears maturity to determine the optimal harvest time.
Step 2: Select net harvest area

Determine the net harvest area following established protocols to ensure accurate yield determination. This may involve calculating the minimum number of plants and area to be harvested based on research or production goals. Choose a representative area of the field, avoiding sections with unusual soil conditions or other factors that could affect results.

Step 3: Locate and mark the net harvest area by placing four pegs — one at each corner. The size of the harvest area should be representative for the field. When marking net harvest area, consider crop establishment method. For example, if line-seeded, pegs should be placed centrally between rows on both sides (Fig. 1 left). If plants are in random geometry (e.g. randomly broadcasted), only plants that root inside the delineated area should be harvested.

This user manual is based on fieldwork conducted in the Southern coastal region of Bangladesh. As such, certain aspects of the user manual or module may not be applicable to other regions of Bangladesh or different agro-ecological settings.
Agricultural Water Insecurity

Water is integral to food systems. Productive water is crucial for food production, including crops, fisheries, and livestock, and also for food processing and transformation. As the largest global water consumer, the agricultural sector uses 70% of the world's freshwater. In low-income and less developed countries, agriculture accounts for over 90% of all water withdrawals (Fujs and Kashiwase, 2023). The availability, accessibility, reliability, and use of agricultural water is crucial for agricultural productivity, economic growth and environmental sustainability. Assessing agricultural water [in]security provides a comprehensive understanding of how water influences agricultural development, as well as the material and psychological well-being of those who access and use water for agriculture.

Climate change, coupled with land use changes, population growth, biodiversity loss, urbanization; and other anthropogenic drivers are intensifying pressure on limited freshwater resources (HLPE, 2015). Water availability varies geographically, but across regions there are marked inequalities in access to and use of water, which are shaped by policy incoherence, poor management and governance of water resources; political, social, economic factors including intersecting inequalities by gender, class, ethnicity, caste, race, age, disability etc. To date, there is very little data that provides insights into the complexity of these intersectional inequalities in productive water access, use for agricultural activities.

Building on the Water Insecurity Experiences (WISE) Scales framework (Young et.al. 2021; 2019), we designed, and pilot tested an Agricultural Water Insecurity Experience (AgWISE) module to evaluate productive water insecurity, i.e. analyse issues related to the adequacy, reliability, accessibility, and safety of water related to agriculture. This AgWISE module aims to provide a more holistic understanding of agrifood systems water insecurity – focusing on crop fields, kitchen gardens, livestock, and fisheries, understand water insecurity from an intersectional perspective, i.e. how gender, class, age and other contextual factors impact the experience of productive water access, use and control, as well as document the material (physical and economic) and psychological impacts of these challenges.
Measuring Agricultural Water Insecurity Experiences (AgWISE)

We define agricultural water insecurity as “the lack of reliable access to sufficient, quality water needed for agricultural activities of a household”. This includes challenges in ensuring a consistent and sufficient water supply for maintaining productive agricultural practices and supporting the household's agricultural needs (Michel, 2023). Agricultural water insecurity is difficult to measure because of the multiple uses of water, and the diverse outcomes of productive water insecurity amongst diverse uses and users of water.
Our focus in developing and piloting this module was to document gender

disaggregated experiences in the access to, use and control of productive water for food production, including crops, fisheries, and livestock, as well as to analyse how cross-cutting social variables – such as class, caste, ethnicity, age etc. shape water [in]security. These issues are critical as multiple push and pull factors have resulted in a substantial migration of the mostly male rural labour force to urban areas resulting in what is considered as an increasing feminization of agriculture. Feminization of agriculture implies a lot of things, particularly the growing presence, visibility, and involvement of women in all agricultural activities both as wage workers and as unpaid family labourers (Najjar, 2021). Several studies point out that male outmigration is not associated with improved outcomes for women, who are increasingly engaged in agricultural production (de Brauw et al., 2021; Slavchevska et al., 2020). This is particularly relevant in Bangladesh’s southern coastal deltaic regions, where anthropogenic changes - food systems policy shifts have dramatically altered the ecological and social dimensions of the region, resulting in freshwater becoming a highly contested resource – especially in the dry season
(November to May).

In the context of an increasing feminization of agriculture, women's participation in agricultural activities is increasing (Asadullah and Kambhampati, 2021), however, women’s experiences with productive water resources have been overlooked. In literature, policies and projects, there is a tendency to frame largely
women’s challenges with water as related to the domestic sector, i.e. water for domestic (i.e. not productive) use (Joshi et al., 2022).

Addressing this gap, the AgWISE module was designed to document experiences of water insecurity amongst women and men across different age groups and socio- economic characteristics, such as land ownership, caste or ethnic group, age and household composition (e.g., female- vs. male-headed households).
Like other WISE Scales (Young et al., 2024), the AgWISE modules can have many uses:
Identify populations vulnerable to agricultural water insecurity
• Identify gender and other intersectionality gaps in water for productive uses and disparities by other characteristics
• Assess the frequency and severity of water insecurity experiences
• Help to understand causes and consequences of agricultural water insecurity, including health and psychosocial burdens
• Track trends in household/ individual experiences of water insecurity over time
• Monitor and evaluate the impact of water policies and programs
Agricultural Water Insecurity Module

The AgWISE module comprises 13 questions designed to assess how often agricultural water-related problems were encountered over the past 12 months1 and the material and psychological impacts of these problems. Each question is formulated to reflect the experiences of anyone in the household in last 12 months (to capture all seasons in a year). Responses to items are scored as: 0= never, 1= in 1 or 2 months, 2= in some but not every month), 3= in almost every month.
The AgWISE module is designed to assess the impact of water stress on food systems. Table 1 includes several mandatory questions, labeled as follows:
• ""Interruptions,"" ""Change,"" and ""Decision"" (Items 2-4) address the challenges related to water access, availability, and use in food production.
• ""Food"" (Item 5) focuses on negative changes in consumption and diets.
• ""Worry,"" ""Angry,"" ""Sleep,"" and ""Harassment"" (Items 1, 6-8) relate to the emotional risks associated with water issues.

These eight items are essential for any agricultural setting. Additional questions labeled ""Crop,"" ""Homestead Garden,"" ""Livestock,"" ""Capture Fishery,"" and ""Aquaculture"" (Items 9-13) are designed to evaluate the material (physical and economic) losses in agricultural enterprises due to water insecurity. However, because agricultural practices vary by location, one or more of items 9-13 may be omitted if key informants determine they are not relevant. Nevertheless, the surveyed population must be engaged in at least one of these activities (Items 9- 13), and one of these items should be retained.

The items are meant to capture experiences of the respondent, to be able to understand disparities in agricultural water insecurity by individual characteristics like age and gender. Calculation of AgWISE Scores

AgWISE module scores are determined by adding the responses for each of the items. Each response has a value from 0-3, such that when 13 items are asked, the total score ranges from 0 to 39. Higher scores signify greater water insecurity. The range will depend on the number of items that are included in the module.

Because we are in the early days understanding how these items work, we are provisionally recommending a cut-point for agricultural water insecurity as an AgWISE score of 13 or higher when the range is 0-39. This follows the cut-off of 12 to indicate “moderate-to-high water insecurity” for the 12-item HWISE and IWISE Scales (range 0-36). It remains to be seen if an appropriate cut-off score will always be the number of items in the module.

2. Interruptions
Please think about your water sources, how often were there interruptions in accessing and using this water during the last 12 months?

There can be several interruptions to water availability, use and access: a drought may dry up the canal, ponds or river water sources or depletion of water level you use and require you to find alternative sources; floods could damage water infrastructure and sources; increased salinity can render fresh water sources inappropriate for crop, fish or livestock use; or influential local individuals might capture and divert water from canals; or costs of water can increase due to widespread demand and reduced in availability. Please recall your experience of such events in the last 12 months.
3. Change

In the past 12 months, how often did water problems related to agriculture, aquaculture and related food processing activities result in a change in your day-to- day life, livelihood activities or other plans?

This question refers to activities including paid and unpaid agricultural work, and income-generating activities from food production and processing. For example, seasonal water shortages or floods impacted water availability and income; forced you to migrate; switch from farming to non-farming jobs; or altered your time and labour needs or required additional resources. Please recall your experience of such events in the last 12 months.
4. Decision
In the last 12 months, how often did decisions made by others about your key water sources affect the way you accessed and used water?

This question refers to decisions that resulted in interruptions in water access and use due to formal i.e. officially enforced regulations and interventions or by water management organizations; or informally due to pressure or interference by influential/powerful local individuals. Please recall your experience of such events in the last 12 months.
5. Food
Still thinking about the last 12 months, how often did you have to change or reduce what you normally eat because of problems with water for food production/processing?

For example, droughts, water scarcity, the quality of water, floods or extreme events could destroy field crops, homestead gardens, livestock operations, or fishing activities – affecting the production of, or access to food items you typically consume; cause post-harvest losses; reducing your food stock; limit income or cash for purchasing food and push you to seek alternative foods or adjust your diet. Please recall your experience of such events in the last 12 months.
This question is not related to a lack of water for washing, preparing, or cooking food.
6. Angry
In the last 12 months, how often did you feel angry because of problems you were experiencing with water for food production/processing?

This question refers to anger or other negative emotions you may have experienced due to issues with water [insecurity] i.e. water availability, accessibility, control or decision-making. This includes difficulties in obtaining sufficient agricultural water; concerns about water quality; disruptions affecting your daily life and schedule; adjustments to your diet; reduced production or income; and any other related water issues that cause anger or feelings of frustration and anxiety. This could also include anger from the inability to deal with events like loss of crops due to flooding, droughts or extreme climatic events; saline water intrusion, water conflicts leading to crop damage, livestock health, fish death.
Please recall your experience of such events in the last 12 months.
7. Sleep
In the last 12 months, how often did you have difficulties sleeping because of issues with water for food production/processing?

This question exclusively refers solely to a loss of or inadequate hours of sleep or disruptions in sleep, inability to sleep due to disruptions in access to, use and control of water for production/processing activities. This could also include anger from the inability to deal with events like loss of crops due to flooding, droughts or extreme climatic events; saline water intrusion, water conflicts leading to crop damage,
livestock health, fish death. Please recall your experience of such events in the last 12 months.
This question does not address sleeplessness due to individual or family health issues.
8. Harassment
In the past 12 months, how often did you experience harassment while collecting or using water for food production/processing?

There are many reasons why people might feel challenged or harassed because of problems with water. This could include verbal and sexual harassment while fetching or accessing water; threats issued publicly or in private; intimidation by others while accessing and using water for productive activities. Please recall your experience of such events in the last 12 months.
9. Crop
Now thinking specifically about crop production, in the last 12 months, how often did water-related problems harm crop production/processing?

Your field crops require irrigation at specific periods from sources such as canals, wells, boreholes, taps, rivers, streams, deep tubewells or shallow tubewells (one or all these sources). Water-related issues like drought, flooding, salinity can damage/delay/lower your crop production or adequate quantity, and quality water might be a challenge for post-harvest operations (e.g., parboiling of paddy1).
In this question, we aim to understand how frequently these occurrences have impacted irrigation activities and water for food processing in last 12 months.

Now thinking specifically about homestead gardens, in the last 12 months, how often did water-related problems cause issues for your homestead garden?

Your homestead garden require water from sources such as canals, wells, boreholes, taps, tubewell, rivers, or streams, and you might use one or all of these sources for home gardening. Water-related issues like drought, flooding, salinity, irrigation problems can damage your garden due to insufficient, excessive or poor-quality water.
In this question, we want to know how frequently these occurrences have impacted your gardening productivity/processing in the last 12 months.

Implementing the AgWISE Module
Can AgWISE phrasing be adopted to the local context?

All survey items require correct linguistic and contextual translation. Certain phrases may need to be adapted to ensure respondents understand their meaning in the local context. Translations should be piloted/pretested and translated back to English (or the text used in the study) ensure that the intended meaning is maintained (Boateng et al. 2018).
Can any items be dropped?

Yes. The items listed in this module were designed to measure agricultural water insecurity in a specific location in Bangladesh. However, agricultural activities can vary widely in different socio-ecological systems/ contexts. We recommend that this module serves as a framework, and that future use/users build on this design to adapt to specific local contexts. However, the WISE approach / scale is not to be changed. We encourage researchers to retain all of items 1-8 and drop / amend items 9-13.
Who should answer these questions?

Any adults (18 years and above) directly involved with water for agricultural activities in the household can answer agricultural water insecurity questions. In rural areas, both men and women are typically engaged in various tasks such as irrigation, homestead gardening, livestock and poultry rearing, and, in some contexts, capturing fish in open bodies of water. The items are designed to capture individual experiences with water; hence it is appropriate to ask these questions separately to both male and female members of the same household to understand differences by gender. However, the questions could be asked to members of a household as well. The WISE frameworks are designed for use at the Household and Individual scales.
Can this module be administered to women and other marginalized groups?

Yes. This module can be administered to anyone who uses water for agriculture. In many local contexts, it is advisable to have female enumerators conduct interviews with women. Globally, farming systems are often highly gendered; for example, Bangladesh primarily has a male-dominated farming system, while in parts of Africa, female-led systems are more common. Therefore, the outcomes of applying this module must be context-specific and cannot be generalized across different farming systems.
Can I ask this of the household instead of individuals?

The WISE frameworks are designed for use at the Household and Individual scales. Our focus in this module was to capture experiences of the respondent, to be able to understand gendered disparities in agricultural water insecurity and to analyze the impact of factors like class, age, landownership etc. In some cases, it might make more sense to ask about the experiences of the household, in which the items can be modified by adding the phrase “you or anyone in your household”. For example, “In the past 12 months, how often did you or anyone in your household worry about problems with water (too much, too little, not clean, conflicts about water, other problems)?”
Why was 12 months recall period selected?

Problems with agricultural water vary across seasons based on agricultural year (for example Kharif I, Kharif II Rabi season in Bangladesh). Water insecurity intensifies during the dry season or when rains are delayed, too light, or too heavy. Conversely, during the monsoon, excess water also exacerbates water insecurity. Therefore, we used a 12-month recall period to better capture experiences with water insecurity.
Can AgWISE capture seasonality?

Seasonality is an important part of agriculture. Seasonal variations in temperature and precipitation change adequacy, reliability, accessibility of water for productive use. We designed this AgWISE module to capture experiences of water [in]security across seasons. However, a one- or three-month recall period may be more
appropriate for understanding variation across the year. In such cases, it is recommended to implement the module in every season of the year.
How to ask and score AgWISE items with a recall period shorter than a year?

We recommend using phrasing similar to that which has been used for the HWISE and IWISE modules. These have been implemented using 3-day, 1-week, 1-month, and 3-month recall periods. For a 1-month recall, the phrasing and scoring have been “never” (0 days, scored 0), “rarely” (1-2 days, scored 1), “sometimes” (3-10 days, scored 2), “often or always” (11 days or more, scored 3) (Young et al., 2019).
How long it will take to complete the AgWISE module?
The estimated time is 3-4 minutes to ask the 13 items. This does not include the time it takes to describe the study's purpose before asking the questions.
What if a participant responds with “don’t know” or “not applicable”?

Don’t know"" or ""not applicable"" responses are coded as missing. As mentioned, the module should be designed with consultation and validation with the key informants, with the assumption that all items of AgWISE are relevant and can be answered.
Enumerators should employ the suggested probes to ensure that participants fully understand each question before making any response as “don’t know.”
Is qualitative data collection necessary?

After the survey items have been collected and analyzed, it can be insightful to conduct focus group discussions or key informant interviews to explore the context- specific experiences. This could include items like “What do you (or your household) use water for?”, What are the sources of water?”, “What were the problems with water (too much, too little, poor quality)?”, “How were the crops affected?” “What caused the water problems?”, “During dry season, which water uses get the priority under water stress?”. These could be asked of particular groups if the quantitative data suggest particular issues among, e.g., rural women but not urban women. We
also suggest collecting socio-demographic data of the respondents along with AgWISE module.
How were the AgWISE items developed?

We developed AgWISE items based on the Individual and Household Water Insecurity Scales (IWISE/ HWISE) frameworks (Young et al., 2019; 2021; 2024) to evaluate adequacy, reliability, accessibility of water for productive use (crop including kitchen gardens, livestock, and fisheries), and the experience of these impacts on production, livelihoods, food security and psychosocial stresses.
How and where have they been tested?

This AgWISE module has been tested in the Khulna and Satkhira districts of Bangladesh which are located in the southwest part of the country, a coastal area. To get a gender disaggregated overview of the experience of agricultural water insecurity, we interviewed women and men from 514 households separately, and then we disaggregated the data to assess class, ethnicity, age and other divides.
What is the evidence of their validity?
We are currently analyzing the survey data and will soon publish the findings.

We are systematically processing and serving our clients of any volume and in turn we are making more good sales since we now have capacity to produce one ton per hour as opposed to 200kg per hour using the previous miller, she says. Figure 1: A Morta Hammer Mill at Perisha Headquarters at Likuni in Lilongwe In the same way, as Mwai Kukada of Agriche Foods Malawi in Blantyre attests, the UU initiative has enabled him to procure a noodle making machine, which he will be using to make bean-enriched noodles for Malawians of all age ranges. The procurement of this noodles making machine marks a strategic investment in our production capabilities. The implementation of this advanced equipment is expected to enhance our efficiency, product quality, and overall competitiveness on the market, explains Kukada. Figure 2: Noodles making machine procured by Agriche Foods. Ukama Ustawi, a bilingual word collectively translating to partnerships as well as well-being and development , has been supporting the agribusiness sector to scale climate adaptation and mitigation interventions through the grants to MSMEs. This has led to transformation of livelihoods for different people not only in Malawi, but also in Burundi, Zambia, Uganda and Rwanda, where this project is covering. In Uganda for instance, UU focused on increasing capacities and efficiency of SAWA Agricultural Development Company Limited (SADCL), an MSME situated in Mpigi District, which is involved in bean value chain, through provision of portable technologies and machinery. With the grant, SADCL has purchased a digital moisture meter, vacuum sealer, and a digital weighing scale to improve its processing capacities and efficiency. According to the Managing Director Charles Katabalwa, the weighing scale, for instance, will assist in measuring the weights of the grain from the smallholder farmers under the Seed Grain Credit Model (SGCM) and Community Production and Marketing Activity (COPMAS) under the company. The weighing scale will enable us to provide precise measurements to our clients, which will improve our customer confidence and reduce customer dissatisfaction. It will provide an inclusive gender perspective in grain sales as it is easy to read the figures displayed on the LCD by either male or female. For the moisture content meter, it will play a great role for SADCL in affecting the sale weight, quality, and ability to store grain for long term, explains Katabalwa. In Uganda, smallholder farmers and aggregators suffer mold growth setback on the harvested grain due to high moisture content, because molds thrive in moist environments this can grow across the entire production and later lead to mycotoxin contamination like aflatoxin. With digital moisture meter, this will be a thing of the past, as it will reduce mold growth and help in giving confidence at harvest and sell of healthy grain produce. Figure 3: grain Moisture Meter purchased by SADCL. The process of vacuum sealing will enable us to reduce on any occurrence of bacteria growth in the precooked dehydrated bean product and flour thereby extending the shelf life without adding any preservatives, as well as enabling sale of the products for a longer time span. It will also prevent cross contamination of the company products from external influences thence improving food quality and safety, he adds. Figure 4: Vacuum sealing machine purchased by SADCL With the same grant secured under UU, Operations Manager for Morning Beverages Limited (MBL) in Zambia, Kondwani Chiwowa is heavily relieved. Following laborious process of sorting beans manually, inefficiencies in speed and resource utilization have been the order of the day at his company. On top of that, the old sealing machines are overburdened, eventually causing overheating issues. The packaged beans would spoil and we had some returns from the market. But now apart from the sealing machine, were also have a Bean Sorting Machine. Today the damages have reduced by 75%. Besides that, speed and efficiency have been enhanced, says Chiwowa. With the 100 liters jacket oil pot we are procuring, our production will increase to about 600 kilograms (kgs) of beans in a day against the current 120 kgs we are producing now. Our deliveries will not be delayed because even when we have an emergency order, we know in the shortest period we will be able to cook and deliver, boasts Pamela Tembo of Beyond Bridge Investment Limited, another processor who benefitted from UU grants, whose company specializes in producing frozen pre-cooked beans. Make sure to distinguish activities which were carried out from activities which were planned but not carried out.
Step 2: Review the definitions of the scores 0 through 9, so that you understand what the possible values are and where the project being reviewed belongs on the innovation readiness scale.

Step 3: Use the innovation readiness scale to determine the cumulative readiness level of COMPLETED activities conducted as part of the project. IMPORTANT: No activities that have been planned but not yet completed should be considered when determining the readiness level.
Step 4: In a professional, academic 3rd person voice, concisely justify why you selected this readiness level in a maximum of 300 words.

IMPORTANT: Keep in mind that the audience consist of academic researchers. Never refer to yourself in the first person in this summary. Refer to all actions in the past tense. Some notes that will help you:

column2: Innovation development refers to a new, improved, or adapted output or groups of outputs such as technologies, products and services, policies, and other organizational and institutional arrangements, with high potential to contribute to positive impacts when used at scale.

column1: These are the definitions of the scaling readiness levels you need to learn to apply:

column2: Level 9: The innovation is validated for its ability to achieve a specific impact under uncontrolled conditions.

Level 4: The innovation is being tested for its ability to achieve a specific impact under fully controlled conditions.
Level 3: The innovation’s key concepts have been validated for their ability to achieve a specific impact.
Level 2: The innovation’s key concepts are being formulated or designed.
Level 1: The innovation’s basic principles are being researched for their ability to achieve a specific impact.
Level 0: The innovation is at idea stage.

column1: Here are some further clarifications on scoring:
Levels 0, 1, 2 and 3 represent development stages, prior to testing.

column2: Level 0 involves formulating the idea.
Level 1 involves researching the building blocks of the innovation and investigating the feasibility of the idea.
Level 2 involves formulating a plan for what the innovation will entail and how it will be developed, based on the research in Level 1.

column1: Levels 4, 6, and 8 represent testing stages, during which the innovation is actively evaluated for its ability to achieve specific impacts under varying conditions:

column2: Level 4 involves testing in a fully controlled environment,

Introducción

El estudio se enmarca en la iniciativa AgriLAC Resiliente, del CGIAR, que busca transformar los sistemas agroalimentarios de América Latina y el Caribe mediante soluciones innovadoras y sostenibles adaptadas a los desafíos climáticos. Específicamente, esta actividad responde al objetivo de impulsar la innovación tecnológica para mejorar la productividad agrícola y la sostenibilidad, mediante el uso de drones multiespectrales para el monitoreo de cultivos en los departamentos de Totonicapán y Zacapa.

Estas herramientas permiten generar datos clave para la toma de decisiones agronómicas, optimizando el manejo de recursos en regiones caracterizadas por condiciones climáticas y edáficas contrastantes. Al trabajar con parcelas agrícolas dentro de las Redes de InnovaHubs, este proyecto aporta evidencia científica sobre el potencial de la tecnología para transformar los sistemas de producción a pequeña escala, promoviendo prácticas agrícolas resilientes y sostenibles que fortalecen la seguridad alimentaria en comunidades vulnerables.

La agricultura de pequeña escala es una de las principales actividades económicas en Guatemala, desempeñando un rol crucial en la seguridad alimentaria del país. Sin embargo, enfrenta desafíos significativos, como la variabilidad climática, el acceso limitado a tecnología y la necesidad de prácticas agrícolas más sostenibles.

El uso de drones permite obtener datos precisos y rápidos sobre el estado de los cultivos, incluyendo la identificación de zonas con problemas de crecimiento, monitoreo del desarrollo vegetativo y evaluación de prácticas de manejo. Estas ventajas se traducen en información clave para la toma de decisiones, mejorando la productividad de los pequeños agricultores.
Caracterización de la zona de estudio

Totonicapán está ubicado en el altiplano frío de Guatemala, se caracteriza por su clima templado con temperaturas moderadas y precipitaciones bien distribuidas durante el año. Su topografía montañosa y suelos fértiles lo hacen ideal para el cultivo de maíz, el cual es el principal grano básico de la región.

Por otro lado, Zacapa, está situado en el trópico de humedad limitada, con un clima más cálido y seco. Los suelos son menos profundos y requieren prácticas intensivas para sostener la productividad. Las precipitaciones son más esporádicas, lo que hace que el manejo del riego sea crítico.
Cobertura vegetal y uso del suelo
Según el Mapa de Cobertura Vegetal y Uso de la Tierra de Guatemala 2020 del MAGA, las áreas de estudio presentan las siguientes características:

En el municipio de Totonicapán predomina cobertura de bosque de coníferas a un 41%, seguido por un 30% del terreno con cobertura de cultivos como maíz y frijol y un 15% de boque mixto. Por otro lado, dentro de la zona de interés para el monitoreo, el 87% está dedicada a granos básicos y solo un 8% de bosque mixto, igual la zona urbana, 8%.

El municipio de Zacapa muestra una combinación de cultivos anuales en un 7%, como maíz y sorgo dispersos, otros cultivos de ciclo más largo como café 25%, junto con áreas de pastizales y vegetación arbustiva baja como cobertura principal a un 40%. En la zona de interés para el monitoreo se resalta vegetación arbustiva baja en un 82%, sin embargo, hay presencia de cultivos de ciclo corto, como el maíz en un 4%, igual que bosque mixto a un 6%
Suelos
Para las zonas de monitoreo, el Mapa de Clasificación Taxonómica de Suelos del MAGA indica lo siguiente:

En Totonicapán los suelos son completamente de tipo andisoles, caracterizados por alta fertilidad y buena retención de humedad y alta carga de materia orgánica, adecuados para cultivos de granos básicos, mientras que en Zacapa predomina totalmente suelos inceptisoles, con contenido orgánico variable, capacidad de retención de agua baja, lo que limita su productividad sin prácticas de manejo adecuadas.

Clima
Según el estado del clima en Guatemala (INSIVUMEH, 2023), las zonas de monitoreo tienen las siguientes características:

Totonicapán se caracteriza por un clima templado con una temperatura mínima promedio de 10°C y una máxima promedio de 22°C. Las condiciones climáticas favorecen la agricultura, con una precipitación anual promedio de 1,200 mm que permite el desarrollo de cultivos básicos como el maíz y el frijol. Estas condiciones, junto con su topografía montañosa, lo convierten en una región de alta productividad agrícola, aunque también enfrenta desafíos asociados a la fragmentación de parcelas y la necesidad de prácticas sostenibles.

En contraste, Zacapa se localiza en una región de clima cálido y seco, caracterizado por temperaturas que oscilan entre una mínima promedio de 18°C y una máxima promedio de 32°C. La precipitación anual es más limitada, con un promedio de 800 mm, lo que demanda un manejo cuidadoso de los recursos hídricos para garantizar la sostenibilidad de los cultivos predominantes, como el maíz y el sorgo. A pesar de estas limitaciones, Zacapa destaca por la implementación de prácticas agrícolas adaptadas a su entorno, que buscan optimizar el uso del agua y mejorar la productividad en condiciones de humedad limitada.

La zona de monitoreo en el municipio de Zacapa presenta condiciones muy particulares, en contraste con el resto del municipio que se considera como cálido y seco, en el área de vuelo se registran acumulados de lluvia de entre 1000 – 2000 mm y temperaturas medias de entre 18-23 °C, esto se debe a su ubicación en zonas de montaña dentro del municipio (anexo 7).

En el Anexo 6 y Anexo 7 se hace un análisis específico del clima y su comportamiento en las zonas de monitoreo, destacando que, tanto en Zacapa como en Totonicapán hubo acumulados mensuales de lluvia por debajo de lo normal en los meses de monitoreo.
Relieve y topografía

Según el Mapa orográfico de Guatemala (URL, 2022), Totonicapán, ubicado en el altiplano occidental, cuenta con elevaciones que varían entre 2,000 y 3,000 metros sobre el nivel del mar, presentando una topografía montañosa. Para le caso de Zacapa, situado en el valle del río Motagua, con presenta elevaciones entre 300 y 500 metros sobre el nivel del mar, caracterizado por llanuras y colinas bajas.

En las zonas de monitoreo, las elevaciones obtenidas a partir los vuelos de dron (Anexo 9) fueron de 2,367-3,831 msnm para Totonicapán y en Zacapa, las parcelas identificadas están ubicadas en altitudes desde 473 hasta 1,005 msnm.
Metodología
Delimitación de la zona de estudio

Como base para la identificación de sitios de vuelo se cuenta las ubicaciones de parcelas agrícolas que corresponden a las Redes de InnovaHubs (centros de innovación) que hacen parte de la iniciativa AgriLAC Resiliente del CGIAR. Estas parcelas en su mayoría corresponden a granos básicos maíz y frijol.
Para la delimitación de las áreas posibles de vuelo se usaron las siguientes fuentes de datos:
o Base de datos de ubicación de parcelas de las Redes de InnovaHubs.
o Mapa de uso del suelo y cobertura vegetal escala 1:50,000 - MAGA 2020, el cual contiene la delimitación de cultivos anuales (maíz y frijol).
Para la definición de las áreas de vuelo se consideraron los siguientes criterios:
o Se ajustan las áreas de vuelo a 6.5 km².
Las áreas de vuelo abarcan la mayor cantidad de parcelas de la base de datos de las Redes de InnovaHubs.
o El área delimitada abarca la mayor cantidad de cultivos anuales que muestra el mapa uso del suelo y cobertura vegetal MAGA 2020.
Se priorizaron los departamentos de Totonicapán y Zacapa, en la Figura 1 se observan las zonas de monitoreo delimitadas.

El primer vuelo en cada sitio de trabajo se realizó únicamente con una cámara RGB, esto con el fin de establecer una línea base para diferenciación de uso de suelo. Para los siguientes vuelos, en ambos sitios, se utilizaron cámaras con las bandas del infra rojo cercano, verde y azul (NIR,G,B). Esta programación permitió cubrir desde la emergencia y establecimiento del cultivo hasta el desarrollo completo de su fase vegetativa.
Procesamiento de datos

Las imágenes obtenidas mediante los drones tienen una resolución espacial de 30 cm/píxel para las imágenes RGB (color) e imágenes para el cálculo de NDVI (NIR,G,B). El Modelo Digital de Elevación (DEM) tiene una resolución espacial de 1 m/píxel. Toda la información geoespacial está en el sistema de referencia de coordenadas Datum WGS84. Las imágenes NDVI para cada momento de vuelo fueron calculadas utilizando la banda del azul e infra rojo cercano.

Datos in situ

Los puntos de muestreo fueron seleccionados estratégicamente en función de la representatividad de las parcelas agrícolas monitoreadas en los departamentos de Totonicapán y Zacapa. Estos puntos cumplen con los siguientes criterios:

Discusión

Los resultados obtenidos a partir del análisis de NDVI y los datos agronómicos permitieron una comprensión integral del estado de las parcelas de maíz en Totonicapán y Zacapa, dos regiones con contrastantes características agroecológicas. La relación entre los índices de vegetación y las etapas del ciclo del cultivo fue evidente: los valores de NDVI más altos y consistentes en Totonicapán reflejan mejores condiciones de crecimiento y manejo agronómico, mientras que los valores más bajos y variables en Zacapa están asociados con suelos menos fértiles y mayor estrés ambiental. La progresión del NDVI entre las fases vegetativa inicial y media demuestra la utilidad del índice para monitorear dinámicas fenológicas del cultivo.
Implicaciones para los Pequeños Productores de Maíz

Los hallazgos tienen implicaciones prácticas para los pequeños productores de maíz en ambas regiones. En Totonicapán, los altos valores de NDVI y el enfoque en parcelas pequeñas y bien manejadas resaltan la importancia de mantener prácticas sostenibles, como el manejo de rastrojo y el uso de semillas criollas. En Zacapa, los valores más bajos de NDVI y la mayor variabilidad sugieren la necesidad de intervenciones específicas, como la incorporación de cultivos de cobertura y el acceso a herramientas de diagnóstico de fertilidad.

Los pequeños productores podrían beneficiarse de un monitoreo regular basado en NDVI para identificar áreas problemáticas y ajustar las prácticas de manejo en tiempo real. Sin embargo, el costo y la complejidad técnica del uso de drones y análisis satelitales representan barreras significativas para su adopción directa, subrayando la necesidad de apoyo técnico y subsidios para facilitar el acceso a estas tecnologías.
Limitaciones del Estudio y Áreas de Mejora
El estudio presenta varias limitaciones:
1) Condiciones Climáticas: Las restricciones para realizar vuelos en condiciones de nubosidad afectaron la obtención de datos continuos.
2) Tamaño de Parcelas: La gran variabilidad en el tamaño de las parcelas entre Zacapa y Totonicapán complicó la comparación directa.
3) Disponibilidad de Datos In Situ: La falta de mediciones complementarias de biomasa o rendimiento limitó la validación de los datos de NDVI.
4) Costos: El alto costo de los vuelos con drones y el procesamiento de imágenes representa una barrera para estudios más
extensos.

Áreas de mejora incluyen el desarrollo de algoritmos más robustos para la delimitación de parcelas pequeñas, el diseño de campañas multitemporales para capturar el ciclo completo del cultivo, y la integración de datos de sensores de bajo costo para

validar los índices de vegetación. Además, considerar incorporación de datos agronómicos consistentes para correlación con la información geoespacial obtenida con los Drones.
Conclusiones

1. Los valores de NDVI más altos y consistentes en Totonicapán reflejan mejores condiciones agroecológicas y prácticas sostenibles, mientras que Zacapa mostró menor vigor vegetal y mayor variabilidad, asociado con suelos menos fértiles y estrés ambiental.

2. La progresión del NDVI entre las fases vegetativa inicial y media permite un monitoreo efectivo de las etapas fenológicas del cultivo, demostrando la utilidad del índice para la agricultura de precisión.
3. El uso de drones proporciona datos complementarios para el análisis multiescala, pero su adopción a gran escala requiere superar barreras económicas y técnicas.

4. De acuerdo con los datos climáticos registrados durante el año 2024, correspondiente al período de monitoreo del cultivo, se observó un comportamiento atípico en el régimen de lluvias. El inicio del período lluvioso se retrasó varios días y la distribución de la precipitación a lo largo del ciclo presentó irregularidades. Estas condiciones influyeron directamente en las variaciones observadas en los datos agronómicos del período, en comparación con años anteriores. Asimismo, estas particularidades climáticas contribuyeron a una mayor similitud en los datos obtenidos mediante drones, lo que explica la proximidad en los valores de NDVI entre Zacapa y Totonicapán en ambas etapas de crecimiento del cultivo.
Recomendaciones
1) Para productores:
• Continuar con las técnicas de innovación en cultivos, por sus buenos resultados.
En Totonicapán, continuar con el manejo sostenible del rastrojo y el uso de semillas criollas.
En Zacapa, implementar cultivos de cobertura y rotación de cultivos para mejorar la estructura del suelo y la fertilidad.
2) Para extensionistas:
• Facilitar capacitaciones en el uso de tecnologías de monitoreo, como índices de vegetación y herramientas de diagnóstico.
• Realizar más análisis con otras herramientas de teledetección como imágenes de satélite, comparando diferentes tipos de resoluciones espaciales.
Promover subsidios o financiamiento para tecnologías de bajo costo, como sensores portátiles para monitoreo in situ.
3) Para Tomadores de decisiones:
• Diseñar políticas que incentiven la adopción de prácticas sostenibles en regiones con suelos vulnerables, como Zacapa.
Realizar más proyectos para correlación de datos agronómicos con información geoespacial.

Step 3: Use the innovation readiness scale to determine the cumulative readiness level of COMPLETED activities conducted as part of the project. IMPORTANT: No activities that have been planned but not yet completed should be considered when determining the readiness level.
Step 4: In a professional, academic 3rd person voice, concisely justify why you selected this readiness level in a maximum of 300 words.

column1: Here are some further clarifications on scoring:
Levels 0, 1, 2 and 3 represent development stages, prior to testing.

column2: Level 0 involves formulating the idea.

column2: Level 4 involves testing in a fully controlled environment,

I. INTRODUCTION

The Asian Mega-Deltas (AMD) initiative aims to support the creation of resilient, inclusive, and productive deltas in Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, Myanmar, and Vietnam. The AMD initiative uses a transdisciplinary impact pathway approach towards protecting against threats to nutrition security; breaking down investment barriers; strengthening inclusive, gender-equitable governance of the natural resources on which the system depends, and planning development based on risk and vulnerability for sighting to devise policies that create adaptation opportunities and mitigate the impacts of future threats. In line with this initiative, Work Package (WP) 2: Nutrition-sensitive agri-food systems study was conducted in Cambodia which specifically aims to:
1. Assess changes in the deltaic food consumption patterns in relation to demand-side drivers of change to reveal socially differentiated nutrition outcomes.
2. Evaluate how the deltaic agroecosystems and food production practices are transforming in response to multiple drivers to reveal socially differentiated nutrition outcomes; and
3. Identify nutrition-sensitive policies and interventions to support equitable and sustainable consumption and production of nutritious foods in deltas in the face of rapid change.

On December 13, 2022, the International Institute of Rural Reconstruction (IIRR) together with the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT (ABC), Council for Agricultural and Rural Development (CARD), and Scaling Up Nutrition Civil Society Alliance (SUN CSA) organized the consultation workshop in Phnom Penh, Cambodia to present the preliminary results regarding policies that support nutrition-sensitive agri-food systems in the Mekong Delta and current nutrition sensitive agri-food systems literature and interventions to generate feedback/inputs from stakeholders representing various universities, organizations, private companies, and government agencies and to further validate these results. 80 workshop participants (33 are women), 64 face-to-face participants, and 16 virtual participants, who were professionally and actively involved in multidisciplinary sectors including agriculture, health, education, and economic sectors attended (see participant list in annex 1).

This workshop served as an avenue for actors within food systems to exchange information on ongoing activities and networks related to nutrition-sensitive agri-food systems in Cambodia. It enables IIRR and its partners to share and discuss the preliminary results regarding policies that support nutrition-sensitive food systems in the Mekong Delta and current nutrition-sensitive agri- food systems literature and interventions.
This workshop aimed to:
1. Exchange information on ongoing activities related to nutrition-sensitive food systems in Cambodia;
2. Present and validate the results of the literature and policy review of the AMD WP2 study; and
3. Generate inputs and additional information from the stakeholders to further improve the work related to nutrition-sensitive food systems in the Mekong Delta.
This workshop report summarizes the research findings as presented in the workshop and the key points from the discussion that followed.
II. METHODOLOGY
The workshop used a participatory approach to discuss among the participants for contributing inputs to improve the draft report.

The program started at 9:00 am with the national anthem of Cambodia. Mr. H.E. Chea Samnang, Deputy Chairman of Council for Agriculture and Rural Development (CARD) presided over the workshop to officially open with key messages to promote food security and nutrition through partnership building, resource mobilization to meet national roadmaps, policies, and sustainable development goal (see annex 2 for the agenda). After that, the facilitator team asked all participants to attend a group photo. Mr. Or Thy, Country Director of IIRR Cambodia introduced the background of the project, objectives, and program overview. In addition to the project information, Dr. Deborah Nabuuma Associate Scientist of Alliance Bioversity International and CIAT introduced the overall AMD project, including AMD for climate and livelihood resilience, AMD critical development challenges, and focus areas (adapting deltaic production systems, nutrition- sensitive agri-food systems, De-Risking delta-oriented value chains, inclusive-gender equitable governance and policy for natural resources, evidence-based delta development planning, improving climate and livelihood resilience in AMD) (see annex 3 for the AMD presentation)

IIRR Associate Researcher, Mr. Arvin Carandang presented preliminary results of the policies and literature reviewed relevant to the nutrition-sensitive agri-food systems in the Mekong Delta (see annex 4 for the presentation of policy and literature review). After the presentation, the participants generated questions and clarifications in line with the presented results. The facilitators noted the participants' recommendations and suggestions to include them in the study and action plan for AMD WP2 in 2023.

III. KEY FINDINGS AND FEEDBACK
3.1. Literature Review-Feedback and Recommendation

Mr. Arvin Carandang presented literature review results and discussed the nutrition-sensitive agriculture projects in Cambodia such as the Market Linkages for Smallholders (MALIS) Project and Enhanced Homestead Food Production (EHFP). Highlighted on the discussion are the significance of project design, planning, extension, and appropriate policies in developing nutrition-sensitive agriculture interventions to target specific population for best solutions, effect of higher income and social factors such as ethnicity, gender, beliefs and women’s workload and environmental factors.

Following the presentation, the participants provided feedback on the result presented and discussed that highlighted alone is the right of mothers to decide on what to feed the family specifically children, but that should also include fathers since they also have the right to make a decision in the family. The study was conducted with limited time and scope should integrate the effects of social protection in the study. The participants also mentioned that since the study was conducted in a short time, the way to provide the recommendations raised cannot apply to all sectors. The researcher should meet directly with relevant institutions. Researchers should focus on consumer behaviors, including children, and women to ensure that those target groups receiving healthy food. The key messages should be disseminated through media channels. Food fortification as a priority task in improving food nutrition in Cambodia should be included in the study recommended. The study needs to review the relation between climate and nutrition/ food system: how does climate change affect to food system? For example, rice production was affected by climate change.
3.2. Policy Review-Feedback and Recommendation from plenary sessions

Policies relevant to nutrition-sensitive agriculture and food systems were reviewed based on themes of transparency, sustainable food supply chains, and equal and equitable access (see annex 6 for the list of policies). A total of 40 policies were reviewed for the study. Results of the review were also presented highlighting the gaps identified and opportunities, linkage between nutrition and agriculture as an intervention and challenges to accessing information related to food systems. It also mentioned that policy agenda expressed at the national level are usually not well- communicated on the ground.

The participants provided more recommendations regarding the food nutrition policy. They mentioned that the study should include key policies to identify gaps and recommendations to improve the key documents because it cannot be covered all aspects. All sectors and key stakeholders should be involved in this assignment to find the gaps and develop a common way forward with a clear action plan, roles, and responsibilities. The Ministry of Agriculture Forestry and Fisheries (MAFF) has a master plan for agricultural development 2030 that was approved in September 2022. The policy implemented by MAFF and supported by relevant ministries that responds to genuine needs, which is illustrated by indicators by 2030. Ecological agriculture is important for promoting food security and nutrition, which has already been implemented in Kampong Cham, Battambang, and Preah Vihear provinces by MAFF. To promote ecological agriculture, MAFF established Conservation Agriculture and Sustainable Intensification Consortium that is attended by multi-ministries. The General Directorate of Agriculture (GDA) established good

agricultural practice standards by using QR Code to promote nutrition and healthy food. Rural infrastructure plays significant roles in promoting nutrition that needs to develop from the grass root level. Agriculture input suppliers, producers and sellers need to think about sanitary, phyto- sanitary standards and nutrition facts. A national mechanism should work for nutrition budget to allocate budget to relevant ministries, and then it is easy to work and collect data as well. Multi- sectoral works have been guided by national policies, but there should be a clear budget to implement the policies. The capacity building approach should be focused and have common understanding, for example digital capacity building process.
Policy of food fortification guideline should be included in the study. The ministry of planning set up indicators of food fortification and water.

The study talked about food and nutrition but not the sources of food and food safety especially in the production, processing and selling where roles of the producers, processors, small and medium enterprises, consumers or local farmers, agricultural cooperatives should be highlighted.

It is noted that NGOs are able to join the Scaling Up Nutrition Civil Society Alliance (SUN CSA), UN Network, SUN Donor Network to promote food security and nutrition in collaboration with the government.

The study should focus on food safety in good aquaculture practice and livestock, climate change (drought and flood) which is also part of the agri-food systems approach. Environmental impact should be considered in promoting agri-food systems.

The Royal University of Agriculture (RUA) has a food and nutrition faculty that is very relevant to this study. The study should consider food quality, nutrient contents, and ingredients (nutrition facts) that need to test specifically and disseminate the nutrition facts/food ingredients to consumers.

The Royal University of Phnom Penh (RUPP) would collect primary data for AMD2 and analyze food availability, food accessibility, and market linkages of the Mekong Delta. Water study is an essential element to incorporate in AMD3.

It should be noted that WVI implement a project entitled Commercialization of Aquaculture for Sustainable Trade (CAST) that promote food safety and market linkages for fish products from producers to consumers through UNICA and Denish Care Foods companies.

Most of the participants agreed that the literature review should add more information related to some programs/projects conducted by several Ministries such as ASPIRE Program – MAFF, AIMS – Ministry of Commerce, HARVEST 2 &3, Agricultural Census, Population census -2019, Cambodian Demographic Development Health Survey – 2022 – MOP, especially the literature on market and supply chains part. Regarding gaps, it is important to study more on the impacts of chemical fertilizers and pesticides, market information systems as well as nutrition facts analysis.

Participants were divided into four groups to discuss how to make the NSAFS guidance realistic and useful for the Mekong Delta, incorporating context-specific interventions, and identifying any missing elements. Key recommendations included the need for scientific studies to respond to current needs, scaling up successful pilot projects, involving key stakeholders, and integrating the guidance into national and sub-national planning processes. General information about the Agroecology Initiative

Soil data interpretation and recommendations guidance
• Liming is necessary when the pH is low. No liming is needed under high pH. Gypsum can be used to reduce soil pH, especially in highly alkaline soils. Very high pH should be managed appropriately.
• When calcium is low, apply high calcium limestone. When both calcium and magnesium are low, apply dolomitic limestone.

• When soil organic carbon is low, employ good agriculture management practices like application of organic matter, organic residues, compost/manure, mulch or plant green manure cover crops, practice agroforestry, soil conservation (conservation agriculture, erosion control), intercropping, cover cropping, controlled grazing

• When the soil nutrient(s) is(are) low, address by applying good agriculture management practices like organic matter, organic residues, compost/manure, mulching, planting green manure cover crops or leguminous crops; practice agroforestry, soil conservation (conservation agriculture, erosion control), intercropping/rotations, cover cropping, or application of the appropriate nutrient-based organic fertilisers

• The medium and high concentrations of nutrients are okay for moderate to optimum crop productivity. However, they need to be maintained by applying organic matter, organic residues, compost/manure, mulching, planting green manure cover crops or leguminous crops; or applying the appropriate nutrient-based organic fertilisers

Note: The ideal soil nutrient concentrations should range from medium to optimum, and these may vary with crops. Very high concentrations of some nutrients, like Aluminium, may be toxic to plants or impair availability of other soil chemical parameters.

Permanent link to cite or share this item https://hdl.handle.net/10568/169333 External link to download this item DOI Abstract/Description In Kenya, the CGIAR Agroecology Initiative (AE-I) has two agroecological living landscapes (ALLs), one in Kiambu County and a second in Makueni County. Work package 1 (WP1) of the AE-I entailed two key components: ALL establishment, and innovation co-design. In line with broader agroecology approaches and ontologies, both were to be achieved through transdisciplinary co-design processes. This report provides an overview of the innovation co-design process, its results, the scientific performance of co-designed practices and related reflections. First, the report introduces the three-pronged co-design approach, which included a preparatory phase, a co-design phase, and a trial phase; and outlines the many different steps involved in the process. It then provides details of the specific practices co-designed across the three identified focus areas in which most attention was required: soil management, water management, and integrated pest management. The respective practices for the Kiambu ALL included the use of compost manure, mulch, and chili-based biopesticides, and farmyard manure, planted terraces, and neem-based biopesticides in Makueni. In the first cycle of trials, each of these practices was put under trial on 10 farmers fields. The experimental design included on 5x6 m controlled test trial plot, and a second 5x6 m uncontrolled control plot. While the inputs used (including seeds, seedlings, and treatments) were centrally provided, and kept constant, the trial participants used their conventional practice in the control plots. With a few exceptions, this conventional practice is largely organic in Kiambu, and followed permaculture principles in Makueni. Third, the agronomic assessment of two consecutive experimentation cycles (October 2023-March 2024; May 2024-September 2024) revealed generally positive performance of the co-designed practices. A preliminary contextual climate analysis showed that both areas received excessive rainfall in the second cycle, with more than twice the long-term average in April and May. Experienced flooding and water logging considerably influenced agricultural production during that cycle. Considering gross productivity, yields only significantly improved in the Makueni ALL, while differences in Kiambu ALL were not significant. In Makueni, only farmyard manure had a significant effect on maize yields, while all three practices significantly improved bean yields. Considering pest and disease pressure, pests were significantly lower for cabbages in the IPM trials in Kiambu, but not for compost or mulch. In Makueni, pests were significantly lower for both maize and beans in the IPM trial, as well as for beans in the manure trial. Despite experiencing difficulties related to planting timing, the climatic conditions, the quality of the inputs used, and market constraints, the participating farmers evaluated the practices and their participation in the trials very positively. In the last two sections, the report discussed adoption and scaling approaches, and broader reflections on successes and challenges with the co-design process, and recommends a continuation of highly methodical and structured transdisciplinary innovation co-design. This report complements the detailed co-design report prepared by the WP1 Kenya team in 2023 (Fuchs et al., 2023b). Executive summary

In Kenya, the CGIAR Agroecology Initiative (AE-I) has two agroecological living landscapes (ALLs), one in Kiambu County and a second in Makueni County. Work package 1 (WP1) of the AE-I entailed two key components: ALL establishment, and innovation co-design. In line with broader agroecology approaches and ontologies, both were to be achieved through transdisciplinary co-design processes. This report provides an overview of the innovation co-design process, its results, the scientific performance of co-designed practices and related reflections. First, the report introduces the three-pronged co-design approach, which included a preparatory phase, a co-design phase, and a trial phase; and outlines the many different steps involved in the process. It then provides details of the specific practices co-designed across the three identified focus areas in which most attention was required: soil management, water management, and integrated pest management. The respective practices for the Kiambu ALL included the use of compost manure, mulch, and chili-based biopesticides, and farmyard manure, planted terraces, and neem-based biopesticides in Makueni. In the first cycle of trials, each of these practices was put under trial on 10 farmers’ fields. The experimental design included on 5x6 m controlled test trial plot, and a second 5x6 m “uncontrolled” control plot. While the inputs used (including seeds, seedlings, and treatments) were centrally provided, and kept constant, the trial participants used their conventional practice in the control plots. With a few exceptions, this conventional practice is largely organic in Kiambu, and followed permaculture principles in Makueni. Third, the agronomic assessment of two consecutive experimentation cycles (October 2023- March 2024; May 2024-September 2024) revealed generally positive performance of the co-designed practices. A preliminary contextual climate analysis showed that both areas received excessive rainfall in the second cycle, with more than twice the long-term average in April and May. Experienced flooding and water logging considerably influenced agricultural production during that cycle. Considering gross productivity, yields only significantly improved in the Makueni ALL, while differences in Kiambu ALL were not significant. In Makueni, only farmyard manure had a significant effect on maize yields, while all three practices significantly improved bean yields. Considering pest and disease pressure, pests were significantly lower for cabbages in the IPM trials in Kiambu, but not for compost or mulch. In Makueni, pests were significantly lower for both maize and beans in the IPM trial, as well as for beans in the manure trial. Despite experiencing difficulties related to planting timing, the climatic conditions, the quality of the inputs used, and market constraints, the participating farmers evaluated the practices and their participation in the trials very positively. In the last two sections, the report discussed adoption and scaling approaches, and broader reflections on successes and challenges with the co-design process, and recommends a continuation of highly methodical and structured transdisciplinary innovation co-design. 1. Introduction

In Kenya, the CGIAR Agroecology Initiative (AE-I) has two agroecological living landscapes (ALLs), which are localized at the sub-national and sub-county level in Kiambu County and in Makueni County. The AE-I team engages with numerous and diverse stakeholders in the ALLs, as well as with core agroecology stakeholders at the national level. Formal partnerships with the Inter-sectoral forum for agrobiodiversity and agroecology (ISFAA) and PELUM Kenya provide anchorage and scaling of engagements at the sub-national ALL level. The Initiative’s interaction and engagement with the ALLs is organized via central points referred to as so-called “ALLs host centers”. These include the Community Sustainable Agriculture and Healthy Environment Program (CSHEP) in Ndeiya, Kiambu County, which focuses on organic agriculture, and the Drylands Natural Resource Centre (DNRC) in Mbumbuni, Makueni County, focusing on permaculture. The ALLs host centers represent and provide a physical space where food system actors can meet, interact, and co-create knowledge.

Work package 1 (WP1) of the AE-I, which focused on transdisplinary co-creation of innovations in the ALLs, entailed two key components: the establishment of flourishing multi-stakeholder partnerships and collaboration in the designated ALLs (also referred to as “ALL establishment”), and the co-design of on-farm innovations. In line with broader agroecology approaches and ontologies, both were to be achieved through transdisciplinary co- design processes. This report provides an overview of the innovation co-design process, its results, the scientific performance of co-designed practices and related reflections. It complements the detailed co-design report prepared by the WP1 Kenya team in 2023 (Fuchs et al., 2023b).

The innovation co-design workshops that led to the identification of innovative practices for on-farm experimentation were embedded in a broader engagement and co-creation process that involved diverse stakeholders (see Fuchs et al., 2023b for more details). The co-design workshops that led to the first cycle of on- farm experimentation were held in August 2023, and involved about 45 persons per ALL. Stakeholders included farmers, ALL host centers, the AE-I team, and additional research, technical, and extension stakeholders, including from Kenya Agriculture and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO), County Agricultural Extension Department and Participatory Ecological Land Use Management (PELUM) Association. The leads of both ALL host centers participated in the co-design workshops in both ALLs, as did the zonal manager of PELUM-Kenya, one of the key scaling partners.

Farmers were purposively selected from a total of 15 farmer groups per ALL, half of which had previously been trained by the ALL host centers, and half of which had not. The identified farmer groups were invited to observe gender and age balance in their selection of representatives who would participate in the workshop.

In view of the practices and test crops selected, and the agricultural cycles in the Kenyan ALLs, two consecutive rounds of co-design workshops were held with the trial participants and other stakeholders in April 2024, and October 2024 respectively. These led to the establishment of a second and third cycle of trials.

This methodological guidance handbook was developed in the context of the CGIAR Initiative on Agroecology (also referred to as Agroecology Initiative). The Agroecology Initiative is a collaborative partnership of eight CGIAR entities (Alliance Bioversity-CIAT, IMWI, CIMMYT, CIP, ICARDA, IFPRI, IITA, WorldFish), as well as CIFOR-ICRAF, and the French research institute CIRAD under the auspices of the Agroecology Transformative Partnership Platform (TPP). Funded by the CGIAR System Council, the initiative was implemented in eight countries from 2022 to 2024 – five in Africa (Burkina Faso, Kenya, Senegal, Tunisia, Zimbabwe), two in Asia (India, Lao PDR), and one in the Americas (Peru).

The Agroecology Initiative aimed to promote the application of contextually appropriate agroecological principles by farmers and communities in various contexts, with support from other food system actors. The Agroecology Initiative operates through so-called agroecological living landscapes (ALLs) in each country. The ALLs are geographically bound landscapes in which smallholder farmers, agroecology practitioners, researchers, and other development actors identify, test, and promote agroecological innovations across sectors and scales.

The handbook was developed under work package 1 (WP1) of the Agroecology Initiative, which focused on the co-creation of innovations in the ALLs. WP1 entailed two key components: establishing flourishing multi- stakeholder partnerships and collaboration in the designated ALLs (referred to as “ALL establishment”), and co- designing on-farm innovations. Both components were achieved through transdisciplinary co-design processes, in line with broader agroecology approaches and ontologies. The handbook aims to guide stakeholders in the ALLs in pursuing agroecological transformation processes through a participatory action research approach called the Vision-to-Action (V2A) process. The V2A process was piloted and implemented in all 11 ALLs established under the Agroecology Initiative with the support of country teams and partners.

The handbook was developed iteratively over the course of two years.
