Aim

This protocol aims to provide a guide for the collection of data and calculation of local enteric methane (CH4) emission factors (EF = CH4 kg/head/year) for cattle production systems in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) based on the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Tier 2 method (IPCC, 2006, 2019) and necessary additions to increase the accuracy of the Tier 2 EF. Tier 2 enteric CH4 estimations are essential for improved accuracy in reporting national greenhouse gas (GHG) inventories and developing locally suitable mitigation strategies in line with the Paris Climate Change Agreement (https://unfccc.int/most-requested/key-aspects-of-the-paris- agreement). The use of the Tier 2 method is more accurate than the Tier 1 method currently used by most LMICs. It incorporates local animal activity data and diet characteristics, in contrast to the Tier 1 method which uses activity data averaged at a continental level. The approach described in this protocol takes into account seasonal differences in feed availability, feed quality, and related variations in animal performance since there is limited inclusion of seasonality in Tier 2 IPCC 2006 and 2019 guidelines. The energy requirement calculations in this protocol are based on net energy equations described in the revised IPCC method of 2019 (IPCC, 2019), with the initial method described in the IPCC (2006). Some examples in published literature where the IPCC Tier 2 method has been used include Du Toit, Meissner, and Van Niekerk (2013), (Du Toit et al., 2013); Kouazounde et al. (2015), Wilkes, Wassie, Tadesse, et al. (2020), Wilkes, Wassie, Fraval, and van Dijk (2020), Wilkes, Pica-Ciamarra, and Opio (2020), Ndao, Moulin, Traoré, Diop, and Bocquier (2019) and Gurmu et al. (2024).

ILRI Manual 39 (https://hdl.handle.net/10568/109579) provided a technically sound methodological foundation to generate Tier 2 emission factors based on CSIRO’s (Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organization) metabolizable energy method (Marquardt, Ndung’u, Onyango, & Merbold, 2020). This protocol maintains the validity of the methodological approaches while replacing CSIRO-derived equations with IPCC equations, as this is internationally used to estimate livestock GHG inventories. This revision intends to provide a standardized operational procedure for data collection and emission factor calculation for cattle systems and beyond with the aim to enhance the comparability of results with emission factors widely used in national livestock GHG inventories. We plan to continue updating this protocol as more data becomes available.
ix
1. Introduction

It is necessary to have data at the level of the individual animal, herd management, as well as feed composition and quality to generate context-specific enteric CH4 emission factors (EFs; CH4 kg/head/year). The IPCC Tier 2 method estimates EF for different age and sex classes of cattle within different production systems (dairy and other cattle) as well as productivity levels (high vs low).

The key considerations for the Tier 2 method are the development of emission factors and the collection of detailed activity data. Animal activity data is used to calculate daily net energy (NE) requirements by the animals based on predefined equations described in the IPCC (2019) by adding equations from IPCC (2000) and NRC (2001) to improve the accuracy of EFs. The following net energy requirements need to be calculated depending on the age/sex class of the animal: Net energy for maintenance (NEm), net energy for travel (NEt), net energy for lactation (NEl), net energy for pregnancy (NEp), net energy for growth (NEg), net energy for mobilized energy (NEmob), and net energy for work (NEw). The daily NE requirements per animal are converted to daily gross energy intake (GEI) based on feed characteristics data and constants defined in the IPCC (2019) guidelines. The daily GEI is then converted to daily CH4 production (kg/d) using CH4 conversion factors (Ym; percentage of feed energy converted to CH4) provided by IPCC (2019). Seasonal EFs are calculated by multiplying daily CH4 output values by the number of days in each season. The seasonal CH4 values for each animal are summed across the year to obtain EF (CH4 kg/animal/year). Herd level average EF are then calculated by aggregating up the data from individual animals. The approach outlined herein is grounded in one-year-long field measurements of animal production and feed biomass availability and quality over time. These measurements are strategically distributed to capture seasonal variations. It is recommended to track animal movements, especially in situations where animals traverse significant distances in search of pasture and water, such as in a
pastoral setup.

This protocol outlines data collection at a sub-national level, often within a specific production system or administrative unit. The EFs derived at the subnational level can ultimately be aggregated at a national scale for inventory purposes. The following datasets are collected during subsequent farm visits over a one-year (12 months) period for calculating EFs:

● Animal activity data including live weight (LW), LW change (weight gain or loss), milk production and quality (fat, protein contents, etc.), movements in search of feed and water (i.e.; GPS data), and pregnancy (females), castration (males), and lactation status (mature females).
● Feed characteristics and feeding practices, including type and quality of feed and proportional amount in the diet on a dry matter (DM) basis, collected by season.
● Herd composition and entries/exits, including the number and age of animals, births, deaths, sales, and purchases.
● Number of work hours spent on cultivation of cropland and or threshing
Due to resource constraints, collecting data for an entire country or region (e.g. production system

within a country) is often not possible. Careful selection of sampling areas, or study sites, is important to ensure that the selected sites are representative and capture the diversity of the target region for which the EF should represent. Researchers are strongly encouraged to work with a statistician to design an optimal study that achieves their objectives. This includes identifying representative study sites and potential stratification needed, determining appropriate sample sizes, and ensuring transparency in the study's limitations and applicability.

To increase the usefulness of the data collected, especially towards inventory development at a national scale, it is important for researchers to be familiar with the livestock classifications used in the national inventory and to align their data collection with these classifications. This is not intended to limit researchers from developing more context-specific classifications, however, the livestock classes used should be compatible with the inventory classification. Subsections 1.1–1.4 below provide general guidelines for identifying an appropriate sampling design and approach, including selecting representative study sites and sample sizes for data collection.
1.1. Study design and approach

The study design and approach taken to sample farm herds for calculation of context-specific enteric methane (CH4) emission factors depends on the specific objectives of the study and the characteristics and diversity of the main cattle production systems in the target regions. Whether used to inform the development of a national inventory, to collect data for informing mitigation strategies in a specific local context or to provide answers to research questions for a study with a specific target population (e.g. smallholder-owned herds within a project study site), these considerations will guide the design and sampling plan. This is because the levels of stratification required and the sample size per stratum needed to capture the diversity will vary. When used to contribute to national inventory, the sample of farm herds need to represent the entire target region of interest, and also capture the variation in herd sizes and composition, feeding and other management practices, as well as any other relevant variables.

Due to the various potential uses of the data collected using this protocol, a wide range of study designs and approaches may be developed. For this guidance we provide a checklist of issues that researchers should consider and recommend working with a statistician to finalize the design and sampling plan. Documenting the study design and sampling processes in a protocol is an important step in the process to ensure clarity and reproducibility. The protocol provides an explanation of the applicability and potential for extrapolation of the results to the target region (e.g. production system) and beyond (e.g. country). It will also explain hierarchical structures and/or stratification variables in the study, the criteria used to select sites and farms, the sample sizes at each level and the methods used to calculate these. This information is critical for both summary statistics and formal statistical analysis, providing details on structure, clustering or weighting that needs to be incorporated into the models.
All studies have to work within the logistical constraints and resources available. While it might not be possible to cover the entire diversity in the target cattle production systems, the most
important requirement is to be honest and transparent in reporting to ensure that results are interpreted appropriately by others.
1.2. Study site selection

For a large-scale survey to calculate emission factors it may be possible to sample across the entire target region (e.g. production system, country) but in almost all cases resources are not available for this. In this situation, we must select sites within the larger target region from which to select the sample. The following considerations need to be made when settling on study sites within a larger administrative unit or production system:
Consideration 1: What is the target region that our estimates should apply to? (To what extent can I generalize my results?)

This means looking at what cattle production systems or other categorizations represent the target region. If prior classification of these systems exists, it should be used as the basis for selecting sites. Where such classifications are not available, expert opinion can guide the identification of the most prevalent systems. The study design should include sites that capture the most important production systems in terms of their contributions to GHG emissions in the national inventory.

Warning: If the study sites do not adequately represent the full variation in environments, it will be difficult to generalize results. For example, if there is significant contrast in the topography within the study site that is likely to influence feeding practices from one site to another, or if there is a substantial difference in herd sizes across the target region, the selection of study sites should capture this diversity. Therefore, establishing the classifications or seeking expert input must precede farm selection to ensure representativeness.
Consideration 2: What is the objective of the study?
The objectives of the study and target region guide both the site selection and the sampling frame for farm selection (see next section).

This protocol is primarily intended to generate context-specific enteric methane (CH4) emission factors, but the data may be captured within different types of projects. For instance, a project focused on characterizing the site or target region may align well with this guideline, but other project objectives may lead to narrower site selection.
For example:
• If the wider project aims to establish a baseline prior to interventions, site and farm selection criteria may not cover all production systems.

A project may focus only on specific households, for example herd sizes less than 10 animals, within the intervention scope, rather than representing the entire diversity of cattle-keeping households.

Projects comparing interventions may match criteria across those testing different interventions but still fail to capture all production systems. In such cases, it is important to clearly document the
specific target region that the study represents and care must be taken if the intention is to extrapolate those results to national enteric methane (CH4) emission factors.
Consideration 3: How many sites are needed?

There is no easy answer to this question. The sites should cover the diversity of the target region in terms of the categorizations, or strata, that have been defined (e.g. production systems, geographical area etc.) and the more replicates (number of sites) you have per category the better. However, resource constraints often limit the number of sites, making it more economical to survey more farms in fewer sites. Studies should aim to balance resource constraints with representativeness by maximizing the number of sites covered, especially in diverse target regions.
Checklist for selecting sites:

1. Target region: Clearly define the target region and study objectives to ensure the selected sites represent the dominant production systems in the region. Site selection need to be aligned with the most prevalent systems contributing to GHG emissions in the national inventory. Where prior classifications do not exist, expert opinion can guide the identification of representative systems.

2. Site diversity: Ensure that the selected sites capture the full diversity of the target area in terms of production systems, feed practices, and other relevant factors e.g. herd characteristics. The more diverse the sites, the more robust the findings. Where prior classifications do not exist, expert opinion should guide the identification of these systems.

3. Documenting site selection: Include information on the criteria used to select sites and households, the sample sizes at each level, and the methods used to calculate these. This documentation is necessary for any formal statistical analysis and future applicability of the study results. Also, including variance estimates used in arriving at sample sizes in a study protocol enhances transparency and provides a strong basis for the study design.
1.3. Sampling farms

Farms need to be carefully selected to ensure the heterogeneity of the target region is captured. If sites within the target region are required, rather than sampling across the whole region, then the selection of farms will be within the sites. Aim

This protocol is a guide for the collection of data and calculation of context-specific enteric methane (CH4) emission factors (EFs = CH4 kg/head/year) for small ruminants (sheep/goat) production systems in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) based on the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Tier 2 method (IPCC 2006 and 2019).

Tier 2 enteric CH4 estimations are essential for accurately reporting national greenhouse gas (GHG) inventories for livestock and developing locally suitable mitigation strategies in line with the Paris Climate Change Agreement (Wilkes et al. 2017). The use of Tier 2 approaches is more accurate than the Tier 1 methodology currently used by most LMICs. It incorporates local animal activity data and diet characteristics, in contrast to Tier 1 approaches which use activity data averaged at a continental level. The approach described in this protocol uses year-long farm level data accounting for seasonal variations in feed availability, feed quality, and related variations in animal performance. Unless otherwise stated, the energy requirement calculations are based on net energy equations described in the revised IPCC method of 2019 (IPCC., 2019); the initial method described in IPCC (2006). Some of the examples in literature where the IPCC Tier 2 method has been used to estimate enteric methane emissions from small ruminants include Wilkes et al. (2020a), Goopy et al. (2021) and Ndao et al. (2019).

The protocol is primarily intended for use in smallholder mixed crop-livestock systems but can be adapted for other production systems (e.g., pastoral). Where such variations are necessary, the changes required have been described in the manual.
1.0 Introduction
Climate change is increasingly becoming a global challenge, and agriculture is one of the sectors

contributing to greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Specifically, ruminants produce methane (CH4), a highly potent GHG that accounts for over 60% of agricultural GHG emissions (Gerber et al., 2013). Global efforts are being made to reduce these emissions and mitigate further global warming. Some of the specific action points recommended by the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) for reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions include, improving the accuracy of GHG emissions estimation, regularly reporting national GHG inventories, and documenting actions taken to reduce these emissions (UNFCCC, 2015). Most low- and middle- income countries (LMICs) still rely on the IPCC Tier 1 method for their GHG inventory reporting. Tier 1 is the most basic method, relying on enteric CH4 emission factors (EFs; kg CH₄/head/year) assigned to each continent without distinguishing between regions. This can result in over- or underestimations unless countries ensure their systems are accurately represented. Consequently, the use of Tier 1 is expected to result in high uncertainty in the emissions reported (IPCC 2019). Countries using the Tier 1 approach for their national inventory reporting, particularly where the livestock sector contributes a significant proportion of national emissions, are therefore encouraged to move to higher Tier methods, which are more accurate and allow for accounting of strategies to improve production and reduce emissions. This protocol provides a methodology for calculating emissions from small ruminant production using a Tier 2 approach, using the IPCC
method, which is an improvement over Tier 1.

To use the Tier 2 methodology, context-specific enteric CH₄ Emission Factors (EFs) that reflect the dominant livestock production systems within a country are required. This protocol outlines data collection at a sub-national level, within a specific production system or geographical regions. The EFs derived at the sub-national level can then be aggregated to a national scale for inventory purposes. The following datasets are collected during subsequent farm visits over a one-year (12 months) period for calculating EFs:

● Animal activity data including live weight (LW), LW change (gain or loss), milk production and quality, movements in search of feed and water (i.e.; GPS data), and pregnancy (mature female), castration (males), and lactation status (mature females).
● Feed characteristics and feeding practices, including type and quality of feed and proportional amount in the diet on a dry matter (DM) basis, collected by season.

● Flock/herd composition and entries/exits, including the number and age of animals, births, deaths, sales, and purchases. Where sheep are shorn, fleece yield data can be obtained from farmers' sale records or memory recall.

To calculate EFs, animal activity data1 is used first to estimate daily net energy (NE) requirements for each animal based on predefined equations described in the IPCC 2019. Where the provided equation is not appropriate, equations from other more context-relevant literature (e.g. ARC 2000, AFRC, 1993, 1998) are recommended.

The following net energy requirements are also calculated for each animal depending on the age and sex: Net energy for maintenance (NEm), net energy for travel (NEt), net energy for lactation (NEl), net energy for pregnancy (NEp), net energy for growth (NEg), net energy for mobilized energy (NEmobilized), and net energy for wool production (NEwool).

Daily Net Energy (NE) requirements for each animal are summed and converted into daily Gross Energy Intake (GEI) using feed characteristics and constants from the IPCC 2019 guidelines. GEI is then converted to daily methane (CH₄) production based on IPCC factors. Seasonal Emission Factors (EFs) are calculated by multiplying daily CH₄ output by the number of days in each season. The seasonal CH₄ values for each animal are summed to obtain EF (CH₄ kg/animal/year). The average EF at the flock/herd level is calculated by aggregating data from individual animals. Therefore, this flock/herd level EF can then be extrapolated up to the appropriate level (e.g. production system, country), adjusting for the sampling design, for emissions reporting.

Due to resource constraints, collecting data for an entire country or region (e.g. production system within a country) is often not possible. Careful selection of sampling areas, or study sites, is important to ensure that the selected sites are representative and capture the diversity of the target region for which the EF should represent. Researchers are strongly encouraged to work with a statistician to design an optimal study that achieves their objectives. This includes identifying representative study sites and potential stratification needed, determining appropriate sample sizes, and ensuring transparency in the study's limitations and applicability.

To increase the usefulness of the data collected, especially towards inventory development at a national scale, it is important for researchers to be familiar with the livestock classifications used in the national inventory and to align their data collection with these classifications. This is not intended to limit researchers from developing more context-specific classifications, however, the livestock classes used should be compatible with the inventory classification.

Subsections 1.1–1.4 provide general guidelines for identifying an appropriate sampling design and approach, including the selection of representative study sites and determining sample sizes for data collection. Subsections 1.5–1.7 outline guidelines on the data to be collected, quality considerations, and the materials required for data collection. Section 2 details the collection of animal characteristics data, while Section 3 focuses on liveweight data collection. Section 4 describes the collection of animal activity data. Sections 5 address milk yield and quality while Section 6 addresses biomass yield and quality data collection. Finally, Section 7 outlines the equations used to calculate

1.1 Study design and approach

The study design and approach taken to sample farm flocks/herds for calculation of context-specific enteric methane (CH4) emission factors depends on the specific objectives of the study and the characteristics and diversity of the main small ruminant production systems in the target regions. Whether used to inform the development of a national inventory, to collect data for informing mitigation strategies in a specific local context or to provide answers to research questions for a study with a specific target population (e.g. smallholder-owned flocks within a project study site), these considerations will guide the design and sampling plan. This is because the levels of stratification required and the sample size per stratum needed to capture the diversity will vary. When used to contribute to national inventory, the sample of farm flocks/herds need to represent the entire target region of interest, and also capture the variation in flock/herd sizes and composition, feeding and other management practices, as well as any other relevant variables.

Due to the various potential uses of the data collected using this protocol, a wide range of study designs and approaches may be developed. For this guidance we provide a checklist of issues that researchers should consider and recommend working with a statistician to finalize the design and sampling plan. Documenting the study design and sampling processes in a protocol is an important step in the process to ensure clarity and reproducibility. The protocol provides an explanation of the applicability and potential for extrapolation of the results to the target region (e.g. production system) and beyond (e.g. country). It will also explain hierarchical structures and/or stratification variables in the study, the criteria used to select sites and farms, the sample sizes at each level and the methods used to calculate these. This information is critical for both summary statistics and formal statistical analysis, providing details on structure, clustering or weighting that needs to be incorporated into the models.

All studies have to work within the logistical constraints and resources available. While it might not be possible to cover the entire diversity in the target small ruminant production systems, the most important requirement is to be honest and transparent in reporting to ensure that results are interpreted appropriately by others.
1.2 Site selection

For a large-scale survey to calculate emission factors it may be possible to sample across the entire target region (e.g. production system, country) but in almost all cases resources are not available for this. Where it is not possible to do this, sites within the target region should be selected, from which the sample of flocks/herds and animals will then be chosen. The following considerations should be made when selecting sites within a larger target region:
Consideration 1: What is the target region that our estimates should apply to? (To what extent can I generalize my results?)

This means looking at what small ruminant production systems or other categorizations represent the target region and ensuring the sites represent this diversity. If prior classification of these systems exists, it should be used as the basis for selecting sites. Where such classifications are not available, expert opinion can guide the identification of the most prevalent systems. For calculating GHG emissions for the national inventory care must be taken to ensure that the sites capture all the relevant production systems within a country.

Establishing the potential categorizations within the target region must precede site and farm selection to ensure representativeness. Categorization may be used to stratify the sample (e.g. different production systems) or used to balance the sample (e.g. ensure the variation in flock/herd sizes is captured).

Warning: If the chosen sites do not adequately represent the full variation in environments, it will be difficult to extrapolate results to national level. For example, if there are significant differences in feeding practices across the target region then sites must be chosen to capture this diversity. If strata have been identified (e.g. production system) then sites need to be selected within each stratum.
Consideration 2: What is the objective of the study?

This guideline is primarily intended to generate context-specific enteric methane (CH4) emission factors for region or country-level reporting, but these data may also be captured within different types of projects.

For example, a project focused on characterizing the site or target region may align well with this guideline, but other project objectives may lead to narrower site selection. If the wider project aims to establish a baseline prior to interventions, site and farm selection criteria may not cover the diversity in the target region. Alternatively, a project may focus only on specific farm flock/herd types, for example smallholder farms having less than 10 animals, rather than representing the entire diversity of small ruminant-keeping households. Projects comparing interventions may match criteria across those testing different interventions but still fail to capture all production systems. In such cases, it is important to clearly document the specific target region that the study represents, and care must be taken if the intention is to extrapolate those results to context-specific enteric methane (CH4) emission factors.
Consideration 3: How many sites are needed?

Sorry, there is no easy answer to this question. The sites should cover the diversity of the target region in terms of the categorizations, or strata, that have been defined (e.g. production systems, geographical area etc.) and the more replicates (number of sites) you have per category the better. However, resource constraints often limit the number of sites, making it more economical to
survey more farms in fewer sites. Studies should aim to balance resource constraints with representativeness by maximizing the number of sites covered, especially in diverse target regions.
Checklist for Selecting Sites:

1. Target Region: Clearly define the target region and study objectives to ensure the selected sites represent the relevant production systems. Site selection needs to be aligned with the most prevalent systems contributing to GHG emissions in the national inventory. Where prior categorizations do not exist, expert opinion can guide the identification of representative systems.

2. Site Diversity: Ensure that the selected sites capture the full diversity of the target region in terms of production systems, feed practices, and other relevant variables e.g. flock characteristics. The more diverse the sites, the more robust the findings and potential for scaling the EF.

3. Documenting Site Selection: Include information on the criteria used to select sites and farms, the sample sizes at each level, and the methods used to calculate these. This documentation is necessary for any formal statistical analysis and future scaling of results. Also, including EF average and variance estimates used in arriving at sample sizes in a study protocol enhances transparency.
1.3 Sampling farms

Farms need to be carefully selected to ensure the heterogeneity of the target region is captured. If sites within the target region are required, rather than sampling across the whole region, then the selection of farms will be within the sites. Various sampling methods can be employed, and complex studies often involve a combination of approaches. Below are common methods and their applications:

• Completely random sampling: Randomly select farms within the target region or site. This method is ideal as it ensures distribution of the sample across the whole area but is usually not achievable with available resources.

• Stratified random sampling: This is similar to completely random sampling but in this case randomly select households within each level of the stratification variable (e.g., production system, geographical area etc.). This method must be applied when EFs need to be estimated for each stratum rather than across the entire target region.
o Emission factors often vary across production systems, so stratifying by this variable is crucial when multiple systems need to be evaluated.

o For other important variables which influence emission factors, such as flock size or management practices, then the random sampling should ensure that they are represented proportionally to their presence in the system (e.g. if 30% of all flocks are less than 30 animals then 30% of all sampled flocks/herds should be the same). If there is a specific interest in estimating EFs at different levels of these variables (e.g. zero-grazing
versus pasture grazing animals) then this should be included as a stratification variable.
Note that in studies designed to compare interventions, each intervention group would constitute a separate stratum.

Abstract

Zambia is one of the most vulnerable countries in the world to climate change. Smallholder tilapia farmers in the country are particularly vulnerable, as they lack the expertise and resources to implement mitigation strategies in response to adverse weather conditions. Among climate-driven environmental stressors, such as water supply and temperature variability, temperature can lead to loss of production and low growth among tilapia farmers in the short term. As such, it is important to observe and manage fluctuations in pond temperature beyond favorable production conditions.

The AICCRA project developed an air-water temperature relationship algorithm used to forecast pond water temperatures for integration with the data hub of the Intelligent Agricultural Systems Advisory Tool (iSAT) and an early temperature warning decision tree matrix. The project team will develop the matrix into a dashboard based on input data and water quality parameter thresholds for critical scenarios for tilapia and catfish (Clarius Gariepinus). When predicted temperatures approach their thresholds, this activates a color-coded alarm corresponding with a specific action protocol to regulate pond temperatures. The purpose is to mitigate the impact of high-risk (24°C for minimum and 32°C for maximum) and emergency (12°C for minimum and 40°C for maximum) temperature scenarios on cultured stock.

In each case, the messages include information about the current temperature, predictions, the impact of temperature on fish health, monitoring parameters, monitoring frequency and mitigation steps. The prediction tool’s early warning system is based on thresholds derived from mean pond temperatures. It is, however, important to note that normal pond temperatures between 12°C and 18°C are not optimal for growth and feed conversion efficiency in tilapia. Future work will focus on developing priority, low-cost pond monitoring equipment for temperature, oxygen levels and pH that can store data in an online database. Additionally, hydrological data for surface water and pond water replacement rates needs to be integrated.

1. Introduction

The largest number of small-scale farmers in Zambia are found in Northern and North-Western provinces (Figure 1), where knowledge transfer largely stimulates sector growth (DOF 2015; Genschick et al. 2017; Kaminski et al. 2018). However, some wetlands of international importance, such as the Bangweulu, Lake Tanganyika and Lake Mweru-wa-Ntipa wetlands, are located in Northern and Luapula provinces and need protection against unnecessary impact from aquaculture (Hoevenaars and Ng’ambi 2019). In Northern Province, culturing Nile tilapia is not allowed, as they are able to escape from the facilities and disturb the ecology of native tilapia species (Bhole 2014). Best management practices promote the culture of green-headed tilapia (Oreochromis macrochir), Tanganyika bream (O. tanganicae) and red-breasted tilapia (Coptodon rendalli) in Luapula, Northern and Muchinga provinces (Hoevenaars and Ng´ambi 2019). From site visits, species farmed in Northern and Luapula provinces include red-breasted tilapia, green-headed tilapia and banded tilapia (Tilapia sparmanii).

The National Adaptation Programme of Action on Climate Change (2007) promotes the development of aquaculture, while the National Aquaculture Development Plan of Zambia has identified aquaculture zones in the north as target development areas because of their water availability (MOAL and FAO 2015). Lack of technical skills and quality inputs such as fingerlings and feed are some of the main challenges in promoting smallholder growth (Avadí et al. 2022). Farmers learn aquaculture practices from WorldFish workshops and from each other. With adequate support, some farms (such as Hopeways) have developed into hatcheries to further support income and obtain a beneficial position in the value chain. Smallholder farmers often lack the resources and information needed to manage environmental variables that affect their fish culture systems. As one of the most vulnerable countries to climate change (Eckstein et al. 2018), Zambia was classified as being at high to extreme risk in the 2018 Climate Change Vulnerability Index (Maplecroft 2017). The change in temperature in Zambia is projected to increase 1.9°C by 2050, while rainfall will decrease, with the northern region experiencing the least change in water availability (Hamududu et al. 2020). Climate-related weather changes, such as flooding and insufficient rain, lead to dried up ponds and compromised water quality, adversely affecting aquaculture and fisheries in the rural Northern and Luapula provinces.

Drought, flooding and cold temperatures in winter are key environmental risks, while high temperatures pose an occasional risk. Not all farms measure their pond temperature, and frequency is low among those that do. Additionally, farmers have limited knowledge of the physiological and ecological responses of fish and culture systems to temperature changes. However, farmers believe drought poses the highest risk, as its impacts have increased in recent years along with low oxygen measurements and increasingly stressed fish. Climate-smart priority activities include harvesting rainwater (GIZ 2020), while some farmers have indicated that they intend to drill boreholes and pump water during times of drought. Technology and seasonal environmental monitoring will, however, provide more reliable information for implementing mitigation strategies.

Aquaculture farmers must become more resilient and responsive to climate change by planning for and reacting quickly to adverse weather events and changes in environmental trends. The National Sustainable Development Goals promote climate-smart agriculture practices and enhance investment in water capture. Most farmers have access to surface water streams and springs that flow year-round, as well as community wells. However, drilling boreholes equipped with solar pumps would serve as a long-term intervention to provide a reliable water source. It is also possible to store surface water upstream for water replacement purposes for both operation and emergency protocols. Additionally, readily available pond fertilizer can improve overall pond health and

nutrient cycling, while integrating aquaculture with small livestock, particularly chickens, provides fertilizer for culture ponds.

Under the World Bank-funded Accelerating Impact of CGIAR Climate Research for Africa project, WorldFish leads the work on integrated aquaculture–agriculture systems to promote resilience to climate change for smallholder fish farmers in Northern and Luapula provinces. Small-scale aquaculture in the north practices integrated farming systems by combining fish farming with crop and livestock farming to obtain optimal productivity in land use, despite unfavorable seasonal weather conditions (ACF and FSRP 2009). Modeling optimization strategies of land use outputs will improve production viability to ensure sustainable livelihoods for smaller-scale commercial farms.

Climate-smart farming relies on accurate environmental information and temperature predictions to proactively implement mitigation measures to improve the resilience of farming operations to adverse events. Continuous monitoring will also ensure that farming systems recover fully from environmental challenges by learning how long to apply mitigation measures.

This report describes the technical approach and results of WorldFish’s journey toward providing climate-smart information systems (CIS) for aquaculture by developing a temperature-based, early warning alert system for fish farmers in Zambia. WorldFish is working toward improving access to CIS for farmers in Northern and Luapula provinces. Specifically, WorldFish aims to integrate aquaculture climate advisories into iSAT, which is managed by the International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics.
This key objectives of the project were as follows:
• Develop an air–water temperature relationship algorithm to forecast pond water temperatures using air temperature trend data.
• Develop a decision support tree that translates risk scenarios for water temperature forecasts into an early warning alert system with associated mitigation measures.
Integrate the alert system into iSAT with the ability to send real-time alerts to farmers in Northern and Luapula provinces.
• Optimize environmental monitoring protocols and equipment, and conceptualize medium- and long-term interventions needed to build resilience to climate change trends.

Once piloted in Northern and Luapula provinces, WorldFish will update the advisory to include other fish species, such as catfish (Clarius Gariepinus), and then upscaled to other provinces in Zambia and Malawi. Social inclusion of rural women was a key consideration during the development of the advisory tool, particularly in overcoming known barriers to access technology and technical knowledge by incorporating local languages (Kwaku et al. 2023). Advisories will be available both on smartphones and via USSD protocols to allow those without smartphones to access the advisories.

2. Climate-smart information systems for fish farmers in Zambia and climate-smart
agriculture

CIS use technology to provide farmers with climate-related information to promote resilience to climate change. They integrate environmental information with enhanced productivity, adaptive capacity to climate variability and risk management. CIS collect weather data from various sources to illustrate patterns and predict changes, and they communicate (in advance) mitigation measures linked to specific environmental scenarios. Therefore, historical and real-time data are implemented in models that are continuously optimized to support informed decision-making. Empirical models are site-specific and serve as predictive tools when applied to situations that resemble the input parameters for which the model was developed.

Models have been used to analyze data on aquaculture ponds, describe pond dynamics and develop decision support systems for management purposes (Piedrahita et al. 1997). Decision tree models provide a structured and systematic approach to decision-making based on the analysis of historical climatic conditions. Through WorldFish, the aim of the current project is to develop an algorithm of the air–water temperature relationship to link the decision tree to the iSAT decision support system. Existing datasets of past climate information and aquaculture pond monitoring data from four pilot monitoring farms (provided by WorldFish) were analyzed by the team at the University of Stellenbosch to estimate trends for the relationship between water temperature and air temperature.

3. Environmental tolerances and monitoring
3.1. Thermal tolerances

The exotic Nile tilapia (O. Niloticus) (farmed in the southern provinces), three-spotted bream (O. andersonii), green-headed bream (O. macrochir), red-breasted bream (C. rendalli) and Tanganyika bream (O. tanganicae) all have an optimal thermal temperature within 24°C–32°C (Table 1). Nile tilapia, three-spotted bream and Tanganyika bream are fast-growing and omnivorous, and they tolerate a wide range of environmental conditions and temperatures between 8°C and 42°C, though Tanganyika bream does not tolerate cold (Hoevenaars and Ng’ambi 2019). Their upper lethal limits are near 42°C (Table 1), and their lower lethal limits are approximately 8°C–12°C.

Several authors have summarized the general influence of temperature, including Balarin and Haller (1982), Chervinski (1982), Philippart and Ruwet (1982) and Wohlfarth and Hulate (1983). The preferred range is between 28°C and 35°C, with no reproduction occurring below 20°C and poor growth between 10°C and 15°C. Temperature effects can also be reflected in reduced productivity at altitudes up to 1000 m. When fish are fed to satiation, growth at the preferred temperature is typically three times greater than at 22°C. Genetic selection for heat-tolerant tilapia strains should be considered in ecoregions with a high risk for warm temperature stress.
3.2. Monitoring abiotic (water quality) and biotic (fish stress) factors

Ponds are carefully managed for a balanced environment between algae, fish, microbes and nutrient cycling, so it is important to monitor water quality. Phytoplankton and nitrifying bacteria remove toxic ammonia from the water, while bacteria convert organic nutrients into inorganic forms (such as nitrogen, phosphorus and carbon) through a mineralization process that allows phytoplankton to absorb them. Nitrifying bacteria derive nitrate from ammonia, while denitrifying bacteria convert nitrate to nitrogen gas under anaerobic conditions. Rural pond farmers lack appropriate monitoring equipment and methods, and they often do not monitor critical variables, such as ammonia. This leaves them at risk for missing a water quality scenario (Table 2) that may impair fish growth (and thus production) or result in loss of stock because of fish deaths. Temperature fluctuations beyond the optimal thermal range cause stress, which is exacerbated by high stocking densities and other environmental stressors, such as pH, ammonia and low dissolved oxygen (DO), ultimately impacting production performance. Sufficient DO levels of more than 5 mg/L optimize the thermal growth coefficient in tilapia when food macronutrient levels are adequate (Mengistu et al. 2020). Aeration influences DO levels, so it is important that farmers manage it in parallel with temperature, as the partial pressure capacity of DO decreases with rising temperatures. Fish will come to the water’s surface to gasp for air when oxygen levels are low (less than 2 mg/L), especially in the early morning. Temperature drives the demand for oxygen, but tilapia is relatively resilient to limited oxygen by obtaining it at the air-water interface (Lowe-McConnell 1957).

From site visits to smallholder farms in the northern provinces, it was evident that Hopeways monitors water quality, including temperature, conductivity, pH, DO and total dissolved solids, twice daily (morning and afternoon), while the other farms do not. Three other farms, which were not visited, collect water quality data.
There are several tools and devices available for recording water temperature in pond aquaculture systems.

There are traditional thermometers that are simple and inexpensive, thermometers that float on the surface of the water and submersible thermometers that are lowered into the pond at different depths. Data loggers are another option, as are wireless sensors, which farmers can deploy in different areas of the pond to transmit temperature data to a central receiver or a computer system. All of these options provide farmers with real- time monitoring, and farmers can integrate them into automated systems for better control or to implement mitigation strategies. These actions include adjusting feed inputs, modifying aeration systems, changing water circulation or taking any necessary steps to improve the water quality and conditions in the pond. Through training and international support, rural farmers already implement climate mitigation strategies. During drought, farmers will relocate fish to ponds that retain water better, often because of recharge from groundwater. Additionally, farmers aim for a minimum pond depth of 1.5–2 m to help regulate the temperature.

4. Environmental mitigation strategies
4.1. Elevated temperatures

During extended hot periods, farmers typically observe the response of their fish to factors such as reduced DO and, if needed, will relocate their fish to other ponds. Additionally, tank water flow rates increase during times when the temperature appears to affect the fish (Table 2). During elevated temperatures, farmers need to lower both the stocking density and feeding rate, as fish eat less when they are stressed. Typically, adult fish are fed twice daily, while small fish are fed four times per day to maintain a positive energy balance to invest metabolic energy in growth (Riche et al. 2004), while optimal water temperature promotes feed conversion efficiency (Mengistu et al. 2020).

To buffer and control warm water temperatures, farmers can optimize shading to reduce the amount of direct sunlight on the water surface, use aerators or sprayers to increase water circulation within the pond, or add ice during emergencies.
4.2. Cold temperatures

During extended cold periods, farmers must take close note of the well-being and decreased growth of their fish and harvest or relocate their fish to ponds where they seem to perform better. When water temperature drops below 20°C, tilapia eat less, and feeding stops entirely at about 16°C (Balarin and Haller 1982; Chervinski 1982). To guard against cold temperatures, farmers should consider the following factors:
• Choose a location for your tilapia pond with maximum sunlight exposure. This helps warm the water naturally during the day.
Insulate the sides and bottom of the pond to reduce heat loss. Use materials like expanded polystyrene foam or geotextile liners to provide thermal insulation.
• Consider using supplemental heating techniques during extreme cold periods. If needed, use electric heaters or solar-powered heaters to raise the water temperature.
• Constructing a greenhouse can create a microclimate that traps heat and protects the pond.

For mitigation strategies during high-risk scenarios, farmers can flush their ponds with warm water and increase the mixing of warmer water, move fish to ponds with more sunlight, or reduce feeds (Table 2).

5. The relationship between air temperature and pond water temperature

Most smallholder farms do not use sophisticated water quality monitoring equipment and can likely only access air temperature information from local weather stations. Several factors can influence the relationship between air temperature and pond temperature, including sunlight exposure, wind speed, pond depth and the presence of vegetation or other thermal regulators. However, in general, some patterns can help understand their relationship. One is the lag effect, where water has a higher heat capacity than air, making it longer to heat up or cool down. Another is solar radiation, where the sun’s energy directly warms the surface of the pond. Wind can also affect the rate of heat exchange between the air and water. In shallow ponds, the water temperature is more likely to closely follow variations in air temperature.

6. Decision support tool

We developed a decision support matrix/tool by analyzing existing knowledge of the temperature thresholds for tilapia, as well as the potential effects of temperature on other water quality variables (Figure 2). A decision matrix tool provides decision-making support in pond management strategies in response to adverse weather conditions. There are various strategies available for managing pond temperatures, and each has its advantages and disadvantages.

The decision matrix was developed using python language, and it can be replicated with other programming languages. The main components of a decision tree model are root or decision nodes, chance nodes, representing one of the possible choices available at that point in the tree structure, and the result of a combination of decisions or events. The decision matrix tool entails a combination of conditional statements that generate different warning messages based on a predictive pond temperature value. It evaluates the value of the predicted pond temperature against predefined temperature levels and, depending on the result, prints different messages with instructions for monitoring and mitigation.

Tables 1 and 2 employ four levels of predefined temperatures (12°C, 24°C, 32°C and 40°C) to classify the risk levels of pond temperature alert messages. These messages are broadly classified into three categories: (1) high risk, (2) emergency and (3) normal (Figure 2). The specific temperature levels and response strategies may vary depending on the aquaculture setup and the species being cultivated. In each case, the messages include information about the current temperature, predictions, the impact of temperature on fish health, monitoring parameters, monitoring frequency and mitigation steps.

For more resilient livelihoods and greater food security in Zambia, it is vital that increased demand for fish is met by increased production through methods such as aquaculture, and that fish production methods are sustainable. Aquaculture refers to the farming of fish and other aquatic animals. Cecilia Zulu is one of a new cohort of women in Zambia now embarking on aquaculture. She proudly shows off her two fishponds, which total 560 square metres. My husband began the aquaculture project, but as time passed, he handed over the operations and management to me, Cecilia explains. Business accelerators for aquaculture SMEs Cecilia received capacity development and training on aquaculture production through an Aquaculture Accelerator led by WorldFish, a CGIAR research center that leads scientific research on aquatic food systems. The training that Cecilia enjoyed focused particularly on climate-smart elements of aquaculture, which has helped her to be an effective and efficient fish farmer in a fast changing climate in Southern Africa. Climate-smart aquaculture makes use of climatic information to plan aquaculture production. For effective production, aquaculture farmers must understand changes in climate variability, which impacts the timing of cycles of production. With climate-smart aquaculture, farmers can select sites for fishpond construction, design fishponds for flood or drought-prone area, select appropriate fish species to stock, time fish harvests and control water quality in the fishpond. In her training, Cecilia and other fish farmers like her learned about key concepts in relation to the weather, climate change, resilience, mitigation, vulnerability, gender, and the importance of integrating both aquaculture and agriculture systems in her community. Complementary extension information on fish farming, as well as continued mentorship and coaching, is provided through the private sector and government. Short impact statement

The aquaculture practices among smallholder fish farmers in Northern Zambia are undergoing a remarkable transformation driven by climate smart aquaculture solutions implemented by the AICCRA project in the region. For a long time, fish farmers have faced challenges of low temperatures, erratic rainfall pattern affecting water quality in the fishponds, limited access to fingerlings and knowledge on land-based aquaculture best management practices in the face of climate change.

Today, thanks to the AICCRA project, smallholder fish farmers are embracing innovative approaches to aquaculture. The project has not only improved their farming techniques but also significantly enhanced their livelihoods by empowering them with climate-smart aquaculture technologies; strengthening their resilience through access to important weather information; and linked them to aquaculture markets to sustainably improve income and food security and quality of life. The project is transforming the way fish farming is practiced in the region, creating more resilient communities and sustainable farming systems.
Introduction

AICCRA Zambia is scaling access to and use of climate-smart services and innovations to help Zambian farmers and communities safeguard their livelihoods in the face of climate change. AICCRA is Accelerating Impacts of CGIAR Climate Research for Africa. Climate change is threatening Zambia’s aquaculture and livestock systems, impacting agriculture businesses and undermining livelihoods. It is increasingly urgent for fish farmers in Zambia to be able to anticipate climate-related events and take appropriate preventative actions. AICCRA Zambia is working with

local and national partners to scale actionable climate information, de-risk investments into agribusinesses and boost the knowledge and use of climate-smart aquaculture technologies which promote gender and social inclusion.
Intervention description

Since 2021, the International Water Management Institute (IWMI), in partnership with WorldFish and other local organizations, has collaborated with SMEs in the aquaculture value chain to scale actionable climate-smart agriculture (CSA) and climate information services (CIS) innovation bundles. These efforts aim to enhance smallholder farmers’ water and food security while building resilience to climate shocks.

The project partners with the private sector to co-design and implement accelerator grants for startups/SMEs, reducing the risks associated with scaling innovations. This approach enhances the climate resilience of value chains, promotes social inclusion, and ensures the sustainable use of land and water resources. Under the aquaculture innovation bundle, six SMEs in the aquaculture sector received accelerator grants to scale the adoption of climate-smart aquaculture among smallholder fish farmers. These SMEs are: EUNIMOS Investment, Kasakalabwe Multipurpose Cooperative Society, Kasama Arts Theatre, Triple Blessings Centre, HopeWays, and ADSEK Enterprise Limited (https://hdl.handle.net/10568/117963).

Each SME offers unique services within the aquaculture value chain, operating under a business model that integrates CSA and CIS extension services. The ultimate goal is to empower farmers to adopt climate-smart technologies, increasing their resilience and productivity while creating demand for SME products, including seeds, feed, and agro-veterinary supplies.
To facilitate the adoption of climate-smart technologies, the project implemented several interventions:

• Technical Support and Capacity Building WorldFish provided technical support to SMEs, enhancing their capacity to deliver high-quality CSA and CIS extension services. See https://hdl.handle.net/20.500.12348/5596. Training sessions focused on integrated fish- livestock systems and Gender Equality and Social Inclusion (GESI). These ensured that CSA approaches and CIS access addressed and reduced gender and social disparities, empowering women, girls, and disadvantaged groups. https://hdl.handle.net/20.500.12348/5596. See

• Multistakeholder Platforms. A multistakeholder platform was established to promote integrated aquaculture-agriculture systems. This platform facilitated information sharing and strengthened linkages between private sector actors and smallholder farmers (https://hdl.handle.net/10568/127029).

• Radio Programs and Roadshows. The SMEs conducted joint live radio programs on local stations such as Yangeni and Mano. These programs disseminated CSA and CIS information to smallholder farmers. Additionally, roadshows showcased everyday
challenges farmers face, such as floods, droughts, and pests, while providing practical solutions and contact information for SMEs.

• Digital Information Sharing. The partnership created a WhatsApp group to enhance information dissemination. Managed by SMEs, the group includes members from the Zambia Meteorological Department (ZMD), Extension officers from the department of fisheries, WorldFish, and lead farmers. Daily weather bulletins from ZMD are shared directly with farmers, helping them plan their farming activities effectively.
Results of the intervention

In Northern Zambia, the livelihoods of smallholder fish farmers are being transformed through innovative climate-smart aquaculture solutions introduced in partnership with SMEs engaged by the AICCRA project. Six SMEs were enlisted to scale the adoption of these technologies in the region: EUNIMOS Investment, HopeWays, Kasakalabwe Multipurpose Cooperative Society, Kasama Arts Theatre, Triple Blessings Centre, and ADSEK Enterprise Limited.

Over 15,700 farmers have adopted sustainable farming practices, gained access to millions of fingerlings, and secured fish output markets offering premium prices for farmed fish. The project has introduced practical solutions to mitigate the impacts of climate change, such as integrated farming systems. Farmers now combine aquaculture with livestock and crop farming, utilizing livestock droppings as pond fertilizers to enhance phytoplankton growth, which improves fish nutrition and increases oxygen levels in the ponds.

Furthermore, farmers have adopted the design of modern fishponds capable of withstanding flooding and drought, significantly reducing fish losses during climate shocks. Before this initiative, farmers frequently lost fish during flash floods as they escaped from poorly designed ponds. Similarly, erratic rainfall caused water levels to drop, leading to fishponds drying out and forcing farmers to harvest fish prematurely, often before they reached market size. Focus Group Discussions with the beneficiaries revealed that farmers now receive timely weather information updates from the Zambia Metrological Department (ZMD) via WhatsApp and radio, helping them plan farming activities more effectively.
The farmers shared experiences, explaining how the training he received transformed the fish farming practices:

“It has helped me reduce fish losses and improve water management and water quality in the fishponds. I use the information to prepare my fishponds, so they don’t get flooded, preventing fish from escaping. My ponds are designed with an inlet that allows water to enter and an outlet to drain excess water. When there’s too much rainfall, I use the outlet to prevent overflow.”

“In cases of inadequate rainfall, when water levels go down, I dig deeper into the water source to channel more water into the ponds using the drainage system connected to each inlet. This process requires climate information on early warning systems to help me prepare when to drain the fishpond and when to increase water flow from the underground source using the drainage.” Paul explains the process for managing water quality and water levels in his fishponds.

“Before this initiative, we didn’t pay attention to weather forecasts, now, farmers rely on this information to make decisions, reducing climate risks.” Collins explains improvements made in using climate information.

Furthermore, discussions with the farmers revealed that the AICCCRA project has brought tangible improvements to the lives of smallholder farmers. The farmers have stressed that they have seen notable changes in their aquaculture operations and incomes. While precise income figures are difficult to capture due to partial harvest practices, farmers report significant improvements in their livelihoods.

“Our knowledge has advanced; we know about fishpond modern fishpond construction, temperature monitoring, water quality, feeding practices, and biosecurity. This has helped us improve our farming practices to optimise production amid climate shocks, ensuring food security and a steady income.” Florence explains how access to enhanced knowledge on aquaculture has helped to improve farming practices and yield.
“Previously, our management was very poor,” said Nathan. “We used to lose a lot of fish, but now we have seen improvements. The fish grow, and we don’t lose as many.”

Farmers acknowledged the broader socioeconomic benefits of their improved practices. With better yields, households can address urgent household needs, from school uniforms for their children to medical expenses, enhancing their overall quality of life.

Introduction

Oat (Avena sativa L.) is an annual crop used for human food and livestock feed worldwide. Oats serve as an annual forage grass and are greatly valued for their nutrient-rich grain, robust adaptability, high yield, and large market demand. As compared to the other crops, oat is broadly adapted to marginal environments with low fertility soils and tolerates acidic soils. Oat mostly grows in cool moist climates at temperatures ranging from 5 to 26°C and rainfall over 500 mm. Oats are important in feeding ruminant animals for their high dry matter production and low cost. Oats are very palatable (soft), good in protein compared to other grains and considered excellent feed for all livestock.

Oat grains are rich in beneficial nutrients like protein, starch, unsaturated fatty acids, soluble dietary fiber fat-soluble vitamins and -glucans. The outer layer of tissues of the oat grain called bran is rich in minerals, vitamins and antioxidants. Among the β cereals, oat is valued as a low-cost protein source and has higher protein concentration than other cereals which provides a considerable nutritive advantage. Oat produces an abundance of excellent fodder when other succulent better-quality fodders are scarce, and it can be fed green, and the surplus converted into hay and silage for use during the scarcity period. Among other cultivated forage crops, oat is widely utilized in the highland farming systems of Ethiopia. The introduced varieties of oat are mixed up and conceived as one variety by farmers, they do not utilize different oat varieties for various purposes or farming practices, such as different varieties for different soil types, early or late-maturing varieties, seed sizes and forage types.

Common vetch (Vicia sativa) is an important annual forage legume, which is grown both in Ethiopia and in other parts of the world. In most highlands smallholder crop- livestock farmers sow common vetch mixed with oat for livestock feed. Most of the locally available vetch cultivars cannot produce seed under frost prone areas of highland conditions. However, the Vicia species found elsewhere in the world exhibit considerable diversity, and this could be explored to find seed-producing material suitable for the frost prone areas of Ethiopia. Therefore, the oat and vetch trials were conducted to select best-bet; high grain and biomass yielder; and disease and pest resistance oat and vetch accessions for frost prone areas.
Description of the Study Area
The experiments were conducted at Debre Birhan Agricultural Research Center (DBARC) during the 2024 main cropping season. The main station of DBARC is located

The average annual temperature is 13°C with mean minimum and maximum of 6°C and 20°C, respectively. The mean annual rainfall of the area is 897.8 mm. The center soil type is also classified as vertisols and clay loam textural class. The area is also characterized by mixed crop-livestock production and dairying is the major component of the production system.
Experimental Design and Layout

A total of 135 oat accessions sourced from the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) genebank and Ethiopian Biodiversity Institute (EBI) were used for the screening trial. The experiment was designed in a simple observation with two rows, 50 cm spacing between plots, and 20 cm between rows. Planting was done by hand drilling at a seed rate of 100 kg/ha. Fertilizer was applied at a rate of 150 Kg ha-1 Urea and 162 Kg ha-1 NPSB uniformly for each plot. Hand weeding was practiced two times to control grass and legume weeds.

Sixty accessions sourced from ILRI genebank and DBARC were used for the study. Seed, fertilizers and other agronomic practices were applied as per the recommendation for vetch. The experimental design was simple observation with two rows, 0.5 m spacing between the plot and 30 cm between the rows.
Data Collection and Measurement

Data on emergency date, plot coverage, days to first heading, days to 50% heading, numbers of tiller per plants, leaf length, leaf width, leaf length per plant and reactions to major diseases and pest data were taken. The agronomic data on the date of harvesting, plant height, leaf to stem ratio, total fresh weight, sample fresh weight, sample dry weight, days to maturity and grain yield were collected.

The Sustainable Intensification of Mixed Farming Systems Initiative aims to provide equitable, transformative pathways for improved livelihoods of actors in mixed farming systems through sustainable intensification within target agroecologies and socio-economic settings.

Through action research and development partnerships, the Initiative will improve smallholder farmers' resilience to weather-induced shocks, provide a more stable income and significant benefits in welfare, and enhance social justice and inclusion for 13 million people by 2030.

Activities will be implemented in six focus countries globally representing diverse mixed farming systems as follows: Ghana (cereal–root crop mixed), Ethiopia (highland mixed), Malawi: (maize mixed), Bangladesh (rice mixed), Nepal (highland mixed), and Lao People's Democratic Republic (upland intensive mixed/ highland extensive mixed).

Introduction

Feed is one of the major production inputs that affect the production and productivity of Livestock. In many parts of Ethiopia, animals are kept on poorquality natural pasture and crop residues. However, the contribution of natural pasture was declining from time to time as a result of the expansion of crop production, poor management and seasonal availability. One of the possible options to alleviate feed shortage is introducing and utilizing improved forage crops for the given production system. Improved forage crops species are very important because of their high biomass yield and good nutritional value.

Adaptation trials of selected grass and legume forage varieties are currently underway at various MFS sites across Ethiopia. This report highlights the progress of the adaptation trials conducted at the MFS site in the North Shewa Zone of the Amhara region. Oat and vetch varieties have been chosen to diversify and intensify the mixed farming systems and provide food, feed and other products and services in the North Shewa frost prone and high-altitude areas.

Oats are an annual grass, cultivated in the highlands of Ethiopia primarily under rain- fed conditions for grain, forage and fodder. They provide high yields of palatable, moderate-quality forage, mainly for sheep, dry dairy cows, beef cattle and horses. Oats are the preferred food/feed crop for livestock mainly in the central highlands of Ethiopia due to the production of soft straw, in addition to grain. Oats are well adapted to grow in cool and moist climates. In comparison to other cereal crops, oats exhibit broad adaptability to marginal environments, particularly those with low fertility soils and cool wet conditions. Furthermore, in contrast to most other cereal crops, oats display a remarkable tolerance to waterlogged conditions.

Adaptation and number of annual forage legumes in the highlands of Ethiopia are comparatively very low than mid and low altitudes due to mainly climatic factors. Among many annual forage legumes, the adaptation of vetch is better and more promising than others in highland areas. One attraction of vetch is its versatility, which permits diverse utilization as either ruminant feed or green manure. Vetch is an annual forage legume widely adapted to the highlands of Ethiopia. Forage Legumes like vetch are rich sources of nitrogen for livestock with cheaper prices compared to concentrates, especially in developing countries. Vetch has a higher crude protein content compared to many other tropical herbaceous legumes. The contribution of vetch in crop-livestock production systems in different parts of the world are well recognized. Its high value as a protein supplement for ruminants on low quality diets has been recorded. Thus, it is very essential to evaluate and identify improved oat and vetch varieties that are more adapted and well performing to the existing agro- ecological conditions of the North Shewa zone Amhara region to alleviate feed shortage both in quantity and quality.
v
Experimental Design and Layout

Fifteen oat varieties were sourced from Holetta Agriculture Research Center (HARC), Debre Birhan Agriculture Research Center (DBARC), and the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI). A Randomized Complete Block Design (RCBD) was employed with three replicates. Plots measured 2 m x 1.6 m and consisted of six rows spaced 20 cm apart. Seeds were drilled at a rate of 100 kg/ha. Plot spacing was 0.5 m, and block spacing was 1 m.
The fertilizer application consisted of 150 kg/ha Urea and 162 kg/ha NPSB applied uniformly to each plot. Urea was applied in two splits: half at planting and half at the knee-height stage.

Six vetch varieties were sourced from Debre Birhan and Holetta Agricultural Research Centers. Variety trials were conducted at two locations: the main station of Debre Birhan Agricultural Research Center (DBARC) and Bakello site in 2024.

Each variety was planted in 2 m x 1.6 m plots (3.2 m2) within a randomized complete block design. Plots were sown with 30 kg/ha of seed using a seed drill. Rows were spaced at 30 cm within plots, with 0.5 m between plots and 1 m between blocks. 126 kg/ha of NPSB fertilizer was applied. The experiments were replicated at both locations.
Data Collection and Measurement

Data on emergency date, plot coverage, days to first heading, days to 50% heading, number of branches per plant, leaf length, leaf width, and leaf length per plant were recorded. Data on disease and pest reactions were also collected. Agronomic data included date of harvesting, plant height, total fresh weight, sample fresh weight, sample dry weight, days to maturity, and grain yield. Nutritional quality parameters analyzed included dry matter (DM), crude protein (CP), ash, nitrogen (N), Neutral Detergent Fibre (NDF), Acid Detergent Fiber (ADF), Acid Detergent Lignin (ADL), Metabolized energy (ME), and In-vitro Dry Matter Digestibility (IVDMD). Standard laboratory procedures were used for all nutritional analyses.

Duncans Multiple Range Test (DMRT) was used to determine which varieties differed significantly. However, parameters like number of tillers, total fresh weight, dry matter and straw yield showed statistically non-significant differences (Table 1).
